title: Spanish B1
description: The third step in Latin American Spanish, from A2 to CEFR level B1, the level of the Instituto Cervantes DELE B1 exam. Lessons cover the present subjunctive for wishes, advice, feelings, doubt, purpose and future time, negative commands, the subjunctive in relative clauses, the pluperfect and narrative connectors, the future perfect and conditional perfect, the passive, the imperfect subjunctive with ojalá and hypothetical si clauses, reporting requests and speech with tense changes, concession, cause and conditions, building an argument, formal and informal register, idioms, verbs of change, and the e-mails, compositions and talks the DELE B1 asks for. About 600 new words build on the roughly 1,730 from Spanish A1 and A2, with Mexican usage as the standard and Spain's words noted. Conjugation drills add the present and imperfect subjunctive and the pluperfect to the A1 and A2 forms, and a reading list suggests graded readers and free resources for this level. Unlocks when Spanish A2 is complete.
author: Erudior

lessons.title: I hope you…: the present subjunctive and wishes
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In Spanish A1 and A2 you met a few phrases that didn't follow the rules you knew: *¡Que te
mejores!* (Get well soon!), *¡Que le vaya bien!* (All the best!), *No te preocupes* (Don't
worry), and the e-mail opening *Espero que estés bien* (I hope you're well). You learned them as
chunks. They all contain the same verb form, the present subjunctive, and B1 is built around it.

This lesson does three things. It explains what the subjunctive is for, it teaches every form of
the present subjunctive, and it puts it to work in the most natural place to start: wishes and
hopes, with *querer, desear, esperar, preferir* and *ojalá*. The theme is celebrations, good
wishes and New Year's resolutions. The next three lessons use the same forms for advice (02),
feelings (03) and doubt (04).

When you complete this lesson, the present subjunctive opens in your conjugation drills for every
verb you know.

## Two moods: facts and the rest

Every Spanish verb form belongs to a **[[mood]]**: a set of forms that shows how the speaker presents
the action. Everything you have learned so far (present, preterite, imperfect, future…) belongs
to the **[[indicative]]**, the mood for facts and for things the speaker states as real. The
**[[subjunctive]]** is the mood for actions that are wanted, influenced, felt about, doubted or not
real (yet).

![A chart in two columns. Left, "Indicativo: facts", with the examples Sé que vienes (I know you're coming) and Veo que estás bien (I see you're well). Right, "Subjuntivo: the rest", with four boxes: deseos (Quiero que vengas), influencia (Te pido que vengas), sentimientos (Me alegra que vengas) and duda (Dudo que vengas).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Compare:

- *Sé que vienes a la fiesta.* — I know you're coming to the party. (a fact: indicative)
- *Quiero que vengas a la fiesta.* — I want you to come to the party. (a wish: subjunctive)

English often uses an infinitive here ("I want you to come"), or an ordinary verb ("I hope you
come"). Spanish can't say ~~*Quiero tú venir*~~. It builds two clauses joined by *que*:

| main clause | *que* | new subject + subjunctive |
|---|---|---|
| *Quiero* | *que* | *(tú) vengas.* |
| *Espero* | *que* | *mis papás estén bien.* |
| *Mi abuela desea* | *que* | *todos tengamos salud.* |

The first part is the **[[main clause]]**: it makes sense alone (*Quiero*). The part after *que* is a
**[[noun clause]]**: it works like the object of *quiero*, the way a noun would (*Quiero un café* /
*Quiero que vengas*). The main verb decides the mood. A verb of wishing calls for the subjunctive
after it.

## The forms of the present subjunctive

### Regular verbs: the "other" vowel

To make the **[[present subjunctive]]**, take the yo form of the present, drop the *-o*, and add the
endings with the "other" vowel:
*-ar* verbs switch to *e*, *-er* and *-ir* verbs switch to *a*.

| | hablar (hablo) | comer (como) | vivir (vivo) |
|---|---|---|---|
| (que) yo | hable | coma | viva |
| tú | hables | comas | vivas |
| él, ella, usted | hable | coma | viva |
| nosotros | hablemos | comamos | vivamos |
| (vosotros) | (habléis) | (comáis) | (viváis) |
| ellos, ellas, ustedes | hablen | coman | vivan |

The yo and él forms are the same, so speakers add a pronoun when it isn't clear: *Quiere que yo
hable* (She wants me to speak) / *Quiere que él hable* (She wants him to speak). The *vosotros*
forms in brackets are used in Spain only; you'll see them in tables but never need them.

A memory hook: *hables* looks like an *-er* verb and *comas* like an *-ar* verb. A1's usted
commands (*hable, coma, escriba*) are already subjunctive forms.

![A flow in three steps for three verbs. tener: tengo, drop -o, teng-, add -a, tenga. hablar: hablo, habl-, hable. buscar: busco, busc-, busque (c becomes qu to keep the k sound). Below, a box with the six verbs whose subjunctive doesn't come from the yo form: ser sea, ir vaya, estar esté, dar dé, saber sepa, haber haya.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### An irregular yo carries through

Starting from the yo form pays off: every irregularity in the yo present stays in all six
persons.

| infinitive | yo present | subjunctive |
|---|---|---|
| tener | tengo | tenga, tengas, tenga, tengamos, tengan |
| hacer | hago | haga, hagas, haga, hagamos, hagan |
| decir | digo | diga, digas, diga, digamos, digan |
| poner | pongo | ponga, pongas… |
| salir | salgo | salga, salgas… |
| venir | vengo | venga, vengas… |
| conocer | conozco | conozca, conozcas… |
| ver | veo | vea, veas… |

This lesson's *mantener* (to keep, to maintain) works like *tener*: *mantengo* → *mantenga*.

### Spelling changes

The sound of the stem stays the same, so the spelling changes in front of the new vowel:

| ending | change | example |
|---|---|---|
| -car | c → qu | buscar → busque, tocar → toque |
| -gar | g → gu | llegar → llegue, pagar → pague |
| -zar | z → c | empezar → empiece, alcanzar → alcance |
| -ger, -gir | g → j | escoger → escoja, elegir → elija |
| -guir | gu → g | seguir → siga, conseguir → consiga |

These are the same changes as the yo preterite (*busqué, llegué, alcancé*) and the usted commands
(*busque, llegue*).

### Stem changers

*-ar* and *-er* stem changers change in the same persons as the present, so *nosotros* keeps the
plain stem: *quiera, quieras, quiera, queramos, quieran*; *pueda, puedas, pueda, podamos,
puedan*. *-ir* stem changers also change in *nosotros*, to *i* or *u*:

| | pensar (e → ie) | poder (o → ue) | pedir (e → i) | sentir (e → ie, i) | dormir (o → ue, u) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| yo | piense | pueda | pida | sienta | duerma |
| tú | pienses | puedas | pidas | sientas | duermas |
| él | piense | pueda | pida | sienta | duerma |
| nosotros | pensemos | podamos | pidamos | sintamos | durmamos |
| ellos | piensen | puedan | pidan | sientan | duerman |

The same *i* and *u* appear in the gerund you know from A2: *pidiendo, sintiendo, durmiendo*.

### Six verbs to learn by heart

Six verbs don't come from the yo form (*soy, voy, estoy, doy, sé, he* don't end in *-o*):

| ser | ir | estar | dar | saber | haber |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| sea | vaya | esté | dé | sepa | haya |
| seas | vayas | estés | des | sepas | hayas |
| sea | vaya | esté | dé | sepa | haya |
| seamos | vayamos | estemos | demos | sepamos | hayamos |
| sean | vayan | estén | den | sepan | hayan |

- *Estar* has a written accent on every form but *estemos*: *esté, estés, estén*.
- *Dé* has an accent only to tell it apart from the preposition *de*; *des, demos, den* need none.
- *Hay* (there is, there are) becomes *haya*: *Espero que haya pastel* (I hope there's cake).

## Wishes: querer, desear, esperar, preferir

These four verbs take *que* + subjunctive when the second verb has a different subject from the
first (*Quiero que vengas*, *Prefiero que me llames*), and the infinitive when both verbs have
the same subject (*Quiero venir*).

| same subject: infinitive | a different subject: que + subjunctive |
|---|---|
| *Quiero ir a la fiesta.* — I want to go to the party. | *Quiero que vayas a la fiesta.* — I want you to go to the party. |
| *Espero aprobar el examen.* — I hope to pass the exam. | *Espero que apruebes el examen.* — I hope you pass the exam. |
| *Prefiero quedarme en casa.* — I'd rather stay home. | *Prefiero que nos quedemos en casa.* — I'd rather we stayed home. |
| *Deseamos descansar.* — We want to rest. | *Les deseamos que descansen.* — We hope you (all) get some rest. |

- *Esperar* is A1's verb "to wait". Here it means "to hope": *Espero que te guste* (I hope you
  like it). With *que* + subjunctive it is nearly always "hope". Short answers: *Espero que sí*
  (I hope so), *Espero que no* (I hope not).
- *Desear* (to wish) is warmer and more formal than *querer*: the verb of cards and toasts. With a
  noun, *Te deseo mucha felicidad* (I wish you lots of happiness); with a clause, *Te deseo que se
  cumplan tus deseos* (I hope your wishes come true).
- *Preferir* is a stem changer (*prefiero*), and with *que* the second verb is subjunctive:
  *Prefiero que me llames* (I'd rather you called me).

## Ojalá: "let's hope"

*Ojalá* expresses a strong wish. It never changes form, and it is followed by the subjunctive,
with or without *que* (both are correct and common in Mexico):

- *Ojalá (que) no llueva mañana.* — I hope it doesn't rain tomorrow.
- *Ojalá que te den el trabajo.* — I really hope they give you the job.
- *¿Vienes el sábado? — ¡Ojalá!* — Are you coming on Saturday? — I hope so!

The word comes from Arabic: dictionaries trace it to a Hispanic Arabic phrase meaning roughly "if
God wills", from the centuries when Arabic was spoken in Spain (honors lesson 04h1 says more).
Spanish speakers use it with no religious meaning at all.

With the present subjunctive, *ojalá* wishes for something that can still happen. Lesson 13 adds
*ojalá* + another form for wishes that are unlikely or impossible (*Ojalá tuviera…*, "If only I
had…").

## Wishes with que alone

Sometimes the main clause is understood and only *que* + subjunctive is said: *(Espero) que te
vaya bien.* This is how A1's and A2's chunks work:

| chunk | literally | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *¡Que te vaya bien!* | (I hope) that it goes well for you | All the best! Take care! (a goodbye) |
| *¡Que te mejores!* | (I hope) that you get better | Get well soon! |
| *Espero que estés bien.* | I hope that you are well | I hope you're well. |
| *No te preocupes.* | (a negative command) | Don't worry. |

*¡Que te vaya bien!* changes with the person: *¡Que le vaya bien!* (usted), *¡Que les vaya bien!*
(ustedes). *Preocupes* is the subjunctive of *preocuparse*, used for a negative command (lesson
05). Honors lesson 04h1 has many more wishes with *que*.

## Celebrations and good wishes

At a birthday you blow out the candles (*soplar las velas*) and make a wish (*pedir un deseo*),
hoping it comes true (*que se cumpla*). A card or message of congratulations is *una
felicitación*.

In much of Mexico, New Year's Eve has its own customs, as in a 2024 roundup by the news site
adn40: many families eat twelve grapes at midnight, one for each month, making a wish with each
one, and some people walk around the block with a suitcase so that the new year brings travel.
Many also make New Year's resolutions, *los propósitos de Año Nuevo*: to keep up a habit
(*mantener un hábito*), to get over something hard (*superar algo difícil*), to reach a goal
(*alcanzar una meta*). Good wishes often name things money can't buy: *la paz* (peace), *la
tranquilidad* (peace of mind), *el bienestar* (well-being), *la armonía* (harmony), *la
esperanza* (hope). *¡Próspero Año Nuevo!* is the classic greeting on cards.

![A New Year's card with stars and a clock at midnight. It reads: ¡Feliz Año Nuevo 2027! Querida tía Rosa: Te deseamos un año lleno de paz, salud y felicidad. Que se cumplan todos tus deseos y que alcances tus metas. Ojalá que nos veamos pronto en Oaxaca. Con cariño y de corazón, Daniel y Mariana.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

For messages: *de corazón* (from the heart) and *sinceramente* (sincerely): *Te lo digo de
corazón* (I mean it from the bottom of my heart). For a death there is *el pésame*
(condolences): *Mi más sentido pésame* (My deepest condolences) is the standard formula (more in
honors 04h1). *La bendición* is a blessing; older relatives often say goodbye with *¡Que Dios te
bendiga!* (God bless you).

## Dialogue: Noche de Año Nuevo

It's December 31 in Puebla. The Ortega family is waiting for midnight with the grapes ready.

> Abuela: Ya casi son las doce. ¿Todos tienen sus uvas? Quiero que cada uno pida doce deseos.
>
> Daniel: ¡Doce! Yo solo tengo tres: que me den la beca, que mi equipo gane la liga y que mi hermana deje de usar mi cargador.
>
> Mariana: Muy chistoso. Yo deseo que este año todos estemos sanos y que haya paz en la familia.
>
> Papá: Ojalá. Y yo espero cumplir por fin mis propósitos.
>
> Mamá: ¿Cuáles? ¿Los del año pasado?
>
> Papá: Los mismos: hacer ejercicio, ahorrar y aprovechar más el tiempo libre.
>
> Abuela: Mijo, yo prefiero que pases más tiempo con tus hijos. Eso es lo importante.
>
> Mamá: ¡Ya va a empezar! Diez, nueve, ocho…
>
> Todos: ¡Feliz Año Nuevo!
>
> Abuela: Les deseo de corazón un año próspero. Que Dios los bendiga y que les vaya muy bien a todos.

Translation:

> Grandma: It's almost twelve. Does everyone have their grapes? I want each of you to make twelve wishes.
>
> Daniel: Twelve! I only have three: that they give me the scholarship, that my team wins the league and that my sister stops using my charger.
>
> Mariana: Very funny. I wish that this year we'll all be healthy and that there'll be peace in the family.
>
> Dad: Let's hope so. And I hope to finally keep my resolutions.
>
> Mom: Which ones? Last year's?
>
> Dad: The same ones: exercise, save money and make better use of my free time.
>
> Grandma: Son, I'd rather you spent more time with your children. That's what matters.
>
> Mom: It's about to start! Ten, nine, eight…
>
> Everyone: Happy New Year!
>
> Grandma: I wish you all, from the bottom of my heart, a prosperous year. God bless you, and I hope everything goes very well for all of you.

Notes: every wish for someone else has *que* + subjunctive (*que cada uno pida, que me den, que
gane, que deje, que estemos, que haya, que pases, que les vaya*), but Dad's hope is for himself,
so he uses the infinitive (*espero cumplir*). *Las uvas* = grapes. *Cumplir un propósito* is to
keep a resolution (*cumplirse* is for wishes that come true). *Mijo* (from *mi hijo*) is an
affectionate way, very common in Mexico, for a parent or grandparent to address a son or a
grandson (and often any younger man). *Aprovechar*
= to make the most of, to use well.

## Pronunciation

- *Ojalá* is stressed on the last syllable: *o-ja-LÁ*.
- *Haya* (from *haber*), *halla* (finds) and *allá* (over there) differ only in spelling and stress:
  with yeísmo, *haya* and *halla* sound the same, *A-ya*; *allá* is *a-YÁ*.
- Keep the stress where the present has it: *hable* is *HA-ble*, *hablé* (preterite) is *ha-BLÉ*.
  *Esté* (subjunctive) is *es-TÉ*, like *está*; *este* (this) is *ES-te*.

## Common mistakes

- An infinitive with a new subject: ~~*Quiero tú venir*~~ → *Quiero que vengas.*
- *que* + subjunctive with the same subject: ~~*Quiero que yo vaya*~~ → *Quiero ir.*
- The indicative after a wish: ~~*Espero que vienes*~~ → *Espero que vengas.* ~~*Ojalá que
  llueve*~~ → *Ojalá que llueva.*
- Forgetting the spelling change: ~~*busce*~~ → *busque*; ~~*llege*~~ → *llegue*.
- Changing the stem of *-ar* and *-er* verbs in nosotros: ~~*piensemos*~~ → *pensemos*. Only *-ir*
  verbs change there: *pidamos, durmamos*.
- Leaving the accent off *dé* and *esté*: *Espero que me dé la dirección* (I hope she gives me the
  address).

## Key points

- Two moods: the indicative states facts; the subjunctive follows wishes, influence, feelings
  and doubt.
- Pattern: main clause + *que* + a new subject + subjunctive (*Quiero que vengas*). Same subject →
  infinitive (*Quiero venir*).
- Forms: yo present minus *-o* + the "other" vowel (*hable, coma, viva; tenga, conozca*), with
  spelling changes (*busque, llegue, alcance, escoja, siga*) and stem changes (*-ir* verbs change
  in nosotros too: *pidamos*).
- Learn six by heart: *sea, vaya, esté, dé, sepa, haya*.
- *querer, desear, esperar* (to hope), *preferir* + *que* + subjunctive; *ojalá (que)* +
  subjunctive; *¡Que te vaya bien!*

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: I want you to…: advice, requests and permission
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 01 you wished things for other people: *Quiero que vengas.* Wanting is the gentlest way
to influence what someone does. This lesson adds the rest of the family: asking, advising,
recommending, insisting, demanding, allowing and forbidding. The sentence has the same shape as in
lesson 01, a main clause, *que* and a new subject in the subjunctive, so the work here is learning
the verbs and the small words around them.

In A2 you gave advice with *deberías*, *yo que tú* and *es importante* + infinitive (*Es importante
dormir bien*). Now you can aim that advice at one person: *Es importante que duermas bien.* The
theme is parents, teenagers and the rules at home and at school.

## Verbs of influence

| verb | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| *pedir* (A1) | to ask (someone to do) | *Te pido que me llames.* — I'm asking you to call me. |
| *aconsejar* | to advise | *Le aconsejo que descanse.* — I advise you (usted) to rest. |
| *recomendar* (A1) | to recommend | *Te recomiendo que veas esa serie.* — I recommend you watch that series. |
| *sugerir* | to suggest | *Sugiero que salgamos temprano.* — I suggest we leave early. |
| *exigir* | to demand, to require | *La escuela exige que los alumnos lleguen a tiempo.* — The school requires students to arrive on time. |
| *insistir en* | to insist (on) | *Mi mamá insiste en que yo coma verduras.* — My mom insists that I eat vegetables. |
| *rogar* | to beg, to ask (formally) | *Les rogamos que apaguen sus celulares.* — Please turn off your phones (literally "we beg you"). |
| *ordenar* | to order (someone to do) | *El director ordena que todos salgan al patio.* — The principal orders everyone out to the yard. |
| *permitir* | to allow | *No permiten que usemos el celular en clase.* — They don't allow us to use our phones in class. |
| *dejar* (A2) | to let | *Mis papás no dejan que mi hermano salga entre semana.* — My parents don't let my brother go out on weeknights. |
| *prohibir* | to forbid, to ban | *Te prohíbo que hables así.* — I forbid you to talk like that. |

*Pedir* means "to ask someone to do something" or "to ask for something"; asking a question is still
*preguntar* (A1). *Rogar* is strong in conversation but common in polite written notices: *Se
ruega no fumar* (Please do not smoke). *Ordenar* also means "to tidy" (*ordenar el cuarto*), so
context decides.

### Who does the action: the indirect object

With most of these verbs, the person you influence appears twice: as an indirect object pronoun
in the main clause, and as the subject of the subjunctive verb.

- *Te pido que me llames.* — *te* = you, and *llames* = you call.
- *Les prohíben que salgan.* — *les* = them, and *salgan* = they go out.
- *A Sofía le aconsejo que hable con su maestra.* — I advise Sofía to talk to her teacher.

The pronoun and the verb ending point to the same person. *Te pido que me llames* has two
different pronouns because *te* is the person asked and *me* is the person to be called.

### Dejar, permitir, prohibir + infinitive

*Dejar, permitir* and *prohibir* very often take a plain infinitive instead of *que*: the
pronoun already says who is allowed or forbidden.

| with que + subjunctive | with an infinitive |
|---|---|
| *No me dejan que salga.* | *No me dejan salir.* — They don't let me go out. |
| *Te permito que uses mi carro.* | *Te permito usar mi carro.* — I'm letting you use my car. |
| *Nos prohíben que comamos en el salón.* | *Nos prohíben comer en el salón.* — We aren't allowed to eat in the classroom. |

Both columns are correct; the infinitive is the more common choice in conversation. You'll also
hear *aconsejar, recomendar* and *sugerir* with an infinitive (*Te recomiendo probar los
chilaquiles*). With *pedir, exigir, rogar* and *insistir en*, use *que* + subjunctive when someone
else is to act.

### Two verbs with two meanings

*Insistir en que* and *decir que* take the subjunctive when they push someone to act, and the
indicative when they insist on or report a fact:

- *Insiste en que vengas.* — He insists that you come. (influence: subjunctive)
- *Insiste en que no fue su culpa.* — He insists it wasn't his fault. (a claim: indicative)
- *Mi mamá dice que llegues temprano.* — My mom says you should come home early. (a command)
- *Mi mamá dice que llegas temprano.* — My mom says you come home early. (a fact)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing the form after a verb of influence
  accDescr: Start with a verb of influence such as pedir, aconsejar, exigir or prohibir. If you are telling someone else to act, use que plus the subjunctive, for example Te pido que me llames. With dejar, permitir and prohibir, an infinitive is also correct, for example No me dejan salir. If the verb only reports information, for example Dice que llega tarde, use the indicative.
  A["A verb of influence: pedir, aconsejar, exigir, prohibir…"] --> B{"Is someone else told to act?"}
  B -- yes --> C["que + subjunctive: Te pido que me llames."]
  C --> D["dejar, permitir, prohibir: an infinitive also works: No me dejan salir."]
  B -- "no, it reports a fact" --> E["indicative: Dice que llega tarde."]
```

## Impersonal expressions

An **[[impersonal expression]]** is *es* + an adjective or noun with no personal subject: *es
importante, es necesario, es mejor, es urgente, es fundamental, es buena idea*. In A2 you used them
with an infinitive for general advice. To say who should do it, use *que* + subjunctive:

| general (infinitive) | for someone (que + subjunctive) |
|---|---|
| *Es importante dormir ocho horas.* — It's important to sleep eight hours. | *Es importante que duermas ocho horas.* — It's important for you to sleep eight hours. |
| *Es mejor hablar con calma.* — It's better to talk calmly. | *Es mejor que hablemos con calma.* — It's better if we talk calmly. |
| *Es necesario tener permiso.* — You need permission. | *Es necesario que tus papás firmen el permiso.* — Your parents need to sign the permission form. |
| *Es fundamental poner límites.* — Setting limits is essential. | *Es fundamental que los papás pongan límites.* — It's essential for parents to set limits. |

English often uses "for you to" or "if we" here; Spanish uses *que* and the subjunctive.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Infinitive or subjunctive after an impersonal expression
  accDescr: Start with an impersonal expression such as es importante or es mejor. If it is about one person or group, use que plus the subjunctive, for example Es importante que duermas bien. If it is a general statement about everyone, use the infinitive, for example Es importante dormir bien.
  F["An impersonal expression: es importante, es mejor…"] --> G{"About one person or group?"}
  G -- yes --> H["que + subjunctive: Es importante que duermas bien."]
  G -- "no, in general" --> I["infinitive: Es importante dormir bien."]
```

## The forms in use: -ir verbs and irregulars

Advice is full of the verbs from lesson 01's tables. Watch the *-ir* stem changers in *nosotros*
and the irregular yo forms:

- *Te sugiero que duermas más y que pidas ayuda.* — I suggest you sleep more and ask for help.
- *El entrenador nos pide que durmamos bien antes del partido.* — The coach asks us to sleep well
  before the game.
- *Les aconsejo que tengan paciencia y que no se vayan a dormir enojados.* — I advise you to be
  patient and not go to bed angry.
- *Insisto en que sepas la verdad.* — I insist that you know the truth.

Two verbs from this lesson have their own patterns. *Prohibir* puts a written accent on the *i* when
it's stressed: *prohíbo, prohíbes, prohíbe, prohíben*; subjunctive *prohíba, prohíbas, prohíban*
(*prohibimos, prohibamos* have none). *Criar* (to raise, to bring up a child) does the same: *crío,
crías, cría, crían*; subjunctive *críe, críes, críen*. *Exigir* changes *g* to *j* before *o* and
*a*: *exijo, exija*. *Rogar* is *ruego, ruegas…* with *gu* before *e*: *ruegue, roguemos*.

## Rules at home

*La adolescencia* (adolescence) is when the rules get argued about. Raising children (*la
crianza*, from *criar*) means setting limits (*poner límites*) and teaching responsibility (*la
responsabilidad*); teenagers (*los adolescentes*) ask for more freedom (*la libertad*) and
respect (*el respeto*). Some families are strict about discipline (*la disciplina*); others
negotiate. A rule can be *una regla* (everyday) or *una norma* (more formal, like a school's *normas
de convivencia*, rules for getting along together).

In Mexico, the money parents give children each week is often called *la mesada* or *el domingo*
(BBVA México's financial-education page uses both; the second name comes from the custom of giving
it on Sunday). Chores are *los quehaceres*, and a parent who is annoyed *regaña* (scolds): *Mi papá
me regaña si no hago mis quehaceres.* In Spain the allowance is usually *la paga*, and besides
*regañar* you'll also hear *reñir*.

![A poster on a fridge titled "Reglas de la casa, familia Treviño", with six rules, each beside a small picture: a stack of plates, "Lavar los platos después de cenar"; a trash bag, "Sacar la basura los martes y viernes"; a cell phone crossed out over a table, "Nada de celulares en la mesa"; a clock showing ten, "Llegar antes de las 10 p. m. (fines de semana: 11)"; a door with two people, "Pedir permiso para invitar amigos"; coins, "Mesada: los domingos, si cumples con tus quehaceres".](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

A parent explaining the poster might say: *Les pido que laven los platos después de cenar. No
permito que haya celulares en la mesa. Y es importante que pidan permiso antes de invitar amigos.*
Children who follow the rules *obedecen* (obey: *obedezco, obedezca*); a responsible child is
*responsable* (one form for both genders), and *respetar las reglas* is to respect the rules.

## Dialogue: ¿Me dejas ir?

Valeria is sixteen and lives in Guadalajara. She wants to go to a concert on Saturday.

> Valeria: Mamá, ¿me dejas ir al concierto del sábado? Van todas mis amigas.
>
> Mamá: ¿Y a qué hora termina?
>
> Valeria: Como a las once. Te pido que me des permiso, porfa. Te prometo que regreso temprano.
>
> Mamá: Mira, no te prohíbo que vayas, pero hay reglas. Primero, quiero que termines tus quehaceres hoy.
>
> Valeria: Ya lavé los platos y saqué la basura.
>
> Mamá: Bien. Segundo, te exijo que tengas el celular prendido toda la noche.
>
> Valeria: Ay, mamá, ya tengo dieciséis años. Respeta un poco mi libertad.
>
> Mamá: Respeto tu libertad, pero soy responsable de ti. Y tu papá insiste en ir él a recogerlas.
>
> Valeria: ¿Papá? ¿En la puerta del concierto? ¡No, por favor!
>
> Mamá: Es eso o no vas. Y te aconsejo que no sigas discutiendo, porque estás a punto de perder la mesada.
>
> Valeria: Está bien, está bien. Pero dile que se estacione en la esquina, no en la entrada.
>
> Mamá: Trato hecho. Es importante que todos lleguen bien a su casa.

Translation:

> Valeria: Mom, will you let me go to the concert on Saturday? All my friends are going.
>
> Mom: And what time does it end?
>
> Valeria: Around eleven. Please give me permission. I promise I'll come back early.
>
> Mom: Look, I'm not forbidding you to go, but there are rules. First, I want you to finish your chores today.
>
> Valeria: I already washed the dishes and took out the trash.
>
> Mom: Good. Second, I insist that you keep your phone on all night.
>
> Valeria: Oh, Mom, I'm sixteen now. Respect my freedom a little.
>
> Mom: I respect your freedom, but I'm responsible for you. And your dad insists on picking you girls up himself.
>
> Valeria: Dad? At the concert door? No, please!
>
> Mom: It's that or you don't go. And I advise you to stop arguing, because you're about to lose your allowance.
>
> Valeria: OK, OK. But tell him to park on the corner, not at the entrance.
>
> Mom: Deal. It's important that everyone gets home safely.

Notes: *porfa* is the informal short form of *por favor*. *Te prometo que regreso* is indicative:
a promise states a fact about the future, it isn't a wish. *Te exijo que* is strong; with a friend
you would say *te pido que*. *Dile que se estacione* is *decir* + subjunctive: tell him to park. *Tu papá insiste en ir él*
has the infinitive because Dad is both the one who insists and the one who goes (same subject,
as in lesson 01). *Recogerlas* (to pick them up) has *las* for Valeria and her girl friends.
*Discutir* = to argue (lesson 16); *estar a punto de* = to be about to (lesson 10);
*estacionarse* = to park (A2); *¡Trato hecho!* = Deal!

## Pronunciation

- *Prohíbo* has no *h* sound and three syllables: *pro-Í-bo*. The accent splits *oi* into two
  syllables. *Prohibimos* has no accent mark: the stress is on *BI*.
- *Crío* is two syllables, *CRÍ-o*; in *criamos* the stress moves to the *a*: *CRIA-mos*.
- *Exijo, exija* have the Spanish *j*, a breathy *h* from the throat: *e-KSI-ho*.
- In *ruegue* and *regañar*, *gue* is *ge* as in "get" (the *u* is silent), and *ñ* is like the *ny*
  in "canyon": *RUE-ge, re-ga-ÑAR*.

## Common mistakes

- The indicative after a verb of influence: ~~*Te pido que me llamas*~~ → *Te pido que me
  llames.*
- Adding *de* before *que*: ~~*Te sugiero de que…*~~ → *Te sugiero que…* (but *insistir en que*
  keeps its *en*; the RAE's *Diccionario panhispánico de dudas* counts dropping it as an error).
- Forgetting the -ir change in nosotros: ~~*Nos piden que pedamos*~~ → *que pidamos*.
- Leaving out the accent: ~~*prohibe*~~ → *prohíbe*; ~~*crian*~~ → *crían*.
- *Pedir* for a question: ~~*Le pedí dónde vive*~~ → *Le pregunté dónde vive.*

## Key points

- Verbs of influence + *que* + subjunctive: *pedir, aconsejar, recomendar, sugerir, exigir,
  insistir en, rogar, ordenar, permitir, dejar, prohibir.*
- The indirect object pronoun and the subjunctive ending name the same person: *Te pido que me
  llames.*
- *dejar, permitir, prohibir* + infinitive is common: *No me dejan salir.*
- *Insistir en que* and *decir que*: subjunctive to push someone to act, indicative to state a fact.
- Impersonal expressions: + infinitive in general (*Es importante dormir*), + *que* + subjunctive
  for someone (*Es importante que duermas*).

lessons.title: I'm glad you came: feelings and reactions
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lessons 01 and 02 used the subjunctive for things that haven't happened yet: wishes and requests.
This lesson adds the third big group, feelings, and here the subjunctive often describes something
that is true. *Me alegra que estés aquí* (I'm glad you're here): you *are* here. Spanish still uses
the subjunctive, because the sentence isn't reporting the fact; it's reacting to it.

You know the verbs already. In A1, *gustar* and *encantar*; in A2, *preocupar, molestar* and
*sorprender* (*Me preocupa el examen*). Now they can take a whole clause: *Me preocupa que no
estudies.* You'll also learn a new form for reacting to something that has happened, *Me alegra que
hayas venido*, and the words for moods and emotions.

## Gustar-type verbs + que

With *gustar*-type verbs, the thing that causes the feeling is the subject, and the person who
feels it is an indirect object (*me, te, le, nos, les*). That subject can be a noun, an
infinitive or a clause with *que*:

| subject | example |
|---|---|
| a noun | *Me molesta el ruido.* — The noise bothers me. |
| an infinitive (same person) | *Me molesta esperar.* — I hate waiting (it bothers me to wait). |
| *que* + subjunctive (someone else) | *Me molesta que lleguen tarde.* — It bothers me that they arrive late. |

A clause counts as one singular thing, so the verb stays singular even when the clause is about
many people: *Me molesta que lleguen tarde*, not ~~*Me molestan que lleguen*~~.

The common ones:

- *Me alegra que…* — I'm glad that… (*alegrar* = to make glad)
- *Me encanta que…* — I love it that…
- *Me gusta que…* — I like it that…
- *Me molesta que…* — It bothers me that…
- *Me preocupa que…* — It worries me that…
- *Me sorprende que…* — I'm surprised that…
- *Me da miedo / pena / rabia / vergüenza que…* — It scares me / makes me sad or embarrassed /
  makes me furious / embarrasses me that…

*Dar* + a noun of feeling is very common: *el miedo* (fear), *la rabia* (rage, fury), *la
vergüenza* (embarrassment, shame) and *la pena*, which in Mexico often means embarrassment, as you
saw in A2's *me da pena*, and in many other countries usually means sorrow or pity. *Me da rabia que me mientan* (It makes me
furious when people lie to me).

## Personal verbs and estar + adjective

Other emotion verbs have the person who feels as the subject:

| verb | example |
|---|---|
| *alegrarse de que* | *Me alegro de que te guste tu nuevo trabajo.* — I'm glad you like your new job. |
| *sentir que* | *Siento que estés enfermo.* — I'm sorry you're sick. |
| *lamentar que* | *Lamentamos que el vuelo se retrase.* — We regret that the flight is delayed. |
| *temer que* | *Temo que no haya boletos.* — I'm afraid there won't be tickets. |
| *estar contento / feliz de que* | *Estoy feliz de que vivas cerca.* — I'm happy you live nearby. |
| *estar harto de que* | *Estoy harta de que no me escuches.* — I'm fed up with you not listening to me. |
| *estar orgulloso de que* | *Mis papás están orgullosos de que yo estudie medicina.* — My parents are proud that I'm studying medicine. |

- *Alegrarse* keeps its *de*: *Me alegro de que…* The RAE's *Diccionario panhispánico de dudas*
  gives *Me alegro de que…* as the correct form and counts dropping the *de* as a mistake. *Me
  alegra que…* (from *alegrar*, a gustar-type verb) needs no *de*. Both mean the same.
- *Sentir* (A1's *Lo siento*) means "to be sorry" with the subjunctive. With the indicative,
  *sentir que* means "to feel, to sense that": *Siento que algo no está bien* (I feel something
  isn't right).
- *Lamentar* is more formal than *sentir*: airlines and companies *lamentan* things. *Temer* (to
  fear) is formal too; in conversation people say *Me da miedo que…* And *Me temo que* + indicative
  is a polite way to give bad news: *Me temo que no hay boletos* (I'm afraid there aren't any
  tickets).
- *Harto* (fed up) and *orgulloso* (proud) agree with the person: *harta, orgullosos.*

### Same person: the infinitive

When the person who feels is also the one who acts, use the infinitive, as in lessons 01 and 02:

- *Me alegra verte.* — I'm glad to see you. (I feel, I see)
- *Me alegra que me veas.* — I'm glad you see me. (I feel, you see)
- *Siento llegar tarde.* — I'm sorry I'm late.
- *Estoy harto de esperar.* — I'm fed up with waiting.

## Something that has happened: the perfect subjunctive

*Me alegra que vengas* reacts to a coming or a present action. To react to something that has
already happened, use the **[[perfect subjunctive]]**: *haya, hayas, haya, hayamos, hayan* + the
participle, exactly like A1's perfect with the *haber* forms changed.

| present perfect (A1) | perfect subjunctive |
|---|---|
| *Has venido.* — You've come. | *Me alegra que hayas venido.* — I'm glad you've come. |
| *Ha llovido mucho.* — It has rained a lot. | *Me sorprende que haya llovido tanto.* — I'm surprised it has rained so much. |
| *No han llamado.* — They haven't called. | *Me preocupa que no hayan llamado.* — I'm worried they haven't called. |
| *Hemos ganado.* — We've won. | *Mi abuelo está orgulloso de que hayamos ganado.* — My grandpa is proud that we've won. |

Irregular participles are the same as always: *Me sorprende que no hayan vuelto* (I'm surprised
they haven't come back), *Me encanta que hayas escrito* (I love that you've written). The perfect
subjunctive has no drill of its own: practice it in sentences.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Which form after a verb of feeling
  accDescr: Start with a feeling such as me alegra, me molesta, siento or estoy harto de. If the person who feels is also the one who acts, use the infinitive, for example Me alegra verte. If someone else acts, use que plus a subjunctive. If the action is now or still to come, use the present subjunctive, Me alegra que vengas. If it has already happened, use the perfect subjunctive, haya plus participle, Me alegra que hayas venido.
  A["A feeling: me alegra, me molesta, siento, estoy harto de…"] --> B{"Does the same person feel and act?"}
  B -- yes --> C["infinitive: Me alegra verte."]
  B -- no --> D{"When is the action?"}
  D -- "now or still to come" --> E["present subjunctive: Me alegra que vengas."]
  D -- "it has happened" --> F["haya + participle: Me alegra que hayas venido."]
```

## Reacting to news

When someone tells you news, short exclamations with *qué* do the work:

- *¡Qué bueno que estés mejor!* — I'm so glad you're better!
- *¡Qué lástima que no puedas venir!* — What a shame you can't come!
- *¡Qué raro que no conteste!* — How strange that she isn't answering!
- *¡Qué padre que te hayan dado la beca!* — How great that they gave you the scholarship! (*padre*
  = great, Mexican informal, A2)
- *Es una lástima que cierren la librería.* — It's a pity they're closing the bookstore.

*La lástima* is pity: *¡Qué lástima!* (What a pity!) works alone too. In Mexico, as in much of Latin
America, you'll often hear the indicative after *¡Qué bueno que…!*, especially for something that
has already happened (*¡Qué bueno que viniste!*); studies of Mexican speech have recorded the
indicative after other expressions of feeling too. It's normal in conversation, but the
subjunctive is the standard choice and the safe one in writing and in exams.

## Words for feelings

| noun | adjective or phrase |
|---|---|
| *la alegría* (joy) | *alegre* (A2: cheerful) |
| *la tristeza* (sadness) | *triste* (A1) |
| *el orgullo* (pride) | *orgulloso* (proud) |
| *la decepción* (disappointment) | *decepcionado* (disappointed) |
| *el enojo* (anger; Spain *el enfado*) | *enojado* (A1: angry) |
| *la emoción* (emotion; excitement) | *emocionado* (excited; moved) |
| *el estrés* (stress) | *estresado* (stressed) |
| *la soledad* (loneliness, solitude) | *solo* (A1: alone) |
| *la envidia* (envy) | *¡Qué envidia!* (Lucky you!) |

Your general mood is *el estado de ánimo*; you can be *de buen humor* (in a good mood) or *de mal
humor* (in a bad mood). *Aliviado* is relieved: *Estoy aliviada de que no haya sido nada grave* (I'm
relieved it wasn't anything serious). *Aguantar* is to put up with, to stand: *No aguanto que me
interrumpan* (I can't stand being interrupted; *interrumpir* = to interrupt).

### False friends

- *Decepcionado* = disappointed, not "deceived" (that's *engañado*).
- *Sensible* = sensitive (*Mi hijo es muy sensible*); "sensible" is *sensato*.
- *La ilusión* = excitement, hope, a happy expectation: *Tengo mucha ilusión por el viaje* (I'm
  really looking forward to the trip). It also means "illusion". *Me hace ilusión* (I'm excited
  about it) is very common in Spain; in Mexico you'll more often hear *Me emociona*.
- *Emocionado* = excited (*Estoy emocionada por el concierto*) or moved (*El abuelo estaba
  emocionado en la boda*), not "emotional" in the sense of upset.

![Five cartoon faces in a row, each with a caption: a smiling face with a medal, orgulloso; a sad face above a gift box broken in two, decepcionado; a frowning face with angry eyebrows, crossed arms and a stack of papers, harto; a face with closed eyes and a small smile wiping a drop of sweat from its forehead, aliviado; a grinning face with stars for eyes above a ticket that says BOLETO, emocionado.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Dialogue: Buenas y malas noticias

Andrés calls his friend Carmen. They both live in Mexico City.

> Andrés: ¿Carmen? ¿Tienes un minuto? Tengo noticias.
>
> Carmen: Claro. Te oigo de buen humor. ¿Qué pasó?
>
> Andrés: ¡Me dieron el trabajo en Monterrey!
>
> Carmen: ¡No puede ser! ¡Qué bueno que te lo hayan dado! Estoy muy orgullosa de ti.
>
> Andrés: Gracias. Estoy emocionado, pero también un poco triste. Me da tristeza que vivamos tan lejos.
>
> Carmen: A mí también. Pero me alegro de que por fin tengas un trabajo que te guste. Estabas harto de tu jefe.
>
> Andrés: Harto es poco. Me daba rabia cómo me hablaba… bueno, eso ya es pasado.
>
> Carmen: ¿Y tu mamá qué dijo?
>
> Andrés: Le preocupa que esté solo allá, pero está feliz. Lo único malo es que no vamos a vernos tan seguido.
>
> Carmen: Es una lástima, pero Monterrey no está en la luna. Te voy a visitar.
>
> Andrés: ¡Más te vale! Me encanta que siempre veas el lado bueno.

Translation:

> Andrés: Carmen? Do you have a minute? I have news.
>
> Carmen: Sure. You sound like you're in a good mood. What happened?
>
> Andrés: They gave me the job in Monterrey!
>
> Carmen: No way! I'm so glad they gave it to you! I'm really proud of you.
>
> Andrés: Thanks. I'm excited, but also a little sad. It makes me sad that we'll live so far apart.
>
> Carmen: Me too. But I'm glad you finally have a job you like. You were fed up with your boss.
>
> Andrés: Fed up doesn't begin to cover it. The way he talked to me made me furious… well, that's in the past now.
>
> Carmen: And what did your mom say?
>
> Andrés: She's worried that I'll be alone there, but she's happy. The only bad thing is that we won't see each other as often.
>
> Carmen: It's a shame, but Monterrey isn't on the moon. I'll visit you.
>
> Andrés: You'd better! I love that you always look on the bright side.

Notes: *Te oigo de buen humor* = I hear you're in a good mood (you sound…). Every reaction to
someone else's news has *que* + subjunctive (*que te lo hayan dado, que vivamos, que tengas, que
esté, que veas*); *Me daba rabia cómo me hablaba* has no *que*, so its verbs are ordinary
indicative. *Seguido* = often (common in Mexico). *¡Más te vale!* = You'd better! *La luna* = the moon.

## Pronunciation

- *Vergüenza* has *ü*: the *u* is pronounced, *ber-GUEN-sa*. Without the dots it would be silent.
- *Harto* starts with a vowel sound: the *h* is silent, *AR-to*.
- *Sensible* is stressed on the second syllable, *sen-SI-ble*, unlike English "SEN-si-ble".
- *Aliviado, emocionado, decepcionado* are stressed on the next-to-last syllable:
  *a-li-BIA-do, e-mo-sio-NA-do, de-sep-sio-NA-do*.
- *Estrés* ends in a stressed *-trés*, and Spanish needs a vowel before *s* + consonant: *es-TRÉS*.

## Common mistakes

- A plural verb because the clause is about several people: ~~*Me molestan que lleguen tarde*~~ →
  *Me molesta que lleguen tarde.*
- The indicative after a feeling: ~~*Me alegra que estás aquí*~~ → *que estés aquí.*
- *que* with the same person: ~~*Me alegra que yo esté aquí*~~ → *Me alegra estar aquí.*
- Dropping *de* with *alegrarse* and *estar* + adjective: ~~*Me alegro que…, Estoy harto que…*~~ →
  *Me alegro de que…, Estoy harto de que…*
- The present instead of the perfect for something done: *Me alegra que vengas* (that you're
  coming) vs *Me alegra que hayas venido* (that you've come).
- False friends: *estoy decepcionado* (disappointed), *es muy sensible* (sensitive).

## Key points

- Emotion + *que* + subjunctive, even when the thing felt about is true: *Me alegra que estés
  aquí.*
- Gustar-type verbs keep a singular verb before a *que* clause: *Me molesta que griten.*
- *alegrarse de que, sentir que, lamentar que, temer que; estar contento / harto / orgulloso de
  que*; same person → infinitive (*Me alegra verte*).
- Perfect subjunctive: *haya* + participle for what has happened: *Me alegra que hayas venido.*
- Reactions: *¡Qué bueno que…!, ¡Qué lástima que…!, Es una lástima que…*

lessons.title: I doubt it's true: doubt, denial and possibility
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The last group of subjunctive triggers in this module is about how sure you are. In A2 you gave
opinions with *creo que, pienso que* and *me parece que* (*Creo que tienes razón*), and you
hedged with *quizás, tal vez* and *a lo mejor*, all with the indicative. Opinions like *creo que*
state what you take to be true, so they keep the indicative. As soon as you doubt, deny or merely
allow a possibility, Spanish switches to the subjunctive (and after *quizás* and *tal vez* you now
get a choice of mood): *No creo que tengas razón. Es posible que tengas razón.*

This lesson sorts the expressions into the two groups, gives you a decision chart, and practices
them on a theme where certainty matters: science, space, myths and the unknown.

## Certainty: the indicative

These all present something as true (or as what the speaker believes is true):

| expression | example |
|---|---|
| *creo que, pienso que* | *Creo que hay vida en otros planetas.* — I think there's life on other planets. |
| *me parece que* | *Me parece que el experimento funciona.* — It seems to me the experiment works. |
| *estoy seguro de que* | *Estoy segura de que la Luna influye en las mareas.* — I'm sure the Moon affects the tides. |
| *es verdad / es cierto que* | *Es cierto que la Tierra gira alrededor del Sol.* — It's true that the Earth goes around the Sun. |
| *es evidente / es obvio que* | *Es evidente que el clima está cambiando.* — It's clear the climate is changing. |
| *está claro que* | *Está claro que necesitamos más datos.* — Clearly we need more data. |

*Cierto* (certain, true) has a trap: before a noun it means "a certain": *un cierto miedo* (a
certain fear), *cierta persona* (a certain person). After *es* it means "true": *Es cierto.*

## Doubt and denial: the subjunctive

Make those same expressions negative, or use a verb of doubt or denial, and the subjunctive
follows:

| certainty (indicative) | doubt or denial (subjunctive) |
|---|---|
| *Creo que es un ovni.* | *No creo que sea un ovni.* — I don't think it's a UFO. |
| *Pienso que tiene razón.* | *No pienso que tenga razón.* — I don't think she's right. |
| *Me parece que existe.* | *No me parece que exista.* — I don't think it exists. |
| *Estoy seguro de que viene.* | *No estoy seguro de que venga.* — I'm not sure he's coming. |
| *Es verdad que funciona.* | *No es verdad que funcione.* — It isn't true that it works. |
| — | *Dudo que los fantasmas existan.* — I doubt ghosts exist. |
| — | *El científico niega que el experimento tenga errores.* — The scientist denies that the experiment has errors. |

*Dudar* (to doubt) is the clearest case: *Dudo que…* is followed by the subjunctive. *No dudo
que…* (I don't doubt that…) is usually followed by the indicative, since not doubting is being
sure, though you'll also hear the subjunctive.

A question with *¿Crees que…?* can take either mood. *¿Crees que es verdad?* sounds like a
neutral question; *¿Crees que sea verdad?* sounds more doubtful. Both are correct; for now,
recognize the second and use whichever comes naturally.

## Possibility and probability: the subjunctive

Anything that is only possible, likely or unlikely takes the subjunctive:

- *Es posible que llueva esta noche.* — It might rain tonight.
- *Es probable que encuentren agua en ese planeta.* — They'll probably find water on that planet.
- *Es improbable que el cometa choque con la Tierra.* — It's unlikely that the comet will hit Earth.
- *Es imposible que un ser humano viva sin oxígeno.* — It's impossible for a person to live
  without oxygen.
- *Es difícil que lleguemos a tiempo.* — We're unlikely to get there on time.
- *Puede (ser) que tengas razón.* — You may be right.

*Es difícil que* + subjunctive usually means "it's unlikely that", not "it's hard": *Es difícil
que llueva hoy* (It probably won't rain today). For "hard to do", use the infinitive: *Es difícil
explicarlo.*

*Puede que* (it may be that) is very common in conversation and always takes the subjunctive: *Puede
que no venga* (He might not come). *Puede ser que* means the same.

## Quizás, tal vez, a lo mejor

A2's three words for "maybe" behave differently:

- *Quizás* and *tal vez* (before the verb) take either mood. The subjunctive sounds a little
  less sure: *Quizás tiene razón* / *Quizás tenga razón* (Maybe she's right). Both are correct.
- *A lo mejor* takes only the indicative: *A lo mejor tiene razón*, never ~~*a lo mejor
  tenga*~~. It's informal and very common in Mexico.

So if you aren't sure which mood to use after "maybe", *a lo mejor* + indicative is always safe.

![A horizontal scale titled "How sure are you?", from 100% sure on the left to 0% on the right, with seven boxes from left to right: Es evidente que / Estoy seguro de que, marked indicativo; Creo que, indicativo; Es probable que, subjuntivo; Quizás / Tal vez and A lo mejor (ind.), marked ind. o subj.; Es posible que / Puede que, subjuntivo; No creo que / Dudo que, subjuntivo; and at the right end Es imposible que, subjuntivo.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The scale is rough (how sure *creo que* is depends on the speaker), but the moods under it are
reliable.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Indicative or subjunctive after an opinion or a possibility
  accDescr: Ask first whether the speaker presents the idea as true, with creo que, es evidente que, estoy seguro de que or es verdad que. If yes, use the indicative. If the speaker denies or doubts it, with no creo que, dudo que or no es verdad que, use the subjunctive. If the speaker only allows a possibility, with es posible que, es probable que or puede que, use the subjunctive. If it is one of the words for maybe, quizás or tal vez take either mood, and a lo mejor takes the indicative.
  A{"Is it presented as true? creo que, es evidente que, es verdad que…"} -- yes --> B["indicative: Creo que es verdad."]
  A -- no --> C{"Doubt or denial? no creo que, dudo que, niego que…"}
  C -- yes --> D["subjunctive: Dudo que sea verdad."]
  C -- no --> E{"Possibility? es posible que, es probable que, puede que…"}
  E -- yes --> F["subjunctive: Es posible que sea verdad."]
  E -- "no, a word for maybe" --> G["quizás, tal vez: either mood; a lo mejor: indicative"]
```

## Science, space and myths

Science is a good place to practice doubt: a theory (*una teoría*) is tested by experiments (*los
experimentos*), which check (*comprueban*) or prove (*demuestran*) whether it is right. A
scientist wants data (*los datos*; one piece is *un dato*) before saying something exists
(*existe*). A discovery is *un descubrimiento*.

Mexico has its own space history. Rodolfo Neri Vela became the first Mexican in space when he
flew on the space shuttle *Atlantis* from November 26 to December 3, 1985 (mission STS-61-B,
according to UNAM's *Gaceta*); the mission put Mexico's Morelos II satellite into orbit. On June 4,
2022, the engineer Katya Echazarreta, born in Guadalajara, became the first Mexican-born woman in
space, on a Blue Origin flight of about ten minutes (*Expansión*, June 6, 2022).

Then there are beliefs (*las creencias*) that science can't prove. In Mexico and several other
Spanish-speaking countries, the unlucky day is traditionally *martes 13*, Tuesday the 13th, not
Friday, and an old saying warns *En martes 13, ni te cases ni te embarques* (On Tuesday the
13th, don't get married or set sail), as the Mexican news site adn40 noted in 2025. A
superstition (*una superstición*) like this one, a myth (*un mito*), a ghost story (*un
fantasma* is a ghost) or a UFO sighting (*un ovni*, from *objeto volador no identificado*) is the
perfect topic for *no creo que, dudo que* and *puede que*.

Other space words: *la estrella* (star), *la luna* (moon; *la Luna* with a capital for Earth's
moon in scientific writing), *la nave espacial* (spaceship), *el universo* (universe) and *el
extraterrestre* (alien; also an adjective: *vida extraterrestre*).

## Dialogue: Una luz en el cielo

Paola studies physics. Her cousin Iván is visiting her family in a village in Oaxaca. They are
looking at the night sky.

> Iván: ¡Mira, Paola! Esa luz se está moviendo. Estoy seguro de que es un ovni.
>
> Paola: No creo que sea un ovni. Es un avión, o tal vez un satélite.
>
> Iván: ¿Un satélite? Pero brilla muchísimo.
>
> Paola: Algunos brillan mucho. Es posible que sea la Estación Espacial Internacional.
>
> Iván: Siempre tienes una teoría. ¿De verdad crees que estamos solos en el universo?
>
> Paola: Yo no digo eso. Es probable que haya vida en otros planetas, pero dudo que los extraterrestres vengan de visita a Oaxaca.
>
> Iván: ¿Por qué no? A lo mejor les gustan las tlayudas.
>
> Paola: Ja, ja. Mira, es evidente que en el universo hay millones de estrellas. Pero hasta hoy nadie ha demostrado que existan los extraterrestres.
>
> Iván: Puede que todavía no lo hayan comprobado. Y mi abuela dice que vio un fantasma en la casa vieja.
>
> Paola: La abuela también cree que el martes 13 trae mala suerte. Son creencias, no ciencia.
>
> Iván: Bueno, quizás tengas razón. Pero es cierto que la luz se movía raro, ¿no?
>
> Paola: Es cierto que se movía. ¡Por eso es un satélite!

Translation:

> Iván: Look, Paola! That light is moving. I'm sure it's a UFO.
>
> Paola: I don't think it's a UFO. It's a plane, or maybe a satellite.
>
> Iván: A satellite? But it's really bright.
>
> Paola: Some are very bright. It might be the International Space Station.
>
> Iván: You always have a theory. Do you really think we're alone in the universe?
>
> Paola: I'm not saying that. There's probably life on other planets, but I doubt aliens are coming to visit Oaxaca.
>
> Iván: Why not? Maybe they like tlayudas.
>
> Paola: Ha ha. Look, obviously there are millions of stars in the universe. But so far nobody has proved that aliens exist.
>
> Iván: Maybe they haven't confirmed it yet. And my grandma says she saw a ghost in the old house.
>
> Paola: Grandma also thinks Tuesday the 13th brings bad luck. Those are beliefs, not science.
>
> Iván: OK, maybe you're right. But it's true that the light was moving strangely, right?
>
> Paola: It's true it was moving. That's why it's a satellite!

Notes: *Es posible que sea, dudo que vengan, quizás tengas, puede que no lo hayan comprobado*
(perfect subjunctive, lesson 03) are all doubt or possibility, and *nadie ha demostrado que
existan* denies that something has been shown, so it takes the subjunctive like *no es verdad
que*. *Estoy seguro de que es, es
evidente que hay, es cierto que se movía* state facts. *Las tlayudas* are large crisp tortillas with toppings,
typical of Oaxaca. *El satélite* = satellite; *brillar* = to shine.

## Pronunciation

- *Ovni* is one word with the stress on *O*: *OB-ni* (*v* and *b* sound the same).
- *Extraterrestre* has a single tapped *r* after *t* (*tra*) and a trilled *rr* in the middle:
  *eks-tra-te-RRES-tre*.
- *Superstición*: four syllables, stressed on the last, *su-pers-ti-SIÓN*, with seseo.
- *Dudo que sea* runs together in speech: *DU-do-ke-SE-a*.

## Common mistakes

- The subjunctive after a positive opinion: ~~*Creo que sea verdad*~~ → *Creo que es verdad.*
- The indicative after a negative one: ~~*No creo que es verdad*~~ → *No creo que sea verdad.*
- The subjunctive after *a lo mejor*: ~~*A lo mejor venga*~~ → *A lo mejor viene.*
- Reading *es difícil que* as "it's hard": *Es difícil que gane* = she probably won't win.
- Forgetting *de* in *estar seguro de que*: ~~*Estoy seguro que…*~~ → *Estoy seguro de que…* (the
  RAE's *Diccionario panhispánico de dudas* gives the form with *de*).
- *Un cierto* in the wrong place: *Es cierto* (It's true), but *una cierta duda* (a certain doubt).

## Key points

- Certainty + indicative: *creo que, pienso que, me parece que, estoy seguro de que, es verdad /
  cierto / evidente / obvio que, está claro que.*
- Doubt, denial and negated opinions + subjunctive: *no creo que, no pienso que, no me parece que,
  no estoy seguro de que, no es verdad que, dudo que, niego que.*
- Possibility + subjunctive: *es posible / probable / improbable / imposible / difícil que, puede
  (ser) que.*
- *quizás / tal vez* + either mood; *a lo mejor* + indicative only. *¿Crees que…?* can take
  either.

lessons.title: ¡Que te vaya bonito! Wishes, blessings and set phrases with que
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 01 showed that *¡Que te vaya bien!* is a wish with its main clause left out: *(Espero) que
te vaya bien.* Spanish speakers use this pattern all day long, for goodbyes, meals, bedtime,
exams, birthdays and funerals. This lesson collects the common ones, explains *ojalá* and *Dios
quiera*, adds a group of fixed phrases built from a subjunctive repeated around *lo que*
(*pase lo que pase*, whatever happens), and shows how people in Mexico write messages of
congratulations, get-well wishes and condolences. Everything uses the present subjunctive from
lesson 01; nothing new to conjugate, only new ways to use it.

## Wishes with que alone

The pattern is *que* + a present subjunctive, with the person built into the verb and the
pronoun:

| wish | to a friend (tú) | to usted | to ustedes | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| a goodbye | *¡Que te vaya bien!* | *¡Que le vaya bien!* | *¡Que les vaya bien!* | All the best! Take care! |
| at night | *¡Que descanses!* | *¡Que descanse!* | *¡Que descansen!* | Sleep well! Get some rest! |
| before fun | *¡Que te diviertas!* | *¡Que se divierta!* | *¡Que se diviertan!* | Have fun! |
| a parting | *¡Que tengas buen día!* | *¡Que tenga buen día!* | *¡Que tengan buen día!* | Have a good day! |
| illness | *¡Que te mejores!* | *¡Que se mejore!* | *¡Que se mejoren!* | Get well soon! |

More you'll hear: *¡Que cumplas muchos más!* (Many happy returns! literally "may you have many
more birthdays"), *¡Que sean muy felices!* (to a couple: Be very happy!), *¡Que te salga bien!*
(I hope it goes well for you: before an exam or an interview), *¡Que tengas buen viaje!* (Have a
good trip!).

*¡Que te vaya bonito!* is a warmer version of *¡Que te vaya bien!*, heard especially in Mexico (*bonito*
here works as an adverb, "nicely"). It is also the title of a well-known ranchera by the Mexican
songwriter José Alfredo Jiménez (1926–1973), which has made it a familiar phrase.

### At the table: ¡Que aproveche! and ¡Provecho!

*¡Que aproveche!* (from *aprovechar*, lesson 01: may it do you good) is said to people who are
eating. It is the usual phrase in Spain. In Mexico you'll usually hear *¡Provecho!* or A1's
*¡Buen provecho!* instead, often said even to strangers at the next table in a restaurant;
*¡Que aproveche!* is understood there but much less common. The answer is *Gracias*, or *Igualmente* if the
other person is eating too.

### Worked example 1: one wish for three people

You are leaving a party at 11 p.m. Say good night and wish a good rest to (a) your friend Tomás,
(b) his grandmother, doña Lupe, and (c) his two parents.

1. The wish is *descansar*. Its present subjunctive: *descanse, descanses, descanse, descansemos,
   descansen*.
2. Tomás is *tú*: *¡Que descanses, Tomás!*
3. Doña Lupe is *usted*: *¡Que descanse, doña Lupe!*
4. The parents are *ustedes*: *¡Que descansen!*

For a reflexive verb, the pronoun changes too: *¡Que te diviertas!* → *¡Que se divierta!* → *¡Que
se diviertan!* (*divertirse* is an *-ie* stem changer: *diviertas*).

## Ojalá and Dios quiera

Both introduce a hope and take the subjunctive.

- *Ojalá (que) pases el examen.* — I hope you pass the exam.
- *Dios quiera que no llueva en la boda.* — God willing, it won't rain at the wedding.
- *¿Crees que te den el trabajo? — ¡Dios quiera!* — Do you think they'll give you the job? — I
  hope so!

*Dios quiera* (may God will it) is the subjunctive of *querer* with *Dios* as the subject; it is
followed by *que* + subjunctive, or used alone as an answer. A related phrase is *si Dios quiere* (if God wills), often added to plans: *Nos vemos el lunes, si
Dios quiere.*

*Ojalá* has an interesting history. The RAE's dictionary (2001 edition) traces it to a Hispanic
Arabic expression, *law šá lláh*, "if God wills it"; the Peruvian language column *Castellano
actual* (Universidad de Piura), which reports this, adds that the etymologist Joan Coromines and
others proposed different Arabic phrases (such as *wa-šā' allāh*, "and may God will it"), so the
exact form is debated. Today *ojalá* has no religious meaning for most speakers:
an atheist says *¡Ojalá!* as easily as anyone. *Dios quiera* and *si Dios quiere* keep more of
their religious flavor, though many people use them out of habit.

## Whatever happens: repeated subjunctives

A small group of fixed phrases repeats one verb in the subjunctive around *lo que, como* or
*donde*:

| phrase | literally | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *pase lo que pase* | may happen what may happen | whatever happens, no matter what |
| *cueste lo que cueste* | may it cost what it may cost | whatever it takes, at any cost |
| *digan lo que digan* | let them say what they say | whatever people say |
| *sea como sea* | be it how it may be | one way or another; anyway |

- *Pase lo que pase, te llamo mañana.* — Whatever happens, I'll call you tomorrow.
- *Voy a terminar la carrera, cueste lo que cueste.* — I'm going to finish my degree, whatever it
  takes.
- *Digan lo que digan, es la mejor taquería de la ciudad.* — Whatever people say, it's the best
  taco place in the city.
- *Sea como sea, tenemos que llegar a las ocho.* — One way or another, we have to be there at
  eight.

The first verb and the second are always the same, in the same person. *Digan* is *ellos*
(people in general); you can change the person when it makes sense: *digas lo que digas*
(whatever you say). *Sea como sea* also works as "anyway, at any rate" to wrap up a story.

### Worked example 2: making your own

You want to say "Whatever you do, don't tell your mom" with *hacer*, and "Wherever you go, call
me" with *ir*.

1. *hacer*, tú: subjunctive *hagas*. The pattern is verb + *lo que* + verb: *hagas lo que
   hagas*.
2. Add the main sentence: *Hagas lo que hagas, no le digas nada a tu mamá.* (*No le digas* is a
   negative command, lesson 05.)
3. *ir*, tú: *vayas*. Place, so *donde*: *vayas donde vayas.*
4. *Vayas donde vayas, llámame.*

These two are for recognition; the four in the table are the ones to learn.

## Messages for occasions

Messages for births, weddings, graduations, illness and deaths use the same few patterns:
*deseo / te deseo* + noun, *que* + subjunctive, and *ojalá*. Mexico is a country where many
people are religious, so formulas like *Que Dios te bendiga* (God bless you) and *Dios quiera*
are customary, but they aren't required: a warm message without them is just as correct.

Choosing *tú* or *usted*: use *tú* with friends and family of your generation, *usted* with older people,
your boss or someone you don't know well. In a condolence message to an older person, *usted* is
the safe choice.

| occasion | common phrases |
|---|---|
| congratulations | *¡Muchas felicidades!* *Te felicito de corazón.* *Les deseo lo mejor.* *¡Que sean muy felices!* |
| birthday | *¡Feliz cumpleaños!* *¡Que cumplas muchos más!* *Que se cumplan todos tus deseos.* |
| illness | *¡Que te mejores pronto!* *Ojalá que te recuperes muy pronto.* *Aquí estamos para lo que necesites.* |
| a death | *Mi más sentido pésame.* *Mis condolencias.* *Lamento mucho la pérdida de tu papá.* *Que en paz descanse.* *Un abrazo fuerte.* |

*La condolencia* is almost always plural: *mis condolencias*, *le envío mis condolencias*.
*Que en paz descanse* (may he / she rest in peace) follows the name of the person who died: *Don
Arturo, que en paz descanse, era muy buen vecino.* In printed death notices it is often
abbreviated *Q. E. P. D.* *La pérdida* = loss. *Para lo que necesites* (for whatever you need)
uses the subjunctive for something unknown, a use lesson 08 explains.

![Two cards side by side. Left, a wedding card with two rings: Queridos Ana y Rodrigo: ¡Muchas felicidades en este día tan especial! Les deseamos un matrimonio lleno de amor y armonía. Que sean muy felices y que la vida les dé muchos años juntos. Con cariño, familia Méndez. Right, a plain card with a white flower: Estimada señora Gutiérrez: Lamento profundamente el fallecimiento de su esposo, don Arturo. Fue un excelente vecino. Reciba mi más sentido pésame. Que en paz descanse. Atentamente, Julio Ramos.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The wedding card uses *ustedes* (*les deseamos, que sean*) and two wishes with *que*. The
condolence card uses *usted* (*su esposo, reciba*: an usted command), names the person, says
something kind about him and closes with the formula. *El fallecimiento* (death, passing) is the
formal word; *lamento profundamente* = I deeply regret.

### Worked example 3: a get-well message

Your coworker, Licenciada Herrera, has had an operation. Write two sentences.

1. Register: a colleague you call *usted* → *usted* forms.
2. React: *Lamento mucho lo de su operación* (I'm very sorry about your operation: *la
   operación*; *lo de* = the matter of). *Siento mucho lo de…* works too.
3. Wish: *que* + *mejorarse* in the usted form → *Que se mejore pronto.* Or with *ojalá*: *Ojalá
   que se recupere muy pronto.*
4. Close: *Todos en la oficina le mandamos un abrazo.*

Result: *Licenciada Herrera: Lamento mucho lo de su operación. Ojalá que se recupere muy pronto.
Todos en la oficina le mandamos un abrazo.* (After the colon of a greeting in a letter or
message, the RAE's spelling rules call for a capital letter: *Lamento*.)

## A WhatsApp thread: el examen de manejo

> Lucía: Mañana es mi examen de manejo. ¡Estoy nerviosísima!
>
> Beto: ¡Que te vaya bonito, prima! Vas a pasar, ya verás.
>
> Tía Male: Dios quiera que sí, mija. Te mando mi bendición.
>
> Lucía: Gracias, tía. Pase lo que pase, mañana les cuento.
>
> Beto: Y si no pasas, lo vuelves a intentar. Cueste lo que cueste, vas a tener tu licencia.
>
> Lucía (next day): ¡¡PASÉ!!
>
> Tía Male: ¡Qué bueno, mija! Felicidades. Que disfrutes tu licencia y que manejes con mucho cuidado.
>
> Beto: ¡Eso! Hoy en la noche te invito unos tacos para celebrar.
>
> Lucía: ¡Gracias a todos! Me voy a dormir temprano. ¡Que descansen!

Translation:

> Lucía: Tomorrow is my driving test. I'm so nervous!
>
> Beto: Good luck, cousin! You'll pass, you'll see.
>
> Aunt Male: God willing, sweetheart. I'm sending you my blessing.
>
> Lucía: Thanks, Auntie. Whatever happens, I'll tell you all about it tomorrow.
>
> Beto: And if you don't pass, you'll try again. Whatever it takes, you're going to get your license.
>
> Lucía (next day): I PASSED!!
>
> Aunt Male: Wonderful, sweetheart! Congratulations. Enjoy your license, and drive very carefully.
>
> Beto: Yes! Tonight I'm buying you some tacos to celebrate.
>
> Lucía: Thanks, everyone! I'm going to bed early. Sleep well, all of you!

*Mija* (from *mi hija*) is an affectionate form for a daughter, niece or granddaughter (and
often any younger woman), like *mijo* in lesson 01. *Disfrutar* = to enjoy; *con cuidado* = carefully. *¡Eso!* = That's it! Yes!
*Lo vuelves a intentar* = you try it again (*volver a* + infinitive, A2).

## Common mistakes

- The indicative in a wish: ~~*¡Que descansas!*~~ → *¡Que descanses!*
- The wrong person for usted: ~~*¡Que tengas buen día, señora!*~~ → *¡Que tenga buen día, señora!*
- Breaking a repeated phrase: ~~*Pase que pase*~~, ~~*pase lo que pasa*~~ → *pase lo que pase.*
- *Que en paz descanse* for anyone alive: it is only for someone who has died. For a sleeping
  friend, *¡Que descanses!*
- Assuming religious formulas are required: *Mi más sentido pésame* and *Un abrazo fuerte* are
  enough for anyone.
- Spelling *ojalá* without its accent: the stress is on the last syllable.

## Key points

- *Que* + present subjunctive is a full wish: *¡Que descanses! ¡Que te diviertas! ¡Que tengas
  buen día! ¡Que aproveche!* Change the person for *usted* and *ustedes*.
- *Ojalá (que)* and *Dios quiera (que)* + subjunctive. *Ojalá* goes back to Arabic (the usual
  account: "if God wills"; the exact source is debated).
- Repeated subjunctives: *pase lo que pase, cueste lo que cueste, digan lo que digan, sea como
  sea.*
- Messages: congratulations (*¡Que sean muy felices!*), get well (*Que te mejores pronto*),
  condolences (*Mi más sentido pésame, Mis condolencias, Que en paz descanse*); choose *tú* or
  *usted*, and religious formulas are optional.
