lessons.title: Querida consejera: advice columns
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

An advice column (*un consultorio sentimental* in a magazine, or a podcast or blog that answers
listeners' letters) is the perfect place to see the whole module working at once. The person who
writes in has feelings and doubts; the columnist, *la consejera* or *el consejero* (adviser),
reacts to those feelings (lesson 03), gives advice (lesson 02), wishes the writer well (lesson
01) and says what she believes or doubts (lesson 04).

This lesson reads two original letters and their replies, shows how to soften advice so it
sounds kind rather than bossy, and walks you through writing a reply of 100–120 words, the length
of the first DELE B1 writing task (an e-mail, letter or post answering a short text).

## Letter 1: Corazón roto en Puebla

> Querida consejera:
>
> Tengo diecinueve años y estudio en Puebla. Hace dos meses mi novio terminó conmigo y todavía no lo supero. Mis amigas me dicen que salga y que lo olvide, pero no puedo. Lo peor es que él me escribe a veces y me dice que me extraña. ¿Debería intentar reconciliarme con él? Me da miedo que vuelva a pasar lo mismo, pero también me da miedo quedarme sola.
>
> Corazón roto en Puebla

> Querida Corazón roto:
>
> Siento mucho que estés pasando por un desamor tan fuerte. Es normal que te sientas así: dos meses no es mucho tiempo. Me alegra que tengas amigas que te quieren, pero no estoy de acuerdo con que tengas que olvidarlo de un día para otro.
>
> Primero, te aconsejo que te desahogues. Escribe lo que sientes o habla con alguien de confianza; llorar también ayuda. Segundo, toma en cuenta una cosa: él terminó contigo. No dudo que te extraña, pero no creo que extrañarte sea lo mismo que querer volver. Antes de reconciliarte, es importante que hablen con sinceridad sobre por qué terminaron.
>
> Y quizás deberías preguntarte qué quieres tú, no qué quiere él. Ojalá que pronto encuentres la respuesta. Mereces a alguien que te trate bien.
>
> Un abrazo,
> La consejera

Translation of the letter: "Dear adviser: I'm nineteen and I study in Puebla. Two months ago my
boyfriend broke up with me and I still haven't gotten over it. My friends tell me to go out and
forget him, but I can't. The worst part is that he texts me sometimes and tells me he misses me.
Should I try to get back together with him? I'm afraid the same thing will happen again, but I'm
also afraid of being alone. Broken heart in Puebla."

Translation of the reply: "Dear Broken heart: I'm very sorry you're going through such a painful
heartbreak. It's normal to feel this way: two months isn't long. I'm glad you have friends who
love you, but I don't agree that you have to forget him overnight. First, I advise you to let it
all out. Write down what you feel or talk to someone you trust; crying helps too. Second, take
one thing into account: he broke up with you. I don't doubt that he misses you, but I don't think
missing you is the same as wanting to get back together. Before you make up, it's important that
you talk honestly about why you broke up. And maybe you should ask yourself what you want, not
what he wants. I hope you find the answer soon. You deserve someone who treats you well. Hugs,
the adviser."

Words: *terminar con alguien* = to break up with someone; *superar* (lesson 01) = to get over;
*desahogarse* = to vent, to let it out; *reconciliarse (con)* = to make up, to get back together (A2's *hacer las paces* is the everyday phrase after a small fight);
*el desamor* = heartbreak, the pain of a love that's over; *la sinceridad* = honesty, sincerity;
*tomar en cuenta* = to take into account (very common in Mexico; *tener en cuenta*, the usual
form in Spain, is also used there); *de confianza* =
trusted; *merecer* = to deserve. *Mis amigas me dicen que salga* is *decir* + subjunctive, a
reported command (lesson 02). *Alguien que te trate bien* has a subjunctive for a person not yet
known, a use lesson 08 explains.

## Worked example 1: what each sentence does

Here is how the reply combines the module's four uses. Each subjunctive has its trigger:

| sentence | trigger | use | lesson |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Siento mucho que estés pasando…* | *siento que* | feeling | 03 |
| *Es normal que te sientas así.* | *es normal que* | value judgment | 02–03 |
| *Me alegra que tengas amigas…* | *me alegra que* | feeling | 03 |
| *Te aconsejo que te desahogues.* | *aconsejar que* | advice | 02 |
| *No creo que extrañarte sea lo mismo…* | *no creo que* | doubt | 04 |
| *Es importante que hablen con sinceridad.* | *es importante que* | impersonal expression | 02 |
| *Ojalá que pronto encuentres la respuesta.* | *ojalá* | wish | 01 |

And the indicative where a fact is stated: *Tienes amigas que te quieren*, *él terminó contigo*,
*dos meses no es mucho tiempo*, *No dudo que te extraña*. After *no dudo que* the columnist uses
the indicative because not doubting is being sure, as lesson 04 said; you'll also hear the
subjunctive (*No dudo que te extrañe*), but the indicative is the more usual choice.

## Softening advice

A good columnist rarely gives orders. From strongest to softest:

| strength | form | example |
|---|---|---|
| a demand | *Te exijo que… / Tienes que…* | *Tienes que dejar de escribirle.* |
| clear advice | *Te aconsejo que… / Te recomiendo que…* + subjunctive | *Te aconsejo que no le escribas.* |
| a softer suggestion | *Deberías* + infinitive (A2) | *Deberías tomarte un tiempo.* |
| a gentle idea | *Quizás deberías… / Yo en tu lugar…* + conditional | *Quizás deberías hablar con él.* |
| a question | *¿Y si…?* / *¿Por qué no…?* + present indicative; *¿Has pensado en…?* | *¿Y si le escribes una carta?* *¿Has pensado en hablar con un psicólogo?* |

*¿Y si…?* takes the present indicative: *¿Y si le llamas?* (What if you call him?), never
~~*¿Y si le llames?*~~. A *si* that means "if" is never followed by the present subjunctive
(lesson 14 adds the past subjunctive for hypotheses).

## Letter 2: Tímido en Mérida

> Querido consejero:
>
> Tengo veintiocho años y trabajo en una oficina en Mérida. Desde niño soy muy tímido. En las reuniones nunca digo nada, aunque tengo buenas ideas, y cuando alguien me gusta, no me atrevo a invitarla a salir. Creo que es por mi autoestima: me da pánico el rechazo. Mi hermana dice que soy demasiado sensible. ¿Es posible cambiar o así soy?
>
> Tímido en Mérida

> Querido Tímido:
>
> Gracias por tu carta tan sincera. Primero, no creo que tengas que cambiar tu forma de ser: la timidez no es un defecto. Pero sí es posible que aprendas a sentirte más cómodo.
>
> Te sugiero que empieces con pasos pequeños. ¿Y si en la próxima reunión preparas una sola idea y la dices? Es probable que nadie note tus nervios. Con el tiempo, es posible que tu autoestima crezca.
>
> Sobre el rechazo: es verdad que a nadie le gusta, pero un "no" no dice nada de tu valor. Me alegra que tengas una hermana que te conoce bien; quizás puedas practicar con ella. Ella seguramente es más comprensiva de lo que crees.
>
> Te deseo mucha suerte. Ojalá que nos escribas pronto con buenas noticias.
>
> El consejero

Translation of the letter: "Dear adviser: I'm twenty-eight and I work in an office in Mérida.
I've been very shy since I was a child. In meetings I never say anything, even though I have good
ideas, and when I like someone, I don't dare ask her out. I think it's because of my self-esteem:
I'm terrified of rejection. My sister says I'm too sensitive. Is it possible to change, or is
this just who I am? Shy in Mérida."

Translation of the reply: "Dear Shy: Thank you for such an honest letter. First, I don't think you
have to change who you are: shyness isn't a flaw. But it is possible for you to learn to feel more
comfortable. I suggest you start with small steps. What if in the next meeting you prepare just
one idea and say it? Most likely nobody will notice your nerves. Over time, your self-esteem may
grow. About rejection: it's true that nobody likes it, but a 'no' says nothing about your worth.
I'm glad you have a sister who knows you well; maybe you can practice with her. She is probably
more understanding than you think. I wish you lots of luck. I hope you'll write to us soon with
good news. The adviser."

Words: *la timidez* = shyness (from A2's *tímido*); *la autoestima* = self-esteem; *el rechazo* =
rejection; *sincero* = sincere, honest; *comprensivo* = understanding (a false friend: "a
comprehensive plan" is *un plan completo* or *integral*); *sensible* = sensitive (lesson 03);
*atreverse a* = to dare to (lesson 22); *el pánico* = panic, terror; *el valor* = worth;
*seguramente* = most likely; *tu forma de ser* = the way you are, who you are. *Quizás puedas* uses the subjunctive after *quizás*; *quizás puedes*
would also be correct (lesson 04). *Una hermana que te conoce bien* is indicative: he really has
this sister.

## Worked example 2: the structure of a reply

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The structure of an advice-column reply
  accDescr: A reply in five steps. First, the greeting, for example Querida Corazón roto. Second, react to the feelings with a verb of emotion and the subjunctive, for example Siento que estés pasando por esto. Third, give two pieces of advice, one clear, Te aconsejo que hables con él, and one softer, Quizás deberías tomarte un tiempo or ¿Y si le escribes? Fourth, give your honest opinion, with creo que plus indicative or no creo que plus subjunctive. Fifth, close with a wish, Ojalá que todo salga bien, and a sign-off such as Un abrazo.
  A["1. Saludo: Querida…"] --> B["2. Reaccionar: Siento que… / Me alegra que… + subjuntivo"]
  B --> C["3. Aconsejar: Te aconsejo que… + subjuntivo; Quizás deberías… / ¿Y si…?"]
  C --> D["4. Opinar: Creo que… + indicativo / No creo que… + subjuntivo"]
  D --> E["5. Despedirse: Ojalá que… + subjuntivo; Un abrazo"]
```

Both replies follow this plan. Notice the balance: the reaction and the wish show that the
columnist is *comprensiva*; the opinion is honest without being harsh.

## Worked example 3: writing a guided reply (100–120 words)

A reader writes: *"Mi mejor amiga y yo no nos hablamos desde hace un mes. Discutimos por una
tontería y ahora las dos somos demasiado orgullosas para llamar. ¿Qué hago?"* ("My best friend and
I haven't spoken for a month. We argued over something silly and now we're both too proud to
call. What should I do?")

1. Plan one sentence for each step of the diagram: react, two pieces of advice, an opinion, a
   wish.
2. Choose the triggers: *Siento que…*, *Te aconsejo que…*, *¿Y si…?*, *No creo que…*, *Ojalá
   que…*
3. Write, then count the words (100–120 is the target; this one is 109, counting the greeting and the sign-off):

> Querida amiga:
>
> Siento mucho que estés lejos de tu mejor amiga por una tontería. Es normal que te sientas triste y orgullosa al mismo tiempo, pero no creo que el orgullo valga más que una amistad.
>
> Te aconsejo que des el primer paso. ¿Y si le mandas un mensaje sencillo y sincero? No es necesario que hables de la discusión enseguida: basta con decirle que la extrañas. Es posible que ella esté esperando lo mismo. Una amistad de tantos años merece esa oportunidad.
>
> Si quieren reconciliarse, es importante que las dos se escuchen sin interrumpir. Ojalá que pronto vuelvan a reírse juntas de esta tontería.
>
> Un abrazo,
> La consejera

4. Check each verb after *que*: wish, advice, feeling, doubt and impersonal expression →
   subjunctive (*estés, sientas, valga, des, hables, esté, se escuchen, vuelvan*); a fact →
   indicative (*la extrañas*); *si* → indicative (*Si quieren, ¿Y si le mandas?*).

(*La tontería* = something silly; *enseguida* = right away; *basta con* = it's enough to; *la
amistad* = friendship, A2; *la discusión* = argument, lesson 16.)

## Common mistakes

- The subjunctive after *si*: ~~*¿Y si le llames?*~~ → *¿Y si le llamas?*
- Advice that sounds like an order: *Tienes que…* is strong; a columnist prefers *Te aconsejo
  que…, Quizás deberías…, ¿Y si…?*
- *Tomar en cuenta* with a preposition: ~~*Toma en cuenta de que…*~~ → *Toma en cuenta que…*
- *Comprensivo* for "comprehensive": *un estudio completo*, not ~~*un estudio comprensivo*~~ in
  that sense.
- Mixing *tú* and *usted* in one reply: pick one (advice columns usually use *tú*).
- Going over the word limit: count, and cut adjectives before you cut a required point.

## Key points

- A reply reacts (*Siento que…*), advises (*Te aconsejo que…*), gives an opinion (*No creo
  que…*) and wishes (*Ojalá que…*): all four subjunctive uses of this module.
- Soften advice: *deberías, quizás deberías, yo en tu lugar* + conditional, *¿Y si* + present
  indicative?, *¿Has pensado en…?*
- New words for feelings and relationships: *el desamor, desahogarse, reconciliarse, la
  autoestima, la timidez, el rechazo, sincero, la sinceridad, comprensivo, tomar en cuenta.*
- Plan, write and count: DELE B1's first writing task asks for 100–120 words.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Don't do that! Negative commands and the full command system
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In A1 you learned the affirmative **[[imperative]]** for *tú* and *usted* (*maneja, maneje*), and in A2 you attached pronouns to it (*estaciónalo, póngase el cinturón*; *estacionar* or *estacionarse* = to park, from A2's honors lesson 16h1). "Don't" was harder: A2 gave you a few negative commands as fixed phrases (*No te preocupes, No lo toques*) and promised the rest for B1. Now you know the present subjunctive from module 1, and that is all you need: almost every command except the affirmative *tú* form is a subjunctive form. This lesson completes the system: **[[negative commands]]** for *tú*, *usted* and *ustedes*, affirmative *ustedes* commands, and **[[nosotros commands]]** ("let's…"). The theme is driving: learning to drive, the rules of the road and the words on a Mexican street.

## Negative tú commands: no + the tú subjunctive

To tell a friend not to do something, put *no* before the *tú* form of the present subjunctive:

| Verb | Affirmative (A1) | Negative (new) | |
|---|---|---|---|
| acelerar | *acelera* | *no aceleres* | (don't) speed up |
| frenar | *frena* | *no frenes* | (don't) brake |
| escribir | *escribe* | *no escribas* | (don't) write |
| tener | *ten* | *no tengas* | (don't) have |
| hacer | *haz* | *no hagas* | (don't) do |
| decir | *di* | *no digas* | (don't) say |
| salir | *sal* | *no salgas* | (don't) go out |
| ir | *ve* | *no vayas* | (don't) go |
| ser | *sé* | *no seas* | (don't) be |

The affirmative *tú* command comes from the present (*él acelera → acelera*), but the negative comes from the subjunctive (*que tú aceleres → no aceleres*). Everything you learned about subjunctive forms in lesson 01 applies:

- Irregular yo: *tengo → no tengas, digo → no digas, conduzco → no conduzcas.*
- Stem changers: *no pierdas el tiempo, no vuelvas tarde, no pidas permiso* (-ir verbs keep their change: *pedir → no pidas*).
- Spelling changes keep the sound of the stem: *buscar → no busques, llegar → no llegues, cruzar → no cruces, empezar → no empieces.*
- The irregulars: *no vayas, no seas, no estés, no des.*

*No cruces la calle sin mirar.* — Don't cross the street without looking.
*No llegues tarde a la clase de manejo.* — Don't be late for your driving lesson.
*No seas impaciente con los ciclistas.* — Don't be impatient with cyclists.

## usted and ustedes: one form for both

*usted* and *ustedes* commands were subjunctive forms all along: *maneje* (usted) is the same word as *que él maneje*. So the negative just adds *no*:

| | Affirmative | Negative |
|---|---|---|
| usted | *Frene aquí.* — Brake here. | *No frene de golpe.* — Don't brake suddenly. |
| ustedes | *Crucen por el cruce.* — Cross at the crosswalk. | *No crucen a media calle.* — Don't cross in the middle of the street. |

You can now also produce affirmative *ustedes* commands freely (A2 showed them for recognition): *Abróchense el cinturón de seguridad* — Fasten your seat belts (*abrocharse* = to fasten). *Tengan cuidado con la grúa* — Be careful with the tow truck. In Spain, a group of friends gets *vosotros* commands (*cruzad, no crucéis*); Latin America uses *ustedes* for everyone.

## Where the pronouns go

The rule from A2 still holds for affirmative commands: pronouns attach to the end, with a written accent if the stress ends up on the third syllable from the end or earlier. In negative commands, they move in front of the verb, in the same order (reflexive, indirect, direct):

| Affirmative | Negative |
|---|---|
| *Estaciónalo aquí.* — Park it here. | *No lo estaciones aquí.* — Don't park it here. |
| *Distráete un rato.* — Take your mind off things for a while. | *No te distraigas.* — Don't get distracted. |
| *Póngase el casco.* — Put on your helmet. (usted) | *No se quite el casco.* — Don't take off your helmet. |
| *Dígaselo al agente.* — Tell the officer. | *No se lo diga.* — Don't tell him. |

*ponerse* = to put on (clothes, a helmet); *quitarse* = to take off.

![A table titled Estacionar el carro: los mandatos. Columns: Persona, Afirmativo (pronoun at the end, attached) and Negativo: no + subjuntivo (pronoun before the verb). Rows: tú: estaciona, estaciónalo / no estaciones, no lo estaciones. usted: estacione, estaciónelo / no estacione, no lo estacione. ustedes: estacionen, estaciónenlo / no estacionen, no lo estacionen. nosotros: estacionemos, estacionémoslo / no estacionemos, no lo estacionemos. Every cell except tú affirmative is shaded yellow, meaning it is a subjunctive form; tú affirmative is the él form of the present.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Seven of the eight cells are subjunctive forms; only the affirmative *tú* command is different.

## Nosotros commands: "let's…"

To say "let's do something", Spanish uses the *nosotros* form of the subjunctive:

- *Crucemos aquí.* — Let's cross here.
- *No estacionemos en la banqueta.* — Let's not park on the sidewalk.
- *Esperemos a que pase el peatón.* — Let's wait for the pedestrian to cross.

Three details:

1. *ir* has its own affirmative form: *vamos* (let's go), not the subjunctive *vayamos*. The negative is regular: *no vayamos* (let's not go). The RAE's *Diccionario panhispánico de dudas* notes that *vamos* is used for "let's go" more often than *vayamos*, which is now mostly literary.
2. With nos, the final -s drops: *sentemos + nos → sentémonos* (let's sit down), *pongamos + nos → pongámonos el cinturón* (let's put on our seat belts), *vamos + nos → vámonos* (let's go, let's leave). The same happens before *se lo*: *digamos + se lo → digámoselo* (let's tell him). In the negative nothing is dropped: *no nos sentemos, no nos vayamos.*
3. In everyday speech, *vamos a* + infinitive is often used instead: *Vamos a cruzar* (Let's cross) means the same as *Crucemos* (in another context, "we're going to cross"). *Vámonos* is used constantly; forms like *crucemos, estacionemos* sound a little more planned or formal, as in instructions and announcements.

## Softer ways to tell someone what to do

A string of commands can sound bossy. You already have softer options:

- A question with the conditional (A2): *¿Podrías frenar un poco?* — Could you slow down a bit?
- *Mejor* (better) + a command: *Mejor no tomes esa calle; hay mucho tránsito.* — Better not take that street; there's a lot of traffic.
- Advice with the subjunctive (lesson 02): *Te recomiendo que no uses el celular.* *Es mejor que no rebases aquí.* (*rebasar* = to pass, A2).
- *Hay que* + infinitive for a general rule: *Hay que respetar el límite de velocidad.*

## Commands on signs and in rules

Mexican road signs and printed rules use two forms you can now read:

- The infinitive, often after *No* or *Prohibido*: *NO ESTACIONARSE* (No parking), *PROHIBIDO REBASAR* (No passing), *NO TIRAR BASURA* (Don't throw trash).
- The usted command: *CEDA EL PASO* (Yield; *ceder* = to give up), *DISMINUYA SU VELOCIDAD* (Reduce your speed; *disminuir* = to reduce), *MANEJE CON PRECAUCIÓN* (Drive carefully). Some painted signs say *NO REBASE*: a negative *usted* command.

## The street and the car

![A top-down drawing of a street. A sidewalk (la banqueta) runs along the top, with a green bike lane (la ciclovía) and a cyclist (el ciclista) below it. The road has two lanes (el carril) in each direction and a yellow center line. A pedestrian (el peatón) walks across white crosswalk stripes (el cruce). A round speed-limit sign showing 40 stands on the lower sidewalk (la señal de tránsito). On the right, the road enters a traffic circle with a monument in the middle (la glorieta).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*El tránsito* is the official Mexican word for traffic (*el Reglamento de Tránsito*, *el agente de tránsito*); A2's *el tráfico* means the same and is just as common in conversation.

![A drawing of the inside of a car seen from the driver's seat, with labels: el parabrisas (the windshield), el espejo retrovisor (the rearview mirror), el volante (the steering wheel), el claxon (the horn, in the middle of the wheel), el cinturón de seguridad (the seat belt), el freno (the brake pedal, the wider one) and el acelerador (the gas pedal).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

A few phrases with these words: *Un buen conductor es prudente: no toca el claxon sin razón y pisa el freno antes del cruce.* — A good driver is careful: he doesn't honk for no reason and steps on the brake before the crosswalk. *Respeta las señales de tránsito.* — Obey the road signs. *Anota las placas del carro.* — Write down the car's license plate.

## The rules of the road in Mexico City

Traffic rules in Mexico are set by each state, so they differ. In Mexico City, the *Reglamento de Tránsito* (in the text published by the city's Secretaría de Seguridad Ciudadana in 2019) sets these default speed limits where no sign says otherwise: 50 km/h on main roads (*vías primarias*), 40 km/h on secondary roads, 20 km/h in school and hospital zones and 80 km/h in the central lanes of expressways. It also requires the driver and every passenger to wear a seat belt, motorcyclists and their passengers to wear a helmet, and it forbids using a phone while the vehicle is moving. If you break a rule, *un agente de tránsito* can give you *una multa* (a fine), and a car parked where it shouldn't be can end up behind *la grúa*.

## Dialogue: La clase de manejo

Valeria, 17, is learning to drive. Her uncle Toño is teaching her in his car on a Sunday morning.

> Tío Toño: Antes de arrancar, abróchate el cinturón y ajusta el espejo. No, no lo toques así: con cuidado.
>
> Valeria: Ya. ¿Ahora qué hago?
>
> Tío Toño: Pon las dos manos en el volante y sal despacio. No aceleres tanto, ¡estamos en una calle de cuarenta!
>
> Valeria: Perdón. ¿Doy vuelta en la esquina?
>
> Tío Toño: Sí, pero primero pon la direccional. Y fíjate en el peatón: no frenes de golpe, frena poco a poco.
>
> Valeria: Ay, tío, hay un ciclista en el carril.
>
> Tío Toño: Tranquila. No lo rebases aquí; espera a que tengas espacio. Muy bien.
>
> Valeria: Ahora viene la glorieta. Me pone nerviosa.
>
> Tío Toño: No te distraigas y no te preocupes. Los que ya están en la glorieta tienen preferencia. Entremos cuando no venga nadie… ¡ahora!
>
> Valeria: ¡Lo logré! Estacionemos aquí para descansar, ¿no?
>
> Tío Toño: Aquí no, que es zona de grúa. Vámonos a la siguiente cuadra. Y no le digas a tu mamá que tocaste el claxon tres veces.

*Uncle Toño: Before you start, fasten your seat belt and adjust the mirror. No, don't touch it like that: carefully. — Valeria: Done. What do I do now? — Uncle Toño: Put both hands on the wheel and pull out slowly. Don't speed up so much, we're on a forty street! — Valeria: Sorry. Do I turn at the corner? — Uncle Toño: Yes, but first put your turn signal on. And watch the pedestrian: don't brake suddenly, brake little by little. — Valeria: Oh, uncle, there's a cyclist in the lane. — Uncle Toño: Easy. Don't pass him here; wait until you have room. Very good. — Valeria: Here comes the traffic circle. It makes me nervous. — Uncle Toño: Don't get distracted and don't worry. The ones already in the circle have the right of way. Let's go in when nobody's coming… now! — Valeria: I did it! Let's park here to take a break, OK? — Uncle Toño: Not here, it's a tow zone. Let's go to the next block. And don't tell your mom you honked the horn three times.*

(*arrancar* — to start (a car), pull away; *ajustar* — to adjust; *con cuidado* — carefully; *la direccional* — the turn signal, in Mexico; *fijarse en* — to watch, to pay attention to; *tener preferencia* — to have the right of way; *esperar a que* + subjunctive — to wait until.) Find the negative commands (*no lo toques, no aceleres, no frenes, no lo rebases, no te distraigas, no te preocupes, no le digas*), the nosotros commands (*entremos, estacionemos, vámonos*) and the *que* that gives a reason in *Aquí no, que es zona de grúa* (common in speech: "since…").

## Pronunciation

- Keep the stress of the subjunctive when you add *no*: *no a-ce-LE-res, no CRU-ces, no te dis-TRAI-gas*.
- The nosotros command with *nos* keeps its stress on the same syllable, so it needs an accent: *sen-TÉ-mo-nos, pon-GÁ-mo-nos, VÁ-mo-nos*.
- *claxon* has an x that sounds like ks: KLAK-son. *grúa* has two syllables: GRÚ-a. *peatón* has three: pe-a-TÓN.
- *ciclovía*: ci-clo-VÍ-a, four syllables, with *c* = s in Latin America (si-klo-BÍ-a).

## Common mistakes

- Using the affirmative form after *no*: ~~No acelera~~, ~~No dilo~~ → *No aceleres, No lo digas.* (*No acelera* is a statement: "He doesn't speed up.")
- Using the indicative: ~~No te distraes~~ → *No te distraigas.*
- Attaching the pronoun in a negative command: ~~No tócalo~~ → *No lo toques.*
- Forgetting the spelling change: ~~no cruzes, no busces~~ → *no cruces, no busques.*
- Keeping the *-s* before *nos*: ~~sentémosnos, vámosnos~~ → *sentémonos, vámonos.*
- ~~No vamos~~ for "let's not go": that means "we aren't going". Say *No vayamos.*

## Key points

- Negative *tú* commands: *no* + the *tú* subjunctive: *no aceleres, no corras, no vayas, no seas.*
- *usted* and *ustedes* commands are subjunctive forms, affirmative and negative: *frene / no frene, crucen / no crucen.*
- Pronouns: attached to affirmative commands (*estaciónalo*), before negative ones (*no lo estaciones*).
- *nosotros* commands = the nosotros subjunctive (*crucemos, no estacionemos*); *vamos / no vayamos*; drop the *-s* before *nos*: *vámonos, sentémonos.* In conversation, *vamos a* + infinitive is common.
- Softer: *¿Podrías…?, Mejor no…, Te recomiendo que…*; signs: *No estacionarse, Ceda el paso.*

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: So that everyone can help: para que, sin que and purpose
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In A2 you used *para* + infinitive to say why you do something: *Ahorro para viajar* (I'm saving to travel). That works when the person who acts and the person who benefits are the same. But often you do something so that *someone else* can do something: you donate so that children have school supplies, you explain so that a new volunteer understands. For that, Spanish needs *para que* + subjunctive. This lesson teaches it, together with its partner *sin que* (without someone doing something). Both introduce an **[[adverbial clause]]**: a clause that works like an adverb, telling you why, how or when. The theme is volunteering: NGOs, donations and helping a community after *un desastre* (a disaster).

## para + infinitive or para que + subjunctive?

The question to ask is: is the subject the same?

- Same subject: *para* + infinitive. *(Yo) estudio para (yo) aprender.*
- Different subject: *para que* + subjunctive. *(Yo) te lo explico para que (tú) lo entiendas.*

![A two-by-two chart titled ¿El mismo sujeto o un sujeto diferente? Columns: El mismo sujeto + infinitivo, and Un sujeto diferente + que + subjuntivo. Row para: Ahorro para comprar útiles (I save, I buy) / Dono para que los niños tengan útiles (I donate, the children have). Row sin: Ayudamos sin esperar nada (we help, we don't expect) / Ayudamos sin que nadie nos lo pida (we help, nobody asks). A note at the bottom: para que and sin que always take the subjunctive.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

More examples:

- *Recaudamos fondos para comprar cobijas.* — We're raising funds to buy blankets. (We raise, we buy.)
- *Recaudamos fondos para que las familias tengan cobijas.* — We're raising funds so the families have blankets.
- *La ONG organiza talleres para que los jóvenes encuentren trabajo.* — The NGO runs workshops so that young people find work. (*el taller* = workshop)
- *Habla más fuerte para que todos te oigan.* — Speak louder so everyone can hear you.
- *Esta organización lucha contra la pobreza para que las familias necesitadas reciban apoyo.* — This organization fights poverty so that families in need get support. (*luchar* = to fight)
- *La campaña es muy solidaria: todo lo que donas llega a la comunidad.* — The campaign really shows solidarity: everything you donate reaches the community.

Why the subjunctive? A purpose is something you want to happen, not a fact: when you donate, the children don't have the supplies *yet*. That is the same "not real yet" idea you met with *querer que* in lesson 01, and it's why *para que* takes the subjunctive every time, never the indicative.

Notice that English often hides the change of subject behind "for … to": *I brought chairs for the volunteers to sit on* → *Traje sillas para que los voluntarios se sienten.* Spanish needs the full clause.

### The past: one sentence pointing ahead

When the main verb is in the past, *para que* takes a different subjunctive, the imperfect subjunctive, which you'll learn in lessons 13 and 15 (*Donamos ropa para que los niños tuvieran…*). For now, use *para que* with a main verb in the present, the future or a command.

## ¿Para qué? Asking about purpose

*¿Para qué?* asks "what for?", about the purpose. A2's *¿Por qué?* asks "why?", about the cause. The answer to *¿Para qué…?* usually starts with *para*:

- *—¿Para qué es el dinero? —Para reconstruir la escuela.* — "What's the money for?" "To rebuild the school."
- *—¿Para qué necesitan voluntarios? —Para que la escuela abra en enero.* — "What do they need volunteers for?" "So the school can open in January."
- *—¿Por qué donas? —Porque me importa mi comunidad.* — "Why do you donate?" "Because I care about my community."

## sin + infinitive or sin que + subjunctive

*sin* (without) works the same way. With the same subject, use the infinitive; with a different subject, *sin que* + subjunctive:

- *Los voluntarios trabajan sin descansar.* — The volunteers work without resting. (They work, they don't rest.)
- *Ayudo a mi vecina sin que me lo pida.* — I help my neighbor without her asking me.
- *No firmes nada sin leerlo.* — Don't sign anything without reading it.
- *No firmes nada sin que yo lo lea.* — Don't sign anything without me reading it.

Like *para que*, *sin que* always takes the subjunctive: what didn't happen isn't a fact. You'll also see it in the past (*Salió sin que nadie lo viera* — He left without anybody seeing him); that form waits for lesson 15, but you can already recognize it.

## Two more ways to express purpose

- *a fin de que* + subjunctive means the same as *para que* but belongs to formal writing: notices, reports, letters. *Le pedimos que llegue temprano a fin de que podamos empezar a tiempo.* — We ask you to arrive early so that we can start on time. Recognize it; in speech, say *para que*. (*a fin de* + infinitive is the formal *para* + infinitive.)
- **A command + *que* + subjunctive.** In conversation, *que* alone can mean "so that" after a command: *Ven, que te explique cómo funciona.* — Come here, so I can explain how it works. *Acércate, que te vean.* — Come closer, so they can see you. Recognize this; it's informal and very common.

## Reading: a campaign poster

![A poster with a pink header: CAMPAÑA «MANOS QUE AYUDAN». Reconstruyamos juntos la escuela de San Isidro. Under a heart: Las lluvias de octubre dañaron la escuela. In bold: Necesitamos voluntarios para que los niños vuelvan a clases en enero. Then: Dona útiles escolares, cobijas y agua. Centro de acopio: Centro Comunitario, Av. Juárez 15. Sábados de 9:00 a 14:00. No necesitas experiencia: te explicamos todo para que puedas ayudar desde el primer día. At the bottom: Organiza: ONG Puentes, with a WhatsApp number.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The poster is invented, but its language is typical. *Dañar* = to damage; *los útiles escolares* = school supplies; *la cobija* = blanket (Mexico; *la manta* in Spain); *el centro de acopio* = collection center, the place where donations are gathered after a disaster in Mexico. Notice the nosotros command in the slogan (*Reconstruyamos*, lesson 05) and the two *para que* clauses. *Volver a clases* = to go back to school (here *volver a* + a place; with an infinitive, A2's *volver a* means "to do again").

## Text: Un sábado en el centro de acopio

Andrés, a university student in Puebla, writes a post for his college's volunteer page.

> Hace un mes, después de las inundaciones, mi amiga Paola me invitó a colaborar con una ONG que apoya a familias damnificadas. Al principio tenía dudas: no sabía si iba a ser útil. Pero me involucré, y hoy quiero contarles cómo es un sábado en el centro de acopio.
>
> Llegamos a las ocho para recibir las donaciones. La gente trae agua, comida, ropa y cobijas, y nosotros lo separamos todo para que los camiones salgan antes de las doce. Nadie trabaja solo: la coordinadora nos organiza en equipos para que cada uno sepa qué hacer. Lo que más me gusta es que la comunidad colabora sin que nadie se lo pida. Una señora de la colonia nos trae tamales todos los sábados, y no acepta ni un peso.
>
> En la tarde vamos al albergue. Ahí ayudamos a los niños con la tarea para que no se atrasen en la escuela, y escuchamos a los papás, que muchas veces solo necesitan hablar. El esfuerzo es grande, pero vale la pena.
>
> Si quieres ayudar, no necesitas experiencia ni dinero. El voluntariado es gratuito y te enseñan todo. Ven un sábado, que te presente al equipo. La solidaridad no es solo dar cosas: es estar.

*A month ago, after the floods, my friend Paola invited me to help out with an NGO that supports families affected by the disaster. At first I had doubts: I didn't know if I was going to be useful. But I got involved, and today I want to tell you what a Saturday at the collection center is like. — We arrive at eight to receive the donations. People bring water, food, clothes and blankets, and we sort it all so that the trucks leave before twelve. Nobody works alone: the coordinator organizes us into teams so that everyone knows what to do. What I like most is that the community helps without anyone asking them. A lady from the neighborhood brings us tamales every Saturday and won't accept a single peso. — In the afternoon we go to the shelter. There we help the children with their homework so they don't fall behind at school, and we listen to the parents, who often just need to talk. The effort is huge, but it's worth it. — If you want to help, you don't need experience or money. Volunteering is free and they teach you everything. Come one Saturday, and I'll introduce you to the team. Solidarity isn't just giving things: it's being there.*

(*la inundación* — flood; *útil* — useful (lesson 08); *valer la pena* — to be worth it; *el equipo* — team; *atrasarse* — to fall behind; *separar* — to sort, to separate; *la colonia* — neighborhood, in Mexico.) Count the purposes: three *para que* clauses with different subjects (*los camiones salgan, cada uno sepa, no se atrasen*), one *para* + infinitive with the same subject (*para recibir*), one *sin que*, and the informal *Ven…, que te presente* at the end.

## Dialogue: La primera vez

Mariana is a new volunteer; Héctor coordinates the shelter.

> Mariana: Buenos días, vengo a ayudar. ¿Qué hago?
>
> Héctor: ¡Bienvenida! Primero ponte este chaleco para que la gente sepa que eres voluntaria.
>
> Mariana: ¿Y para qué es esta lista?
>
> Héctor: Para anotar todo lo que entra. Así nadie se lleva nada sin que lo sepamos.
>
> Mariana: Entendido. ¿Y las cajas de medicinas?
>
> Héctor: Déjalas en la mesa del fondo para que la doctora las revise. No las abras sin guantes.
>
> Mariana: Perfecto. ¿Necesitan algo más?
>
> Héctor: Sí, que vuelvas el sábado. Con gente como tú, vamos a reconstruir todo.

*Mariana: Good morning, I've come to help. What do I do? — Héctor: Welcome! First put on this vest so people know you're a volunteer. — Mariana: And what's this list for? — Héctor: To write down everything that comes in. That way nobody takes anything without us knowing. — Mariana: Got it. And the boxes of medicine? — Héctor: Leave them on the table at the back so the doctor can check them. Don't open them without gloves. — Mariana: Perfect. Do you need anything else? — Héctor: Yes, for you to come back on Saturday. With people like you, we're going to rebuild everything.*

(*el chaleco* — vest; *los guantes* — gloves.)

## Pronunciation

- *para que* is said as one unit, with the stress on *pa-*: PA-ra-ke. Don't stress *que*.
- *¿Para qué?* is different: *qué* has an accent and carries stress: pa-ra-KÉ.
- *ONG* is spelled out: o-e-ne-JE (o, ene, ge). *recaudar*: re-kau-DAR, with *au* as one syllable.
- *damnificado*: dam-ni-fi-KA-do; say the *m* clearly before *n*.

## Common mistakes

- *para que* + indicative: ~~para que los niños tienen útiles~~ → *para que los niños tengan útiles.*
- *para que* + infinitive: ~~para que entender~~ → *para entender* (same subject) or *para que entiendas* (different subject).
- A different subject with *para* + infinitive: ~~Te lo explico para entender~~ (that means "so I understand") → *para que lo entiendas.*
- Translating "for … to" word for word: ~~para los niños tener útiles~~ → *para que los niños tengan útiles.*
- Mixing up *¿Para qué?* (what for?) and *¿Por qué?* (why?).
- *sin que* + indicative: ~~sin que nadie lo sabe~~ → *sin que nadie lo sepa.*

## Key points

- Same subject: *para / sin* + infinitive. Different subject: *para que / sin que* + subjunctive.
- *para que* and *sin que* always take the subjunctive: a purpose or something that doesn't happen isn't a fact.
- *¿Para qué?* asks about purpose; answer with *para* + infinitive or *para que* + subjunctive.
- *a fin de que* = formal *para que*; *Ven, que te explique* = informal purpose after a command (recognition).
- After a past main verb, these clauses take the imperfect subjunctive (lessons 13 and 15).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: When I get there: cuando + subjunctive and time clauses
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You've used *cuando* since A1: *Cuando era niña, vivía en Puebla* (When I was a girl, I lived in Puebla). Every time, it was about something real: a habit or a past event. But when you talk about the future, "when" points at something that hasn't happened yet, and Spanish marks that with the subjunctive: *Cuando llegue, te escribo* (When I get there, I'll write to you). This lesson teaches that contrast with *cuando* and the other time words (*en cuanto, tan pronto como, hasta que, después de que, mientras*), and the one that always takes the subjunctive: *antes de que*. These are **[[time clauses]]**, a kind of adverbial clause like the purpose clauses of lesson 06. The theme is moving abroad: emigrating, settling in somewhere new and the paperwork in between.

## cuando: three times, two moods

Look at where the action of the *cuando* clause sits in time:

![A timeline with a dashed line marked HOY. On the left, one dot: PASADO, indicativo: Cuando llegué, te escribí (When I arrived, I wrote to you). In the middle, a row of small dots around today: COSTUMBRE, indicativo: Cuando llego, siempre te escribo (I always write when I arrive). On the right, one yellow dot: FUTURO, subjuntivo: Cuando llegue, te escribo / escribiré (When I arrive, I'll write to you).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- Past (it happened): indicative. *Cuando llegué a Monterrey, no conocía a nadie.* — When I arrived in Monterrey, I didn't know anyone.
- Habit (it happens regularly): indicative. *Cuando voy a mi pueblo, siempre visito a mi abuela.* — When(ever) I go to my hometown, I always visit my grandmother.
- Future (it hasn't happened yet): subjunctive. *Cuando vaya a mi pueblo, voy a visitar a mi abuela.* — When I go to my hometown, I'm going to visit my grandmother.

The main clause can be in the present, the future, *ir a* + infinitive or a command; the *cuando* clause stays subjunctive:

- *Cuando tenga la residencia, busco trabajo.* — When I have my residence permit, I'll look for a job.
- *Cuando tenga la residencia, buscaré trabajo.*
- *Cuando tenga la residencia, voy a buscar trabajo.*
- *Cuando tengas la residencia, búscate un trabajo.* — When you have your residence permit, find yourself a job.

English says "when I *have*", not "when I will have". Spanish doesn't use the future there either (~~Cuando tendré la residencia~~): it uses the subjunctive.

Even with the same subject in both halves, *cuando* takes a conjugated verb: *Cuando (yo) llegue, (yo) te llamo.* There's no infinitive version of *cuando* for this.

## The same contrast with other time words

| Connector | Future: subjunctive | Habit or past: indicative |
|---|---|---|
| *en cuanto* (as soon as) | *En cuanto llegue, te mando un mensaje.* | *En cuanto llego, te mando un mensaje.* / *En cuanto llegué, te mandé un mensaje.* |
| *tan pronto como* (as soon as) | *Tan pronto como tengas la visa, compra el boleto.* | *Tan pronto como tuvo la visa, compró el boleto.* |
| *hasta que* (until) | *No me voy hasta que termines.* | *No me fui hasta que terminaste.* |
| *después de que* (after) | *Después de que se vayan los invitados, limpiamos.* | *Después de que se fueron los invitados, limpiamos.* |
| *mientras* (while) | *Mientras estés en Canadá, llámame los domingos.* | *Mientras estuvo en Canadá, me llamaba los domingos.* |

*Tan pronto como* is a little more formal than *en cuanto*. *Mientras* + subjunctive can also mean "as long as" (*Mientras pagues a tiempo…*), a use you'll study in lesson 18.

A note on *después de que* in the past: standard Spanish uses the indicative (*Después de que se fueron…*), because it's a fact. You may see the imperfect subjunctive after it in newspapers (*después de que se fueran*); that is a journalistic habit. Recognize it, but write the indicative.

## antes de que: always the subjunctive

*antes de que* (before) is different: it always takes the subjunctive, even about the past, because at the moment of the main action, the "before" event hadn't happened yet.

- *Despídete de tu abuela antes de que nos vayamos.* — Say goodbye to your grandmother before we leave.
- *Quiero empacar antes de que lleguen mis papás.* — I want to pack before my parents arrive.

In the past it takes the imperfect subjunctive (*antes de que llegaran*), which comes in lesson 15.

## Same subject: the infinitive

With *antes de, después de* and *hasta*, Spanish prefers the infinitive when the subject is the same, just as with *para* in lesson 06:

- *Voy a empacar antes de salir.* — I'm going to pack before I leave. (I pack, I leave.)
- *Voy a empacar antes de que salgas.* — I'm going to pack before you leave.
- *Después de instalarme, voy a buscar una escuela de idiomas.* — After I settle in, I'm going to look for a language school.
- *Trabajé hasta terminar.* — I worked until I finished.

## Questions with cuándo take the indicative

A question with *¿cuándo?* asks for information; it doesn't take the subjunctive. Use the present, *ir a* or the future:

- *¿Cuándo llegas?* / *¿Cuándo vas a llegar?* / *¿Cuándo llegarás?* — When are you arriving?
- *No sé cuándo me dan la residencia.* — I don't know when they'll give me my residence permit. (an indirect question: also indicative)

Only *cuando* without an accent, joining two clauses, takes the subjunctive for the future.

## Which mood? A quick check

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing the mood after cuando and other time words
  accDescr: First, if the word is antes de que, use the subjunctive. Otherwise, if it is a question with cuándo, use the indicative or the future. Otherwise, ask whether the action has happened or happens regularly. If it is a past event or a habit, use the indicative. If it is still in the future, use the subjunctive.
  A["Time word + clause"] --> B{"Is it antes de que?"}
  B -- yes --> S1["Subjunctive: antes de que llegues"]
  B -- no --> C{"Is it a question with cuándo?"}
  C -- yes --> I1["Indicative or future: ¿Cuándo llegas?"]
  C -- no --> D{"Past, habit, or future?"}
  D -- "past or habit" --> I2["Indicative: cuando llegué / cuando llego"]
  D -- future --> S2["Subjunctive: cuando llegue"]
```

## Text: A new stage in Querétaro

Kevin, from Texas, has just moved to Querétaro for work. He writes to Laura, a Mexican friend who emigrated to Houston years ago.

> Querida Laura:
>
> ¡Por fin di el paso! Llevo dos semanas en Querétaro y todavía estoy instalándome. Fue la decisión más difícil de mi vida, pero no me arrepiento.
>
> Te cuento cómo fue el trámite, por si alguien te pregunta. Primero pedí la visa de residente temporal en el consulado de México en Dallas. Cuando la tuve, empaqué mis cosas y crucé la frontera. Al llegar, pasé por migración, y ahora tengo un plazo de treinta días para cambiar la visa por la tarjeta de residente en una oficina del Instituto Nacional de Migración. En cuanto tenga la tarjeta, voy a pedir el permiso de trabajo; mi empresa me ayuda con todo.
>
> El choque cultural es más pequeño de lo que pensaba, pero existe. Aquí la gente come tarde y casi nadie llega a las fiestas a la hora de la invitación. Mis compañeros dicen que me voy a integrar rápido, siempre y cuando aprenda a decir "ahorita" como ellos.
>
> ¿Y tú? ¿Todavía sientes nostalgia cuando escuchas mariachi? Cuando vengas a México en diciembre, ven a verme. Te prometo unas enchiladas queretanas. Y no te vayas sin que te presente a mis vecinos: son los mejores.
>
> Un abrazo,
> Kevin

*Dear Laura: I finally took the plunge! I've been in Querétaro for two weeks and I'm still settling in. It was the hardest decision of my life, but I don't regret it. — Let me tell you how the paperwork went, in case anyone asks you. First I applied for the temporary resident visa at the Mexican consulate in Dallas. When I had it, I packed my things and crossed the border. When I arrived, I went through immigration, and now I have a thirty-day deadline to exchange the visa for the resident card at an office of the National Migration Institute. As soon as I have the card, I'm going to apply for the work permit; my company is helping me with everything. — The culture shock is smaller than I thought, but it's real. Here people eat late and hardly anyone arrives at parties at the time on the invitation. My coworkers say I'll fit in fast, as long as I learn to say "ahorita" like they do. — And you? Do you still feel homesick when you hear mariachi? When you come to Mexico in December, come and see me. I promise you some enchiladas queretanas. And don't leave without me introducing you to my neighbors: they're the best. — Hugs, Kevin*

(*llevar* + time — to have been somewhere for; *arrepentirse* — to regret, lesson 11; *el trámite* — paperwork, an official procedure; *por si* — in case; *siempre y cuando* + subjunctive — as long as, lesson 18; *ahorita* — in a moment, or right now, in Mexico.) Find the past *cuando* (*Cuando la tuve*), the habit (*cuando escuchas*) and the futures (*En cuanto tenga, Cuando vengas*).

The procedure in the text follows the Mexican government's consular information as of November 2026: a temporary resident visa is issued by a Mexican consulate, and within 30 calendar days of entering Mexico the holder must apply to the Instituto Nacional de Migración (INM) for the resident card; temporary residence covers stays of more than 180 days and up to four years. Rules change, so anyone actually moving should check the consulate's current page.

## Dialogue: Antes de que te vayas

Sofía is moving from Guadalajara to Toronto to work as a nurse. Her mom helps her pack.

> Mamá: ¿Ya empacaste los papeles de la embajada?
>
> Sofía: Sí, todo está en esta carpeta. No la abras, que está muy bien organizada.
>
> Mamá: Ay, hija. ¿Y cuándo vas a regresar?
>
> Sofía: No sé, mamá. Primero quiero establecerme. Cuando tenga un departamento y un poco de dinero, te compro un boleto para que vengas.
>
> Mamá: Mientras estés allá, cuídate mucho. Y llámame en cuanto aterrice el avión.
>
> Sofía: Te lo prometo. Antes de que me vaya, ¿me haces tus chilaquiles?
>
> Mamá: Claro. Pero no llores, que si lloras tú, lloro yo.
>
> Sofía: Es una etapa nueva, mamá. Tantos emigrantes lo han hecho antes. Hasta que me acostumbre, voy a extrañar todo.
>
> Mamá: Y nosotros a ti. Ándale, termina de empacar antes de que llegue tu tía.

*Mom: Did you pack the papers from the embassy? — Sofía: Yes, it's all in this folder. Don't open it, it's very well organized. — Mom: Oh, sweetheart. And when are you going to come back? — Sofía: I don't know, Mom. First I want to settle down. When I have an apartment and a little money, I'll buy you a ticket so you can come. — Mom: While you're there, take good care of yourself. And call me as soon as the plane lands. — Sofía: I promise. Before I leave, will you make me your chilaquiles? — Mom: Of course. But don't cry, because if you cry, I'll cry. — Sofía: It's a new stage, Mom. So many emigrants have done it before. Until I get used to it, I'm going to miss everything. — Mom: And we'll miss you. Come on, finish packing before your aunt arrives.*

(*la carpeta* — folder; *aterrizar* — to land; *¡Ándale!* — come on, in Mexico.)

## Emigrar or inmigrar?

You *emigras* from your country and *inmigras* to a new one: the same person is *un emigrante* for Guadalajara and *un inmigrante* for Toronto. *La migración* covers both, and in Mexico it also names the immigration desk at an airport or border (*pasar por migración*). People planning to move talk about *planear la mudanza*, the *plazo* for each paperwork step and the moment you finally *das el paso*.

## Pronunciation

- *en cuanto*: link the words: en-KWAN-to. *tan pronto como*: tan-PRON-to-KO-mo.
- *emigrar* (e-mi-GRAR) and *inmigrar* (in-mi-GRAR): the only difference is the first syllable, so say it clearly.
- *consulado*: kon-su-LA-do; *embajada*: em-ba-HA-da, with *j* like a strong English h.

## Common mistakes

- The future after *cuando*: ~~Cuando llegaré, te llamo~~ → *Cuando llegue, te llamo.*
- The subjunctive for a past event: ~~Cuando llegue a México, conocí a Laura~~ → *Cuando llegué a México, conocí a Laura.*
- The subjunctive in a question: ~~¿Cuándo llegues?~~ → *¿Cuándo llegas?*
- The indicative after *antes de que*: ~~antes de que se van~~ → *antes de que se vayan.*
- *antes de que* with the same subject: ~~Empaco antes de que salga~~ (if it's you who leaves) → *Empaco antes de salir.*

## Key points

- *cuando, en cuanto, tan pronto como, hasta que, después de que, mientras*: subjunctive for the future (*cuando llegue*), indicative for habits and the past (*cuando llego, cuando llegué*).
- Never the future after *cuando* in a time clause.
- *antes de que* always takes the subjunctive.
- Same subject: *antes de / después de / hasta* + infinitive.
- *¿Cuándo…?* questions (direct and indirect) take the indicative or the future.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: I'm looking for one that…: the subjunctive in relative clauses
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In A2 (lesson 18) you joined sentences with *que, donde, quien* and *lo que*: *Tengo un celular que tiene buena cámara* (I have a phone that has a good camera). The part after *que* is a **[[relative clause]]**: it describes a noun, the way an adjective does. Until now, every relative clause described something real. But when you shop, you often describe something you're looking for and haven't found yet, something that may not even exist: *Busco un celular que tenga buena cámara* (I'm looking for a phone that has a good camera). That relative clause takes the subjunctive. This lesson shows when, and adds *lo que, el que, donde* and *como* + subjunctive for "whatever, whoever, wherever, however". The theme is shopping online: products, materials, reviews and returns.

## Known or unknown? The antecedent decides

The noun that a relative clause describes is its **[[antecedent]]** (*un celular* in the examples above). The question is always about the antecedent:

- Known and real (you have it, you've seen it, it exists): indicative.
- Wanted, unknown, or nonexistent (you're looking for one, you don't know if there is one, there isn't one): subjunctive.

| Known, real: indicative | Wanted, unknown or nonexistent: subjunctive |
|---|---|
| *Tengo una licuadora que hace mucho ruido.* — I have a blender that makes a lot of noise. | *Quiero una licuadora que no haga ruido.* — I want a blender that doesn't make noise. |
| *Compré unas botas que son impermeables.* — I bought some boots that are waterproof. | *Necesito unas botas que sean impermeables.* — I need some boots that are waterproof. |
| *Hay una tienda en línea que vende muebles de madera.* — There's an online store that sells wooden furniture. | *¿Hay alguna tienda en línea que venda muebles de madera?* — Is there an online store that sells wooden furniture? |
| *Hay algo aquí que me gusta.* — There's something here I like. | *No hay nada que me guste.* — There's nothing I like. |

The same sentence can go either way, depending on what you mean. *Busco la mochila que es resistente al agua* (indicative): you know which one, maybe you saw it yesterday. *Busco una mochila que sea resistente al agua* (subjunctive): any backpack, as long as it's water-resistant. Both are correct; they say different things. Clues: *un, algún, ningún, nadie, nada* and *buscar, querer, necesitar* usually point to an unknown antecedent; *el, este, mi* to a known one.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Indicative or subjunctive in a relative clause
  accDescr: Start with the noun that the relative clause describes, the antecedent. If it exists and the speaker knows it or has it, use the indicative, as in Tengo una licuadora que hace ruido. If the speaker is looking for one, asking whether one exists, or saying there is none, use the subjunctive, as in Busco una licuadora que no haga ruido, Hay alguna que no haga ruido?, and No hay ninguna que no haga ruido.
  A["The noun the clause describes: the antecedent"] --> B{"Does it exist, and do I know it or have it?"}
  B -- "yes" --> C["Indicative: Tengo una licuadora que hace ruido."]
  B -- "I'm looking for one" --> D["Subjunctive: Busco una licuadora que no haga ruido."]
  B -- "I'm asking if one exists" --> E["Subjunctive: ¿Hay alguna que no haga ruido?"]
  B -- "there isn't one" --> F["Subjunctive: No hay ninguna que no haga ruido."]
```

## The personal a with an unknown person

You learned in A1 that a person as a direct object takes *a*: *Veo a Lupita.* With an unknown, unspecified person, the *a* is usually dropped: you're not thinking of anyone in particular.

- *Busco un técnico que sepa arreglar aparatos.* — I'm looking for a technician who knows how to fix appliances. (any technician)
- *Busco al técnico que arregló mi licuadora.* — I'm looking for the technician who fixed my blender. (a specific person: *a + el = al*)

But *alguien* and *nadie* always keep the *a* as objects, even though the person is unknown: *¿Conoces a alguien que hable japonés? No conozco a nadie que lo hable.* You'll also hear *Busco a un técnico que…* with the *a*; it isn't an error, and the point to learn here is the mood.

## lo que, el que: "whatever", "whoever", "any one that"

*lo que* means "what" or "the thing that". With the indicative, it refers to something definite; with the subjunctive, it means "whatever":

- *Hago lo que me dices.* — I do what you tell me. (you've told me)
- *Haz lo que quieras.* — Do whatever you want.
- *Compra lo que necesitas.* — Buy what you need. (we know what it is: the list is on the table)
- *Compra lo que necesites.* — Buy whatever you need.

*el que, la que, los que, las que* work the same way, for people or things:

- *El que llegue primero escoge el asiento.* — Whoever arrives first chooses the seat.
- *Llévate la que te guste.* — Take whichever one you like.
- *Llévate la que te gusta.* — Take the one you like. (I know which one: the red one)

And *donde, como, cuando* + *quieras* (or another subjunctive) are very common: *Siéntate donde quieras* (Sit wherever you like), *Hazlo como quieras* (Do it however you want), *Ven cuando puedas* (Come whenever you can).

## Prepositions with relatives

When the relative clause needs a preposition (*with, in, for*), Spanish puts it before the relative word, never at the end like English: *el amigo con el que hablé* (the friend I talked with). Use *el que, la que, los que, las que*, agreeing with the antecedent; *quien* (A2) also works for people. These **[[relative pronouns]]** combine with the subjunctive too:

- *Esta es la tienda en la que compré mi computadora.* — This is the store where (in which) I bought my computer.
- *Busco una tienda en la que pueda pagar en efectivo.* — I'm looking for a store where I can pay in cash.
- *Es el modelo con el que tuve problemas.* — It's the model I had problems with.
- *Necesito una mesa en la que quepan seis personas.* — I need a table that six people can fit at. (*caber* = to fit; *quepan* is its subjunctive)

In formal writing you'll see *el cual, la cual, los cuales, las cuales* instead of *el que* after a preposition or a comma: *La empresa, la cual tiene tiendas en todo el país, ofrece envío gratis.* — The company, which has stores all over the country, offers free shipping. In speech, *el que* or *que* is normal.

## Reading a product page

![An online store page for an invented blender, the Licuadora Remolino 600, model LR-600. It shows a picture of the blender, four of five stars from 128 ratings, the price 1,299 MXN, a green box headed Características (glass jar of 1.5 liters, 600 W motor with 3 speeds, stainless steel blades), a box headed Tamaño (20 × 18 × 40 cm), a box headed Envío gratis (arrives Thursday the 19th), a button Agregar al carrito, and a section Reseñas de clientes with a four-star review by Lupita R.: Muy práctica y fácil de lavar. Busco una que haga menos ruido, pero por este precio está bien.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The store and brand are invented. *Las características* are the features; *el vaso* here is the blender's jar; *las cuchillas de acero inoxidable* are stainless-steel blades. *Agregar al carrito* = add to cart. In Lupita's review, *Busco una que haga menos ruido* is subjunctive: she hasn't found one.

## Text: Tres reseñas

Three customers review the same wireless headphones on an online store.

> ★★★★★ Daniela M.: Llevaba meses buscando unos audífonos inalámbricos que fueran ligeros y que no costaran una fortuna, y por fin los encontré. Son muy cómodos, el sonido es de buena calidad y el envío llegó en dos días. El repartidor fue muy amable. Los recomiendo a cualquiera que haga ejercicio.
>
> ★★☆☆☆ Jorge R.: El producto no es malo, pero el material es muy delgado: parece plástico barato. Yo busco algo duradero, que aguante el uso diario. A la semana se rompió el estuche. Pedí un reembolso y me lo dieron sin problemas, eso sí.
>
> ★★★★☆ Ana L.: Prácticos y útiles para el home office. Lo único: no hay ningún modelo que tenga cable de repuesto, así que si lo pierdes, tienes que comprar uno nuevo. Si buscas unos audífonos que te duren años, mejor invierte un poco más.

*Daniela M.: I'd been looking for months for wireless headphones that were light and didn't cost a fortune, and I finally found them. They're very comfortable, the sound is good quality and the shipment arrived in two days. The delivery person was very friendly. I recommend them to anyone who works out. — Jorge R.: The product isn't bad, but the material is very thin: it looks like cheap plastic. I'm looking for something long-lasting, that can stand daily use. After a week the case broke. I asked for a refund and they gave it to me without any problems, I'll say that. — Ana L.: Handy and useful for working from home. The only thing: there's no model that comes with a spare cable, so if you lose it, you have to buy a new one. If you're looking for headphones that will last you years, you'd better spend a bit more.*

(*los audífonos* — headphones; *una fortuna* — a fortune; *delgado* — thin; *el estuche* — case; *de repuesto* — spare; *aguantar* — to stand, to put up with, lesson 03; *el home office* — working from home, lesson 15; *invertir* — to invest, lesson 14.) *fueran* and *costaran* are imperfect subjunctive forms (lesson 13): after a past verb (*Llevaba meses buscando*), the subjunctive moves into the past. You only need to recognize them here. Find the present subjunctives: *cualquiera que haga ejercicio, algo… que aguante, ningún modelo que tenga, unos audífonos que te duren*.

## Dialogue: La licuadora nueva

Rosa and her husband Martín are shopping online on the couch.

> Rosa: Necesitamos una licuadora nueva. La vieja ya no sirve.
>
> Martín: A ver… ¿Cómo la quieres?
>
> Rosa: Quiero una que tenga vaso de vidrio, no de plástico, y que sea fácil de lavar.
>
> Martín: Esta tiene vaso de vidrio y cuesta mil doscientos noventa y nueve pesos. ¿Qué dicen las reseñas?
>
> Rosa: Que es muy práctica, pero hace mucho ruido. ¿No hay ninguna que sea más silenciosa?
>
> Martín: Hay una de metal que dice "motor silencioso", pero no la venden en ninguna tienda que haga envíos a Mérida.
>
> Rosa: Ay, qué mala suerte. Bueno, pide la de vidrio. Lo que cueste el envío, lo pago yo.
>
> Martín: El envío es gratis. Llega el jueves. ¿A qué hora quieres que venga el repartidor?
>
> Rosa: Cuando sea, mientras alguien esté en la casa. Y fíjate bien en el tamaño: no quiero un aparato que no quepa en el mueble.

*Rosa: We need a new blender. The old one doesn't work anymore. — Martín: Let's see… What kind do you want? — Rosa: I want one that has a glass jar, not plastic, and that's easy to wash. — Martín: This one has a glass jar and costs 1,299 pesos. What do the reviews say? — Rosa: That it's very practical, but it makes a lot of noise. Isn't there one that's quieter? — Martín: There's a metal one that says "quiet motor", but they don't sell it in any store that ships to Mérida. — Rosa: Oh, what bad luck. OK, order the glass one. Whatever the shipping costs, I'll pay it. — Martín: Shipping is free. It arrives Thursday. What time do you want the delivery person to come? — Rosa: Whenever, as long as someone's home. And check the size carefully: I don't want an appliance that doesn't fit in the cabinet.*

(*servir* — here, to work, to be usable; *silencioso* — quiet; *el mueble* — piece of furniture, here a cabinet; *cuando sea* — whenever, any time; honors 08h2 does more of these.) Other materials you'll see in product descriptions: *de madera* (wooden), *de cuero* (leather), *de tela* (fabric), *de metal*, *de vidrio*; and *el pedido* is the order you place.

## Pronunciation

- *haga, tenga, sea*: the subjunctive ending is unstressed: HA-ga, TEN-ga, SE-a.
- *inalámbrico*: i-na-LAM-bri-ko, stressed on the third syllable from the end (hence the accent).
- *reembolso*: re-em-BOL-so; the two e's are pronounced separately in careful speech, often blended in fast speech.

## Common mistakes

- Indicative for something you're looking for: ~~Busco un departamento que tiene terraza~~ (if you haven't found it) → *Busco un departamento que tenga terraza.*
- Subjunctive for something you have: ~~Tengo un celular que tenga buena cámara~~ → *Tengo un celular que tiene buena cámara.*
- After *no hay nada / nadie / ningún*: ~~No hay nada que me gusta~~ → *No hay nada que me guste.*
- Dropping the *a* before *alguien / nadie*: ~~No conozco nadie que…~~ → *No conozco a nadie que…*
- A preposition at the end, English style: ~~el amigo que hablé con~~ → *el amigo con el que hablé.*

## Key points

- Relative clause + indicative when the antecedent is known and real; + subjunctive when it's wanted, unknown or nonexistent.
- Typical subjunctive triggers: *busco / quiero / necesito un…, ¿hay algún…?, no hay ningún / nada / nadie que…*
- The personal *a* usually drops before an unspecified person (*Busco un técnico que…*) but stays with *alguien, nadie*.
- *lo que, el que* + subjunctive = whatever, whoever, any one that; *donde / como / cuando quieras*.
- Prepositions go before the relative: *en la que, con el que*; *el cual* is formal.

lessons.title: Honors: Ready for the earthquake: Mexico's drills and seismic alert
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Most people who live in central or southern Mexico know two sounds: the wail of the *alerta sísmica* and the question that follows, *¿Está temblando?* Earthquake safety is one of the places where Mexican Spanish is full of the grammar of this module: commands (*No corras, no grites, no empujes*), purpose (*para que todos salgan a tiempo*) and time clauses (*cuando suene la alerta*). This lesson reads and writes that kind of language, and tells the story behind it: the earthquakes of 19 September, the seismic alert system and the national drills.

This lesson is language practice, not safety training. The advice quoted here comes from Mexico City's civil protection guide, summarized in my own words; for real preparation, follow the official guidance where you live (in Mexico, your state's Protección Civil and the Coordinación Nacional de Protección Civil).

## Sismo, temblor, terremoto

Three words for one event, used differently:

- *el temblor* is the everyday word, for any earthquake, big or small: *¿Sentiste el temblor de anoche?* The verb is *temblar* (e → ie): *¡Está temblando!* (It's shaking!)
- *el sismo* is the word of the news and of official texts: *un sismo de magnitud 7.1*. The national seismological service is the *Servicio Sismológico Nacional* (SSN), run by the UNAM.
- *el terremoto* (A2) is usually kept for a strong, destructive one.

After a big *sismo* come *las réplicas* (aftershocks). If a building is badly damaged it can *derrumbarse* (collapse), leaving *escombros* (rubble), where rescue teams search for survivors. In Mexico many of those rescuers are volunteers: *los brigadistas*, a word also used for the members of a school's or an office's emergency team.

## Three earthquakes on the same date

Mexico has had three major earthquakes on 19 September:

| Year | Time | Magnitude | Epicenter | What happened |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1985 | 7:17 a.m. | 8.1 | Off the coast of Michoacán | Severe damage in Mexico City; the official figure was about 6,000 dead, though the true number was never known precisely. |
| 2017 | 1:14 p.m. | 7.1 | Near Axochiapan, Morelos (Puebla–Morelos border), 57 km deep | Buildings collapsed in Mexico City, Morelos and Puebla; Expansión's state-by-state figures add up to about 370 deaths, most of them in Mexico City. |
| 2022 | about 1:05 p.m. | 7.7 | Off Coalcomán, Michoacán | The federal government confirmed two deaths. |

The 2017 earthquake struck on the 32nd anniversary of 1985. The SSN's head said at the time that the date was only a coincidence: earthquakes can't be predicted, and nothing about 19 September makes them more likely.

## The seismic alert: how a few seconds are won

After 1985, the Mexico City government and the Centro de Instrumentación y Registro Sísmico (CIRES), a nonprofit, developed an early-warning system. It has worked for Mexico City since 1991, and on 14 September 1995, for a magnitude 7.3 quake in Guerrero, it gave what Expansión calls the world's first public early earthquake alert. Today the Sistema de Alerta Sísmica Mexicano (SASMEX) has sensors along the Pacific coast (96 of them since 2012, according to Expansión).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How the seismic alert works
  accDescr: An earthquake begins near the Pacific coast. Sensors near the epicenter detect it, and at least two stations must agree on an estimate. If the estimate is strong enough, a radio signal goes to the city, which is far away. Loudspeakers and phones sound the alert. Because the radio signal is much faster than the seismic waves, the shaking arrives tens of seconds later, so people have time to leave or move to a safe place.
  A["Earthquake near the Pacific coast"] --> B["Sensors near the epicenter detect it"]
  B --> C{"Do two stations agree it is strong enough?"}
  C -- no --> N["No alert"]
  C -- yes --> D["A radio signal reaches the city in an instant"]
  D --> E["Loudspeakers and phones sound: alerta sísmica"]
  E --> F["Tens of seconds later, the shaking arrives"]
```

The trick is speed: a radio signal travels almost instantly, while seismic waves take time to cross the hundreds of kilometers between the coast and the capital. That's why the alert gives tens of seconds of warning for a quake on the coast, and little or none for one that starts close to the city or outside the sensor network. *A veces tiembla y no suena la alerta*: it doesn't mean the system failed.

The national drills now also test alerts sent straight to cell phones: for the drill of 19 September 2026, at 12:00, the test message was to reach more than 80 million phones, according to the head of the Coordinación Nacional de Protección Civil.

## The national drill

*Un simulacro* is a drill: everyone practices leaving buildings as if there were a real earthquake. The Simulacro Nacional is held across the country; in 2026 there were two, on 6 May (11:00) and 19 September (12:00). Each drill has a *hipótesis* (scenario), for example a magnitude 7.7 earthquake with its epicenter near Tehuacán, Puebla, for central Mexico in September 2026. Offices and schools *evacúan* their buildings, walk to *la zona de seguridad* and count their people.

![A floor plan of an invented primary school, ground floor. Three classrooms and a staircase along the top, an office, a library and bathrooms along the bottom, and a hallway between them with green arrows pointing right: la ruta de evacuación. A yellow backpack by the door of classroom 1 is labeled la mochila de emergencia; the staircase is labeled las escaleras; a green door at the end of the hallway is labeled la salida de emergencia. A dashed path leads outside to a green schoolyard with a round sign of four arrows pointing to a dot: la zona de seguridad.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*La ruta de evacuación* is the evacuation route; *la salida de emergencia* the emergency exit; the sign with four arrows pointing to the middle marks *la zona de seguridad* or *punto de reunión* (meeting point). Every family is encouraged to keep *una mochila de emergencia*, which Mexico City's guide calls *la maleta de vida*.

## The language of the instructions

Official guides mix three forms, and you can now read and write all of them. Mexico City's civil protection guide, for example, uses *tú* commands throughout; posters in offices often use the infinitive or *usted*.

| Infinitive (posters, lists) | tú | usted / ustedes | nosotros |
|---|---|---|---|
| *No correr.* | *No corras.* | *No corra. / No corran.* | *No corramos.* |
| *Mantener la calma.* | *Mantén la calma.* | *Mantenga la calma. / Mantengan…* | *Mantengamos la calma.* |
| *No usar el elevador.* | *No uses el elevador.* | *No use el elevador. / No usen…* | *No usemos el elevador.* |
| *Alejarse de las ventanas.* | *Aléjate de las ventanas.* | *Aléjese… / Aléjense…* | *Alejémonos…* |

(*mantener la calma* — to stay calm; *alejarse de* — to move away from.) The famous three rules for leaving a building are *no correr, no gritar, no empujar*; the Mexico City guide writes them as *No corras, no grites y no empujes*. Many explanations add a purpose with *para que*: *No empujes, para que nadie se caiga* (Don't push, so nobody falls).

### Example 1: Turning a poster into spoken instructions

A poster in an office says:

> EN CASO DE SISMO: Mantener la calma. No usar el elevador. Dirigirse a la zona de seguridad. No regresar al edificio sin autorización.

You're the floor's *brigadista* and want to say it aloud to your coworkers (*ustedes*), and then, as one of the group, encourage them (*nosotros*).

- *ustedes*: *Mantengan la calma. No usen el elevador. Diríjanse a la zona de seguridad. No regresen al edificio sin autorización.*
- *nosotros*: *Mantengamos la calma. No usemos el elevador. Dirijámonos a la zona de seguridad. No regresemos al edificio sin autorización.*

Points to check: *mantener* is irregular like *tener* (*mantengan*); *dirigirse* (to head for) changes g → j before a (*diríjanse*, with an accent because the pronoun is attached); the nosotros form drops its *-s* before *nos* (*dirijámonos*); in the negative nothing attaches (*no regresemos*).

### Example 2: Explaining the reasons with para que

A teacher explains the rules to a class of ten-year-olds (*ustedes*). Each rule gets a reason with *para que* + subjunctive (a different subject) or *para* + infinitive (the same subject):

- *Caminen en fila para que nadie se pierda.* — Walk in a line so nobody gets lost.
- *No hablen durante la evacuación, para que todos oigan a la brigadista.* — Don't talk during the evacuation, so everyone can hear the rescue volunteer.
- *Cuando suene la alerta, dejen las mochilas para salir más rápido.* — When the alert sounds, leave your backpacks to get out faster. (*ustedes* leave, *ustedes* get out: *para* + infinitive)
- *Revisamos la mochila de emergencia cada seis meses para que la comida no caduque.* — We check the emergency backpack every six months so the food doesn't expire. (*caducar* = to expire)

The *cuando* clause takes the subjunctive too (*cuando suene*), because it is about a future moment (lesson 07).

### Example 3: Reading a news report

> *Sismo de magnitud 6.4 sacude el centro del país*
>
> Un sismo de magnitud 6.4 se sintió esta mañana en la Ciudad de México y en cinco estados. La alerta sísmica sonó unos 50 segundos antes de que llegara el movimiento, y miles de personas evacuaron oficinas y escuelas. Protección Civil informó que no hay edificios derrumbados, aunque algunas bardas se cayeron. Se esperan réplicas en las próximas horas, por lo que las autoridades piden que la población revise sus casas y que no regrese a ningún edificio dañado hasta que lo revisen los especialistas.

*Magnitude 6.4 earthquake shakes central Mexico. A magnitude 6.4 earthquake was felt this morning in Mexico City and in five states. The seismic alert sounded about 50 seconds before the shaking arrived, and thousands of people evacuated offices and schools. Civil Protection reported that no buildings have collapsed, although some walls fell down. Aftershocks are expected in the coming hours, so the authorities are asking people to check their homes and not to go back into any damaged building until specialists have inspected it.*

This report is invented, but it is written the way Mexican news reports are. (*sacudir* — to shake; *la barda* — wall, fence, in Mexico; *por lo que* — so, therefore; *dañado* — damaged.) Grammar to notice: *antes de que llegara* is the past of *antes de que* (imperfect subjunctive, lesson 15); *piden que… revise* and *que no regrese* are influence + subjunctive (lesson 02); *hasta que lo revisen* is a future time clause (lesson 07).

## Before, during and after: a short guide in Spanish

A summary in the style of the official guides (tú), to read aloud:

> Antes. Prepara tu mochila de emergencia con agua, comida que no se eche a perder, una linterna con pilas, un radio, medicinas y copias de tus documentos. Platica con tu familia y decidan dónde se van a reunir.
>
> Durante. Cuando suene la alerta, mantén la calma. Si puedes salir, sal por la ruta de evacuación sin correr, sin gritar y sin empujar. Si estás en un piso alto y no alcanzas a salir, ve a la zona de menor riesgo y aléjate de las ventanas. No uses el elevador ni las escaleras mientras tiembla.
>
> Después. Sigue las indicaciones de los brigadistas. Si tu casa tiene daños, no regreses hasta que la revisen. Usa linternas, no velas, por si hay una fuga de gas, y usa el celular solo para emergencias, para que las líneas no se saturen.

*Before. Pack your emergency backpack with water, food that won't spoil, a flashlight with batteries, a radio, medicine and copies of your documents. Talk with your family and decide where you'll meet. — During. When the alert sounds, stay calm. If you can get out, leave by the evacuation route without running, shouting or pushing. If you're on a high floor and can't get out in time, go to the lowest-risk area and move away from the windows. Don't use the elevator or the stairs while it's shaking. — After. Follow the rescue volunteers' instructions. If your house is damaged, don't go back until it's been inspected. Use flashlights, not candles, in case there's a gas leak, and use your phone only for emergencies, so the lines don't get overloaded.*

(*echarse a perder* — to spoil; *las pilas* — batteries; *platicar* — to talk, in Mexico; *alcanzar a* + infinitive — to manage to, in time; *la vela* — candle; *la fuga* — leak; *saturarse* — to get overloaded.)

## Common mistakes

- Mixing persons on one poster: ~~Mantén la calma y no use el elevador~~ → keep to one: *Mantén la calma y no uses el elevador.*
- An affirmative form after *no* in a hurry: ~~No corre~~ → *No corras* (or *No corra* for usted).
- Using the singular for a building's rubble: *el escombro* exists, but the usual word is plural: *los escombros del edificio*.
- *el sismo* is masculine: ~~la sismo~~. *La alerta sísmica* is feminine.
- Thinking the alert always gives warning: if the earthquake starts near you, there may be no alert at all.

## Key points

- *el temblor* (everyday), *el sismo* (news, official), *el terremoto* (a big one); *las réplicas* follow.
- Mexico's 19 September earthquakes: 1985 (M8.1), 2017 (M7.1), 2022 (M7.7); the date is a coincidence.
- SASMEX, developed by CIRES after 1985, has alerted Mexico City since 1991 and gives tens of seconds of warning for coastal quakes.
- Instructions appear as infinitives (*No correr*), *tú / usted / ustedes* commands (*No corras, No corran*) and nosotros commands (*No corramos*); reasons come with *para que* + subjunctive.
- For real safety advice, use the official guides.
