lessons.title: Honors: Whatever, whenever, whoever: the open-ended subjunctive
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 08 ended with a handful of short phrases: *Haz lo que quieras, Siéntate donde quieras, Ven cuando puedas.* They are among the most useful bits of Spanish you'll ever learn, because English "-ever" words (whatever, whoever, wherever, whenever, however) have no single Spanish equivalent. Spanish builds them from a relative word plus a subjunctive, most often *sea* (from *ser*) or *quieras* (from *querer*). This lesson sorts them out: the everyday ones (*lo que sea, cuando sea, como quieras*), the formal written ones (*quienquiera que, dondequiera que*), the indefinite *cualquier cosa*, and the way Mexicans use some of them in conversation as a shrug or to change the subject.

## Two families: sea and quieras

![A chart titled Cualquier opción: + sea · la opción que tú prefieras: + quieras. Rows for lo que, quien, donde, cuando and como. With sea: lo que sea (whatever, anything), quien sea (whoever, anyone), donde sea (wherever, anywhere), cuando sea (whenever, any time), como sea (any way at all; anyway). With quieras: lo que quieras (whatever you want), quien quieras (whoever you want), donde quieras (wherever you want), cuando quieras (whenever you want), como quieras (however you want). A note at the bottom: Formal, written: quienquiera que / dondequiera que + subjuntivo.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

**With *sea*: any option at all.** *Sea* is the subjunctive of *ser*: *lo que sea* is literally "what it may be". These phrases mean that the choice doesn't matter:

- *Tengo tanta hambre que me como lo que sea.* — I'm so hungry I'll eat anything.
- *Eso lo puede hacer quien sea.* — Anyone can do that.
- *Con este plan tienes internet donde sea.* — With this plan you have internet anywhere.
- *Llámame cuando sea, de día o de noche.* — Call me any time, day or night.
- *Hay que terminarlo hoy como sea.* — We have to finish it today, one way or another.

**With *quieras*: the option you choose.** These hand the choice to the listener, so they're polite and generous. They change with the person: *lo que quieras* (tú), *lo que quiera* (usted), *lo que quieran* (ustedes).

- *Pide lo que quieras, yo invito.* — Order whatever you want, it's on me.
- *Invita a quien quieras.* — Invite whoever you want.
- *—¿Te veo en el centro o en tu casa? —Como quieras.* — "Shall I meet you downtown or at your place?" "Whatever you prefer."

Other verbs fit the same frame: *cuando puedas* (whenever you can), *donde te quede cerca* (wherever is close for you), *lo que necesites* (whatever you need). And *a cualquier hora* means "at any time of day": *En esta farmacia te atienden a cualquier hora.*

### How this differs from lesson 08

In lesson 08 the subjunctive described a noun that was wanted or unknown: *Busco una licuadora que no haga ruido*. Here there's no noun at all: *lo que, quien, donde* contain the "thing", "person" or "place" themselves. The logic is the same, though: the subjunctive marks something open, not yet chosen. And the same contrast with the indicative applies: *Hago lo que quiero* (I do what I want: a fact about me) vs *Haz lo que quieras* (Do whatever you want: open). *Vivo donde nací* (I live where I was born: a real place) vs *Puedes vivir donde quieras* (any place).

## cualquier cosa, cualquiera

A2 taught *cualquier* before a noun (*cualquier día, cualquier persona*: any day, any person) and *cualquiera* on its own (*—¿Qué lámpara quieres? —Cualquiera.*). Two points to add:

- *cualquier cosa* = anything (at all): *No le regales cualquier cosa; piensa en algo especial.* — Don't give her just anything; think of something special.
- *cualquiera* (with *-a*, as a pronoun) = anyone, any one: *Cualquiera puede aprender a cocinar.* — Anyone can learn to cook. *¿Cuál quieres? —Cualquiera.* — "Which one do you want?" "Any one." Before a noun it loses the *-a*: never ~~cualquiera cosa~~.

In everyday Mexican conversation, and in many other countries, *cualquier cosa* also opens a short offer of help at the end of a conversation: *Cualquier cosa, me avisas* — If anything comes up, let me know. (It's a fixed formula: the full idea would be *Si necesitas cualquier cosa, avísame*.)

## The formal words: quienquiera que, dondequiera que

Formal writing has one-word versions, followed by *que* + subjunctive:

- *quienquiera que* (whoever): *Quienquiera que haya escrito esto conoce bien el tema.* — Whoever wrote this knows the subject well. The plural is *quienesquiera*, which is rare.
- *dondequiera que* (wherever): *Dondequiera que vivas, recuerda de dónde vienes.* — Wherever you live, remember where you come from.

(*cuandoquiera* and *comoquiera* exist too, but are rarer still; just recognize them.) In speech, people use *quien sea* or *el que sea* and *donde sea* instead.

Watch the spelling. The RAE's *Diccionario panhispánico de dudas* says *dondequiera* is written as one word; *donde quiera* in two words is a different thing: *donde* + *quiera* from *querer*, "where he / she / you (usted) wants": *Usted puede sentarse donde quiera.* — You can sit wherever you like.

## In conversation: shrugs and "anyway"

Some of these phrases have a life of their own in everyday speech. These notes describe common informal usage in Mexico; they aren't dictionary definitions.

- *Lo que sea* as an answer can sound indifferent, even rude, if said flatly: *—¿Qué quieres de cenar? —Lo que sea.* Softened, it's friendly: *Lo que sea está bien, gracias* or *Lo que tú prefieras.*
- *Como sea* can mean "anyway" to close a topic and move on: *Bueno, como sea, ¿qué hacemos el sábado?* — Well, anyway, what are we doing on Saturday? It can also sound dismissive (*—Llegaste tarde. —Como sea.* — "You were late." "Whatever."), so watch your tone.
- *Cuando sea* and *donde sea* are often generous: *Cuando sea, aquí estoy* (I'm here any time).

Module 1's honors lesson 04h1 teaches the related fixed phrases *sea como sea, pase lo que pase, cueste lo que cueste*; this lesson doesn't repeat them.

### Example 1: sea or quieras?

Choose the phrase that fits, and explain why.

1. Your guest asks what to bring to your party. You want to be generous: *Trae ___.*
2. Your little brother is starving and complains about the menu. You tell him: *Si tienes hambre, comes ___.*
3. A coworker asks when to send you the file; you're free all day: *Mándamelo ___.*

Answers: 1. *lo que quieras*: the choice is the guest's, and *quieras* sounds hospitable. 2. *lo que sea*: any food at all, the choice doesn't matter (said a bit sharply). 3. *cuando quieras* or *cuando sea*: both work; *cuando quieras* is more courteous, *cuando sea* stresses that any time is fine.

### Example 2: From formal to everyday

A notice in a coworking space reads: *Quienquiera que use la cocina debe dejarla limpia.* Say it in everyday Spanish to a friend.

- *El que use la cocina, que la deje limpia.* or *Quien use la cocina tiene que dejarla limpia.*

Steps: *quienquiera que* → *el que* or *quien* (the subjunctive stays: *use*, because the person isn't known); *debe* + infinitive → *que* + subjunctive or *tiene que*, which sound more conversational.

### Example 3: Reading the tone

In each exchange, is the answer friendly or a little dismissive?

> A: —¿Vamos al cine o a cenar? —Lo que tú quieras, me da igual.
>
> B: —Te dejé el informe en tu escritorio. —Ajá, como sea.
>
> C: —Gracias por todo. —De nada, cualquier cosa, me avisas.

A is friendly: *lo que tú quieras* hands over the choice (*me da igual* = it's all the same to me). B sounds dismissive: *como sea* here means "whatever". C is warm: *cualquier cosa, me avisas* offers more help. (*el informe* — report; *el escritorio* — desk; *ajá* — uh-huh.)

## Dialogue: Un fin de semana sin planes

Lucía and her friend Beto plan a weekend in Mexico City.

> Lucía: ¿Qué quieres hacer el sábado?
>
> Beto: Lo que sea, mientras no tenga que madrugar.
>
> Lucía: Perfecto. Podemos ir a Coyoacán a la hora que quieras; ahí hay gente a cualquier hora.
>
> Beto: ¿Y a comer?
>
> Lucía: Donde tú digas. Yo como lo que sea: tacos, pozole, quesadillas…
>
> Beto: Bueno, como sea, primero vamos al mercado. ¿Invitamos a alguien?
>
> Lucía: A quien quieras. Pero no invites a cualquiera, que luego no se quieren ir.
>
> Beto: Ja, ja. Entonces nos vemos a las once. Si cambias de idea, cualquier cosa, me avisas.

*Lucía: What do you want to do on Saturday? — Beto: Whatever, as long as I don't have to get up early. — Lucía: Perfect. We can go to Coyoacán at whatever time you want; there are people there at any time of day. — Beto: And to eat? — Lucía: Wherever you say. I eat anything: tacos, pozole, quesadillas… — Beto: Well, anyway, first let's go to the market. Shall we invite someone? — Lucía: Whoever you want. But don't invite just anyone, because then they never want to leave. — Beto: Ha ha. Then see you at eleven. If you change your mind, if anything comes up, let me know.*

(*madrugar* — to get up very early; *mientras* + subjunctive — as long as, lesson 18; *donde tú digas* — wherever you say, another open-ended subjunctive.) Note *Pero no invites a cualquiera*: *cualquiera* as a pronoun here means "just anyone", with a hint of "anybody at all, not chosen with care".

## Common mistakes

- ~~cualquiera cosa~~ → *cualquier cosa* (the *-a* drops before a noun).
- Writing the formal word in two parts: ~~donde quiera que vayas~~ (for "wherever you go") → *dondequiera que vayas*; and ~~quien quiera que~~ → *quienquiera que*.
- The indicative for an open choice: ~~Haz lo que quieres~~ → *Haz lo que quieras.* (*Hago lo que quiero* is fine as a fact.)
- Forgetting the person: to a stranger, *lo que quiera* or *como quiera* (usted), not *lo que quieras*.
- *quienquiera* without *que* before a verb: ~~Quienquiera llame…~~ → *Quienquiera que llame…*

## Key points

- + *sea* = any option at all: *lo que sea, quien sea, donde sea, cuando sea, como sea.*
- + *quieras* (or another subjunctive) = the listener's choice: *lo que quieras, como quieras, donde quieras, cuando puedas.*
- *cualquier cosa* = anything; *cualquiera* = anyone, any one; *a cualquier hora* = at any time.
- Formal: *quienquiera que, dondequiera que* + subjunctive, written as one word.
- In conversation, *lo que sea* and *como sea* can sound dismissive; *lo que quieras* and *cualquier cosa, me avisas* sound friendly.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: It had already happened: the pluperfect
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 3 is about telling things in detail, and a good story often has to step back in time.
"When the police arrived, the thief had already fled." The arrival is the moment you are telling;
the escape happened before it. English marks that earlier step with "had" + a past participle,
and Spanish does the same with the **[[pluperfect]]** (*el pretérito pluscuamperfecto*): *Cuando llegó
la policía, el ladrón ya había huido.*

You already know both pieces: the present perfect from Spanish A1 (*he visto*) and the imperfect
from Spanish A2 (*había* is the imperfect of *haber*). A2's optional honors lesson 04h2 previewed
the pluperfect; this lesson teaches it fully for everyone. From this lesson on, the pluperfect is one
of your conjugation drills. The theme is crime and detective stories, told without anything
graphic.

## The forms

The pluperfect is a **[[compound tense]]**: a form of *haber* followed by a **[[participle]]**. Here *haber*
is in the imperfect:

| | *haber* (imperfect) | + participle |
|---|---|---|
| yo | había | llegado |
| tú | habías | visto |
| él, ella, usted | había | huido |
| nosotros, nosotras | habíamos | resuelto |
| (vosotros, vosotras) | (habíais) | (dicho) |
| ellos, ellas, ustedes | habían | desaparecido |

(*Vosotros* is Spain's plural "you"; in Mexico *ustedes* covers every plural "you".)

Three things to notice:

- The participle never changes. It doesn't agree with anybody: *ella había llegado, ellas
  habían llegado, la policía había detenido a dos hombres.*
- Nothing goes between *había* and the participle. *No*, object pronouns and reflexive
  pronouns go in front of *había*, all of them: *No lo había visto* (I hadn't seen it), *Se
  habían escondido* (They had hidden), *Ya me lo había dicho* (She had already told me).
- *Yo había* and *él había* look the same, so add the subject when it isn't clear: *Yo ya había
  cerrado la puerta, pero él no.*

### Participles: regular, accented and irregular

Regular participles end in *-ado* (-ar verbs) and *-ido* (-er and -ir verbs): *denunciado,
detenido, confesado, desaparecido*. After the vowels *a, e, o*, the *i* of *-ido* takes an
accent: *leído, creído, caído, traído, oído*. After *u* it doesn't: *huido, construido,
destruido*.

These irregular participles are the ones learners miss most often:

| verb | participle | verb | participle |
|---|---|---|---|
| hacer | hecho | abrir | abierto |
| decir | dicho | cubrir | cubierto |
| ver | visto | descubrir | descubierto |
| poner | puesto | escribir | escrito |
| volver | vuelto | describir | descrito |
| devolver | devuelto | romper | roto |
| resolver | resuelto | morir | muerto |

*Resolver* (to solve) is new in this lesson: *El caso estaba resuelto* (The case was solved),
*Nadie había resuelto el caso* (Nobody had solved the case).

Don't confuse the pluperfect with A2's *había* = "there was, there were", which stays singular in standard
Spanish (see Common mistakes): *Había dos testigos* (There were two witnesses). In *Los testigos habían visto al ladrón* (The
witnesses had seen the thief), *habían* is the pluperfect and agrees with *los testigos*.

## The past before the past

![A timeline titled "The past before the past". On the left, at 22:10 (10:10 p.m.), a running figure: el ladrón huyó. In the middle, at 22:40, a police car: llegó la policía. On the right: ahora. A curved arrow points back from 22:40 to 22:10, labeled "looking back from 22:40". A box at the top reads: Cuando llegó la policía, el ladrón ya había huido. A line at the bottom reads: preterite = the moment you are telling; pluperfect = an event before that moment.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

A story has a moment of telling: the event you're describing now, usually in the preterite. The
pluperfect looks back from that moment to something that had happened earlier:

- *Cuando llegó la policía, el ladrón ya había huido.* — When the police arrived, the thief had
  already fled.
- *La detective sabía que el sospechoso había mentido.* — The detective knew that the suspect had
  lied. (*mentir* = to lie)
- *Me enteré de que habían detenido a mi vecino.* — I found out that they had arrested my
  neighbor.

Compare two sentences that differ only in one verb:

- *Cuando llegó la policía, el ladrón huyó.* — When the police arrived, the thief fled (he ran
  when he saw them).
- *Cuando llegó la policía, el ladrón ya había huido.* — When the police arrived, the thief had
  already fled (he was gone before they came).

When you tell events in the order they happened, the preterite is enough: *El ladrón entró por la
ventana, tomó el collar y huyó.* Spanish speakers don't put every verb into the pluperfect; they
use it when the story jumps back. *Antes de* and *después de* also make the order clear, so the
preterite is normal with them: *Huyó antes de las once* (He fled before eleven), *Después de
cenar, salí* (After dinner, I went out).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Preterite or pluperfect?
  accDescr: A decision chart for one past event in a story. First question: did it happen before the moment you are telling? If no, use the preterite, for example llegó, abrió. If yes, second question: is the order already clear because you tell events in order or use antes de or después de? If yes, the preterite is fine, for example Entró, tomó el collar y huyó. If no, because the story jumps back in time, use the pluperfect, for example ya había huido.
  A["A past event in your story"] --> B["Did it happen before the moment you are telling?"]
  B -- no --> P1["Preterite: llegó, abrió"]
  B -- yes --> C["Is the order already clear? (told in order, antes de, después de)"]
  C -- yes --> P2["The preterite is fine: Entró, tomó el collar y huyó"]
  C -- "no: the story jumps back" --> Q["Pluperfect: ya había huido"]
```

### Words that go with it

| word | example |
|---|---|
| *ya* (already) | *Ya habían cerrado la tienda.* — They had already closed the store. |
| *todavía no, aún no* (not yet) | *Todavía no habíamos resuelto el caso.* — We hadn't solved the case yet. |
| *nunca antes, nunca* (never before) | *Nunca antes había visto un juicio.* — I had never seen a trial before. |
| *para entonces* (by then) | *Para entonces, el sospechoso había desaparecido.* — By then, the suspect had disappeared. |
| *antes* (before) | *Yo ya lo había visto antes.* — I had seen him before. |
| *la noche anterior, el día anterior* (A2) | *La noche anterior alguien había entrado en la casa.* — The night before, someone had gotten into the house. |



### Explaining a past situation

The pluperfect is the natural way to give the cause of a past state, with *porque*, *como* or
*por eso*:

- *Estaba nerviosa porque no había dormido.* — She was nervous because she hadn't slept.
- *Como nadie había cerrado la ventana, el ladrón entró sin problema.* — Since nobody had closed
  the window, the thief got in without any trouble.


### After verbs of finding out and knowing

What you found out, realized, discovered or knew had usually happened earlier, so these verbs
often lead into the pluperfect: *enterarse de que* (to find out), *darse cuenta de que* (to
realize), *descubrir que* (to discover), *averiguar* (to find out by investigating), *saber que*.

- *La policía averiguó que el carro había desaparecido el lunes.* — The police found out that
  the car had disappeared on Monday.


You'll also use it to report what someone said had happened: *Me dijo que había visto al ladrón*
(He told me he had seen the thief). Lesson 16 does reported speech in full.

## The language of a crime story

*El delito* is the legal word for any offense (*robar es un delito*); *el crimen* usually means a
serious crime, especially a killing, and *el asesinato* is murder. *La víctima* is always feminine, even for a man: *La víctima, un hombre
de 60 años, no vio nada.* *El arma* (weapon) is also feminine, but takes *el* in the singular
because it starts with a stressed *a*: *el arma, las armas, un arma peligrosa.*

You *denuncias* a crime when you report it to the authorities: *Fui a denunciar el robo*, *Puse
una denuncia* (I filed a report); in Mexico you'll also hear *levantar una denuncia*. The police *detienen* a suspect (*detener* = to arrest, and also to stop: *Detuvo el carro en la esquina*, She stopped the car
at the corner). *Detener* is conjugated like *tener*: *detengo, detuve, detén,
detendré.* Then come *el juicio* (the trial), *el juez* or *la jueza*, and, for *el culpable*,
*la cárcel* (jail, prison).

![A detective's evidence board for case 214, a robbery at a jewelry store. Pinned on the board: a photo of a man with a mustache, labeled el sospechoso; a card with a large fingerprint, labeled la huella; a plastic evidence bag with a pistol inside, labeled el arma; a movie ticket for 9:30 p.m. with a sticky note reading ¿Estuvo en el cine?, labeled la coartada. Red string connects the items. A woman in a jacket stands at the right pointing at the board, labeled la detective.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*La coartada* is an alibi; *la huella* is a footprint or a mark, and *la huella digital* a
fingerprint.

## Story: *El collar de jade*

> El martes por la noche, don Ernesto Ávila llamó a la policía. Alguien había entrado en su casa
> de Coyoacán y el collar de jade de su abuela había desaparecido. La detective Inés Robles llegó
> a las once.
>
> —¿A qué hora salió usted de la casa? —preguntó la detective.
>
> —A las ocho. Cuando regresé, a las diez y media, la ventana estaba rota y la caja fuerte, abierta.
>
> —¿Alguien más tenía la llave?
>
> —Solo mi sobrino Julián, pero él no fue. Esa noche había ido al cine y tiene coartada: aquí está
> su boleto.
>
> La detective miró la ventana con atención. El vidrio estaba afuera, en el jardín, no adentro.
> Nadie había roto esa ventana desde afuera: alguien la había roto desde adentro.
>
> En la caja fuerte no había ninguna huella, ni siquiera de don Ernesto. Alguien la había limpiado
> con cuidado. La detective empezó a tener una sospecha: ¿por qué un ladrón tan cuidadoso había
> hecho tanto ruido con la ventana?
>
> Al día siguiente, la detective visitó tres joyerías del centro. En la tercera averiguó algo
> importante: don Ernesto había vendido un collar de jade en marzo, siete meses antes del "robo".
>
> —Usted tenía deudas, ¿verdad? —le dijo la detective—. Ese fue su motivo. Vendió el collar y
> luego inventó el robo para cobrar el seguro.
>
> Don Ernesto se quedó callado un minuto. Después confesó todo. Julián era inocente: nunca había
> existido ningún ladrón.

Translation:

> On Tuesday night, don Ernesto Ávila called the police. Someone had gotten into his house in
> Coyoacán, and his grandmother's jade necklace had disappeared. Detective Inés Robles arrived at
> eleven.
>
> "What time did you leave the house?" the detective asked.
>
> "At eight. When I got back, at ten thirty, the window was broken and the safe was open."
>
> "Did anyone else have the key?"
>
> "Only my nephew Julián, but it wasn't him. That night he had gone to the movies, and he has
> an alibi: here's his ticket."
>
> The detective looked carefully at the window. The glass was outside, in the garden, not inside.
> Nobody had broken that window from outside: someone had broken it from inside.
>
> There were no fingerprints at all on the safe, not even don Ernesto's. Someone had wiped it
> carefully. The detective began to have a suspicion: why had such a careful thief made so much
> noise with the window?
>
> The next day, the detective visited three jewelry stores downtown. At the third, she found out
> something important: don Ernesto had sold a jade necklace in March, seven months before the
> "robbery".
>
> "You were in debt, weren't you?" the detective said to him. "That was your motive. You sold
> the necklace and then made up the robbery to collect the insurance."
>
> Don Ernesto said nothing for a minute. Then he confessed everything. Julián was innocent:
> there had never been any thief.

Notes: *la caja fuerte* = safe; *el vidrio* = glass (lesson 08's word); *roto* = broken (participle of *romper*); *ni siquiera* = not
even; *cuidadoso* = careful; *limpiar* = to clean, here to wipe; *la joyería* = jewelry store; *la deuda* = debt
(lesson 18's word); *inventar* = to make up; *cobrar el seguro* = to collect the insurance (*el
seguro* in this sense is lesson 18's word); *quedarse callado* = to go quiet. *Don* is a
respectful title used with a first name. Coyoacán is a real borough of Mexico City; the story and
its people are invented.

The imperfect sets the scene (*estaba rota, tenía deudas*), the preterite moves the story
(*llamó, visitó, confesó*), and the pluperfect reaches back to what had happened before
(*había ido al cine, había vendido*). Lesson 10 puts the three together.

## Pronunciation

- *había, habían*: the *h* is silent and the stress is on the *í*: a-BÍ-a, a-BÍ-an. The *b*
  between vowels is soft, with the lips not quite closed. *Habíamos* is a-BÍ-a-mos.
- *huir, hui*: usually one syllable, *wee*-r and *wee* (some speakers say *hu-ÍR* in two). For
  spelling, the Real Academia's 2010 rules count *ui* as one syllable however it is pronounced, so
  they write *hui* and *huis* without an accent. *Huyó* is u-YÓ, with the Mexican *y* sound.
- *averiguar, averigüé*: in *-guar* the *u* is pronounced (a-be-ri-GWAR). In *averigüé* the
  two dots (*la diéresis*) keep that *w* sound before *e*: a-be-ri-GWÉ.
- *la coartada*: four syllables, co-ar-TA-da. *El juez*: one syllable, HWES (z = s).

## Common mistakes

- Regular participles for irregular verbs: ~~había resolvido, habían hacido~~ → *había resuelto,
  habían hecho*.
- Making the participle agree: ~~La policía había detenida al sospechoso~~ → *había detenido*.
- Splitting the tense: ~~Había ya huido~~, ~~Había lo visto~~ → *Ya había huido, Lo había visto*.
- Using the pluperfect for events told in order: *Entró, tomó el collar y huyó* is a sequence, so
  the preterite is right; ~~había entrado, había tomado y había huido~~ would make every step
  "earlier than" a moment the story never gives.
- Making "there were" plural: *Había dos testigos*, not ~~Habían dos testigos~~, in standard
  Spanish. You'll hear *habían* in this sense in casual speech in much of Latin America, but the
  Real Academia's *Diccionario panhispánico de dudas* recommends the singular.
- Forgetting the accents: *había, habíamos* (and *leído, caído*), but *huido* and *construido*
  have none.


## Key points

- Pluperfect = *había, habías, había, habíamos, habían* + participle: *había huido, habían
  resuelto*. The participle never changes.
- Pronouns and *no* go before *había*: *Ya lo había visto. No se habían ido.*
- It tells what had happened before a past moment: *Cuando llegó la policía, el ladrón ya había
  huido.* If you tell events in order, use the preterite.
- Typical partners: *ya, todavía no, nunca antes, para entonces*, and verbs of finding out (*me
  enteré de que, averiguó que, se dio cuenta de que*).
- It explains a past situation: *Estaba cansada porque no había dormido.*
- Irregular participles to know: *hecho, dicho, visto, puesto, vuelto, roto, abierto, escrito,
  descrito, descubierto, resuelto, muerto*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Telling it in order: narrative connectors and three past tenses
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You now have three past tenses: the imperfect and the preterite from Spanish A2, and the
pluperfect from lesson 09. A real story needs all three, plus the small linking words that tell
a reader when each thing happened: *al abrir la puerta* (on opening the door), *al cabo de una
hora* (an hour later), *desde entonces* (since then). This lesson puts the tenses together, adds
the time connectors a B1 storyteller uses, and looks at how stories are built, from the first
line to the *desenlace* (the ending). The theme is literature: novels, short stories, poems and
fables.

## Three pasts, three jobs

![A timeline titled "Three pasts in one story". A long shaded bar runs under the whole story, labeled imperfect: the scene (era de noche, llovía). Three dots on the line are labeled preterite: the events (oyó un ruido, abrió la puerta, vio una carta). One dot further left, before the bar's events, is labeled pluperfect: earlier (alguien había dejado una carta), with a curved arrow from abrió la puerta back to it. At the right end: ahora.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Each tense has its own job:

| tense | job | example |
|---|---|---|
| imperfect | the scene: time, weather, descriptions, what was going on | *Era de noche y llovía. Marta leía en la sala.* |
| preterite | the events that move the story forward | *De pronto oyó un ruido. Abrió la puerta.* |
| pluperfect | what had happened before those events | *Alguien había dejado una carta en el suelo.* |

Read the three sentences together and the story has depth: a scene, a chain of events, and a step
back to explain them. A story told only in the preterite is a list; one told only in the imperfect never starts.

### Example: a paragraph taken apart

*Cuando Marta abrió la puerta, no había nadie. El viento soplaba y la calle estaba vacía. Alguien
había tocado el timbre y había huido.*

- *abrió*: preterite, an event.
- *no había nadie*: imperfect of *hay*, part of the scene (there was nobody).
- *soplaba, estaba*: imperfect, the scene.
- *había tocado, había huido*: pluperfect, two things that happened before she opened the door.

(*soplar* = to blow, lesson 01's word; *tocar el timbre* = to ring the doorbell.)

## Connectors of time

These words and phrases organize a story in time.

### *al* + infinitive: when, on (doing)

*Al* + infinitive says "at the moment of doing": *Al abrir la puerta, vio la carta* (When she
opened the door, she saw the letter). The infinitive never changes, and it usually has the same
subject as the main verb. It's common in writing and in careful speech; in conversation you can
always say *cuando abrió*.

- *Al llegar a casa, me di cuenta de que había perdido las llaves.* — When I got home, I realized
  I had lost my keys.
- *Al ver a la policía, el ladrón huyó.* — On seeing the police, the thief fled.

### *en cuanto, tan pronto como, apenas*: as soon as

For something that really happened in the past, these take the indicative, usually the
preterite: *En cuanto llegó, me llamó* (As soon as she arrived, she called me). Lesson 07 taught
them with the subjunctive for the future (*En cuanto llegues, llámame*); in a story about the
past the event is a fact, so the indicative is the normal choice.

*Apenas* has two meanings. Before a clause about an event it means "as soon as" (*Apenas salió el
sol, empezamos a caminar*); with a verb, an amount or an adjective it means "barely, hardly"
(*Apenas dormí*, I barely slept; *Tenía apenas quince años*, She was barely fifteen).

### Time passing: *al cabo de, a partir de, desde entonces, hasta entonces*

| connector | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| *al cabo de* + time | after (a period), … later | *Al cabo de una hora, volvió.* — An hour later, he came back. |
| *a partir de* | from … on | *A partir de ese día, todo cambió.* — From that day on, everything changed. |
| *desde entonces* | since then | *Desde entonces no lo he visto.* — I haven't seen him since then. |
| *hasta entonces* | until then | *Hasta entonces nunca había leído poesía.* — Until then I had never read poetry. |

- *Al cabo de* is a little formal or literary; in everyday Mexican Spanish you'll also hear *a la hora*, *a
  los dos días* (two days later) and *después de una hora*.
- *A partir de* also works for the future: *A partir del lunes, la biblioteca abre a las nueve.*
- *Hasta entonces* looks back from a turning point, so it often goes with the pluperfect or the
  imperfect: what had been true until that moment.
- *Desde entonces* reaches from a past moment toward the present, so it often goes with the
  present perfect or the present: *Desde entonces vive en Puebla.*

### *mientras tanto, de pronto, por último*

- *Mientras tanto* (meanwhile) starts a new sentence about what was happening somewhere else:
  *Marta buscaba la llave. Mientras tanto, su hermano llamaba a la policía.* A2's *mientras* joins
  two clauses in one sentence: *Mientras Marta buscaba la llave, su hermano llamaba.*
- *De pronto* (suddenly) means the same as A2's *de repente*: *De pronto se apagó la luz.*
- *Por último* (lastly, finally) introduces the last step or event in a series: *Primero leyó la
  carta, luego la guardó y, por último, salió de la casa.* A2's *al final* (in the end) also
  closes a story.

### About to, and had just: *estar a punto de, acababa de*

*Estar a punto de* + infinitive means "to be about to". In a story it's usually in the imperfect,
and something interrupts it: *Estaba a punto de salir cuando sonó el teléfono* (I was about to go
out when the phone rang). A2 showed *acababa de* + infinitive (had just): *Acababa de llegar
cuando empezó a llover* (I had just arrived when it started to rain). Both are very common at
turning points.

A2's *anterior* and *al día siguiente* place events around the story's main day: *La noche
anterior había llovido mucho* (The night before, it had rained a lot); *Al día siguiente, el río
estaba seco* (The next day, the river was dry).

## How a story is built

![A story-arc diagram, a curve that rises and then falls. On the left, low: el planteamiento (the beginning), with the connectors Había una vez, Hace mucho tiempo. Rising: el nudo (the conflict), with Un día, De pronto, Al cabo de. At the top: el clímax, with En ese momento, Estaba a punto de. Falling to the right: el desenlace (the ending), with A partir de entonces, Desde entonces, Por último. A small box at the far right: la moraleja (in a fable).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Spanish-language schools usually describe a story in parts like these:

- *el planteamiento* (the setup): who, where, when, in the imperfect. *Había una vez…* (Once upon
  a time…) and *Hace mucho tiempo…* (A long time ago…) are the classic openings.
- *el nudo* (the knot, the conflict): something goes wrong. Events start, in the preterite.
- *el clímax*: the moment of greatest tension.
- *el desenlace* (the ending, the outcome): how it is resolved. A fable (*una fábula*) ends with
  *la moraleja*, the moral.

The names vary from school to school, but the order doesn't.

### Words for talking about books

*El protagonista* or *la protagonista* is the main character (A2's *el personaje* is any
character); *el narrador* or *la narradora* tells the story. *La trama* is the plot, and *el género* is the kind of text:
*la novela*, *el cuento* (short story), *el relato* (a tale, an account, also of real events),
*el poema*, *la fábula*. *El género* also means gender.

Careful with two pairs: *la editorial* is the publisher (*Editorial Colibrí publicó la novela*),
but *el editorial* is a newspaper's editorial. *La portada* is a book's or magazine's cover, and
*el capítulo* a chapter. *El lector* or *la lectora* is the reader.

*La literatura* for young readers is full of *aventuras* (adventures) with *un héroe* or *una
heroína* at the center, and every writer needs *imaginación*. *Narrar* (to narrate, to tell) is a
more formal word than *contar*: *La novela narra la vida de tres hermanas* (The novel tells the
life of three sisters).

![A scene in a small bookstore. On a table stands a book whose cover shows a moon over a house; on the cover, the title La noche de los relojes, the author's name Ana Robles, and at the bottom a hummingbird logo with the words Editorial Colibrí. A young man sits in an armchair reading an open book whose left page is headed Capítulo 3. On a stand, another open book shows a short text in two stanzas. Labels name la portada, el título, la editorial, el poema, el capítulo and el lector.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## A fable: *El tlacuache y el agua*

A *tlacuache* is an opossum, an animal that appears in many Mexican stories. This fable was
written for this course.

> Hace mucho tiempo, en un bosque de Oaxaca, vivía un tlacuache llamado Tomás. Era pequeño, lento
> y muy tímido, y los otros animales se reían de él. Hasta entonces, Tomás nunca había salido
> del bosque.
>
> Un año no llovió. Al cabo de varios meses, el río se secó y los animales empezaron a tener sed.
> Según el venado, al otro lado de las montañas había un manantial, pero nadie había llegado nunca
> hasta allá.
>
> El jaguar dijo que iría, pero al ver las montañas cambió de opinión. El águila estaba a punto de
> salir cuando se lastimó un ala. Mientras tanto, Tomás escuchaba en silencio.
>
> Esa noche, apenas se durmieron los demás, salió del bosque sin decir nada. Al día siguiente,
> todos dijeron: "El tlacuache huyó. Le dio miedo".
>
> Tomás caminó tres noches. Antes de salir, había hablado con las hormigas, y ellas le habían
> explicado un secreto: el agua corre bajo la tierra, cerca de los árboles más verdes.
>
> La tercera noche, de pronto, oyó agua. Acababa de encontrar el manantial. Bebió, descansó y,
> por último, llenó de agua una calabaza.
>
> Una semana después, cuando los animales estaban a punto de perder la esperanza, Tomás regresó
> con la calabaza y con algo más importante: el camino.
>
> A partir de ese día, nadie se rio de él. Desde entonces, cuando no llueve, los animales del
> bosque siguen el camino del tlacuache.
>
> Moraleja: el que hace más ruido no siempre es el más valiente.

Translation:

> A long time ago, in a forest in Oaxaca, there lived an opossum called Tomás. He was small, slow
> and very shy, and the other animals laughed at him. Until then, Tomás had never left the forest.
>
> One year it didn't rain. After several months, the river dried up and the animals began to be
> thirsty. According to the deer, on the other side of the mountains there was a spring, but
> nobody had ever gotten that far.
>
> The jaguar said he would go, but on seeing the mountains he changed his mind. The eagle was
> about to leave when she hurt a wing. Meanwhile, Tomás listened in silence.
>
> That night, as soon as the others fell asleep, he left the forest without saying anything. The
> next day, everyone said: "The opossum ran away. He got scared."
>
> Tomás walked for three nights. Before leaving, he had talked with the ants, and they had
> explained a secret to him: water runs under the ground, near the greenest trees.
>
> On the third night, suddenly, he heard water. He had just found the spring. He drank, rested
> and, lastly, filled a gourd with water.
>
> A week later, when the animals were about to lose hope, Tomás came back with the gourd and with
> something more important: the way there.
>
> From that day on, nobody laughed at him. Since then, when it doesn't rain, the animals of the
> forest follow the opossum's path.
>
> Moral: the one who makes the most noise isn't always the bravest.

Notes: *reírse de* = to laugh at; *secarse* = to dry up; *el venado* = deer; *el manantial* =
spring (of water); *lastimarse* = to hurt yourself (A2); *el ala* = wing (feminine, *el ala, las
alas*, like *el arma*); *le dio miedo* = he got scared; *la hormiga* = ant; *la calabaza* = here
a gourd used as a bottle (also pumpkin, squash); *valiente* = brave.

The parts: the *planteamiento* is the first paragraph (imperfect: *vivía, era*); the *nudo*
starts with *Un año no llovió*; the *clímax* is *de pronto, oyó agua*; the *desenlace* starts
with *A partir de ese día*. The pluperfect steps back twice: Tomás *nunca había salido*, and the
ants *le habían explicado* the secret before he left.

## Pronunciation

- *el héroe*: three syllables, É-ro-e, stress on the first. *La heroína* is e-ro-Í-na.
- *el poema*: three syllables, po-E-ma; don't run *oe* together.
- *el desenlace*: de-sen-LA-se (c = s).
- *la editorial*: e-di-to-RIAL, four syllables, stress on the last.

## Common mistakes

- A conjugated verb after *al*: ~~Al abrió la puerta~~ → *Al abrir la puerta* (or *Cuando abrió
  la puerta*).
- The subjunctive for a past fact: ~~En cuanto llegara, me llamó~~ → *En cuanto llegó, me llamó.*
  (The subjunctive does appear when a past sentence looks ahead to something that hadn't happened
  yet, as in *Me dijo que me llamaría en cuanto llegara*: that's lesson 15's grammar.)
- The wrong gender: *el poema* (like *el problema*), *la protagonista* for a woman, *la editorial*
  for a publisher.
- Every event in the pluperfect. Use it to step back; tell the main events in the preterite.
- Reading *apenas* as only "barely": *Apenas llegó, se fue a dormir* = As soon as he arrived, he
  went to bed.

## Key points

- Imperfect for the scene, preterite for the events, pluperfect for what had happened before.
- *al* + infinitive = when, on (doing): *Al abrir la puerta, vio…*
- *en cuanto, tan pronto como, apenas* + indicative for past facts: *En cuanto llegó, me llamó.*
- *al cabo de* (… later), *a partir de* (from … on), *desde entonces* (since then), *hasta
  entonces* (until then), *mientras tanto* (meanwhile), *de pronto* (suddenly), *por último*
  (lastly).
- *estaba a punto de* (was about to) and *acababa de* (had just) mark turning points.
- A story: *planteamiento*, *nudo*, *clímax*, *desenlace*; a fable adds a *moraleja*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: By then I'll have finished: the future perfect and the conditional perfect
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 09 built the pluperfect from *haber* in the imperfect: *había terminado*. Put *haber* in
the future or the conditional, both from Spanish A2, and you get two more compound tenses:

- the **[[future perfect]]**: *habré terminado* (I will have finished);
- the **[[conditional perfect]]**: *habría terminado* (I would have finished).

They let you look back from the future (*By 2035 I'll have finished my degree*), make a guess
about something that has probably happened (*She must have fallen asleep*), and imagine a past
that didn't happen (*I wouldn't have done it*). The theme is careers and ambitions: success,
failure, changing direction and looking back.

These two tenses aren't among the app's conjugation drills: you practice them in this lesson's
text and questions. You already drill both of their pieces, though: the future and conditional
of *haber* use the stem *habr-*, and the participles are the ones from lesson 09.

## The future perfect

| | *haber* (future) | + participle |
|---|---|---|
| yo | habré | terminado |
| tú | habrás | logrado |
| él, ella, usted | habrá | salido |
| nosotros, nosotras | habremos | abierto |
| (vosotros, vosotras) | (habréis) | (hecho) |
| ellos, ellas, ustedes | habrán | vuelto |

As in every compound tense, the participle never changes and pronouns go first: *Ya lo habré
terminado*, *Se habrán ido*.

### Use 1: finished before a point in the future

![A timeline titled "Looking back from the future". On the left, ahora: 2026. In the middle, a dot at 2030: terminar la carrera. On the right, a flag at 2035: para 2035. A curved arrow points back from 2035 to 2030, labeled "already done by then". A box at the top reads: Para 2035, ya habré terminado la carrera. A line at the bottom reads: future perfect = done before a point in the future.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The future perfect stands at a future moment and looks back at something that will be finished
by then. The future moment is usually named with *para* (by), *dentro de* (in … time), *antes
de*, or a *cuando* clause with the subjunctive (lesson 07):

- *Para 2035, ya habré terminado la carrera.* — By 2035, I'll already have finished my degree.
- *Dentro de cinco años, la empresa habrá crecido mucho.* — In five years' time, the company will
  have grown a lot.
- *Cuando llegues, ya habremos cenado.* — When you arrive, we'll already have had dinner.
- *¿Habrás terminado el informe antes del viernes?* — Will you have finished the report (*el informe*) before Friday?

Without a future reference point, use the plain future or *ir a*: *Mañana termino el informe*,
*Voy a terminarlo mañana*. *Mañana habré terminado el informe* means "by tomorrow it will be
done", a different idea.

### Use 2: a guess about the recent past

In A2's honors lesson 16h2 the simple future made a guess about the present: *¿Dónde está Luis?
—Estará en el tráfico* (He's probably stuck in traffic). The future perfect makes the same kind
of guess about something that has probably already happened:

| what you say | time | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *Estará en la oficina.* | now | He's probably at the office. |
| *Habrá salido temprano.* | the recent past | He must have left early. / He's probably left early. |
| *Salió temprano. / Ha salido temprano.* | the recent past | He left early. (You know it.) |

- *Ana no contesta. —Se habrá quedado dormida.* — Ana isn't answering. —She must have fallen
  asleep.
- *¿Qué habrá pasado?* — I wonder what's happened. / What can have happened?
- *Habrán cerrado la tienda.* — They must have closed the store.

*¿Qué habrá pasado?* is one of the most common uses of the tense in everyday speech. You'll
often hear the same guess made with *seguramente* or *a lo mejor* + preterite (*Seguramente se
quedó dormida*), or with *deber (de) haber* + participle (*Debe de haber salido*, He must have
left). All of these are correct.

## The conditional perfect

| | *haber* (conditional) | + participle |
|---|---|---|
| yo | habría | estudiado |
| tú | habrías | aceptado |
| él, ella, usted | habría | dicho |
| nosotros, nosotras | habríamos | ido |
| (vosotros, vosotras) | (habríais) | (visto) |
| ellos, ellas, ustedes | habrían | puesto |

Notice the accent: *habría, habríamos*, like every conditional form.

### Use: what would have happened

The conditional perfect describes a past that didn't happen: what someone would have done in
other circumstances.

- *Yo no lo habría hecho.* — I wouldn't have done it.
- *En tu lugar, habría aceptado el ascenso.* — In your place, I would have accepted the promotion.
- *Con más tiempo, lo habríamos terminado.* — With more time, we would have finished it.
- *Sin tu ayuda, habría fracasado.* — Without your help, I would have failed.

The condition goes in a phrase: *en tu lugar* (in your place), *con más tiempo*, *sin tu
ayuda*, A2's *yo que tú* (if I were you). The full sentence with *si*, "If I had known, I would
have come", needs a new form (*Si lo hubiera sabido, habría venido*); that's honors lesson 16h1.
Never put *habría* right after a *si* that means "if".

### Regrets and missed chances

With *gustar*, *ser mejor* and similar expressions, the conditional perfect says what you would
have liked, or what would have been better:

- *Me habría gustado estudiar música.* — I would have liked to study music.
- *Habría sido mejor esperar un año.* — It would have been better to wait a year.
- *¿Qué habrías hecho tú?* — What would you have done?

![A picture of two roads splitting at a signpost labeled 2015: ¿Derecho o música? The left road is solid and leads to a courthouse: estudió Derecho, es abogada, labeled lo que pasó (preterite, present). The right road is dashed and leads to a grand piano: habría estudiado música, habría sido pianista, labeled lo que habría pasado (conditional perfect).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

In speech, in Mexico and across Latin America (and in Spain too, less often), you'll hear
*hubiera* where this lesson writes *habría*: *Yo no lo hubiera hecho*, *Me hubiera gustado estudiar
música*. The Real Academia's *Nueva gramática* accepts both in sentences like these, and notes that
*hubiera* is preferred more in the Americas than in Spain. (Only *hubiera* replaces *habría* this
way, not *hubiese*.) Recognize *hubiera*; use *habría* until honors lesson 16h1 explains the
other form.

## Four compound tenses

| tense | *haber* | example | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| present perfect | he, has, ha… | *He terminado.* | I have finished. |
| pluperfect | había, habías… | *Había terminado.* | I had finished. |
| future perfect | habré, habrás… | *Habré terminado.* | I will have finished. |
| conditional perfect | habría, habrías… | *Habría terminado.* | I would have finished. |

## Podcast: *Trayectorias*

An interview from an invented podcast about careers. Lucía Ortega is fictional.

> —Bienvenida a *Trayectorias*, Lucía. Hace diez años usted trabajaba en un banco en Guadalajara.
> ¿Por qué cambió de rumbo?
>
> —Me habían ofrecido un ascenso, pero ya no me sentía bien allí. Tenía cuarenta y dos años y
> pensé: "Si no emprendo ahora, ¿cuándo?".
>
> —¿Y qué negocio emprendió?
>
> —Una panadería. Mi primer negocio propio fracasó a los ocho meses: había rentado un local
> carísimo. Con más experiencia, habría buscado algo más pequeño.
>
> —¿Se arrepintió de dejar el banco?
>
> —De la decisión, no. El fracaso me enseñó mucho. Hay que esforzarse y hacer sacrificios: durante
> dos años casi no tuve vacaciones. Pero valió la pena.
>
> —Muchos emprendedores dicen que el mayor desafío es el dinero.
>
> —Para mí, el mayor reto fue el miedo. El talento ayuda, pero la paciencia es más importante. Eso
> le habría dicho a la Lucía de cuarenta y dos años.
>
> —¿Y el porvenir? ¿Cómo será su trayectoria en cinco años?
>
> —Para 2031 habremos abierto tres panaderías más, si todo sale bien. Soy ambiciosa, pero a estas
> alturas la ambición ya no me quita el sueño.
>
> —¿Le preocupa envejecer?
>
> —No. La madurez me dio algo que no tenía a los treinta: calma. Mis hijos ya se independizaron.
> No sé cómo será mi vejez, pero no tengo ningún arrepentimiento.

Translation:

> "Welcome to *Trayectorias*, Lucía. Ten years ago you worked at a bank in Guadalajara. Why did you
> change direction?"
>
> "They had offered me a promotion, but I didn't feel good there anymore. I was forty-two and I
> thought: 'If I don't start a business now, when will I?'"
>
> "And what business did you start?"
>
> "A bakery. My first business of my own failed after eight months: I had rented a very
> expensive space. With more experience, I would have looked for something smaller."
>
> "Did you regret leaving the bank?"
>
> "The decision, no. The failure taught me a lot. You have to work hard and make sacrifices: for
> two years I hardly had any vacation. But it was worth it."
>
> "Many entrepreneurs say the biggest challenge is money."
>
> "For me, the biggest challenge was fear. Talent helps, but patience is more important. That's
> what I would have told the forty-two-year-old Lucía."
>
> "And the future? What will your career look like in five years?"
>
> "By 2031 we will have opened three more bakeries, if all goes well. I'm ambitious, but at this
> point ambition doesn't keep me up at night anymore."
>
> "Does getting older worry you?"
>
> "No. Maturity gave me something I didn't have at thirty: calm. My children have already moved
> out and become independent. I don't know what my old age will be like, but I have no regrets."

Notes: *la trayectoria* = career path, track record; *la panadería* = bakery; *rentar* = to rent (A1); *el local* =
commercial space, premises; *salir bien* = to go well; *quitar el sueño* = to keep (someone) awake, to worry; *el miedo* = fear; *la paciencia* =
patience; *la calma* = calm. *El reto* and *el desafío* both mean "challenge"; *reto* is the more everyday
word in Mexico. *Maduro* means "mature" for people (*una persona madura*) and "ripe" for fruit
(*un mango maduro*).

Lucía uses three compound tenses: the pluperfect for what had happened before her decision
(*me habían ofrecido, había rentado*), the conditional perfect for the past she imagines (*habría
buscado, le habría dicho*) and the future perfect for a point in her future (*habremos
abierto*).

## Pronunciation

- *habré, habrás*: stress on the last syllable, a-BRÉ, a-BRÁS, like every future form.
- *habría, habríamos*: the *í* is stressed and separate from the *a*: a-BRÍ-a, a-BRÍ-a-mos.
- *br*: the *r* after *b* is a single tap, never the rolled *rr*.
- *el desafío*: de-sa-FÍ-o, four syllables. *El porvenir*: por-be-NIR.

## Common mistakes

- Mixing *habré* and *habría*: *habré* looks forward (*Para junio habré terminado*); *habría*
  imagines (*Yo habría terminado antes*).
- "Would have" + infinitive: ~~habría ir, habría hacer~~ → *habría ido, habría hecho*.
- Making the participle agree: ~~Las tiendas habrán cerradas~~ → *habrán cerrado*.
- *Habría* after *si*: ~~Si habría sabido…~~ is wrong (a *si* that means "if" never takes the
  conditional; *si* meaning "whether" can: *No sé si habría venido*). Until
  honors 16h1, put the condition in a phrase: *Con más información, habría ido.*
- Using the future perfect for an ordinary plan: *Mañana voy al banco*, not ~~Mañana habré ido al
  banco~~, unless you mean "by tomorrow it will be done".
- Overusing it for guesses: if you know it happened, say it plainly: *Salió temprano.*

## Key points

- Future perfect: *habré, habrás, habrá, habremos, habrán* + participle. It looks back from a
  future point (*Para 2035 habré terminado*) and guesses about the recent past (*Se habrá quedado
  dormida; ¿Qué habrá pasado?*).
- Conditional perfect: *habría, habrías, habría, habríamos, habrían* + participle. It imagines a
  past that didn't happen (*Yo no lo habría hecho; En tu lugar, habría aceptado*) and expresses
  regrets (*Me habría gustado…*).
- In speech you'll hear *hubiera* for *habría*; the *si* sentence with *hubiera* is honors 16h1.
- Neither tense has a drill of its own: practice them in sentences.

the lesson.

lessons.title: It was built in the year…: the passive voice
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

History, news and museum guides are full of sentences about what was done rather than who did
it: "The city was founded in 1325", "Two tombs were discovered", "The building was designed by
an Italian architect". English uses the passive for this. Spanish has several ways to say it,
and you know one already: in Spanish A2 (lesson 17) you met the *se* of signs and ads, *Se venden
casas* (Houses for sale), which grammars call the **[[passive se]]**.

This lesson adds the **[[passive voice]]** with *ser* + participle, the written form of history and
the news (*La ciudad fue fundada en 1325*); *estar* + participle for the state that results (*El
museo está cerrado*); and the third-person plural for an unknown doer (*Me robaron la cartera*).
You'll learn to turn an active sentence into a passive one and back, and to choose the form a
Mexican speaker would actually use. The theme is heritage, archaeology and monuments in Mexico
and Latin America; every fact here is dated and was checked against official or reference
sources.

## The *ser* passive

The passive voice turns the object of an active sentence into its subject. The verb becomes
*ser* + participle, and the doer, called the **[[agent]]**, can be added with *por*:

- Active: *Los mexicas fundaron la ciudad en 1325.* — The Mexica founded the city in 1325.
- Passive: *La ciudad fue fundada por los mexicas en 1325.* — The city was founded by the Mexica
  in 1325.

![A chart titled "Active to passive". Top row, active: Los mexicas (subject) — fundaron (preterite) — la ciudad (object) — en 1325. Bottom row, passive: La ciudad (new subject) — fue fundada (ser in the preterite + participle ending in -a) — por los mexicas (agent) — en 1325. Arrows show la ciudad moving from object to subject and los mexicas moving to por los mexicas. A note under the chart: the participle agrees with the new subject: la ciudad fue fundada, los templos fueron construidos. A last line: everyday Spanish: La ciudad se fundó en 1325.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Three rules:

1. *Ser* takes the tense of the active verb: *fundaron → fue fundada*, *descubren → son
   descubiertos*, *han restaurado → ha sido restaurado*, *construirán → será construido*.
2. The participle agrees with the new subject in gender and number, like an adjective: *el
   templo fue construido, la escultura fue restaurada, los objetos fueron excavados, las ruinas
   fueron declaradas patrimonio mundial.* This is the big difference from the compound tenses,
   where the participle never changes (*habían construido*).
3. *Por* + agent is optional. Leave it out when the doer is unknown or obvious: *El museo fue
   inaugurado en 1987.*

Some facts in this form:

- *La Piedra del Sol fue descubierta en el Zócalo de la Ciudad de México en 1790.* — The Sun
  Stone was discovered in the Zócalo of Mexico City in 1790.
- *El Palacio de Bellas Artes fue diseñado por el arquitecto italiano Adamo Boari.* — The Palace
  of Fine Arts was designed by the Italian architect Adamo Boari.
- *El Centro Histórico de la Ciudad de México fue declarado patrimonio mundial por la UNESCO en
  1987.* — The Historic Center of Mexico City was declared a World Heritage site by UNESCO in
  1987.

In Mexico you'll read both *patrimonio mundial* and *patrimonio de la humanidad* (World
Heritage).

### Where you'll meet it

The *ser* passive is mostly written: history books, the news, museum labels, official reports.
It is most natural in the preterite (*fue construido*) and in the compound tenses. In the
present it often describes something regular: *El museo es visitado por miles de personas cada
año.* In conversation, Spanish speakers usually prefer the active, the *se* passive or the
third-person plural (below).

## *ser* or *estar* + participle?

*Ser* + participle is an event: something was done. *Estar* + participle is the state that
results: how something is.

- *La tienda fue cerrada por la policía.* — The store was closed by the police (someone closed it).
- *Hoy la tienda está cerrada.* — Today the store is closed (it isn't open).
- *El templo estaba cubierto de tierra cuando lo encontraron.* — The temple was covered with
  earth when they found it.

With *estar*, the participle agrees too, and you usually don't add *por* + agent.

## The *se* passive: the everyday choice

The *se* passive from A2 works in every tense. The verb agrees with the thing: singular with one
thing, plural with several.

- *Se construyó en el siglo XVI.* — It was built in the 16th century.
- *Se descubrieron dos tumbas.* — Two tombs were discovered. (*la tumba* = tomb)
- *En Taxco se venden joyas de plata.* — Silver jewelry is sold in Taxco. (Taxco, in Guerrero,
  is famous for its silver.)
- *¿Cuándo se inauguró el museo?* — When was the museum opened?

Modern Spanish doesn't normally add *por* + agent to a *se* passive: *Se fundó por los
mexicas* sounds odd (the RAE's *Diccionario panhispánico de dudas* notes that it appears only
occasionally, in legal and administrative language). When you want to name the doer, use the active (*Los mexicas la fundaron*) or the
*ser* passive.

## The third-person plural: someone did it

When the doer is a person (or people) who is unknown or unimportant, Spanish often uses the
verb in the *ellos* form with no subject: *Me robaron la cartera* (My wallet was stolen; literally
"they stole my wallet"); *Restauraron la iglesia el año pasado* (The church was restored last
year). Nobody specific is meant by "they".

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Which passive should I use?
  accDescr: A decision chart. First question: are you describing a state you can see now, the result of an action? If yes, use estar plus participle, for example El museo está cerrado. If no, it is an event. Second question: do you name who did it? If yes, use ser plus participle plus por, which is formal and mostly written, for example La ciudad fue fundada por los mexicas; or use the active, Los mexicas fundaron la ciudad. If no, use se plus verb, the everyday choice, for example Se construyó en 1950; or the third person plural, Restauraron la iglesia.
  A["You want to say what was done, or how something is"] --> B["Is it a state you can see now (a result)?"]
  B -- yes --> E["estar + participle: El museo está cerrado."]
  B -- "no: it's an event" --> C["Do you name who did it?"]
  C -- yes --> S["ser + participle + por (formal, written): La ciudad fue fundada por los mexicas. Or the active: Los mexicas fundaron la ciudad."]
  C -- no --> D["se + verb (everyday): Se construyó en 1950. Or the ellos form: Restauraron la iglesia."]
```

## Words for heritage

![An archaeological site, labeled. In the center, a stepped pyramid (la pirámide) with a small temple on top (el templo). At the foot of the stairs, a carved stone serpent's head (la escultura). In the foreground, low broken stone walls (las ruinas). On the right, a woman in a hat kneels with a brush beside a half-buried carved stone (la arqueóloga), next to a sign reading ZONA ARQUEOLÓGICA. Behind, green hills and two visitors.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*La zona arqueológica* is the usual Mexican term for an archaeological site open to the public,
and the INAH (*Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia*) is the federal institute that
looks after them. *El arqueólogo* or *la arqueóloga* works in *la arqueología*; they *excavan*
(dig), *conservan* (preserve) and *restauran* (restore). *El hallazgo* is a find, especially an
unexpected one. *Las ruinas* is usually plural for the remains of buildings; *la ruina* in the
singular means ruin in general, including financial ruin.

*La herencia* is an inheritance and also a heritage (*la herencia indígena de México*); *el
patrimonio* is heritage as something a country protects (*el patrimonio cultural*). *Indígena*
has one form for both genders: *un pueblo indígena, una lengua indígena.* In Mexico you'll hear
both *pueblos indígenas* (the term in federal law and in the name of the national institute,
the INPI) and *pueblos originarios* (original peoples), which many communities and the Mexico
City government use.

Spanish chroniclers called Moctezuma *el emperador* and his state *el imperio*; in Nahuatl, his
title was *huey tlatoani* (great speaker, ruler). *El conquistador* is the Spanish soldier of the
conquest, *la civilización* a whole culture (*la civilización maya*), and *el monumento* any
historic building or statue. *El arquitecto* designs (*diseña*) buildings; *la arquitectura* is
the art of doing it.

## Dialogue: a tour of the Templo Mayor

A guide (*la guía*) shows a group around the Templo Mayor in Mexico City's historic center. The
people are invented; the facts are real.

> —Bienvenidos al Templo Mayor. Aquí estaba el templo más importante de Tenochtitlan, la ciudad
> que fue fundada por los mexicas en 1325.
>
> —¿Y cómo se descubrió?
>
> —Fue un hallazgo inesperado. El 21 de febrero de 1978, unos trabajadores de la compañía de luz
> estaban excavando en esta esquina cuando encontraron una enorme piedra redonda. Era una
> escultura de Coyolxauhqui, la diosa de la luna.
>
> —¿Y después?
>
> —A partir de ese hallazgo se excavó toda la zona. Los trabajos fueron dirigidos por el
> arqueólogo Eduardo Matos Moctezuma, y se encontraron miles de objetos, algunos de oro.
>
> —¿Por qué el templo está en ruinas?
>
> —Después de la conquista, en 1521, el templo fue destruido por los conquistadores españoles, y
> muchas de sus piedras se usaron para construir la nueva ciudad.
>
> —¿Dónde se conservan los objetos?
>
> —En el Museo del Templo Mayor, que fue inaugurado en 1987. Hoy la sala principal está cerrada,
> pero el resto del museo está abierto.
>
> —¿Y la Piedra del Sol? ¿También está aquí?
>
> —No. Fue descubierta en el Zócalo en 1790 y desde 1964 está en el Museo Nacional de
> Antropología. Pesa más de veinticuatro toneladas.

Translation:

> "Welcome to the Templo Mayor. This is where the most important temple of Tenochtitlan stood,
> the city that was founded by the Mexica in 1325."
>
> "And how was it discovered?"
>
> "It was an unexpected find. On 21 February 1978, some workers from the electric company were
> digging on this corner when they found an enormous round stone. It was a sculpture of
> Coyolxauhqui, the goddess of the moon."
>
> "And after that?"
>
> "Following that find, the whole area was excavated. The work was directed by the archaeologist
> Eduardo Matos Moctezuma, and thousands of objects were found, some of them gold."
>
> "Why is the temple in ruins?"
>
> "After the conquest, in 1521, the temple was destroyed by the Spanish conquistadors, and many
> of its stones were used to build the new city."
>
> "Where are the objects kept?"
>
> "In the Templo Mayor Museum, which was opened in 1987. Today the main hall is closed, but the
> rest of the museum is open."
>
> "And the Sun Stone? Is it here too?"
>
> "No. It was discovered in the Zócalo in 1790, and since 1964 it has been in the National Museum
> of Anthropology. It weighs more than twenty-four tons."

Notes: *inesperado* = unexpected; *la compañía de luz* = the electric company; *la diosa* =
goddess; *construir* = to build (a new word in this lesson: *construyo, construyó*); *la
tonelada* = (metric) ton. Coyolxauhqui is pronounced ko-yol-SHAU-ki. The Sun Stone (*Piedra del Sol*), often called the Aztec calendar, is a different monolith from
the one found in 1978.

The guide mixes the forms as a Mexican speaker would: the *ser* passive for the history (*fue
fundada, fueron dirigidos, fue destruido, fue inaugurado*), the *se* passive for the rest (*se
excavó, se encontraron, se usaron*), and *estar* for how things are today (*está cerrada, está
abierto*).

## Pronunciation

- *el arqueólogo*: ar-ke-Ó-lo-go; *la arqueología*: ar-ke-o-lo-HÍ-a. The *qu* is a plain *k*.
- *indígena*: in-DÍ-he-na, stress on the second syllable.
- *el hallazgo*: a-YAS-go (*ll* = y, *z* = s in Latin America).
- *Coyolxauhqui*: the Nahuatl *x* sounds like English *sh*, as in some Mexican place names (*Xola*, a street and metro station in Mexico City).

## Common mistakes

- Forgetting agreement with *ser*: ~~La ciudad fue fundado~~ → *fue fundada*; ~~Los templos fue
  construido~~ → *fueron construidos*.
- Agreement in the wrong place: with *haber* the participle never changes (*Han restaurado la
  iglesia*); with *ser* and *estar* it agrees (*La iglesia ha sido restaurada*, *está
  restaurada*).
- *De* or *de parte de* for "by": the agent of a passive takes *por*: *diseñado por Adamo Boari*.
- *Ser* for a state: ~~La tienda es cerrada~~ → *La tienda está cerrada* (it's closed now).
- *Se* + plural noun with a singular verb: ~~Se descubrió dos tumbas~~ → *Se descubrieron dos
  tumbas.* (The RAE's *Diccionario panhispánico de dudas* asks for agreement.)
- Translating "I was born" as a passive: ~~Fui nacido~~ → *Nací.* Spanish *nacer* is an ordinary
  active verb.
- Using the *ser* passive in every conversation. It's correct, but it sounds written; *Se construyó en 1950* is what most people would say.

## Key points

- Passive voice: *ser* (any tense) + participle agreeing with the subject, + *por* + agent if
  needed: *La ciudad fue fundada por los mexicas.* Mostly written: history, news, museums.
- Active → passive: object becomes subject, *ser* takes the active verb's tense, the participle
  agrees, the old subject becomes *por* + agent.
- *Estar* + participle = the resulting state: *El museo está cerrado.*
- *Se* passive = the everyday form, no agent: *Se construyó en 1950. Se descubrieron dos tumbas.*
- *Ellos* form for an unknown doer: *Me robaron la cartera.*
