lessons.title: Honors: Realismo mágico: an original story
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lessons 09 and 10 gave you the tools of a storyteller: three past tenses, the pluperfect for
stepping back, and connectors like *al cabo de* and *desde entonces*. This honors lesson uses
them on a longer text in a style that Latin American literature made famous around the world:
*el realismo mágico*, magical realism. You'll read what the term means and who is associated
with it, then an original story of about 900 words written for this course in that manner,
followed by questions on time and inference.

## What magical realism is

In a fantasy novel there are dragons, and everyone knows they are extraordinary. In magical realism the impossible happens in an ordinary, recognizable world, and
nobody in the story finds it very strange. A grandmother floats above her bed; the town worries
about the price of corn. The narrator tells both in the same calm voice. That calm is the
"magic": the reader is surprised, the characters aren't.

Three features usually appear together:

- a realistic setting: a real-looking town, family, politics or history;
- something *sobrenatural* (supernatural) or *inexplicable* (impossible to explain), told as a
  normal fact, often without comment;
- a narrator who doesn't explain or judge it, so the reader has to accept it.

The term has a history. The German art critic Franz Roh used *Magischer Realismus* in 1925 for a
kind of painting, not literature. In 1949 the Cuban writer Alejo Carpentier, in the prologue to
his novel *El reino de este mundo*, spoke of *lo real maravilloso* (the marvelous real), the idea
that Latin American reality itself is full of the marvelous. Critics still argue about where
the borders of the label are and which writers belong inside it, so treat it as a useful
description, not a club with a membership list.

## Three writers often associated with it

- Juan Rulfo (Mexico, 1917–1986) published the short stories of *El llano en llamas* (1953)
  and the short novel *Pedro Páramo* (1955), in which a man goes to the town of Comala to find
  his father and finds a town full of the voices of the dead. Rulfo is often described as a
  forerunner of magical realism rather than a member of it. Gabriel García Márquez said that
  reading *Pedro Páramo*, in 1961, helped him find the way to his own great novel.
- Gabriel García Márquez (Colombia, 1927–2014) wrote *Cien años de soledad* (*One Hundred
  Years of Solitude*, 1967), the story of seven generations of the Buendía family in the invented
  town of Macondo. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1982. He lived for many years in
  Mexico City, where he died.
- Isabel Allende (Chile; born in Lima, Peru, in 1942) began her career as a novelist with
  *La casa de los espíritus* (*The House of the Spirits*, 1982), a family saga in which a woman
  who can see the future lives side by side with the political history of a country.

This lesson quotes none of their books, which are under copyright; *Pedro Páramo* is short
enough for an ambitious B1 reader with a dictionary.

## How the tenses carry the magic

Magical realism leans on the imperfect. When the impossible is told in the imperfect, as a habit
or a description, it becomes part of the scene, as normal as the weather:

- *Las gallinas ponían huevos azules cuando iba a llover.* — The hens laid blue eggs when it was
  going to rain.

The preterite turns the impossible into an event, something that happened once:

- *Ese día, el cielo se puso naranja.* — That day, the sky turned orange.

And the pluperfect lets a story reach back to a prophecy (*una profecía*) or an omen (*un
presagio*) that had come before:

- *Doña Celia había anunciado la fecha de su muerte.* — Doña Celia had announced the date of her
  death.

Watch also for the words that frame the strange as normal: *nadie se sorprendía* (nobody was
surprised), *con toda tranquilidad* (perfectly calmly).

![A timeline of the story's events in the order they happened, numbered 1 to 6: 1, twelve years earlier, Lucía se fue a Chicago; 2, doña Celia anunció su muerte; 3, 31 de octubre, murió y llegaron las mariposas; 4, 1 de noviembre, bajó la niebla; 5, 3 de noviembre, la fecha de la carta; 6, 9 de diciembre, Lucía llegó y la niebla subió. Under event 1, a note: told later, in the pluperfect (se había ido).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## The story: *La niebla de San Isidro*

San Isidro is an invented village in the mountains of Michoacán, one of the two states where
millions of monarch butterflies spend the winter. They arrive in the forests of Michoacán and the State of
Mexico between late October and early November, close to the Day of the Dead, and a tradition
associated especially with the Purépecha people of Michoacán links them with the souls of the
dead coming home. The story builds on that belief.

### 1. La profecía

> En San Isidro nadie se sorprendía de nada. Las gallinas ponían huevos azules cuando iba a
> llover, y el río cantaba en voz baja los domingos. Por eso, cuando doña Celia anunció la fecha
> de su muerte, nadie se asustó.
>
> Doña Celia tenía noventa y tres años y había sido la partera del pueblo durante medio siglo.
> Había traído al mundo a casi todos los vecinos y conocía los secretos de cada familia.
>
> —Me voy a morir el último día de octubre —dijo una tarde, mientras pelaba elotes en el patio—.
> Ese día llegarán las mariposas. Y la niebla no se irá del pueblo hasta que regrese Lucía.
>
> Lucía era su nieta. Se había ido a Chicago doce años antes y nunca había vuelto. Al principio
> escribía cartas; después, solo mensajes de cumpleaños; después, nada.

Words: *la gallina* (hen), *poner huevos* (to lay eggs), *la partera* (midwife), *traer al
mundo* (to deliver a baby), *pelar elotes* (to husk ears of corn), *hasta que regrese* (until
she comes back: lesson 07), *la nieta* (granddaughter), *al principio* (at first).

In short: in a village where strange things are normal, an old midwife announces the day she
will die and makes a prophecy about butterflies, fog and her absent granddaughter.

### 2. Las mariposas

> El 31 de octubre, a las seis de la mañana, doña Celia se murió en su cama, con una sonrisa. En
> ese momento el cielo se puso naranja: millones de mariposas monarca llegaron del norte y
> cubrieron los techos, los árboles y la torre de la iglesia.
>
> —Es su alma, que viene a despedirse —dijo el padre Ramón, y nadie dijo lo contrario.
>
> Para el velorio, las mujeres pusieron una ofrenda con flores de cempasúchil y el pan que le
> gustaba a la difunta. Las mariposas entraban y salían de la casa como invitadas. Al día
> siguiente, después del entierro, todas subieron juntas hacia el bosque.

Words: *la sonrisa* (smile), *ponerse naranja* (to turn orange), *cubrir* (to cover), *el
padre* (here: the priest), *lo contrario* (the opposite), *el velorio* (wake), *el
cempasúchil* (Mexican marigold, the Day of the Dead flower), *la invitada* (guest), *el
entierro* (burial).

In short: she dies on the day she said, the butterflies arrive at that moment, and the town
treats them as her soul saying goodbye.

### 3. La niebla

> Esa misma tarde bajó la niebla. Era una niebla blanca y espesa, tan espesa que la gente se
> perdía entre su casa y la tienda. Los niños jugaban a desaparecer, y los perros dejaron de
> ladrar.
>
> Pasaron dos semanas, luego un mes, y la niebla no se iba. Algunos decían que era un hechizo;
> otros, que era el presagio de un año malo. Don Fermín, el maestro, aseguraba que era un
> fenómeno natural, pero tampoco podía explicar por qué, dentro de la niebla, las cosas pequeñas
> flotaban: las cucharas, los lápices, las llaves.
>
> —Es inexplicable —decía, mientras atrapaba su sombrero en el aire.

Words: *espeso* (thick), *jugar a* (to play at), *dejar de* (to stop doing, A2), *ladrar* (to
bark), *el fenómeno natural* (natural phenomenon), *atrapar* (to catch).

In short: a thick fog covers the village for weeks, and inside it small objects float; the
teacher's scientific explanation can't account for it.

### 4. La carta

> Mientras tanto, en Chicago, Lucía trabajaba de enfermera en un hospital. Su madre la había
> llamado para darle la noticia, pero Lucía no había podido viajar. Una noche de noviembre
> encontró una carta debajo de la puerta de su departamento. No tenía timbre, y la letra era de
> su abuela:
>
> "Querida Lucía: cuando leas esta carta, yo ya me habré ido. No estés triste. Ven a San Isidro:
> la niebla te está esperando. Te quiere, tu abuela".
>
> Lucía miró la fecha: 3 de noviembre, tres días después de la muerte de su abuela. Pero no le pareció
> extraño. Había crecido en San Isidro, y allí las cosas imposibles pasaban todos los días.
> Compró un boleto de avión esa misma noche.

Words: *trabajar de enfermera* (to work as a nurse), *el timbre* (stamp, A2), *la letra* (here:
handwriting), *me habré ido* (I will have gone: lesson 11), *No estés triste* (Don't be sad:
lesson 05), *extraño* (strange).

In short: in Chicago, Lucía receives a letter from her grandmother, dated after her death, and
decides to go home without hesitating.

### 5. El regreso

> Lucía llegó a San Isidro el 9 de diciembre, después de dos aviones y un autobús. Al bajar del
> autobús entró en la niebla y no vio nada. De pronto sintió que algo le tocaba la cara: era una
> mariposa monarca, sola, lejos del bosque.
>
> La siguió por las calles blancas hasta la casa de su abuela. En la puerta, la mariposa se quedó
> quieta un momento. Después voló hacia el cielo, y la niebla empezó a subir detrás de ella, muy
> despacio, como una cortina.
>
> Esa noche, los vecinos encontraron sus cucharas y sus llaves en el suelo, donde las habían
> dejado. Nadie habló de espíritus ni de nada sobrenatural. Solo comentaron, con toda
> tranquilidad, que doña Celia siempre cumplía su palabra.
>
> Lucía nunca volvió a Chicago. A partir de ese invierno, la partera del pueblo fue ella.

Words: *bajar del autobús* (to get off the bus), *quieto* (still), *la cortina* (curtain),
*comentar* (to remark), *cumplir su palabra* (to keep one's word).

In short: Lucía arrives, a butterfly leads her to her grandmother's house, the fog lifts, and
she stays to take her grandmother's place.

## Working with the story

### Example 1: why the imperfect makes the magic normal

*Las gallinas ponían huevos azules cuando iba a llover.* Two imperfects (*ponían, iba a*) make
this a habit: it happened every time. The sentence describes the village the way you'd describe
its weather. Compare *Una gallina puso un huevo azul*: a single event, and suddenly it's news.
The story chooses the habit, and the first line, *nadie se sorprendía de nada*, tells the reader
how to take it.

### Example 2: story order and telling order

The first thing that happened, Lucía leaving for Chicago, is told in the last paragraph of part 1, in the pluperfect: *Se había ido a Chicago doce años antes y nunca había vuelto.* The pluperfect, plus
*antes* (before, earlier), shows the jump back. The picture above shows all six events in story order.

### Example 3: an inference

Why does the fog lift when Lucía reaches the house? The story never says, but it gives three
clues: doña Celia's prophecy (*la niebla no se irá hasta que regrese Lucía*), the letter (*la
niebla te está esperando*) and the butterfly leading Lucía to the door. A careful reader infers
that the prophecy has been fulfilled and that the butterfly is, for the village, doña Celia's
soul. The last line (*siempre cumplía su palabra*) confirms the inference without stating it.

## Common mistakes

- Masculine adjectives with *el alma*: *alma* is feminine. It takes *el* in the singular only
  because it starts with a stressed *a*, and its adjectives stay feminine: *el alma buena, las
  almas buenas*.
- *La difunta* and *muerto*: *el difunto, la difunta* (the deceased) is a noun, respectful and a
  little formal; *muerto* is the everyday adjective (*está muerto*). Don't say ~~está difunto~~.
- *Presagio* and *profecía*: a *presagio* is a sign or omen (a fog, a black butterfly); a
  *profecía* is a prediction that someone says out loud.
- Calling every fantastic story *realismo mágico*: a story set in an invented world with magic
  rules is *fantasía*. The label needs a realistic world.


## Key points

- Magical realism: something supernatural, told calmly as normal, in a realistic world.
- The term: Franz Roh (1925, painting); Alejo Carpentier's *lo real maravilloso* (1949).
- Juan Rulfo (*Pedro Páramo*, 1955), Gabriel García Márquez (*Cien años de soledad*, 1967;
  Nobel 1982) and Isabel Allende (*La casa de los espíritus*, 1982) are the names most often
  linked with it; the boundaries of the label are debated.
- Imperfect = the impossible as habit or scene; preterite = the impossible as an event;
  pluperfect = the prophecy or the past behind it.
- Read for inference: the story gives clues and lets you conclude.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: Maya, mexicas e incas: history in the passive
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 12 taught the passive voice: *ser* + participle for written history (*La ciudad fue
fundada en 1325*), the *se* passive for everyday speech (*Se construyó en el siglo XVI*), and
*estar* for the resulting state. This honors lesson uses all three to read about three great
civilizations of the Americas: the Maya, the Mexica (often called the Aztecs) and the Inca. Four
short texts look at writing and calendars, cities and roads, the ball game, and the rise and
fall of each civilization, ending at the Spanish conquest. (A2's honors lesson 04h1 told the
history of Mexico from Tenochtitlan to the Revolution; this lesson goes back further and
farther south.)

The texts are simplified for B1 readers. Every date was checked against the INAH, UNESCO, UNAM
and other reference sources listed in the course notes; where historians disagree, the text
says so.

![A map in two panels. Left, Mesoamérica: southern Mexico and the start of Central America, with a dot for Tenochtitlan (hoy Ciudad de México) inside a shaded area labeled mexicas, and a shaded area labeled zona maya covering the Yucatán Peninsula and the land south of it, with dots for Chichén Itzá near the northern tip of the peninsula and Palenque at its southwestern edge. Right, Los Andes: the west coast of South America with a long shaded band along the mountains labeled incas, dots for Machu Picchu and Cusco close together, and a dashed brown line running the length of the band labeled Qhapaq Ñan.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## A note on names

Historians usually say *los mexicas* for the people who founded Tenochtitlan; *los aztecas* is
the older, popular name, still very common. *Los mayas* are the people, *el maya* is a language
(really a family of languages: *las lenguas mayas*). *Los incas* is used for the whole people,
although *el Inca* was originally the title of the ruler. All three names are written with a
small letter in Spanish, like other names of peoples: *los mayas, una ciudad inca.*

## 1. Escritura y calendarios

> La escritura maya es una de las más completas de la América antigua. Los textos se tallaban en
> piedra, se pintaban en cerámica y se escribían en códices de papel amate. Cada jeroglífico podía
> representar una palabra o una sílaba; en total se conocen unos 800 signos. Casi todos los
> códices fueron destruidos después de la conquista, y la escritura fue descifrada en gran parte
> en la segunda mitad del siglo XX, a partir del trabajo del lingüista ruso Yuri Knórozov en los
> años cincuenta.
>
> Los mayas también estudiaban el cielo. En el Códice de Dresde se encuentran tablas sobre el
> planeta Venus y los eclipses, y se cree que El Caracol, un edificio redondo de Chichén Itzá, era
> usado como observatorio. Su astronomía estaba unida a las matemáticas: contaban en base 20 y
> usaban un signo para el cero. Uno de los ceros más antiguos tallados en piedra es del año
> 357 d. C.
>
> Los incas, en cambio, no dejaron una escritura que podamos leer. Sus datos se guardaban en
> quipus, cuerdas con nudos de colores. Todavía se discute si los quipus solo registraban números
> o también palabras.

Words: *tallar* (to carve), *la cerámica* (pottery), *el códice* (codex, an early book), *el
papel amate* (bark paper), *la sílaba* (syllable), *descifrar* (to decipher), *el lingüista*
(linguist), *unido a* (linked to), *d. C.* (*después de Cristo*, AD), *la cuerda* (string,
cord), *el nudo* (knot), *registrar* (to record). *Que podamos leer* is the subjunctive after an
unknown antecedent (lesson 08).

In short: Maya writing combined word signs and syllable signs; most of it was read only in the
20th century. The Maya tracked Venus and eclipses and used a zero. The Inca kept records on
knotted cords.

## 2. Ciudades y caminos

> Según la tradición, Tenochtitlan fue fundada en 1325 en una isla del lago de Texcoco. La ciudad
> estaba unida a tierra firme por tres grandes calzadas: hacia el norte, a Tepeyac; hacia el sur,
> a Iztapalapa, y hacia el oeste, a Tlacopan. En 1519, cuando llegaron los españoles, vivían allí
> más de 200 000 personas, según la mayoría de los cálculos.
>
> En Palenque, en Chiapas, gobernó durante casi setenta años K'inich Janaab' Pakal, uno de los
> gobernantes mayas más famosos, que murió en 683. Su tumba fue descubierta en 1952 por el
> arqueólogo Alberto Ruz Lhuillier, debajo del Templo de las Inscripciones. Gracias a los textos
> de la ciudad se conoce bien su dinastía.
>
> En los Andes, los incas construyeron el Qhapaq Ñan, una red de caminos de unos 30 000
> kilómetros que se usaba para el comercio, la comunicación y el ejército. La red fue construida durante
> varios siglos y alcanzó su mayor extensión en el siglo XV. En 2014 fue declarada patrimonio
> mundial. Cerca de Cusco, la capital, se construyó en el siglo XV Machu Picchu, que fue
> declarado patrimonio mundial en 1983.
>
> Todas estas ciudades vivían de la tierra. En Mesoamérica se cultivaban maíz, frijol y calabaza;
> en los Andes, muchas variedades de papa. Una mala cosecha podía significar hambre para
> miles de personas.

Words: *según* (according to), *la tierra firme* (the mainland), *el cálculo* (estimate,
calculation), *gobernar* (to rule, *gobernó*), *la red* (network), *el comercio* (trade), *el
ejército* (army, A2), *la extensión* (extent), *vivir de* (to live on), *la variedad* (variety),
*el hambre* (hunger, feminine: *el hambre, mucha hambre*). Spanish writes large numbers with a
space (*200 000*) or a period in some countries; Mexico also uses a comma (*200,000*).

In short: Tenochtitlan was an island city joined to the shore by three causeways. Pakal ruled
Palenque for almost seventy years. The Inca road network covered about 30,000 km. All three
civilizations depended on their harvests.

## 3. El juego de pelota

> El juego de pelota se practicaba en toda Mesoamérica, de México a Centroamérica.
> La pelota era de hule y era muy pesada, y en muchas versiones solo se podía golpear con la
> cadera. Las canchas se construían en el centro de las ciudades, cerca de los templos, porque el
> juego también tenía un sentido religioso. Se considera que la cancha más grande del mundo maya es
> la de Chichén Itzá.
>
> El juego no desapareció del todo. En Sinaloa, en el norte de México, todavía se juega el ulama,
> un deporte que los especialistas consideran heredero del antiguo juego. En su versión de cadera
> se practica hoy en los municipios de Mazatlán y Escuinapa.

Words: *el hule* (rubber, Mexico; elsewhere *el caucho*), *pesado* (heavy), *golpear* (to hit),
*la cadera* (hip), *la cancha* (court, field), *el sentido* (meaning), *del todo* (completely),
*el heredero* (heir).

In short: the ball game was played all over Mesoamerica with a heavy rubber ball, often
struck only with the hips; Chichén Itzá's court is considered the largest in the Maya world; a descendant, *ulama*,
survives in Sinaloa.

## 4. Apogeo y decadencia

> El apogeo de muchas ciudades mayas fue en el periodo Clásico, más o menos entre los años 250 y
> 900. Después, muchas ciudades del sur fueron abandonadas. Las causas de esa decadencia todavía
> se discuten: se habla de sequías, guerras y problemas políticos. Pero los mayas no
> desaparecieron: hoy millones de personas hablan lenguas mayas.
>
> Los mexicas y los incas vivían su apogeo cuando llegaron los españoles. Tenochtitlan fue
> conquistada el 13 de agosto de 1521. En el Perú, el gobernante inca Atahualpa fue capturado en
> Cajamarca el 16 de noviembre de 1532. La conquista del mundo maya fue mucho más lenta: Nojpetén,
> en lo que hoy es Guatemala, uno de los últimos reinos mayas independientes, cayó el 13 de marzo
> de 1697.

Words: *abandonar* (to abandon), *la causa* (cause), *la sequía* (drought, lesson 17), *capturar*
(to capture), *el reino* (kingdom), *caer* (to fall, *cayó*).

In short: the Maya Classic period ended with many cities abandoned for reasons still debated,
but Maya peoples live on. The Mexica fell in 1521 and the Inca from 1532; the conquest of the
last Maya kingdoms took until 1697.

## Three civilizations compared

| | los mayas | los mexicas | los incas |
|---|---|---|---|
| where | Yucatán Peninsula, Chiapas, Guatemala, Belize, parts of Honduras and El Salvador | central Mexico | the Andes, from Colombia and Ecuador to Chile and Argentina |
| main cities | many city-states: Palenque, Chichén Itzá, Tikal, Calakmul | Tenochtitlan | Cusco, the capital |
| records | glyphs on stone, pottery and codices | painted codices | quipus (knotted cords) |
| apogee | Classic period, about 250–900 | 15th and early 16th centuries | 15th and early 16th centuries |
| conquest | slow: 16th–17th centuries (Nojpetén, 1697) | 1521 | from 1532 (Cajamarca) |

## Worked examples

### Example 1: one fact, three forms

Active: *Alberto Ruz Lhuillier descubrió la tumba de Pakal en 1952.*

1. The object, *la tumba de Pakal*, becomes the subject.
2. *Descubrió* is preterite, so *ser* goes into the preterite: *fue*.
3. The participle of *descubrir* is irregular, *descubierto*, and agrees with *la tumba*:
   *descubierta*.
4. The old subject becomes the agent with *por*.

*Ser* passive: *La tumba de Pakal fue descubierta por Alberto Ruz Lhuillier en 1952.*
*Se* passive, with no agent: *La tumba de Pakal se descubrió en 1952.*

### Example 2: imperfect or preterite in the passive?

The passive keeps the meaning of each tense. Habits and descriptions take the imperfect: *Se
cultivaba maíz* (Corn was grown), *Los textos se tallaban en piedra* (Texts were carved in
stone). Single events take the preterite: *Tenochtitlan fue conquistada en 1521*, *La tumba se
descubrió en 1952*. So in text 3, *el juego de pelota se practicaba en toda Mesoamérica* describes a practice, while *Atahualpa fue capturado* in text 4 is one event on one day.

### Example 3: reading *se cree que* and *se discute*

History texts use the impersonal *se* to show that a claim is an opinion or still open: *se cree
que El Caracol era usado como observatorio* (it's believed that…), *las causas todavía se
discuten* (are still debated). When you read these, the writer is telling you not to take the
claim as settled. Use them yourself when you report something uncertain.

## Common mistakes

- Mixing two passives: ~~se fue construido~~, ~~se fue descubierta~~ → *se construyó* or *fue
  construido*.
- Forgetting agreement: ~~Las calzadas fue construido~~ → *Las calzadas fueron construidas*.
- Capital letters for peoples: ~~los Mayas, los Incas~~ → *los mayas, los incas*.
- Saying Machu Picchu was "discovered" in 1911. The American explorer Hiram Bingham reached it on
  24 July 1911 and made it known abroad, but local farmers knew it, and other visitors had been
  there in 1902. Say *Bingham lo dio a conocer* (made it known).
- Treating *el maya* (a language) and *los mayas* (the people) as the same word.

## Key points

- History texts use the *ser* passive for dated events (*fue fundada en 1325, fue capturado en
  1532*) and the *se* passive for practices and generalizations (*se cultivaba maíz, se jugaba
  con una pelota de hule*).
- *Se cree que, se discute, según* mark claims that aren't settled.
- Maya: glyphs, astronomy, a zero, the Classic period (about 250–900). Mexica: Tenochtitlan,
  its causeways, 1521. Inca: Cusco, the Qhapaq Ñan, quipus, 1532.
- The ball game was played across Mesoamerica and survives as *ulama* in Sinaloa.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: If only I could: the imperfect subjunctive
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Since lesson 01 you've used the present subjunctive for wishes, advice, feelings and doubt:
*Ojalá que te vaya bien* (I hope it goes well for you). Spanish has a second subjunctive, the
**[[imperfect subjunctive]]** (*hablara, tuviera, fuera*), and it opens up a whole new kind of
sentence: the unreal one. With it you can wish for things that probably won't happen (*Ojalá
tuviera un yate* — I wish I had a yacht), describe someone "as if" something were true (*Gasta
como si fuera millonario* — He spends as if he were a millionaire), and, in the next lessons,
say what you would do if things were different and report what people asked in the past.

This lesson builds the forms, which come straight from a tense you know well, the preterite,
and uses them with *ojalá* and *como si*. The theme is dreams, luck and fantasy: winning the
lottery, superpowers, desert islands. Completing it adds the imperfect subjunctive to your verb
drills.

## Building the imperfect subjunctive

There is one recipe for every verb in the language. Take the *ellos* form of the preterite (A1
and A2), drop *-ron*, and add *-ra, -ras, -ra, -ramos, -ran*.

![A three-step chart. Step 1, the ellos preterite: hablaron, comieron, tuvieron, fueron. Step 2, take off -ron: habla-, comie-, tuvie-, fue-. Step 3, add the endings -ra, -ras, -ra, -ramos, -ran: hablara, comiera, tuviera, fuera. A note under the nosotros ending says the vowel before it takes an accent: habláramos, tuviéramos.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| | hablar (hablaron) | comer (comieron) | vivir (vivieron) |
|---|---|---|---|
| (que) yo | hablara | comiera | viviera |
| tú | hablaras | comieras | vivieras |
| él, ella, usted | hablara | comiera | viviera |
| nosotros | habláramos | comiéramos | viviéramos |
| (vosotros) | (hablarais) | (comierais) | (vivierais) |
| ellos, ellas, ustedes | hablaran | comieran | vivieran |

Two things to notice:

1. *Yo* and *él / ella / usted* share a form (*hablara*), as in the imperfect and the
   conditional. Add the pronoun when you need to: *Ojalá yo supiera* (I wish I knew).
2. *Nosotros* takes a written accent on the vowel before the ending: *habláramos, comiéramos,
   fuéramos*. The stress stays where it was in the preterite (*ha-BLA-ron → ha-BLÁ-ra-mos*).

### Every preterite irregularity carries over

Because the recipe starts from the preterite, you already know the irregular ones. If the
preterite is strange, the imperfect subjunctive is strange in the same way.

| Infinitive | ellos preterite | Imperfect subjunctive |
|---|---|---|
| *ser* and *ir* | fueron | fuera (the same for both) |
| *tener, estar, andar* | tuvieron, estuvieron, anduvieron | tuviera, estuviera, anduviera |
| *poder, poner, saber* | pudieron, pusieron, supieron | pudiera, pusiera, supiera |
| *querer, venir, hacer* | quisieron, vinieron, hicieron | quisiera, viniera, hiciera |
| *decir, traer* | dijeron, trajeron | dijera, trajera (no *i*: never ~~dijiera~~) |
| *dar, ver* | dieron, vieron | diera, viera |
| *pedir, sentir, preferir* | pidieron, sintieron, prefirieron | pidiera, sintiera, prefiriera |
| *dormir, morir* | durmieron, murieron | durmiera, muriera |
| *leer, oír, creer, caerse* | leyeron, oyeron, creyeron, se cayeron | leyera, oyera, creyera, se cayera |
| *haber* | hubieron | hubiera (for honors 16h1) |

The *-ir* stem changers keep the vowel change they have in the *ellos* preterite (*pidieron →
pidiera*), and the *-ar* and *-er* stem changers have none (*pensaron → pensara, volvieron →
volviera*). Spelling changes that only touch the *yo* preterite don't matter here: *busqué*,
but *buscaron → buscara*; *llegué*, but *llegaron → llegara*.

### The -se forms

There is a second set of endings, *-se, -ses, -se, -semos, -sen*: *hablase, tuviese, fuésemos*.
It means exactly the same. You'll meet it in books, in older texts and in speakers from Spain,
where both sets are common. In Latin American speech the *-ra* forms are far more frequent:
studies of educated speech in major Spanish American cities have found the *-se* forms in only a
few percent of cases. This course teaches *-ra* and accepts *-se* in every answer.

## Ojalá: "I hope" or "I wish"?

In lesson 01, *ojalá (que)* + present subjunctive expressed a hope: something that may well
happen. With the imperfect subjunctive, the same word expresses a wish that is unlikely or
impossible. English uses two different verbs here; Spanish changes the tense.

| | Spanish | English |
|---|---|---|
| Possible | *Ojalá gane la lotería.* | I hope I win the lottery. (I bought a ticket; who knows?) |
| Unlikely | *Ojalá ganara la lotería.* | If only I won the lottery. (I don't really expect to.) |
| Impossible now | *Ojalá fuera viernes.* | I wish it were Friday. (It's Tuesday.) |
| Impossible | *Ojalá tuviera superpoderes.* | I wish I had superpowers. |

![A horizontal scale from probable on the left to imposible on the right. On the left, under "Ojalá + present subjunctive (I hope)": Ojalá llueva mañana, Ojalá gane mi equipo. In the middle, poco probable: Ojalá ganara el premio mayor. On the right, under "Ojalá + imperfect subjunctive (I wish)": Ojalá fuera invisible, Ojalá tuviera una máquina del tiempo.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Both refer to now or the future; the tense shows how likely the speaker thinks it is, not when
it happens. That makes it a choice, not a rule you can get wrong: the same person might say
*Ojalá venga* on Monday and *Ojalá viniera* on Friday, when the hope has faded. In everyday
speech the line isn't sharp, but the general rule holds: present = it could happen, imperfect
= I don't really expect it.

*Ojalá* takes the subjunctive, never the indicative or the conditional: ~~*Ojalá tengo*~~,
~~*Ojalá tendría*~~ → *Ojalá tuviera*. (*Ojalá* + a past wish, "I wish I had won", needs one more
form: honors 16h1.)

### A1's quisiera, explained

Back in A1 you learned *quisiera* (I'd like) as a polite way to order. Now you can see what it
is: the imperfect subjunctive of *querer*. Its unreal, "softened" meaning makes a request less
direct than *quiero*: *Quisiera un café, por favor* (I'd like a coffee, please); *Quisiera hablar con el gerente* (I'd like to speak to the manager; *el gerente* is lesson 15's word). It is one of
the few cases where the imperfect subjunctive stands alone as the main verb of a sentence.

## Como si: as if

*Como si* (as if, as though) is always followed by the imperfect subjunctive when it talks about
the same time as the main verb, whatever the tense of the main verb:

- *Gasta como si fuera millonario.* — He spends as if he were a millionaire.
- *Me habla como si yo fuera un niño.* — She talks to me as if I were a child.
- *Vive como si el dinero no importara.* — He lives as if money didn't matter.
- *Bailaron toda la noche como si tuvieran veinte años.* — They danced all night as if they
  were twenty.

Never the present subjunctive or the indicative after *como si*: ~~*como si es*~~, ~~*como si
sea*~~ → *como si fuera*. The idea is always unreal or doubtful, so the unreal form fits. You'll
also hear *como si nada* (as if nothing had happened): *Llegó tarde, como si nada.*

## Dreams, luck and fantasy

The words of this lesson's theme:

- *soñar* (*sueño, sueñas…*): to dream. A2's *el sueño* is the noun. To dream about something
  is *soñar con*, never ~~*soñar de*~~: *Sueño con una casa en la playa; Anoche soñé con mi
  abuela.* To dream that something happens: *Soñé que volaba* (I dreamed I was flying).
- *imaginarse*: to picture, to imagine (A2's *imaginar*, used with the pronoun, is very common
  in conversation): *¿Te imaginas?* (Can you imagine?), *Imagínate que ganas* (Imagine you win).
- *la lotería* and *el premio mayor* (jackpot, first prize): Mexico's *Lotería Nacional* goes back
  to 1770, when the Spanish king Carlos III authorized the *Real Lotería General de la Nueva
  España*. A ticket is *un billete*; tickets are also sold in fractions (one twentieth of a whole ticket), and in
  Mexico a fraction is usually called *un cachito*.
- *apostar* (*apuesto, apuestas…*): to bet. *Apuesto a que no gana nadie* (I bet nobody wins).
- *la fortuna* (a fortune; also luck) and *la riqueza* (wealth); *rico* (A1's "tasty") also means rich:
  *Mi tío es rico.* *Heredar* is to inherit: *Heredó una fortuna de su abuela.*
- *el lujo* (luxury) and *lujoso* (luxurious): *un hotel de lujo, un carro lujoso*; *la mansión,
  el yate, el crucero* (cruise), *la isla desierta* (desert island).
- *la fantasía* (fantasy), *el superpoder* (superpower), *invisible*, *la máquina del tiempo*
  (time machine), *eterno* (eternal), *el genio* (genie; also a genius: *Einstein era un genio*).
- *el capricho*: a whim, something you want just because: *Fue un capricho* (It was a whim).
- *la casualidad*: chance, coincidence. *por casualidad* = by chance; *¡Qué casualidad!* = What a
  coincidence! A2's *el destino* (destination) also means fate: *Fue el destino.*
- *ideal* and *perfecto*: *la vida ideal, un día perfecto.*

![A dream scene in a thought bubble above a person sleeping. In the bubble: a big house with columns on a hill, a yacht on the sea, a large cruise ship further out, a tiny island with one palm tree, and a lottery ticket with stars. They are labeled la mansión, el yate, el crucero, la isla desierta and el billete de lotería.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Dialogue: un cachito de suerte

Lupita and her coworker Andrés have bought a lottery ticket together in Guadalajara. The draw
is tonight.

> Andrés: Ya tengo el cachito. Si nos sacamos el premio mayor, lo dividimos a la mitad, ¿eh?
>
> Lupita: Claro. Aunque, la neta, ojalá ganáramos aunque fuera un reintegro. Nunca gano nada.
>
> Andrés: No seas así. Imagínate que ganamos. ¿Qué harías primero?
>
> Lupita: Ay, no sé… Ojalá tuviera una casita en una isla desierta, sin correos ni juntas.
>
> Andrés: ¿Una isla desierta? Yo prefiero un crucero. O un yate, como los millonarios de las películas.
>
> Lupita: Tú hablas como si ya fueras rico. Ayer me pediste prestado para el camión.
>
> Andrés: Es que estoy practicando. Mi tía heredó una fortuna de un tío que ni conocía, y ahora vive como si cada día fuera el último.
>
> Lupita: Pues ojalá yo tuviera una tía así. Bueno, te apuesto un café a que no ganamos.
>
> Andrés: Acepto. Pero si gano yo, me lo pagas en la mansión.

Translation:

> Andrés: I've got the ticket. If we win the jackpot, we split it down the middle, OK?
>
> Lupita: Sure. Although, honestly, if only we won even just our money back. I never win anything.
>
> Andrés: Don't be like that. Imagine we win. What would you do first?
>
> Lupita: Oh, I don't know… I wish I had a little house on a desert island, with no e-mails or meetings.
>
> Andrés: A desert island? I'd rather have a cruise. Or a yacht, like the millionaires in the movies.
>
> Lupita: You talk as if you were already rich. Yesterday you borrowed money from me for the bus.
>
> Andrés: I'm practicing. My aunt inherited a fortune from an uncle she didn't even know, and now she lives as if every day were her last.
>
> Lupita: Well, I wish I had an aunt like that. OK, I bet you a coffee we don't win.
>
> Andrés: Deal. But if I win, you can pay up at the mansion.

Notes: *sacarse la lotería* (to win the lottery) is everyday Mexican speech beside *ganar la
lotería*; *el reintegro* is getting the price of your ticket back, the smallest win (in the Lotería Nacional, when
your ticket's last digit matches the reintegro number). *La neta* (honestly, the
truth) is informal Mexican, lesson 21. *¿Qué harías?* is a conditional (A2); lesson 14 joins it
to *si*. *El camión* is the city bus in much of Mexico. Andrés's last line uses *si* + present
(a real possibility, A2): the imperfect subjunctive with *si* waits for the next lesson.

## Pronunciation

- Keep the stress of the preterite: *tu-VIE-ra, hi-CIE-ra, fue-ra* (one syllable *fue*), and
  *tu-VIÉ-ra-mos, ha-BLÁ-ra-mos* in *nosotros*.
- Don't confuse *hablara* (imperfect subjunctive: ha-BLA-ra) with *hablará* (future: ha-bla-RÁ).
  The spelling differs only by the accent; the stress moves to the end in the future.
- *Ojalá* is stressed on the last syllable: *o-ja-LÁ*.
- *Lujo, lujoso* have the strong *j*: *LU-ho, lu-HO-so*. *Yate* starts with the *y* of *yo*:
  *YA-te*.

## Common mistakes

- Building from the infinitive: ~~*tenera, hacera, podiera*~~ → *tuviera, hiciera, pudiera*.
  Always start from *ellos* in the preterite.
- Leaving out the *nosotros* accent: ~~*tuvieramos*~~ → *tuviéramos*.
- An extra *i* after *j*: ~~*dijiera, trajiera*~~ → *dijera, trajera* (as in *dijeron*).
- The conditional after *ojalá*: ~~*Ojalá podría*~~ → *Ojalá pudiera*.
- The present after *como si*: ~~*Actúa como si es el jefe*~~ → *Actúa como si fuera el
  jefe.*
- *Soñar de*: ~~*Sueño de viajar*~~ → *Sueño con viajar.*
- Thinking *ojalá* + imperfect is about the past. *Ojalá tuviera tiempo* is about now: "I wish I
  had time (but I don't)".

## Key points

- Imperfect subjunctive = *ellos* preterite − *-ron* + *-ra, -ras, -ra, -ramos, -ran*; accent on
  *nosotros* (*tuviéramos*). Irregular preterites carry over: *fuera, tuviera, hiciera, dijera,
  pudiera, supiera, estuviera, quisiera, diera, pidiera, durmiera, leyera*.
- *-se* forms (*hablase*) mean the same: recognize them; *-ra* is the everyday form in Latin
  America.
- *Ojalá* + present = I hope (possible); *ojalá* + imperfect subjunctive = I wish (unlikely or
  impossible), both about now or the future.
- *Quisiera* = I'd like (polite).
- *Como si* + imperfect subjunctive = as if: *Gasta como si fuera millonario.*
- *Soñar con, imaginarse, apostar a que, por casualidad, ¡Qué casualidad!*

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: If I were mayor: hypothetical si clauses
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In A2 you made real conditions with *si* + present: *Si llueve, nos quedamos en casa* (If it
rains, we'll stay home). In A2 you also learned the conditional, the "would" form (*haría,
podría, tendría*), but only for politeness and advice, because a "would" sentence with "if"
needed a form you didn't have yet. Lesson 13 gave you that form, the imperfect subjunctive. Now
the two come together in the classic hypothetical sentence:

*Si fuera alcaldesa, arreglaría los baches.* — If I were mayor, I'd fix the potholes.

A sentence with *si* has two parts: the **[[si clause]]**, which sets the condition, and the main
clause, which says what happens then. This lesson sorts conditions into three kinds, shows which
tenses go together, and practices them on a topic everyone has opinions about: the problems of a
city and what you would change. (We keep to problems and proposals, not parties.)

## Three kinds of condition

![A chart with three rows. Row 1, real or likely: si + present, main clause in the present, future or a command: Si tengo tiempo, te ayudo. Row 2, unlikely or not true now: si + imperfect subjunctive, main clause in the conditional: Si tuviera tiempo, te ayudaría. Row 3, not true in the past: si + pluperfect subjunctive, main clause in the conditional perfect: Si hubiera tenido tiempo, te habría ayudado (honors 16h1).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### 1. Real or likely

This is A2's kind. You think it may well happen. *Si* + present; the main clause in the
present, the future or a command:

- *Si suben los impuestos, la gente se va a quejar.* — If taxes go up, people will complain.
- *Si ves un bache grande, repórtalo en la aplicación de la alcaldía.* — If you see a big
  pothole, report it in the borough's app.

### 2. Unlikely, imaginary or contrary to fact now

You're imagining it, or you know it isn't so.
*Si* + imperfect subjunctive; the main clause in the conditional:

- *Si fuera alcalde, invertiría en transporte público.* — If I were mayor, I'd invest in
  public transportation. (I'm not mayor.)
- *Si la ciudad tuviera más presupuesto, podría arreglar el drenaje.* — If the city had a
  bigger budget, it could fix the drainage system. (It doesn't.)
- *Si no hubiera tanta corrupción, los impuestos alcanzarían para más.* — If there weren't so
  much corruption, taxes would go further.

### 3. Contrary to fact in the past

*Si* + pluperfect subjunctive (*hubiera* + participle), with
the conditional perfect from lesson 11: *Si hubieran invertido en el drenaje, no se habría
inundado la calle* (If they'd invested in drainage, the street wouldn't have flooded). This is
honors 16h1; for now, just recognize it.

### Real or hypothetical: often your choice

The difference between 1 and 2 is often the speaker's view, not the facts. *Si gano, te invito
a cenar* (If I win, I'll take you out to dinner: I might) and *Si ganara, te invitaría a cenar*
(If I won, I'd take you out to dinner: I doubt it) are both correct about the same game.

Note: when *si* means "whenever" about real past habits, it takes the indicative, like any real
condition: *Si llovía, no salíamos* (Whenever it rained, we didn't go out). That's a fact about
the past, not a hypothesis.

### Either clause can come first

The order is free, as in English. When the *si* clause comes first, put a comma after it; when
it comes second, you usually don't need one.

- *Si tuviera más tiempo, haría ejercicio.*
- *Haría ejercicio si tuviera más tiempo.*

### The two classic mistakes

The conditional never goes in the *si* clause, and neither does the present subjunctive:

| Wrong | Right |
|---|---|
| ~~*Si tendría dinero, compraría una casa.*~~ | *Si tuviera dinero, compraría una casa.* |
| ~~*Si tenga dinero, compro una casa.*~~ | *Si tengo dinero, compro una casa.* |
| ~~*Si lloverá mañana, no salimos.*~~ | *Si llueve mañana, no salimos.* |

Memory hook: the "would" goes in the result, never in the *if*. English agrees: "If I had money,
I would buy", not "If I would have money".

The future is also out of a *si* clause of condition (third row above). Careful: in a reported
question, *si* means "whether", and then any tense is fine: *No sé si vendrá* (I don't know
whether he'll come). That *si* is lesson 16's.

### A decision chart

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing the tenses for a si sentence
  accDescr: Start with the question: does the condition refer to the past and is it contrary to fact? If yes, use si plus pluperfect subjunctive with the conditional perfect, honors 16h1. If no, ask: do you think it may really happen? If yes, use si plus present with the present, future or a command. If no, because it is unlikely, imaginary or untrue now, use si plus imperfect subjunctive with the conditional. A note says never use si plus conditional, si plus present subjunctive or si plus future.
  A["A sentence with si (if)"] --> B{"Past and contrary to fact?"}
  B -- "yes" --> C["si + hubiera + participle, habría + participle (16h1)"]
  B -- "no" --> D{"Could it really happen?"}
  D -- "yes, likely" --> E["si + present: present, future or command"]
  D -- "no: unlikely, imaginary, untrue now" --> F["si + imperfect subjunctive: conditional"]
  F --> G["Never: si + conditional, si + present subjunctive, si + future"]
  E --> G
```

## Asking and advising

- *¿Qué harías si…?* (What would you do if…?) is the standard way to ask someone to imagine:
  *¿Qué harías si fueras alcaldesa? ¿Qué harías si te sacaras la lotería?* Answer with the
  conditional: *Arreglaría las calles.*
- *Si yo fuera tú* (If I were you) gives advice, like A2's *yo que tú*, with a conditional after
  it: *Si yo fuera tú, hablaría con el vecino. / Yo que tú, hablaría con el vecino.* Both are
  common; *yo que tú* is shorter and more informal. Note *fuera tú*, with the subject pronoun
  *tú*, not ~~*fuera ti*~~.
- *De* + infinitive can replace a *si* clause in a more formal style; recognize it in the news and
  in speeches: *De ser así, habría que cambiar la ley* (If that were so, the law would have to
  change).

## The city and its problems

When people talk about what a city should change, these words come up:

- Who governs: in Mexico, the head of a *municipio* (municipality) is officially the *presidente
  municipal* (the Constitution's article 115 says each *municipio* is governed by an elected
  *ayuntamiento*, a town council, headed by one), but in everyday speech and the news people
  often say *el alcalde* or *la alcaldesa* (mayor). Mexico City is divided into sixteen
  *alcaldías* (boroughs), each with its own *alcalde* or *alcaldesa*; they replaced the old
  *delegaciones* on 1 October 2018. *La alcaldía* is also the town hall in many Spanish-speaking
  countries. Residents are *ciudadanos* (citizens).
- Money: *el presupuesto* (budget; also an estimate for a job), *el impuesto* (tax), *invertir*
  (*invierto, invirtió*; to invest) and *la inversión*.
- Problems: *la vivienda* (housing), *la desigualdad* (inequality), *el desempleo*
  (unemployment), *la corrupción*, *la delincuencia* (crime in general) and *la inseguridad*,
  which in Mexican news usually means the lack of public safety: *La inseguridad es el problema
  que más preocupa en la colonia* (Crime is the problem that worries the neighborhood most). It
  also means personal insecurity.
- In the street: *el bache* (pothole), *el drenaje* (drainage, sewer system), *el agua potable*
  (drinking water; feminine, *el agua*), *la escasez de agua* (water shortage), and *el
  alumbrado público* (street lighting), which you'll see in the picture.
- Doing something: *la propuesta* (proposal), *la medida* (measure: *tomar medidas*, to take
  measures), *la ley* (law), *la prioridad* (priority), *aumentar* (to increase), *reducir* (to
  reduce: *reduzco; reduje, redujo, redujeron*), *mejorar* (to improve). *La política* is both
  politics and a policy: *una política de vivienda* (a housing policy).

![A simple map of a neighborhood crossroads with five labeled spots: the town hall with a flag and a clock (la alcaldía), a large hole in the road (el bache), a storm drain grate at a corner with water pooling around it (el drenaje), a street lamp that is out (el alumbrado público), and a public water tank with a tap and a jug (el agua potable). Two residents stand on a corner.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Dialogue: if you were mayor

A radio host in Puebla asks three listeners what they would change if they were mayor.

> Locutora: Buenas tardes. Hoy la pregunta es: ¿qué harían si fueran alcaldes de la ciudad? Tenemos a Rosa en la línea.
>
> Rosa: Hola. Si yo fuera alcaldesa, mi prioridad sería el agua. En mi colonia hay escasez casi todas las semanas. Invertiría en el drenaje y en el agua potable antes que en cualquier otra cosa.
>
> Locutora: ¿Y de dónde sacaría el dinero?
>
> Rosa: Si hubiera menos corrupción, el presupuesto alcanzaría. No subiría los impuestos.
>
> Locutora: Gracias, Rosa. Ahora habla Julián.
>
> Julián: Yo arreglaría los baches. Si las calles estuvieran bien, los camiones no se descompondrían tanto y la gente llegaría más rápido al trabajo.
>
> Locutora: Es una propuesta muy concreta. ¿Y si tuviera que elegir una sola medida?
>
> Julián: Mejoraría el alumbrado. Con más luz, habría menos inseguridad en la noche.
>
> Locutora: Muy bien. Y si nuestros oyentes tienen otras ideas, pueden mandarlas por mensaje.

Translation:

> Host: Good afternoon. Today's question is: what would you do if you were mayors of the city? We have Rosa on the line.
>
> Rosa: Hi. If I were mayor, my priority would be water. In my neighborhood there's a shortage almost every week. I'd invest in drainage and drinking water before anything else.
>
> Host: And where would you get the money?
>
> Rosa: If there were less corruption, the budget would be enough. I wouldn't raise taxes.
>
> Host: Thank you, Rosa. Now Julián is on.
>
> Julián: I'd fix the potholes. If the streets were in good shape, buses wouldn't break down so much and people would get to work faster.
>
> Host: That's a very concrete proposal. And if you had to choose just one measure?
>
> Julián: I'd improve the street lighting. With more light, there'd be less crime at night.
>
> Host: Very good. And if our listeners have other ideas, they can send them by text message.

Notes: *¿Qué harían si fueran…?* is the *ustedes* form, to all the listeners. *Alcanzar* (lesson
01, to reach) also means "to be enough": *el presupuesto alcanzaría*. *Hubiera* here is the
imperfect subjunctive of *haber* (there were). The host's last line is a real condition (*si* +
present + present). *Descomponerse* (A2) is to break down.

## Pronunciation

- *Si* (if) has no accent and is unstressed, joined to the next word: *si-fue-ra*. *Sí* (yes)
  is stressed.
- *Escasez*, with seseo: *es-ka-SES*; both *z* and *c* before *e* sound like *s*. The plural is
  rare (*escaseces*).
- *Ciudadano*: *siu-da-DA-no* (two vowels in one syllable at the start). *Bache*: *BA-che*.
- Say the conditional's *-ía* clearly: *arreglaría* = *a-rre-gla-RÍ-a*.

## Common mistakes

- *Si* + conditional: ~~*Si sería alcalde…*~~ → *Si fuera alcalde…*
- *Si* + present subjunctive: ~~*Si tenga tiempo…*~~ → *Si tengo tiempo…* (real) or *Si tuviera
  tiempo…* (hypothetical).
- Mixing the kinds: ~~*Si tuviera tiempo, te ayudo*~~. With an imperfect subjunctive after *si*,
  use the conditional in the main clause: *te ayudaría*.
- Translating "if I were you" word for word with *estar*: ~~*Si estuviera tú*~~ → *Si yo fuera
  tú.*
- *Invertir* is a stem changer like *preferir*: *invierto*, and *invirtió, invirtieron* in the
  preterite, so *invirtiera*. *Reducir* is like *conducir*: *reduzco, redujo, redujera*.

## Key points

- Real: *si* + present → present / future / command. Hypothetical now: *si* + imperfect
  subjunctive → conditional (*Si fuera alcaldesa, arreglaría los baches*). Past: *si* +
  pluperfect subjunctive → conditional perfect (16h1).
- Either clause first; a comma after a *si* clause that comes first.
- Never *si* + conditional, present subjunctive or future in a condition.
- *¿Qué harías si…? Si yo fuera tú… = Yo que tú… De ser así* (formal).
- City words: *el alcalde, la alcaldía, el municipio, el presupuesto, el impuesto, invertir, el
  bache, el drenaje, el agua potable, la escasez, la inseguridad, la propuesta, la medida.*

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: She asked me to: the subjunctive in the past
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 1 taught the subjunctive after verbs of wanting, asking, feeling and doubting, all in the
present: *Mi jefa quiere que termine el informe* (My boss wants me to finish the report). But
much of what we say about work happens in the past: what the manager asked yesterday, what you
were afraid of, what the client wanted. When the main verb moves into the past, the subjunctive
after it moves too, into the imperfect subjunctive from lesson 13:

*Mi jefa quería que terminara el informe.* — My boss wanted me to finish the report.

This matching of tenses is called the **[[sequence of tenses]]**. This lesson shows how it works with
every kind of trigger you know, with the conditional (*Me gustaría que…*), and in one of the
most useful patterns at work: reporting what someone asked or told you to do. The theme is the
office: bosses, colleagues, tasks and deadlines.

## The sequence of tenses

The trigger (*quiero que, me pide que, es importante que, para que…*) works exactly as in
module 1. What changes is the tense of the subjunctive, which follows the tense of the main verb.

![A two-row chart. Top row: a main verb in the present, future, present perfect or a command (quiere, querrá, ha pedido, pídele) points to the present subjunctive: que vengas. Bottom row: a main verb in the preterite, imperfect, pluperfect or conditional (quiso, quería, había pedido, querría, me gustaría) points to the imperfect subjunctive: que vinieras.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Present main verb → present subjunctive | Past or conditional main verb → imperfect subjunctive |
|---|---|
| *Quiero que vengas.* | *Quería que vinieras.* — I wanted you to come. |
| *Me pide que lo llame.* | *Me pidió que lo llamara.* — He asked me to call him. |
| *Es importante que lleguemos a tiempo.* | *Era importante que llegáramos a tiempo.* — It was important for us to arrive on time. |
| *No creo que sea posible.* | *No creía que fuera posible.* — I didn't think it was possible. |
| *Le molesta que no lo inviten.* | *Le molestó que no lo invitaran.* — It bothered him that they didn't invite him. |
| *Busca a alguien que sepa Excel.* | *Buscaba a alguien que supiera Excel.* — She was looking for someone who knew Excel. |

The same happens after the conjunctions of module 2:

- *Te lo explico para que lo entiendas → Te lo expliqué para que lo entendieras.* (so that you
  would understand it)
- *Salió sin que nadie lo viera.* — He left without anyone seeing him.
- *Mandé el informe antes de que la gerente lo pidiera.* — I sent the report before the manager
  asked for it.

And with the *cuando* of lesson 07: in a past story, a future seen from the past takes the
imperfect subjunctive: *Me dijo que me avisaría cuando llegara el cliente* (She said she'd let
me know when the client arrived).

### The conditional counts as past

A main verb in the conditional also takes the imperfect subjunctive. This is how you make polite
requests and wishes about other people:

- *Me gustaría que me ayudaras con la presentación.* — I'd like you to help me with the
  presentation.
- *Preferiría que habláramos mañana.* — I'd rather we talked tomorrow.
- *Sería mejor que usted autorizara el gasto.* — It would be better if you authorized the
  expense.

Compare A2's *Me gustaría ayudarte* (same subject: infinitive) with *Me gustaría que me
ayudaras* (a different subject: *que* + imperfect subjunctive). The rule from lesson 01 still
decides between infinitive and *que*.

After *me gustaría* you will also hear the present subjunctive, especially in Latin America:
*Me gustaría que me ayudes*. The RAE says the imperfect subjunctive is the most normal choice
after a conditional but that the present there can't be called wrong. This course uses the
imperfect subjunctive, which is always right.

### When the clause is in the past but the main verb isn't

The sequence is a strong tendency, not a law. When the main verb is in the present but the
subjunctive clause is about something past, the imperfect subjunctive is also normal: *No creo
que lo supiera* (I don't think he knew), *Me alegra que vinieras* (I'm glad you came; *que hayas
venido* from lesson 03 is just as good). Use that when you need it; when both verbs are about the
same time, follow the chart.

## Asking and telling: decir que + two moods

With *decir* and *escribir* (and *avisar*, *recordar*), the mood after *que* changes the
meaning:

- Information → indicative. *Me dijo que había llamado.* — He told me he had called.
- An instruction → subjunctive. *Me dijo que lo llamara.* — He told me to call him.

| What the boss said | Reported as information | Reported as an instruction |
|---|---|---|
| "Mando el informe." | *Dijo que mandaba el informe.* (he said he was sending it) | |
| "Manda el informe." | | *Me dijo que mandara el informe.* (he told me to send it) |
| "Llámame." | | *Me pidió / me dijo que lo llamara.* |
| "No llegues tarde." | | *Me pidió que no llegara tarde.* |

Commands, requests and advice from the past all come out the same way: *pedir, decir, aconsejar,
recomendar, exigir, rogar* + *que* + imperfect subjunctive. Note how the people change: "Llámame"
(call me) becomes *que lo llamara* (that I call him). Lesson 16 shows every other shift in
reported speech.

## At the office

Many of these words describe the people and things in the picture below:

- People: *el gerente* (manager; *la gerente*, also *la gerenta*), *el supervisor / la
  supervisora*, *el colega / la colega* (colleague; A2's *el compañero de trabajo* is the
  everyday word, *colega* sounds a bit more professional; in Spain *colega* is also an informal
  "buddy").
- Things: *el escritorio* (desk), *el documento*, *el informe* (written report), *la presentación*
  (presentation), *el recordatorio* (reminder), *la fecha límite* (deadline).
- Organizing work: *encargar* (to ask someone to do a job: *Me encargaron el informe*; also to
  order goods), *encargarse de* (to be in charge of, to take care of: *Yo me encargo de las
  copias*), *delegar* (to delegate), *coordinar*, *autorizar* (to authorize).
- Time: *la jornada laboral* (workday, working hours), *las horas extra* (overtime; *horas
  extras* is also correct: grammars accept both forms), *la puntualidad*.
- Results: *el desempeño* (performance at work), *la productividad*, *eficiente*, *la
  evaluación* (appraisal), *evaluar* (*evalúo, evalúas…*: the *ú* is stressed), *el aumento*
  (raise; also an increase), *la renuncia* (resignation: *presentar la renuncia*).
- *El ambiente laboral*: the work environment, the atmosphere among people at work.
- *El home office*: working from home. In Mexico this English loan is the everyday term (*hago
  home office los viernes*). The law calls it *teletrabajo*: a reform of Mexico's Ley Federal del
  Trabajo, published on 11 January 2021, regulates it for people who work more than 40 % of their
  time at home or another place they choose. *El teletrabajo* is also the usual word in Spain.

![An office scene, labeled: a manager (la gerente) pointing at a wall calendar where the 20th is circled in red (la fecha límite), a desk (el escritorio) with a computer, a bound report with a bar chart on its cover (el informe), a sticky note on the monitor that says "¡No olvides!" (el recordatorio), and a wall clock.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Dialogue: what did the manager want?

Valeria comes back from a week off. Her colleague Toño tells her what happened while she was
away.

> Valeria: ¿Qué tal la semana? ¿Me perdí de algo?
>
> Toño: Uf, de mucho. La gerente quería que termináramos el informe trimestral antes del viernes.
>
> Valeria: ¿Antes del viernes? Pero la fecha límite era el día 20.
>
> Toño: Ya sé. Pero el director le pidió que lo presentara en la junta del lunes. Así que nos encargó a todos una parte.
>
> Valeria: ¿Y a mí? ¿Qué me tocó?
>
> Toño: Te dejó un recordatorio en el escritorio. Te pide que revises las gráficas. Ah, y me dijo que te dijera que no te preocuparas, que tienes hasta el miércoles.
>
> Valeria: Menos mal. ¿Y tú hiciste horas extra?
>
> Toño: Dos noches. No me gustó que no nos avisaran antes, pero la gerente nos autorizó el pago. Y quiere que el lunes hagamos home office para que descansemos.
>
> Valeria: Bueno, eso sí está bien. Me gustaría que siempre organizaran así el trabajo.

Translation:

> Valeria: How was the week? Did I miss anything?
>
> Toño: Phew, a lot. The manager wanted us to finish the quarterly report before Friday.
>
> Valeria: Before Friday? But the deadline was the 20th.
>
> Toño: I know. But the director asked her to present it at Monday's meeting. So she gave each of us a part.
>
> Valeria: And me? What did I get?
>
> Toño: She left you a reminder on your desk. She's asking you to check the charts. Oh, and she told me to tell you not to worry, that you have until Wednesday.
>
> Valeria: Thank goodness. And did you do overtime?
>
> Toño: Two nights. I didn't like that they didn't warn us earlier, but the manager authorized the pay. And she wants us to work from home on Monday so that we can rest.
>
> Valeria: Well, that's good. I'd like them to organize the work like that all the time.

Notes: *perderse de algo* (to miss out on something) is common in Mexico. *¿Qué me tocó?* =
What fell to me? (*tocar* = to be someone's turn or share). Look at the tenses: *quería que
termináramos, le pidió que lo presentara, me dijo que te dijera que no te preocuparas* (past →
imperfect subjunctive), but *te pide que revises, quiere que hagamos* (present → present
subjunctive, because the note and the plan are still current). *Que tienes hasta el miércoles*
is information, so it's indicative, and it stays in the present because it's still true.

## Pronunciation

- Keep the stress of each imperfect subjunctive on the same syllable as the preterite *ellos*
  form: *ter-mi-NÁ-ra-mos, pre-sen-TA-ra, pre-o-cu-PA-ras*.
- *Evalúo* has a stressed *ú*: *e-va-LÚ-o*; *evaluamos* doesn't: *e-va-LUA-mos*.
- *Home office* is said much as in English, *jom ÓF-is*, with a Spanish *j* sound for the *h*.
- *Gerente*: *he-REN-te* (*g* before *e* = the *j* sound).

## Common mistakes

- Keeping the present subjunctive after a past verb: ~~*Quería que vengas*~~ → *Quería que
  vinieras.*
- The indicative for an instruction: ~~*Me pidió que lo llamaba*~~ → *Me pidió que lo llamara.*
  (*Pedir* always reports a request: subjunctive.)
- *Que* + subjunctive with the same subject: ~~*Quería que yo terminara*~~ (said about yourself)
  → *Quería terminar.*
- Writing *evaluo* without the accent: → *evalúo, evalúe.*

## Key points

- Sequence of tenses: present / future / command / present perfect + present subjunctive;
  preterite / imperfect / pluperfect / conditional + imperfect subjunctive.
- The triggers are the same as in modules 1 and 2: *Quería que vinieras; Era importante que
  llegáramos; No creía que fuera posible; Salió sin que nadie lo viera.*
- Polite wishes about others: *Me gustaría que…, Preferiría que…, Sería mejor que…* +
  imperfect subjunctive.
- *Decir que* + indicative reports information; + subjunctive reports an instruction: *Me dijo
  que lo llamara* (told me to call him).
- Office words: *el gerente, el colega, el informe, la fecha límite, encargarse de, las horas
  extra, el home office, el desempeño, la evaluación, el aumento, la renuncia.*

complete the lesson.

lessons.title: He said he would call: reported speech with tense changes
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In A2 (lesson 21) you reported what people say with *dice que* (no change of tense) and
*dijo que* + the preterite or the imperfect: *Dijo que estaba cansada.* Since then you've
learned the pluperfect (lesson 09), the imperfect subjunctive (13) and the sequence of tenses
(15). That's everything you need for full **[[reported speech]]**: retelling someone's words after a
past verb like *dijo, contó, explicó, preguntó*, with every tense moved one step into the past.

*"Te llamo mañana." → Dijo que me llamaría al día siguiente.* — He said he would call me the
next day.

This lesson gives the complete set of shifts, the cases where you don't shift, the time and place
words that change with them, reported questions, and the verbs that report. The theme suits it
perfectly: gossip, rumors, misunderstandings and who said what.

## The tense shifts

When the reporting verb is in the past, each tense in the original words moves back:

![Arrows from original words on the left to reported words on the right. "Estoy cansada" goes to dijo que estaba cansada (present to imperfect). "Perdí el vuelo" and "He perdido el vuelo" go to dijo que había perdido el vuelo (preterite and perfect to pluperfect). "Llegaré tarde" goes to dijo que llegaría tarde (future to conditional). "Voy a llamar" goes to dijo que iba a llamar. "Llámame" goes to me dijo que lo llamara (command to imperfect subjunctive). A box at the bottom says the imperfect, pluperfect and conditional don't change.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Original words | Reported after *dijo que…* |
|---|---|
| present: *"Estoy cansada."* | imperfect: *Dijo que estaba cansada.* |
| preterite: *"Perdí el vuelo."* | pluperfect: *Dijo que había perdido el vuelo.* (the preterite is also common: *que perdió el vuelo*) |
| present perfect: *"He terminado."* | pluperfect: *Dijo que había terminado.* |
| future: *"Llegaré tarde."* | conditional: *Dijo que llegaría tarde.* |
| *ir a*: *"Voy a llamar."* | *iba a*: *Dijo que iba a llamar.* |
| command: *"Llámame."* | imperfect subjunctive: *Me dijo que lo llamara.* (lesson 15) |
| present subjunctive: *"Quiero que vengas."* | imperfect subjunctive: *Me dijo que quería que viniera.* |
| imperfect, pluperfect, conditional | no change: *"Era tarde" → Dijo que era tarde.* |

Two notes:

- A present about the future can become an imperfect: *"Vengo mañana" → Dijo que venía al día
  siguiente*, just as correct as *Dijo que vendría al día siguiente*.
- With *dice que* (present), nothing shifts: *Dice que está cansada. Dice que llegará tarde.*

### When not to shift

If what was said is still true now, you may keep the original tense: *Me dijo que vive en
Puebla* (she still lives there). *Me dijo que vivía en Puebla* is also correct and simply doesn't
say whether she still does. Both are fine Spanish; the present underlines that it's still true.
The same goes for general truths: *El profesor explicó que el agua hierve a cien grados.*

### People and possessives

Pronouns and possessives change to fit the person who is reporting, as in English:

- Ana, to me: *"Tu hermano me prestó su carro."* → *Ana me dijo que mi hermano le había prestado
  su carro.*
- Luis, to you: *"Te lo explico yo."* → *Luis me dijo que él me lo explicaba.*

Also *venir* often becomes *ir* and *traer* becomes *llevar* if the place has changed: *"Ven a mi
casa" → Me dijo que fuera a su casa.*

## Time and place words

A report made later, somewhere else, moves the time and place words too:

| In the original | In the report |
|---|---|
| *hoy* | *ese día* |
| *ayer* | *el día anterior* |
| *mañana* | *al día siguiente* |
| *la semana que viene, el mes que viene* | *la semana siguiente, el mes siguiente* |
| *la semana pasada* | *la semana anterior* |
| *ahora* | *en ese momento, entonces* |
| *aquí, acá* | *allí, ahí, allá* |
| *este, esta* | *ese, esa* |

Use them when the day has changed. If you report today what someone said this morning, *hoy* and
*mañana* stay: *Me dijo hace una hora que mañana no hay clase.*

## Reported questions

A question is reported with *preguntar* (or *querer saber*):

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How to report a question
  accDescr: Start with the original question. If it has a question word such as dónde, cuándo, qué or por qué, keep the word with its accent after preguntó: Me preguntó dónde vivía. If it is a yes or no question, use si, without an accent: Me preguntó si iba. In both cases shift the tenses as in statements and drop the question marks.
  A["The original question"] --> B{"Does it have a question word?"}
  B -- "yes: dónde, cuándo, qué, por qué…" --> C["Me preguntó dónde vivía (keep the accent)"]
  B -- "no: a yes/no question" --> D["Me preguntó si iba (si, no accent)"]
  C --> E["Shift the tenses; no question marks"]
  D --> E
```

- yes/no questions take *si* (whether): *"¿Vienes a la fiesta?" → Me preguntó si iba a la fiesta.*
- questions with a question word keep the word, with its accent: *"¿Dónde vives?" → Me preguntó
  dónde vivía. "¿Por qué no me invitaste?" → Me preguntó por qué no lo había invitado.*

The tenses shift exactly as in statements, and the word order becomes that of a statement in
English ("where I lived", not "where did I live"); in Spanish the subject can still follow the
verb: *Me preguntó qué quería mi hermana.* No question marks in the report. In conversation
you'll often hear an extra *que*: *Me preguntó que si iba.* It's normal in speech; in writing,
use *Me preguntó si iba.*

## Verbs that report

*Decir* repeated five times sounds flat. These verbs say *how* something was said (A2 words
first):

| Verb | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *contar, explicar* | to tell, to explain | *Me contó que se había peleado con su novio.* |
| *afirmar, asegurar* | to state, to assure | *Aseguró que no sabía nada.* |
| *advertir* | to warn | *Me advirtió que no confiara en él.* (+ subjunctive: an instruction) |
| *aclarar* | to clarify | *Aclaró que era una broma.* |
| *negar* | to deny | *Negó que fuera verdad.* (+ subjunctive, lesson 04) |
| *admitir* | to admit | *Admitió que había exagerado.* |
| *mencionar* | to mention | *Mencionó que se iba a mudar.* |
| *desmentir* | to deny (a report, a rumor) | *La empresa desmintió el rumor.* |
| *susurrar* | to whisper | *Me susurró que tenía un secreto.* |
| *presumir* | to show off, to boast | *Presumía de que su hijo era el mejor de la clase.* |

*Presumir* (to show off) is very common in Mexico, with *de* or with a direct object: *Le encanta
presumir de su carro nuevo / presumir su carro nuevo.* It also means "to presume" in formal writing.

## Gossip and its words

*El chisme* is a piece of gossip, and gossip in general (*Spain: el cotilleo*); *chismear* is to
gossip, and *un chismoso / una chismosa* is a gossip (also an adjective: *¡Qué chismoso eres!*).
*El rumor* is a rumor; *al parecer* and *por lo visto* (apparently) and *supuestamente*
(supposedly) report what you've heard without vouching for it. *Guardar un secreto* is to keep a
secret. *Una indirecta* is a dig or a hint (*echar indirectas*, to make digs). *El malentendido*
is a misunderstanding; *la discusión* is an argument (also a discussion), and *discutir* is to
argue (also to discuss). *Exagerar, criticar* (*critiqué*) and *la crítica* (criticism; also a
review) complete the set. *El grito* is a shout; *interrumpir*, to interrupt; *la versión*, a
version of a story.

To quote words exactly, use *textualmente* (word for word) and *las comillas* (quotation
marks): *Me dijo, textualmente: "No vuelvo".* In Spanish the period goes after the closing
quotation mark.

## Dialogue: the version that reached Marisol

Marisol hears a rumor at a family party in Monterrey and checks it with her cousin Beto.

> Marisol: Oye, Beto, ¿es cierto que te vas a casar? Mi tía me dijo que ya habías comprado el anillo.
>
> Beto: ¿Qué? ¿Quién te dijo eso?
>
> Marisol: Por lo visto, tu mamá le contó a mi tía que ibas a dar una sorpresa en la cena de hoy.
>
> Beto: Ay, no. Fue un malentendido. Yo le dije a mi mamá que tenía una noticia importante, nada más.
>
> Marisol: ¿Y qué noticia es?
>
> Beto: Que me dieron el trabajo en Canadá. Le pedí que no se lo dijera a nadie hasta la cena.
>
> Marisol: Pues ya lo sabe media familia, pero en otra versión. Al parecer, tu prima Karla agregó que la novia era de Guadalajara.
>
> Beto: ¡Si ni siquiera tengo novia! Esta familia es más chismosa que una telenovela.
>
> Marisol: Mejor desmiéntelo hoy antes de que alguien te pregunte cuándo es la boda.

Translation:

> Marisol: Hey, Beto, is it true you're getting married? My aunt told me you'd already bought the ring.
>
> Beto: What? Who told you that?
>
> Marisol: Apparently, your mom told my aunt you were going to make a surprise announcement at today's dinner.
>
> Beto: Oh, no. It was a misunderstanding. I told my mom I had some important news, that's all.
>
> Marisol: And what's the news?
>
> Beto: That I got the job in Canada. I asked her not to tell anyone until the dinner.
>
> Marisol: Well, half the family already knows, but in a different version. Apparently, your cousin Karla added that the bride was from Guadalajara.
>
> Beto: I don't even have a girlfriend! This family gossips more than a soap opera.
>
> Marisol: You'd better deny it today, before someone asks you when the wedding is.

Notes: every report shifts: *"Ya compró el anillo" → me dijo que ya había comprado el anillo;
"Va a dar una sorpresa" → que ibas a dar una sorpresa; "Tengo una noticia" → que tenía una
noticia; "No se lo digas a nadie" → le pedí que no se lo dijera a nadie.* *Si ni siquiera…* is an
exclamation (I don't even…!), not a condition. *Desmiéntelo* is the tú command of *desmentir*
(*desmiento*) with *lo* attached; *antes de que* + present subjunctive is lesson 07.

## Pronunciation

- *Chisme, chismoso*: *CHIS-me, chis-MO-so*; the *s* before *m* is an *s* sound (before *m* it is
  often slightly buzzed, like a soft English *z*; in some regions it weakens almost to an *h*).
- *Malentendido* is one word: *ma-len-ten-DI-do*.
- In reported questions, the question word is still stressed: *me preguntó DÓN-de vivía*; *si*
  (whether) is not: *me preguntó si-I-ba*.
- *Susurrar* has a trilled *rr* and then a tapped final *r*: *su-su-RRAR*.

## Common mistakes

- Not shifting the future: ~~*Dijo que vendrá*~~ when the moment has passed → *Dijo que
  vendría.* (*Dijo que venía* is also fine.)
- An indicative for a reported command: ~~*Me dijo que lo llamaba*~~ (that means "he said he
  was calling him") → *Me dijo que lo llamara.*
- Dropping the accent on question words: ~~*Me preguntó donde vivía*~~ → *dónde vivía.*
- Keeping *mañana* and *aquí* in a report made days later and elsewhere: → *al día siguiente,
  allí.*
- The period before the closing quotation mark: ~~*"No vuelvo."*~~ at the end of a sentence →
  *"No vuelvo".*

## Key points

- After a past reporting verb: present → imperfect; preterite / perfect → pluperfect (the
  preterite also stays); future → conditional; *ir a* → *iba a*; command or present subjunctive
  → imperfect subjunctive; imperfect, pluperfect, conditional unchanged.
- Facts that are still true may keep the present: *Dijo que vive en Puebla.*
- *hoy → ese día, ayer → el día anterior, mañana → al día siguiente, aquí → allí, este → ese.*
- Questions: *preguntar si…* (yes/no) or *preguntar dónde / cuándo / por qué…* (with the accent).
- Report with variety: *contar, explicar, asegurar, advertir, admitir, mencionar, negar,
  desmentir, susurrar, presumir.*
- *El chisme, el rumor, por lo visto, al parecer, supuestamente, el malentendido, textualmente,
  entre comillas.*
