lessons.title: Honors: Taking part in a discussion
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 19 taught you to build an argument on paper, where nobody interrupts. A live discussion is
different: you have to get a turn, keep it, answer someone who disagrees, admit what is true in
their point and bring the talk back to the topic. Lesson 20's register matters here too: a radio
panel, a meeting at work or a neighbors' assembly calls for polite, fairly formal Spanish. This
honors lesson gives you the phrases for each move, an original transcript of a radio roundtable,
and the skills behind the conversation part of the DELE B1 speaking test.

## Who's who

*Una mesa redonda* (a roundtable, a panel discussion) has guests and *un moderador* or *una
moderadora*, who *modera* the debate: introduces the topic, gives the floor (*da la palabra*, or
formally *concede la palabra*) and keeps time. Each turn to speak is *una intervención*, and to
speak in a discussion is *intervenir* (conjugated like *venir*: *intervengo, intervino,
intervendré*; command *intervén*). At the end, the moderator may ask whether there is *consenso*
(consensus).

Moderators' phrases:

- *Tiene la palabra la doctora Ruiz.* — Dr. Ruiz has the floor.
- *Le doy la palabra a…* — I'll give the floor to…
- *Por cuestión de tiempo, le pido que sea breve.* — For reasons of time, I'll ask you to be brief.
- *Retomemos la pregunta inicial.* — Let's go back to the opening question. (*retomar* = to take up
  again)
- *Para cerrar, ¿llegamos a algún consenso?* — To close, have we reached any consensus?

## Getting, keeping and giving back the floor

| Move | Tú | Usted |
|---|---|---|
| Ask for a turn | *¿Puedo decir algo?* | *Si me permite, quisiera intervenir.* |
| Interrupt politely | *Perdona que te interrumpa, pero…* | *Perdone que lo / la interrumpa, pero…* |
| Keep your turn | *Déjame terminar.* | *Permítame terminar, por favor.* |
| Pick up again | *Como iba diciendo…* | *Como le decía…* |
| Return to the topic | *Volviendo al tema…* | *Si me permite volver al tema…* |
| Give the turn back | *Te escucho.* | *Adelante, por favor.* |

*Perdona que te interrumpa* has the subjunctive because *perdonar que* reacts to something, like
the emotion verbs of lesson 03 (*me molesta que*). Notice the object pronoun: *te* for *tú*, *lo*
or *la* for *usted* (a man or a woman).

## Conceding, reformulating and qualifying

To concede (*conceder*) is to admit part of the other side before you answer it. It makes you
sound fair, and it is the spoken version of lesson 17's *aunque*:

- *Tiene razón en que el agua es cara, pero…* — You're right that water is expensive, but… (*en
  que* + indicative: you accept a fact)
- *Es cierto que…, pero… / Reconozco que…, pero…* — It's true that…, but… / I admit that…, but…
- *Le concedo que el plan es ambicioso.* — I'll grant you that the plan is ambitious.
- *No digo que sea fácil, pero…* — I'm not saying it's easy, but… (*no digo que* + subjunctive)

To reformulate, say it again in other words: *es decir, o sea* (A2 honors), *lo que quiero decir
es que…, en otras palabras…*.

To qualify (*matizar*: *maticé* in the yo preterite) is to accept a statement with a limit: *Sí,
pero habría que matizar: no todos los barrios gastan igual.* The noun is *el matiz* (nuance; plural
*los matices*): *Estoy de acuerdo, con un matiz.*

## Disagreeing without fighting

From softest to firmest:

- *Entiendo lo que dice, pero yo lo veo de otra manera.* — I understand what you're saying, but I
  see it differently.
- *No estoy del todo de acuerdo.* — I don't entirely agree.
- *Tengo una objeción.* — I have an objection. (*la objeción*)
- *Discrepo de usted en ese punto.* — I disagree with you on that point. (*discrepar*, formal)
- *No es que el plan sea malo, sino que es caro.* — It's not that the plan is bad; it's that it's
  expensive. (*no es que* + subjunctive, *sino que* + indicative)

Avoid *¡Eso es mentira!* or *No tiene razón* in a formal discussion: they attack the person, not
the idea.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: A polite disagreement in four moves
  accDescr: Four boxes in a column. First, show you listened: Entiendo lo que dice. Second, concede part of the point: Tiene razón en que... Third, counter with pero and a reason: pero yo lo veo de otra manera, ya que... Fourth, give the turn back: ¿Qué opina usted? A side note says that if the other person interrupts, you can say Permítame terminar.
  A["1. Show you listened: Entiendo lo que dice…"] --> B["2. Concede: Tiene razón en que…"]
  B --> C["3. Counter: …pero yo lo veo de otra manera, ya que…"]
  C --> D["4. Give the turn back: ¿Qué opina usted?"]
  N["If someone interrupts: Permítame terminar."] -.- C
```

## Transcript: a radio roundtable

*Mesa abierta* is an invented call-in program on a city radio station. Today's topic: should
households that use a lot of water pay a higher rate?

> Moderadora (Lucía Ibarra): Buenas tardes. Hoy en la mesa redonda nos acompañan el ingeniero Arturo Salas, la señora Paola Méndez, de una asociación de vecinos, y el señor Javier Cruz, dueño de una lavandería. Ingeniero, tiene la palabra.
>
> Arturo Salas: Gracias. En primer lugar, el agua es un recurso limitado. Si quien gasta más paga más, todos cuidamos más.
>
> Paola Méndez: Perdone que lo interrumpa, ingeniero, pero en mi colonia hay agua solo tres días a la semana. No es que gastemos mucho, sino que no llega.
>
> Arturo Salas: Permítame terminar, por favor. Tiene razón en que el servicio es desigual. Por eso propongo cobrar más solo a partir de cierto consumo.
>
> Javier Cruz: Si me permiten, quisiera intervenir. Una lavandería no es una casa. Reconozco que gasto mucha agua, pero es mi trabajo.
>
> Moderadora: Una objeción importante. Ingeniero, ¿qué le responde?
>
> Arturo Salas: Habría que matizar. Los negocios tienen otra tarifa; yo hablo de los hogares. Lo que quiero decir es que una casa con alberca no debería pagar lo mismo que un departamento pequeño.
>
> Paola Méndez: En eso estoy de acuerdo, con un matiz: primero arreglen las fugas. Se pierde muchísima agua en la calle.
>
> Javier Cruz: Discrepo de la señora en una cosa: arreglar fugas tarda años. Mientras tanto, algo hay que hacer.
>
> Moderadora: Volviendo al tema, por cuestión de tiempo: ¿hay algún consenso?
>
> Arturo Salas: Creo que sí: tarifa más alta para el consumo alto de los hogares, y al mismo tiempo, un plan para las fugas.
>
> Paola Méndez: Con tal de que el plan de fugas empiece este año, lo acepto.
>
> Moderadora: Muchas gracias a los tres por sus intervenciones. Nos escuchamos la próxima semana.

> Moderator (Lucía Ibarra): Good afternoon. On today's roundtable we have the engineer Arturo Salas, Mrs. Paola Méndez, from a neighborhood association, and Mr. Javier Cruz, the owner of a laundromat. Mr. Salas, you have the floor.
>
> Arturo Salas: Thank you. First of all, water is a limited resource. If whoever uses more pays more, we all take more care.
>
> Paola Méndez: Excuse me for interrupting, Mr. Salas, but in my neighborhood there's water only three days a week. It's not that we use a lot; it's that it doesn't arrive.
>
> Arturo Salas: Please let me finish. You're right that the service is uneven. That's why I propose charging more only above a certain level of use.
>
> Javier Cruz: If you'll allow me, I'd like to say something. A laundromat isn't a house. I admit I use a lot of water, but it's my job.
>
> Moderator: An important objection. Mr. Salas, what's your answer?
>
> Arturo Salas: That needs qualifying. Businesses have a different rate; I'm talking about households. What I mean is that a house with a swimming pool shouldn't pay the same as a small apartment.
>
> Paola Méndez: I agree with that, with one qualification: first fix the leaks. A huge amount of water is lost in the street.
>
> Javier Cruz: I disagree with Mrs. Méndez on one thing: fixing leaks takes years. Meanwhile, something has to be done.
>
> Moderator: Back to the topic, since time is short: is there any consensus?
>
> Arturo Salas: I think so: a higher rate for high household use, and at the same time, a plan for the leaks.
>
> Paola Méndez: Provided that the leak plan starts this year, I accept it.
>
> Moderator: Many thanks to all three of you for your contributions. We'll talk again next week.

*La lavandería* = laundromat; *la tarifa* = rate; *el hogar* = household, home; *la alberca* =
swimming pool (Mexico; Spain *la piscina*); *la fuga* = leak; *la colonia* = neighborhood (A2).
In Mexico an engineer is often addressed as *ingeniero* (or *inge*, informally), as a lawyer is
*licenciado*. The guests use *usted* throughout, as is usual on air with people you don't know.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: from blunt to polite

Your colleague says: *Hay que cerrar la oficina los viernes.* Your first thought is *¡Qué mala
idea!* Build a polite answer in three steps:

1. Show you listened: *Entiendo lo que dices…*
2. Concede what you can: *…y tienes razón en que ahorraríamos luz…*
3. Disagree and give a reason: *…pero yo lo veo de otra manera: los clientes llaman los viernes.*

Result: *Entiendo lo que dices, y tienes razón en que ahorraríamos luz, pero yo lo veo de otra
manera: los clientes llaman los viernes.* (*ahorraríamos* is a conditional: "we would save".)

### Example 2: holding your turn

You're explaining your point and someone starts talking over you. Three options, from gentle to
firm:

- *Un momento, ya termino.* — One moment, I'm almost done.
- *Déjame terminar y luego te escucho.* — Let me finish and then I'll listen to you.
- *Perdona, pero no he terminado.* — Sorry, but I haven't finished.

When you finish, give the turn back explicitly (*Ahora sí, te escucho*): it shows that you
interrupted the interruption, not the person.

### Example 3: the moderator's summary

At the end of a meeting, the moderator joins the points with lesson 17 and 18 connectors:
*Aunque no estamos de acuerdo en todo, hay consenso en dos puntos: subir la tarifa para el consumo
alto, siempre que se arreglen las fugas, y revisar el plan en un año.* — Although we don't agree
on everything, there's consensus on two points: raising the rate for high use, as long as the
leaks get fixed, and reviewing the plan in a year.

## The skill behind DELE B1 speaking task 2

In the DELE B1 speaking test, the first task is a short talk you prepare, and the second is a
conversation with the examiner about it, lasting a few minutes (3 to 4, according to the official
exam guide). Expect questions and mild challenges about what you said. The moves in this lesson
are the skills that task tests: answer directly, justify (*porque, ya que*), concede (*Es
cierto que…, pero…*), reformulate when you're stuck (*Lo que quiero decir es que…*) and, if you
didn't understand, ask politely (*¿Me puede repetir la pregunta, por favor?*). Describe your
reasons; don't just say *sí* or *no*. The exam's own guide, from the Instituto Cervantes, has the
official description and sample tasks.

## Common mistakes

- ~~*Perdona que te interrumpo*~~ → *Perdona que te interrumpa.* *Perdonar que* takes the
  subjunctive.
- ~~*Tienes razón que…*~~ → *Tienes razón en que…*: keep the *en*.
- ~~*Discrepo a usted*~~ → *Discrepo de usted* (or *con usted*).
- ~~*Yo intervení*~~ → *Yo intervine.* *Intervenir* is conjugated like *venir*.
- Conceding and then never coming back with *pero*: the listener hears only agreement.
- Using *o sea* in every sentence: in a formal discussion, vary it with *es decir* and *lo que
  quiero decir es que*.

## Key points

- Roles: *la mesa redonda, el moderador / la moderadora, moderar, la intervención, intervenir,
  dar / conceder la palabra, el consenso*.
- Turns: *Si me permite, quisiera intervenir; Perdone que lo interrumpa; Permítame terminar;
  Volviendo al tema; Retomemos…*.
- Concede, then answer: *Tiene razón en que… pero; Es cierto que… pero; No digo que* + subjunctive.
- Qualify and reformulate: *Habría que matizar, con un matiz, Lo que quiero decir es que…*.
- Disagree politely: *Yo lo veo de otra manera, No estoy del todo de acuerdo, Tengo una objeción,
  Discrepo de usted, No es que* + subjunctive, *sino que* + indicative.

lessons.title: Honors: Mexican paperwork: documents and formal requests
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Anyone who lives, studies or works in Mexico meets *los trámites* (A2: official procedures): a
school enrollment, a new ID, a certificate from the university. The language is compact and
formal, and the lists of requirements (*los requisitos*, A2) are full of words you won't hear in
conversation. This honors lesson teaches you to read those lists, to name the usual documents,
and to write a formal request with lesson 20's formulas. Procedures, fees and web addresses change
often, so the facts below are dated, and every real procedure should be checked on the official
page of the agency in charge (most are listed on gob.mx).

## The usual documents

- *El acta de nacimiento* (birth certificate) is issued by the civil registry (*el Registro
  Civil*) of each state. *Acta* is feminine but takes *el* in the singular, like *el agua*: *el
  acta, las actas, el acta original, una copia del acta*. Many people now print it from gob.mx
  after entering their CURP; the fee is set by each state (in September 2023 UnoTV gave 62 pesos
  in Nuevo León, 85 in Mexico City and 210 in Yucatán). The INE accepts it for a voter card whatever its date, as long as it has no
  crossings-out or corrections (as reported in August 2026).
- *La copia certificada* (certified copy) is a copy an authority has stamped as faithful to the
  original. A plain photocopy (*una copia simple*) is not the same thing.
- *El comprobante de domicilio* (proof of address) is usually a recent water, electricity, gas or
  phone bill. For the INE voter card it must be no more than three months old, and it doesn't have
  to be in your name (Bloomberg Línea, 19 August 2026). Other procedures set their own rules.
- *Una identificación oficial vigente* (a valid official ID): most often *la credencial para votar*
  issued by the INE (valid for ten years, as you saw in A2), or a passport.
- *La CURP* (*Clave Única de Registro de Población*) is an 18-character code that identifies each
  resident and citizen; it is managed by RENAPO, part of the Secretaría de Gobernación, and you can
  look yours up free of charge on gob.mx (Mexican consulate in San Antonio, checked November 2026).
- *El RFC* (*Registro Federal de Contribuyentes*) is the tax ID issued by the SAT, Mexico's tax
  authority. You give it, for example, when you ask a business for *una factura*.

Words for the life of a document: a document is *vigente* (valid, in force) during its *vigencia*
(validity period), and then it is *vencido* (expired; *vencer* = to expire). Then you have to
*renovarlo* (*renovar*: *renuevo, renueva*; subjunctive *renueve*). A card is *una credencial*:
*la credencial de estudiante, la credencial del INE*.

![Five documents on a desk, each labeled. La credencial: a green ID card with a photo, the name Laura Pérez Gil, an address and the line Vigencia 2034. El comprobante de domicilio: an electricity bill (Recibo de luz) in her name with her address, a meter reading and a total of 412 MXN. El acta de nacimiento: a page headed Estados Unidos Mexicanos with her name, date and place of birth and her parents. La copia certificada: a gray photocopy with a round stamp and the words Certifico que es copia fiel de su original. El folio: a small slip headed Su número with the number 2026-118-04573 and the words Conserve este papel.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Who you deal with

In Mexico a government agency is often called *una dependencia* (also "dependence" in general:
*la dependencia del petróleo*). The person at the window is *un funcionario* or *una funcionaria*
(civil servant, official). Your case gets *un folio* (a reference number) that you quote whenever
you ask about it: *Mi número de folio es…* Offices often give appointments online (*sacar una cita
en línea*) and ask you to bring *original y copia* (the original and a photocopy) of each document.

## How requirement lists are written

Requirement lists use a few fixed structures:

| Form | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Infinitive instruction | *Presentarse 15 minutos antes de la cita.* | Arrive 15 minutes before your appointment. |
| Passive or impersonal *se* | *No se aceptan documentos vencidos.* | Expired documents are not accepted. |
| Past participle as adjective | *Formato de solicitud llenado y firmado.* | Application form, filled in and signed. |
| Noun phrase with no verb | *Comprobante de domicilio con antigüedad no mayor a tres meses.* | Proof of address no more than three months old. |
| *En caso de que* / *en caso de* | *En caso de que el trámite sea para un menor, deberá acudir el padre o la madre.* | If the procedure is for a minor, the father or mother must attend. |
| Future of obligation | *El solicitante deberá presentar…* | The applicant must present… |

*Acudir* = to go, to attend (formal); *el solicitante* = applicant (from A2's *solicitar*); *la
antigüedad* = age (of a document), length of service. *Sin tachaduras ni enmendaduras* (no
crossings-out or corrections) appears on many lists.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: reading a notice

The invented town of San Pedro de las Flores posts this notice for renewing a sports center card:

> RENOVACIÓN DE CREDENCIAL DEL CENTRO DEPORTIVO MUNICIPAL
>
> Requisitos:
> 1. Credencial anterior (vigente o vencida).
> 2. Identificación oficial vigente (original y copia).
> 3. Comprobante de domicilio con antigüedad no mayor a tres meses.
> 4. En caso de que el usuario sea menor de edad, acta de nacimiento y credencial del padre, la madre o el tutor.
>
> Costo: 150 pesos. Vigencia de la nueva credencial: un año.
> El trámite es personal. No se aceptan documentos con tachaduras.

Questions and answers:

- *Ana's old card expired in March. Can she renew it?* Yes: point 1 accepts a card that is *vigente
  o vencida*.
- *Her electricity bill is from May, and it's now November. Is it good?* No: it is more than three
  months old.
- *Can her brother do it for her?* No: *El trámite es personal* means she must go herself.
- *How long will the new card last?* One year (*Vigencia… un año*).

### Example 2: writing a formal request

Diego needs proof that he studied at an (invented) institute, for a job abroad. He writes to the
school records office (*el departamento de servicios escolares*, often called *control escolar* in
Mexico):

> Asunto: Solicitud de constancia de estudios y copia certificada
>
> A quien corresponda:
>
> Por medio de la presente, solicito una constancia de estudios y una copia certificada de mi
> título de la Licenciatura en Administración, que terminé en julio de 2024 en el Instituto
> Tecnológico de San Pedro (número de expediente 20-1187).
>
> Necesito estos documentos para un proceso de contratación en el extranjero, cuya fecha límite es
> el 15 de diciembre. Por ello, les agradecería que me informaran el costo y el tiempo de entrega,
> y si sería posible recibir la constancia en formato digital.
>
> Adjunto una copia de mi identificación oficial vigente y el comprobante de pago del trámite
> (folio 2026-118-04573).
>
> Quedo a la espera de su respuesta. Sin otro particular, reciban un cordial saludo.
>
> Diego Ramírez Soto

> Subject: Request for proof of studies and a certified copy
>
> To whom it may concern:
>
> I hereby request proof of studies and a certified copy of my degree certificate for the
> bachelor's degree in Business Administration, which I completed in July 2024 at the Instituto Tecnológico
> de San Pedro (file number 20-1187).
>
> I need these documents for a hiring process abroad, whose deadline is 15 December. I would
> therefore be grateful if you could tell me the cost and the processing time, and whether it would
> be possible to receive the certificate in digital form.
>
> I attach a copy of my valid official ID and the receipt for the fee (reference number
> 2026-118-04573).
>
> I await your reply. Kind regards,
>
> Diego Ramírez Soto

Notice the plan: what he asks for, why and by when, the questions (*les agradecería que me
informaran* + imperfect subjunctive), what he attaches, and the closing. *Cuya* (whose) is a formal
relative that agrees with the noun after it: *cuya fecha límite*. *El título* here is the degree
certificate (A1's *título* of a book, in a new sense). *Por ello* = for that reason
(formal *por eso*).

### Example 3: at the window

> Funcionaria: Buenos días. ¿Me permite su folio?
>
> Diego: Sí, aquí está: 2026-118-04573.
>
> Funcionaria: Su constancia ya está lista. Para la copia certificada me falta su identificación.
>
> Diego: Aquí tiene mi pasaporte.
>
> Funcionaria: Lo siento, este pasaporte está vencido desde agosto. ¿Trae otra identificación vigente?
>
> Diego: Tengo mi credencial del INE.
>
> Funcionaria: Perfecto. La copia certificada se la entregamos en cinco días hábiles.
>
> Diego: Muchas gracias. Disculpe las molestias.

> Official: Good morning. May I have your reference number?
>
> Diego: Yes, here it is: 2026-118-04573.
>
> Official: Your certificate is ready. For the certified copy I still need your ID.
>
> Diego: Here's my passport.
>
> Official: I'm sorry, this passport has been expired since August. Do you have another valid ID?
>
> Diego: I have my INE card.
>
> Official: Perfect. We'll give you the certified copy in five business days.
>
> Diego: Thank you very much. Sorry for the trouble.

*¿Me permite…?* (May I have…?) is a very polite way to ask for a document. *Me falta* (I'm missing)
works like *gustar*: *Me faltan dos documentos.*

## Common mistakes

- ~~*el acta certificado*~~ → *el acta certificada*: *acta* is feminine; only the article is *el*.
- ~~*Mi credencial está expirada*~~ is understood, but the usual words are *vencida* or *ya venció*.
- Confusing *la copia certificada* with *una copia simple*: the office that asks for the first
  won't accept the second.
- Writing *Querido señor* in a request. Use *Estimado(a)…* or *A quien corresponda:*.

## Key points

- Documents: *el acta de nacimiento, el comprobante de domicilio, una identificación oficial
  vigente, la credencial (del INE), la CURP, el RFC, la copia certificada*.
- Validity: *vigente, la vigencia, vencido, vencer, renovar* (*renuevo*).
- Offices: *la dependencia, el funcionario / la funcionaria, el folio, la cita, original y copia*.
- Requirement lists use infinitives, *se*, participles, *en caso de que* + subjunctive and the
  future (*deberá*).
- A request: *A quien corresponda / Por medio de la presente solicito… / Les agradecería que* +
  imperfect subjunctive */ Adjunto… / Quedo a la espera de su respuesta*.
- Always check the current requirements on the agency's official page.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: Advertising and persuasion
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lessons 17–19 taught you to persuade with reasons. Advertising persuades with almost none: a
command, a promise, a condition, a picture. Ads are also some of the most frequent Spanish you'll
read on a street in Mexico, on a bus or on your phone, and they pack in a lot of B1 grammar:
commands (lesson 05), *para que* (06), relative clauses with the subjunctive (08) and conditions
(18). This honors lesson shows how ads use them, how slogans play with words, and how to read the
small print before you sign up. All the ads and slogans here are invented.

## The grammar of persuasion

*La publicidad* (advertising; uncountable) is made of *anuncios* (A2: ads) for a *público
objetivo* (target audience). Each choice of grammar does a job.

Commands speak straight to the reader. Many Mexican ads for young people use *tú*; banks,
insurers and services for older customers often use *usted*.

- *¡No esperes más! Descarga la app y pide tu comida en minutos.* — Don't wait any longer!
  Download the app and order your food in minutes.
- *Llámenos hoy mismo.* — Call us today.
- *Ven, prueba y decide.* — Come, try it and decide.

*Para que* + subjunctive sells the benefit to someone else (lesson 06):

- *Un seguro de vida para que tu familia esté tranquila.* — Life insurance so that your family
  can have peace of mind.

A relative clause with the subjunctive describes the thing the reader is looking for, which the
ad then claims to have (lesson 08):

- *¿Buscas un celular que dure todo el día? Lo tenemos.* — Looking for a phone that lasts all day?
  We've got it.

Conditions (lesson 18) set the terms of the offer:

- *Siempre que compres dos, el tercero es gratis.* — As long as you buy two, the third one is free.
- *En caso de que no quedes satisfecho, te devolvemos tu dinero.* — If you're not satisfied, we'll
  give you your money back.

*Que* + subjunctive, the wish of lesson 01, sounds like a toast: *¡Que nada te detenga!* — Let
nothing stop you!

## Words of the trade

*Publicitario* is the adjective (*una campaña publicitaria*, an advertising campaign). A business
*promociona* (promotes) a product, often with *una promoción* (a special deal: *promoción válida
hasta el domingo*). A good ad *atrae* (attracts; *atraer* is conjugated like *traer*: *atraigo,
atrajo*) attention and *persuade* (persuades) the buyer; it is *persuasivo*. The offer is
*irresistible*, at least on the poster. Critics say ads feed *el consumismo* (consumerism), the
habit of buying more than we need. *El eslogan* (plural *los eslóganes*) is the short line you
remember.

## Slogans and wordplay

Slogans use a handful of tricks. These are invented, for invented businesses:

- Rhythm and repetition: *Tortillería La Esquina: siempre calientitas, siempre a tiempo.* (The
  diminutive *calientitas*, "nice and warm", adds affection.)
- Parallel structure: *Lavandería Burbuja: tu ropa, como nueva; tu tiempo, para ti.*
- Double meaning: *Gimnasio Fuerza: no es magia, es constancia.* *La constancia* here means
  perseverance; in lesson 20 it was an official certificate. The slogan works because both senses
  are serious and solid.
- A question that answers itself: *¿Cansado del tráfico? Muévete en bici.*

Wordplay is hard to translate, and some is only funny in one country. When you write a slogan in
Spanish, test it on a native speaker: an accidental double meaning can be embarrassing.

## The small print

The line with an asterisk (*) at the bottom of an ad is *la letra chica* (the small print; Spain
says *la letra pequeña*). Learn these phrases:

| Small print | Meaning |
|---|---|
| *Aplican restricciones.* | Restrictions apply. |
| *Hasta 50 % de descuento.* | Up to 50 % off (so most items may have less). |
| *Desde 99 pesos.* | From 99 pesos (the cheapest version). |
| *Hasta agotar existencias.* | While supplies last. |
| *Precios sujetos a cambio sin previo aviso.* | Prices subject to change without notice. |
| *Consulta términos y condiciones en…* | See terms and conditions at… |
| *Imágenes con fines ilustrativos.* | Pictures for illustration only. |
| *Con tarjetas participantes.* | With participating cards only. |

![An invented ad for an internet company called NubeLink, Internet para tu hogar. In large letters: ¡Internet de hasta 500 megas desde 299 pesos al mes!, with an asterisk. A badge says Instalación gratis, and a line says No esperes más. ¡Contrata hoy! The small print at the bottom: Precio promocional durante los primeros 3 meses; a partir del cuarto mes, 549 pesos al mes. Velocidad sujeta a disponibilidad en tu zona. Plazo forzoso de 12 meses. Aplican restricciones. Consulta términos y condiciones en nubelink.example.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Worked examples

### Example 1: what does it really cost?

Read the NubeLink ad above and answer as a careful consumer.

1. *What do you pay in month 4?* The small print says *a partir del cuarto mes, 549 pesos al
   mes*: from the fourth month, 549 pesos.
2. *How much is the first year?* Three months at 299 and nine at 549: 897 + 4,941 = 5,838 pesos.
   The big number, 299, applies to only a quarter of the year.
3. *Is 500 megas guaranteed?* No: *hasta* (up to) and *sujeta a disponibilidad en tu zona*
   (depending on availability in your area).
4. *Can you cancel after two months?* The ad says *plazo forzoso de 12 meses*: a compulsory
   twelve-month term, so probably not without a penalty.

### Example 2: how does this ad persuade?

> ¿Buscas un café que te despierte de verdad? En Café Nube tostamos el grano cada mañana para
> que cada taza sepa a recién hecho. Ven hoy y, siempre que traigas tu propio vaso, te regalamos
> un pan dulce. Café Nube: despierta tu día.

> Looking for a coffee that really wakes you up? At Café Nube we roast the beans every morning so
> that every cup tastes freshly made. Come today and, as long as you bring your own cup, we'll
> give you a pan dulce. Café Nube: wake up your day.

The techniques, line by line: a question with a relative subjunctive (*un café que te despierte*:
the coffee you want), a benefit with *para que* + subjunctive (*para que sepa*; *saber a* = to
taste of), a *tú* command (*Ven*), a condition (*siempre que traigas*), a gift, and a slogan with
a command (*despierta tu día*) that repeats the key idea. *Tostar* = to roast; *el grano* = the
(coffee) bean.

### Example 3: is it misleading?

In Mexico the Ley Federal de Protección al Consumidor (art. 32) requires advertising to be
truthful, verifiable and clear, and calls information *engañosa* (misleading) when it leads the
consumer into error or confusion, for example through an inexact, false, exaggerated or partial
presentation, even if the claims are technically true (text of the article checked in November 2026;
its first paragraph was last reformed in 2016). Profeco can act on such ads.

Apply the idea to three invented claims:

- *"Sin costo de instalación"* when the small print adds a monthly "equipment fee". Partial, so
  possibly misleading.
- *"El mejor taco de la ciudad"*: an obvious boast that few readers take as a measured fact. It
  proves nothing, but it is unlikely to fool anyone.
- *"Bajamos los precios un 40 %"*, when the "before" price was raised the week before. False
  impression: misleading.

Whether a real ad breaks the law is for Profeco or a court to decide; your job as a reader is to
ask what the ad leaves out.

## Writing an honest ad

A good ad can be persuasive and clear at once. Here is a model for an invented neighborhood
bakery; the conditions are in the main text, not hidden in an asterisk:

> ¿Extrañas el pan de tu abuela? En Panadería Doña Rosa lo hacemos igual: con tiempo y sin prisas.
> Este mes, siempre que compres diez piezas, te regalamos una concha. Promoción válida del 1 al
> 30 de noviembre de 2026, de lunes a sábado. Ven temprano para que te toque el pan recién salido
> del horno.

> Miss your grandmother's bread? At Panadería Doña Rosa we make it the same way: taking our time,
> no rush. This month, as long as you buy ten pieces, we'll give you a concha. Offer valid from 1
> to 30 November 2026, Monday to Saturday. Come early so that you get the bread fresh out of the
> oven.

*La pieza* (piece, the sense from lesson 08) is how Mexican bakeries count bread; *la concha* = a round sweet bun
with a shell pattern on top; *tocarle a alguien* = to get (one's share). The ad still
uses a question, a condition and *para que*, but the dates and the condition are stated plainly.

## Common mistakes

- ~~*los eslogans*~~ → *los eslóganes*: the plural adds *-es* and an accent.
- ~~*una publicidad*~~ for one ad → *un anuncio*. *La publicidad* is advertising in general.
- ~~*atrayó*~~ → *atrajo*: *atraer* follows *traer* in the preterite (*atraje, atrajeron*).
- *Engañoso* (misleading) describes the ad; *engañado* (deceived) describes the customer.
- *La promoción* is a special offer; a promotion at work is *el ascenso* (lesson 11).
- Reading *hasta* as "at least": *hasta 50 %* means "up to", so 50 % is the maximum.

## Key points

- Ads persuade with commands (*tú* or *usted*), *para que* + subjunctive, relative clauses with the
  subjunctive (*¿Buscas un… que…?*), conditions (*siempre que, en caso de que*) and *¡Que…!* wishes.
- Words: *la publicidad, publicitario, el eslogan / los eslóganes, persuadir, persuasivo, el
  público objetivo, la promoción, promocionar, atraer (atraigo, atrajo), engañoso, irresistible,
  el consumismo*.
- Slogans use rhythm, repetition, parallel structure and double meanings.
- Small print: *aplican restricciones, hasta, desde, hasta agotar existencias, sujeto a, plazo
  forzoso*.
- In Mexico, ads must be truthful, verifiable and clear (LFPC art. 32); Profeco can act on
  misleading ones.

the lesson.

lessons.title: Don't pull my leg: idioms, and ser and estar that change the meaning
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

By now you can wish, advise, doubt, imagine and argue in Spanish. What often still gives a
learner away is the lack of the small fixed phrases that native speakers use all day: *Metí la
pata*, *¡Órale!*, *Es pan comido*. This first lesson of the last module teaches a set of
common idioms, the most useful Mexican informal interjections, and a group of adjectives whose
meaning changes with *ser* and *estar*. You already know the basic split from A1 and A2 (*ser*
for what something is, *estar* for states and location); here you'll see where that split
changes the meaning of a word completely.

The theme is humor and everyday conversation in Mexico: jokes, teasing and the phrases friends
use with each other.

## What an idiom is

An **[[idiom]]** is a fixed phrase whose meaning isn't the sum of its words. *Tomar el pelo* is
literally "to take the hair", but it means "to pull someone's leg", to tease them.

Two things matter when you use one:

- The verb still conjugates. Only the verb changes; the rest stays fixed. *Metí la pata*
  (I put my foot in it), *¿Me estás tomando el pelo?* (Are you pulling my leg?), *No le tomes
  el pelo* (Don't tease him), *Ojalá no meta la pata* (I hope she doesn't mess up). All the
  grammar of this course works inside an idiom, the subjunctive too.
- Don't translate word for word. *Costar un ojo de la cara* (to cost an eye from the face)
  is "to cost an arm and a leg". Learn each idiom with its real meaning and one example.

![Four pictures of idioms. 1: a hand pulling a strand of a man's hair, labeled tomar el pelo, to tease, to pull someone's leg. 2: a woman whose head is among clouds, labeled estar en las nubes, to have your head in the clouds. 3: a price tag with an eye drawn on it, labeled costar un ojo de la cara, to cost an arm and a leg. 4: a dog's paw stepping into a cake, labeled meter la pata, to put your foot in it, to mess up.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Idioms with the body, food and animals

| Idiom | Literally | Means | Register |
|---|---|---|---|
| *meter la pata* | to put in the paw | to put your foot in it, to mess up | informal |
| *tomar el pelo (a alguien)* | to take the hair | to pull someone's leg, to tease | informal |
| *costar un ojo de la cara* | to cost an eye from the face | to cost an arm and a leg | informal |
| *no tener pelos en la lengua* | not to have hairs on the tongue | not to mince words, to be blunt | neutral |
| *echar la mano (a alguien)* | to throw the hand | to lend a hand (Mexico) | informal |
| *ser pan comido* | to be eaten bread | to be a piece of cake | informal |
| *dar la lata (a alguien)* | to give the tin can | to pester, to be a pain | informal |
| *ponerse las pilas* | to put your batteries in | to get your act together, to get moving | informal |
| *estar en las nubes* | to be in the clouds | to daydream, to have your head in the clouds | neutral |
| *echarle ganas (a algo)* | to throw desire at it | to give it your all (Mexico) | informal |
| *estar de buenas / de malas* | to be "of goods / of bads" | to be in a good / bad mood | informal |

*La pata* is an animal's leg or paw (for people, *la pierna* and *el pie*), so *meter la pata*
pictures an animal stepping where it shouldn't. Some notes on use:

- *Echar la mano* is very common in Mexico (*¿Me echas la mano con estas cajas?*); in
  most other countries you'll hear *echar una mano*. Both are understood everywhere.
- *Échale ganas* is what Mexicans say to encourage someone before an exam, a new job or a
  hard moment: "go for it, do your best". The *le* refers loosely to the task (*Échale ganas a
  la escuela*), and often nothing follows it: *Le estoy echando ganas* = I'm really trying.
- *Dar la lata* takes an indirect object (*Mi hermanito me da la lata* = My little brother
  pesters me); with *ser pan comido* and *costar un ojo de la cara*, the thing is the subject
  (*El examen fue pan comido* = The exam was a piece of cake).

## Mexican informal interjections

These short reactions are some of the first things you'll hear among friends in Mexico. They
are informal: use them with friends and family, not in a job interview.

| Interjection | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *¡Órale!* | OK, let's do it; wow; come on, hurry | *—¿Vamos por unos tacos? —¡Órale!* |
| *¡Híjole!* | surprise or dismay: oh wow, oh no, yikes | *¡Híjole! Se me olvidó tu cumpleaños.* |
| *¡Aguas!* | watch out! | *¡Aguas con el escalón!* — Watch the step! |
| *¡No manches!* | no way!, you're kidding! | *¿Te ganaste el premio? ¡No manches!* |
| *¡Qué oso!* | how embarrassing! | *Me caí enfrente de todos. ¡Qué oso!* |

Three informal nouns go with them:

- *la neta*: the truth. *La neta, no me gustó la película* (To be honest, I didn't like the
  movie). *¿Neta?* = Really? Seriously?
- *el cuate, la cuata*: a buddy, a good friend (*Es mi cuate desde la prepa* = He's been my buddy since high school). In Mexico it
  also means a twin (*Mis primos son cuates*).
- *la chamba*: a job, work (*Encontré chamba en un restaurante*). Neutral Spanish says *el
  trabajo*.

A word on register. *¡No manches!* is a softened form of a much ruder phrase: it is fine among
friends, but don't say it to your boss. *¡Qué oso!* sounds young and playful. You'll also hear
*güey* (dude) constantly among young friends; it can offend if you use it with strangers, so
recognize it but don't start with it. This course doesn't teach vulgar words; you don't need them to
sound natural.

## Jokes, teasing and sayings

- *El chiste* is a joke you tell: *contar un chiste*. *La broma* is a joke you play or a
  joking remark: *hacer una broma*, *Es broma* (just kidding). *Bromear* is to joke: *No te
  enojes, estoy bromeando.*
- *En serio* is seriously, for real: *¿En serio?* (Really?), *Te lo digo en serio* (I mean
  it). Its opposite is *en broma* (as a joke).
- *El refrán* is a traditional saying with a lesson, a proverb. *El dicho* is any popular
  saying or expression, so every *refrán* is a *dicho*, but not every *dicho* is a *refrán*.
  A few *refranes* every Mexican knows:
  - *Más vale tarde que nunca.* — Better late than never.
  - *Camarón que se duerme se lo lleva la corriente.* — The shrimp that falls asleep is
    carried off by the current (if you don't pay attention, you lose out).

## Ser and estar that change the meaning

A few adjectives mean one thing with *ser* and something quite different with *estar*. With
*ser* you describe what someone or something is like; with *estar*, a state or how it is right
now.

![A chart of eight adjectives whose meaning changes. With ser: listo clever, rico rich, aburrido boring, malo bad, verde green, vivo lively or sharp, atento considerate, orgulloso proud or arrogant. With estar: listo ready, rico tasty, aburrido bored, malo sick or gone bad, verde unripe, vivo alive, atento paying attention, orgulloso de proud of.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Adjective | with *ser* | with *estar* |
|---|---|---|
| *listo* | clever: *Tu hija es muy lista.* | ready: *¿Ya estás lista?* |
| *rico* | rich: *Su familia es rica.* | tasty: *¡Qué rico está el pozole!* (pozole: a hominy soup) |
| *aburrido* | boring: *La clase es aburrida.* | bored: *Estoy aburrido.* |
| *malo* | bad: *Ese hotel es malo.* | sick; (food) gone bad: *Estoy malo de la garganta. La leche está mala.* |
| *verde* | green: *Su carro es verde.* | unripe: *Los plátanos todavía están verdes.* |
| *vivo* | lively, sharp: *Es un niño muy vivo.* | alive: *Mi abuela todavía está viva.* |
| *atento* | considerate, thoughtful: *Es muy atento con sus vecinos.* | attentive, paying attention: *Estén atentos a la explicación.* |
| *orgulloso* | proud, too proud: *Es demasiado orgulloso para pedir ayuda.* | proud of: *Estoy orgullosa de ti.* |

Some honest limits to these pairs:

- *Rico* with food. *Estar rico* is how this dish tastes right now. In Mexico you'll also hear
  *ser rico* for a food in general: *El mole es muy rico* (Mole is a delicious dish). For a
  person, *ser rico* is always "rich".
- *Malo* for health: *estar malo* is common, but *estar enfermo* is the safe, neutral choice.
- *Estar verde* is also informal for "inexperienced, still learning": *Todavía estoy verde en
  la chamba.*
- *Vivo* with *estar* is the exception to "permanent = *ser*": being alive takes *estar*, and
  so does *estar muerto*.

## Dialogue: una broma en la oficina

Valeria and Diego work in the same office in Guadalajara. It's Monday morning.

> Diego: ¿Qué onda, Valeria? Te ves de buenas hoy.
>
> Valeria: ¡Estoy de buenas! El jefe me dijo que me van a dar el proyecto nuevo.
>
> Diego: ¡No manches! ¿En serio? Ayer me dijo que me lo iba a dar a mí.
>
> Valeria: ¿Neta? Híjole… ¿no me estás tomando el pelo?
>
> Diego: Sí, es broma. Te lo dieron a ti, y me alegra mucho. Pero aguas: ese cliente da mucha lata.
>
> Valeria: Ya lo sé. Lo que pide cuesta un ojo de la cara. Si me echas la mano con los números, te invito a comer.
>
> Diego: ¡Órale! Con los números es pan comido. Lo difícil es el cliente: no tiene pelos en la lengua.
>
> Valeria: Entonces tengo que ponerme las pilas. La última vez estaba en las nubes en la junta y metí la pata.
>
> Diego: ¿Qué dijiste?
>
> Valeria: Le dije "Juan", y se llama Julio. ¡Qué oso!
>
> Diego: Bueno, eso ya pasó. Échale ganas. ¿Te cuento un chiste para que te relajes?
>
> Valeria: Mejor no. Tus chistes son muy malos.

> Diego: What's up, Valeria? You look like you're in a good mood today.
>
> Valeria: I am in a good mood! The boss told me they're going to give me the new project.
>
> Diego: No way! Seriously? Yesterday he told me he was going to give it to me.
>
> Valeria: Really? Oh no… you're not pulling my leg?
>
> Diego: Yes, I'm kidding. They gave it to you, and I'm really glad. But watch out: that client is a real pain.
>
> Valeria: I know. What he wants costs an arm and a leg. If you lend me a hand with the numbers, I'll buy you lunch.
>
> Diego: Deal! The numbers are a piece of cake. The hard part is the client: he doesn't mince words.
>
> Valeria: Then I need to get my act together. Last time I was daydreaming in the meeting and I put my foot in it.
>
> Diego: What did you say?
>
> Valeria: I called him "Juan", and his name is Julio. How embarrassing!
>
> Diego: Well, that's over now. Give it your all. Shall I tell you a joke so you can relax?
>
> Valeria: Better not. Your jokes are really bad.

*¿Qué onda?* (What's up?) is A2's greeting among friends; *te ves* = you look. Notice the grammar inside the idioms: *me iba a dar* (reported plan),
*Si me echas la mano…, te invito* (a real condition), *para que te relajes* (purpose +
subjunctive), and *son muy malos* (*ser malo* = bad, not sick).

## Pronunciation

- *¡Órale!* and *¡Híjole!* are stressed on the first syllable: *Ó-ra-le, Hí-jo-le*. The *j* is a
  soft breathy *h* in Mexico.
- *¡Aguas!*: *A-guas*, two syllables; the *gu* before *a* sounds like a soft *gw*.
- *La neta* and *el cuate*: *NE-ta*, *CUA-te* (two syllables: *cua-te*).
- *Bromear*: *bro-me-AR*, three syllables (the *e* and the *a* are separate); *bromeo* is *bro-ME-o*.

## Common mistakes

- Translating idioms word for word: ~~*Cuesta un brazo y una pierna*~~ → *Cuesta un ojo de la
  cara.* ~~*Estás jalando mi pierna*~~ → *Me estás tomando el pelo.*
- Changing the fixed part: ~~*meter el pie*~~ → *meter la pata*; ~~*estar en la nube*~~ →
  *estar en las nubes*.
- Forgetting to conjugate the verb: ~~*Yo meter la pata*~~ → *Metí la pata.*
- *Soy aburrido* when you mean "I'm bored": that says "I'm a boring person". Say *Estoy
  aburrido.* Likewise ~~*Soy listo*~~ for "I'm ready" → *Estoy listo.*
- ~~*Contar una broma*~~ → *contar un chiste*; a *broma* is played or said *en broma*.
- Using *¡No manches!* or *güey* in a formal situation. Keep them for friends.

## Key points

- An **[[idiom]]** has a fixed meaning; only its verb conjugates (*metí la pata, no me tomes el pelo*).
- Learn each idiom with its real meaning and register: neutral, informal, or Mexican informal.
- Mexican interjections: *¡Órale!* (OK, wow), *¡Híjole!* (oh no, wow), *¡Aguas!* (watch out),
  *¡No manches!* (no way), *¡Qué oso!* (how embarrassing); *la neta* (the truth), *el cuate*
  (buddy), *la chamba* (job).
- *Chiste* = a joke you tell; *broma* = a prank or a joking remark; *en serio* / *en broma*.
- Ser / estar: *listo* clever / ready, *rico* rich / tasty, *aburrido* boring / bored, *malo*
  bad / sick, *verde* green / unripe, *vivo* lively / alive, *atento* considerate / paying
  attention, *orgulloso* proud (arrogant) / proud of.

lessons.title: She became a doctor: verbs of change and verbs with prepositions
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

English uses two all-purpose verbs for change: "become" and "get" (*he got nervous, she
became a doctor, they got rich*). Spanish has no single verb for this. It chooses among several
**[[verbs of change]]** according to the kind of change: sudden or slow, chosen or not, a mood or a
profession. You met *convertirse en* in A2 honors; this lesson builds the whole system around
it. The second half covers verbs that always take the same preposition (*contar con, fijarse
en, atreverse a*), which keep that preposition even in questions.

Lesson 21 showed adjectives that change meaning with *ser* and *estar*. The verbs here are
close relatives: they say how someone *came to be* or *came to be in* a state.

## Verbs of change

![A chart of verbs of change. ponerse plus an adjective: a sudden, usually temporary change, se puso rojo. volverse plus an adjective: a lasting change in character, se volvió desconfiado. hacerse plus a noun or adjective: through effort or time, se hizo médica, se hizo rico. convertirse en plus a noun: a transformation, la casa se convirtió en museo. llegar a ser: at the end of a long process, llegó a ser directora. quedarse plus an adjective or sin plus a noun: the result of an event, se quedó ciego, se quedó sin trabajo.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### *ponerse* + adjective: sudden and usually temporary

Moods, colors, health and looks that change quickly: *Se puso rojo cuando lo vieron* (He went
red when they saw him). *Me pongo nerviosa antes de hablar en público* (I get nervous before
speaking in public). *Se puso muy contenta con la noticia* (She was really happy at the news).
*Ponerse* takes adjectives, never a noun for a job.

### *volverse* + adjective: a deep, lasting change in character

Often a change nobody planned: *Después del robo, se volvió muy desconfiado* (After the
robbery, he became very distrustful). *Con los años se ha vuelto más paciente* (Over the years
she has become more patient). *Volverse loco* is to go crazy, also in the everyday sense: *¡Me
voy a volver loca con tanto ruido!* (I'm going to go crazy with all this noise!). *Volverse* is
conjugated like *volver* (*me vuelvo, se vuelve; se ha vuelto*).

### *hacerse* + noun or adjective: by effort, choice or time

Jobs, beliefs and status that someone works toward or reaches over time: *Se hizo médica*
(She became a doctor). *Se hicieron ricos con su negocio* (They got rich with their business).
*Me hice vegetariano hace dos años* (I became a vegetarian two years ago). It is conjugated like
*hacer* (*me hago, se hizo, se ha hecho*). Two set phrases: *hacerse viejo* (to grow old) and
*se hace tarde* (it's getting late).

### *convertirse en* + noun: a transformation

One thing turns into another: *La fábrica se convirtió en un centro cultural* (The factory
became a cultural center). *El pueblo se convirtió en ciudad* (The town became a city). It is the usual verb when the
change is complete and the result is a different kind of thing.

### *llegar a ser*: at the end of a long road

Only for a result reached after a long process, often with effort: *Empezó como mesera y
llegó a ser directora del hotel* (She started as a waitress and went on to become the hotel's
director). It stresses the journey; *se hizo directora* would also be correct.

### *quedarse* + adjective, *quedarse sin* + noun: the result of an event

You know *quedarse* as "to stay". As a verb of change it gives the state someone is left in
after something happens, often a loss: *Se quedó ciego después del accidente* (He went blind
after the accident). *Nos quedamos sorprendidos* (We were left surprised). *Me quedé sin
trabajo* (I lost my job, literally "I was left without work"). *Se quedó sin batería* (Its
battery died).

### One-word verbs of change

Many changes have their own verb, and Spanish often prefers it: *adelgazar* (to lose weight;
*adelgacé* in the yo preterite), *engordar* (to gain weight), *envejecer* (to grow old, lesson
11), *madurar* (to mature; of fruit, to ripen), *enfermarse* (to get sick; Spain more often says
*ponerse enfermo* or *enfermar*), *transformar* (to transform: *La experiencia lo transformó*). In Mexico you'll
also hear *bajar de peso* and *subir de peso* for losing and gaining weight.

### Choosing the verb

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Which verb of change?
  accDescr: A decision chart. First question: is a noun coming after the verb? If yes, ask whether the change came through effort, a job or a belief: if yes, use hacerse, as in se hizo médica; if it is a complete transformation, use convertirse en, as in se convirtió en un museo; if it is the end of a long process, llegar a ser also works. If an adjective comes after the verb, ask whether the change is sudden and temporary, like a mood, color or health: if yes, use ponerse, as in se puso nervioso. If not, ask whether it is the result of an event, often a loss: if yes, use quedarse, as in se quedó ciego or se quedó sin trabajo. Otherwise, for a lasting change in character, use volverse, as in se volvió desconfiado, and for status reached over time, hacerse, as in se hizo rico.
  A["become / get + ..."] --> B{"A noun comes next?"}
  B -- yes --> C{"Effort, a job, a belief?"}
  C -- yes --> D["hacerse: se hizo médica (or llegar a ser, after a long road)"]
  C -- "no, a transformation" --> E["convertirse en: se convirtió en un museo"]
  B -- "no, an adjective" --> F{"Sudden, temporary: mood, color, health?"}
  F -- yes --> G["ponerse: se puso nervioso"]
  F -- no --> H{"The result of an event, often a loss?"}
  H -- yes --> I["quedarse: se quedó ciego, sin trabajo"]
  H -- no --> J["volverse (character): se volvió desconfiado; hacerse (status): se hizo rico"]
```

The boundaries are soft, and speakers don't always agree. *Se puso muy flaco* and *Se quedó
muy flaco* (He got very thin) are both heard in Mexico. Use the chart for your own choices, and
expect variety in what you hear.

## Verbs with a fixed preposition

Some verbs always come with the same preposition, and English often uses a different one or
none: *contar con* (to count on), *fijarse en* (to notice). Learn them as a unit.

| Verb | Means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *atreverse a* | to dare to | *No me atrevo a decírselo.* — I don't dare tell him. |
| *dedicarse a* | to do for a living (A2) | *Se dedica a la fotografía.* — She works as a photographer. |
| *fijarse en* | to notice, to pay attention to | *¿Te fijaste en sus zapatos?* — Did you notice his shoes? |
| *contar con* | to count on; (formal) to have | *Cuenta conmigo.* — Count on me. *El hotel cuenta con alberca.* — The hotel has a pool. |
| *tratarse de* | to be about, to be a matter of | *Se trata de un problema serio.* — It's a serious problem. |
| *burlarse de* | to make fun of | *No te burles de tu hermano.* — Don't make fun of your brother. |
| *interesarse por* | to take an interest in, to ask after | *Se interesó por mi salud.* — He asked after my health. |
| *olvidarse de* | to forget (A2) | *Me olvidé de la cita.* — I forgot the appointment. |
| *soñar con* | to dream of (lesson 13) | *Sueña con viajar a Japón.* — She dreams of going to Japan. |
| *insistir en* | to insist on (02) | *Insistió en pagar.* — He insisted on paying. |
| *arrepentirse de* | to regret (11) | *No me arrepiento de nada.* — I don't regret anything. |
| *depender de, confiar en, enamorarse de, casarse con* | A1 and A2 | *Me enamoré de él y me casé con él.* — I fell in love with him and married him. |

*Contar* without *con* is to count or to tell (A1), so the preposition changes the meaning.
*Interesarse en* is also common in Latin America and correct. *Fíjate que…* is a very common
softener in Mexico before news or an excuse: *Fíjate que no voy a poder ir* (The thing is, I
won't be able to go).

*Tratarse de* has a catch. *Se trata de* has no subject: *Se trata de una mujer que…* (It's
about a woman who…). The RAE's *Diccionario panhispánico de dudas* treats this *se trata de* as
impersonal, so it shouldn't take a subject; when the film or book is the subject, careful usage
says *tratar de* without *se*: *La película trata de una mujer que…* You'll
hear *La película se trata de…* very often in Latin America, but avoid it in careful writing.

### The preposition comes first in questions

English leaves the preposition at the end ("Who can you count on?"). Spanish can't: the
preposition goes before the question word.

- *¿Con quién cuentas?* — Who can you count on?
- *¿A qué te dedicas?* — What do you do for a living?
- *¿De qué se trata?* — What's it about?
- *¿En qué te fijaste?* — What did you notice?
- *¿De quién se burlan?* — Who are they making fun of?

The same happens in relative clauses (lesson 08): *la persona con la que cuento* (the person I
count on), *el tema del que se trata* (the topic it's about).

### Before a clause

The preposition stays before *que*: *Me fijé en que no traía su anillo* (I noticed he wasn't
wearing his ring). *Insisto en que vengas* (I insist that you come: subjunctive of influence,
lesson 02). In speech you'll hear the preposition dropped (*Me fijé que…*), especially in the
Americas, but the RAE's *Diccionario panhispánico de dudas* recommends keeping it in careful
writing.

## Interview: empezar de cero

A local radio station in Puebla interviews Ernesto Ríos, 67, who changed careers in his sixties.

> Locutora: Don Ernesto, usted dice que su vida dio un giro a los sesenta años. ¿Qué pasó?
>
> Ernesto: Me quedé sin trabajo. Fui ingeniero en la misma empresa durante treinta años, y un día cerraron la planta.
>
> Locutora: ¿Cómo se sintió?
>
> Ernesto: Al principio me puse muy triste, y luego me volví un poco amargado. No sabía qué rumbo tomar.
>
> Locutora: ¿Y qué hizo?
>
> Ernesto: Mi nieta me dijo: "Abuelo, échale ganas, tú sabes mucho de historia". Me atreví a empezar de cero: estudié para guía de turistas.
>
> Locutora: ¿Alguien se burló de usted?
>
> Ernesto: Algunos amigos, sí: "¿Estudiante en la tercera edad?". Pero conté con mi familia. Hoy soy guía en el centro histórico.
>
> Locutora: ¿Qué es lo más bonito de la chamba?
>
> Ernesto: Que la gente se interesa por la ciudad. Y que yo me fijo en cosas que nunca había visto.
>
> Locutora: ¿Qué les diría a otros adultos mayores?
>
> Ernesto: Que superarse no tiene edad. Hace falta valentía para enfrentar el miedo, pero vale la pena.

> Host: Don Ernesto, you say your life took a turn at sixty. What happened?
>
> Ernesto: I lost my job. I was an engineer at the same company for thirty years, and one day they closed the plant.
>
> Host: How did you feel?
>
> Ernesto: At first I got very sad, and then I became a bit bitter. I didn't know which way to go.
>
> Host: And what did you do?
>
> Ernesto: My granddaughter said to me: "Grandpa, give it your all, you know a lot about history." I dared to start from scratch: I studied to be a tour guide.
>
> Host: Did anyone make fun of you?
>
> Ernesto: Some friends, yes: "A student, at your age?" But I could count on my family. Today I'm a guide in the historic center.
>
> Host: What's the best thing about the job?
>
> Ernesto: That people take an interest in the city. And that I notice things I had never seen.
>
> Host: What would you say to other older adults?
>
> Ernesto: That bettering yourself has no age limit. It takes courage to face your fear, but it's worth it.

*La locutora* is a radio host; *amargado* = bitter; *la planta* = the plant (factory). *La
tercera edad* is literally "the third age", old age. *El anciano, la anciana* is an elderly
person; it is respectful but can sound blunt to some ears, and Mexican official and polite
language usually says *los adultos mayores*. *La superación* (personal) is self-improvement, a
word you'll see on many bookshop shelves in Mexico, and *superarse* is to better oneself.

![A timeline of Ernesto's life with four numbered pictures: 1980, a graduation cap, se graduó; 2019, an empty cardboard box, se quedó sin trabajo; 2020, a notebook and pencil, empezó de cero; 2022, a small flag in front of a cathedral, se hizo guía.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Pronunciation

- *Adelgazar, adelgacé*: the *z* and the *c* before *e* sound like *s* in Latin America:
  *a-del-ga-SAR, a-del-ga-SÉ*.
- *Hacerse*: *ha-SER-se*; *se hizo* is *se I-so* (the *h* is silent, the *z* is *s*).
- *Valentía* has four syllables with the stress on the *í*: *va-len-TÍ-a*.
- *Ciego*: *CIE-go*, two syllables; *ie* is one diphthong.

## Common mistakes

- Using *ser* or *estar* for a change: ~~*Estuvo nervioso*~~ for "he got nervous" → *Se puso
  nervioso.* ~~*Fue médica*~~ for "she became a doctor" → *Se hizo médica.*
- Forgetting the pronoun: ~~*Puso rojo*~~ → *Se puso rojo*; ~~*Volvió loco*~~ → *Se volvió
  loco.*
- ~~*Se puso doctora*~~: *ponerse* doesn't take a job → *Se hizo doctora.*
- ~~*Convertirse a*~~ → *convertirse en*. (*Convertirse al budismo*, to convert to Buddhism, is
  a different sense.)
- Leaving the preposition at the end, English-style: ~~*¿Quién cuentas con?*~~ → *¿Con quién
  cuentas?*
- Dropping or swapping the preposition: ~~*Me atreví hablar*~~ → *Me atreví a hablar*;
  ~~*Se burlan a mí*~~ → *Se burlan de mí.*

## Key points

- **[[Verbs of change]]**: *ponerse* + adjective (sudden, temporary), *volverse* + adjective
  (lasting change in character), *hacerse* + noun or adjective (effort, job, status),
  *convertirse en* + noun (transformation), *llegar a ser* (after a long road), *quedarse* +
  adjective or *sin* + noun (the result, often a loss).
- One-word verbs often do the job: *adelgazar, engordar, envejecer, madurar, enfermarse*.
- Verbs with a fixed preposition: *atreverse a, fijarse en, contar con, tratarse de,
  burlarse de, interesarse por*; the preposition goes first in questions (*¿Con quién
  cuentas?*) and stays before *que* in careful writing.
- *Se trata de…* has no subject; for a film or a book, *trata de…*
