lessons.title: Writing at B1: e-mails, posts and reviews
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At A2 you wrote short messages of 60–80 words. At B1 your texts get longer and do more: you
tell an experience with all three past tenses, give an opinion with reasons, react with the
subjunctive and recommend. This lesson gives you a method for the two kinds of text the DELE B1
asks for, three model texts, and the words for writing about films, series and shows, the
most common topic of a B1 review. Lesson 24 describes the whole exam; honors lesson 24h2
practices the writing tasks in full.

## What the exam asks you to write

The official *Guía del examen DELE B1* (Instituto Cervantes) describes two writing tasks in 60
minutes. In general terms:

- Task 1: you read a short text (a note, an ad, a letter or a message) and answer it with
  an e-mail, a letter, a forum post or a blog entry of 100–120 words, covering the points
  the instructions list.
- Task 2: you choose one of two options, each introduced by a short news item from a
  magazine, a blog or a social network, and write 130–150 words: for example a
  composition, a diary entry or a short biography.

Both are personal, everyday writing, not essays. The examiners look at whether the text fits
the genre and the task, whether it hangs together, how correct it is, and how much range it
shows (lesson 24 explains the scoring).

## A method in five steps

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Five steps for a B1 text
  accDescr: A chain of five steps. One, read the task and underline every point you must cover. Two, choose tú or usted and the genre's opening and closing. Three, plan one paragraph per idea, with a connector to start each. Four, write, using the three past tenses, the subjunctive where it is needed, and a recommendation. Five, count the words and check agreement, accents and mood.
  A["1. Read the task: underline every point"] --> B["2. Choose tú or usted, opening and closing"]
  B --> C["3. Plan: one paragraph per idea, a connector for each"]
  C --> D["4. Write: three pasts, subjunctive, a recommendation"]
  D --> E["5. Count and check: agreement, accents, mood"]
```

1. Cover every point. If the task asks you to say what you saw, what you liked and what you
   recommend, a missing point costs more than a small mistake. Tick each one off.
2. Choose the register (lesson 20) and keep it: *¡Hola, Sofi!… Un abrazo* to a friend;
   *Estimada señora…, Atentamente* to a stranger.
3. Plan short paragraphs. One idea each, opened with a connector: *Para empezar, Además,
   Sin embargo, Por eso, En resumen* (lessons 10, 17, 19).
4. Use your range. B1 means more than the present tense: the preterite for events, the
   imperfect for the scene, the pluperfect for what had happened before (*Ya había leído el
   libro*), the subjunctive after emotions and recommendations, maybe a hypothetical (*Si
   pudiera, la vería otra vez*).
5. Count and check. Stay inside the word range. Then reread three times, each time for
   one thing (see "Editing your draft" below).

## Writing about films, series and shows

| To say | Spanish |
|---|---|
| what it's about | *Se trata de… / La película trata de…* (lesson 22); *Está ambientada en…* (It's set in…) |
| who's in it | *El reparto es excelente. La protagonista la interpreta…* |
| what you thought | *Me pareció conmovedora / entretenida / previsible.* |
| what you liked | *Lo que más me gustó fue… Me encantó que…* |
| a reservation | *Aunque es un poco larga, vale la pena. Si tuviera que poner un pero…* |
| a recommendation | *Te recomiendo que la veas. Es imprescindible. No te la pierdas.* |

Some words in more detail:

- *El estreno* is a premiere or release; *estrenar* is to release a film or put on a show for
  the first time (*La estrenan en marzo*), and also to use or wear something for the first time
  (*Hoy estreno zapatos*).
- *Interpretar* is to play a role and also to interpret. Here A1's *el papel* (paper) has the
  sense "role": *Interpreta el papel de una maestra* (She plays the role of a teacher).
- *El reparto* is the cast; *el guion* is the script (no accent, RAE 2010 spelling); *la banda
  sonora* is the soundtrack.
- *El público* is the audience; *el espectador, la espectadora* a viewer or member of it;
  *aplaudir* to applaud; *el escenario* the stage.
- *El crítico, la crítica* is a critic; *la crítica* is also criticism or a review (lesson 16),
  like *la reseña* (lesson 08).
- *La comedia*, *el documental*, *el suspenso* (Mexico; Spain *el suspense*): genres. *Los
  efectos especiales* are special effects.
- In Mexican cinemas you can usually choose a *versión doblada* (dubbed) or one with
  *subtítulos* (*subtitulada*).
- *Emocionante* is exciting; *conmovedor* is moving, touching (feminine *conmovedora*);
  *entretenido* is entertaining; *previsible* is predictable; *recomendable* worth
  recommending; *imprescindible* a must, essential.

### Reacting with the subjunctive

You saw the film in the past, so a reaction in the past takes the imperfect subjunctive
(lesson 15): *Me encantó que la directora usara actores no profesionales* (I loved that the
director used non-professional actors). *Me molestó que el final fuera tan previsible.* (It
bothered me that the ending was so predictable.) A recommendation to a friend is about the
future, so it takes the present subjunctive: *Te recomiendo que la veas en el cine.*

![A streaming page for an original series, Las hermanas del puerto. A poster on the left. On the right: the title; Estreno: viernes 13 de noviembre; Reparto: Ana Robles, Tere Cano, Luz Méndez; a row of subtitle options, Subtítulos: español, inglés; a play button for the soundtrack, Banda sonora; and a reviews box with four stars, 120 reseñas.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Three model texts

Each text is original; the word counts were checked by computer.

### 1. A forum post (105 words)

In a forum, Sofía asked: *¿Qué serie me recomiendan para el fin de semana? Me gustan las
historias de familia.*

> ¡Hola, Sofi! Yo te recomiendo *Las hermanas del puerto*, una serie mexicana que se estrenó el
> mes pasado. Se trata de tres hermanas que heredan un restaurante en Veracruz y descubren un
> secreto de su papá. El guion es muy inteligente y el reparto es excelente: la actriz que
> interpreta a la hermana mayor es conmovedora. Además, la banda sonora tiene son jarocho, y te
> va a encantar. Solo tiene ocho capítulos, así que puedes verla en un fin de semana. Un
> consejo: vela en versión original con subtítulos, porque la versión doblada pierde el acento
> de la costa. ¡Después me cuentas qué te pareció!

*Heredar* = to inherit (lesson 13); *el son jarocho* is a traditional music from Veracruz
(honors 24h3). The post answers the question, gives three reasons, adds a practical tip and
ends with a friendly question. *Vela* is *ve* (the command of *ver*) + *la*.

### 2. An e-mail to a friend (111 words)

> Querido Andrés:
>
> ¿Cómo estás? Te escribo para contarte que el sábado fuimos al estreno de la obra de teatro de
> tu prima Lucía. ¡Qué lástima que no pudieras venir! El teatro estaba lleno y el público
> aplaudió de pie al final. La obra es una comedia sobre una familia que se queda sin luz el
> día de una boda. Lucía estuvo increíble en el escenario: me encantó que cantara una canción de
> su abuela. El final es un poco previsible, pero no importa, porque es muy entretenida. Van a
> repetir la función el próximo fin de semana. Te recomiendo que compres los boletos pronto,
> porque se agotan rápido.
>
> Un abrazo,
> Marina

*Aplaudir de pie* = to give a standing ovation; *se agotan* = they sell out. Count the tenses:
preterite for the events (*fuimos, aplaudió, estuvo*), imperfect for the scene (*estaba
lleno*), the present for the play itself, and two subjunctives (*pudieras* after a past
emotion, *compres* after a recommendation). The greeting and the signature are included in the
count.

### 3. A review for a culture blog (136 words)

> Ayer vi en un pequeño cine de mi barrio *El último invierno*, un documental sobre los
> guardianes de la mariposa monarca en Michoacán. Al principio pensé que sería aburrido, pero me
> equivoqué. La directora siguió durante un año a una familia que cuida el bosque, y lo cuenta
> sin narrador, solo con las voces de sus protagonistas. Lo que más me gustó fue que los niños
> explicaran el problema con sus propias palabras. Las imágenes son impresionantes y la música
> es sencilla y conmovedora. No hay efectos especiales: no los necesita. Como espectadora, salí
> con ganas de hacer algo. Si tuviera que poner un pero, diría que algunas escenas son demasiado
> largas. Aun así, es una película imprescindible para quien se interese por la naturaleza. Se
> estrena en plataformas el próximo viernes; no se la pierdan.

> Yesterday, at a small cinema in my neighborhood, I saw *El último invierno*, a documentary
> about the guardians of the monarch butterfly in Michoacán. At first I thought it would be
> boring, but I was wrong. The director followed a family that looks after the forest for a
> year, and she tells the story without a narrator, only with the voices of the people in it.
> What I liked most was that the children explained the problem in their own words. The images
> are stunning and the music is simple and moving. There are no special effects: it doesn't need
> them. As a viewer, I came out wanting to do something. If I had to find a fault, I'd say some
> scenes are too long. Even so, it's a must for anyone interested in nature. It comes out on
> streaming platforms next Friday; don't miss it.

The review uses *pensé que sería* (the future in the past, as a conditional), a past reaction
with the imperfect subjunctive (*fue que… explicaran*), a hypothetical (*Si tuviera…,
diría*), a concession (*Aun así*), *quien* + subjunctive for "anyone who" (lesson 08), and a
plural command to readers (*no se la pierdan*).

## Editing your draft

Reread three times, each time for one thing:

- Agreement. *La película es conmovedora*, *los efectos especiales*, *la serie es
  entretenida*. *El guion, el reparto, el público* are masculine; *la actriz* (plural *las
  actrices*) feminine.
- Accents. *película, crítico, espectáculo, también, así*; but *guion* and *fue* take
  none.
- Mood. After *me gustó que, me encantó que, me sorprendió que*: imperfect subjunctive.
  After *te recomiendo que, espero que*: present subjunctive. After *creo que, es verdad que*:
  indicative.

## Pronunciation

- *Guion*: the *u* is silent before *i*, like *guitarra*. The RAE counts *guion* as one syllable
  for spelling, which is why it has no accent, though many speakers say it in two (*gi-ON*).
- *Actriz, actrices*: *ac-TRIS, ac-TRI-ses* in Latin America.
- *Imprescindible*: *im-pre-sin-DI-ble*; the *sc* is a single *s* sound in Latin America.
- *Previsible*: *pre-vi-SI-ble*, four syllables.

## Common mistakes

- Missing one of the task's points: the most expensive mistake. Plan with the task in front of
  you.
- ~~*Me encantó que la directora usa…*~~ → *Me encantó que la directora usara…* (past emotion,
  imperfect subjunctive).
- ~~*La película se trata de…*~~ in careful writing → *La película trata de…* (lesson 22).
- ~~*El guión*~~ → *el guion* (RAE 2010 spelling).
- ~~*Es muy predictable*~~ (English) → *Es muy previsible.*
- Switching between *tú* and *usted* in one text.
- Writing far fewer or far more words than the task asks: stay inside the range.

## Key points

- DELE B1 writing: a reply of 100–120 words (e-mail, letter, forum post, blog entry) and a text
  of 130–150 words chosen from two options (such as a composition, a diary entry or a short
  biography).
- Method: cover every point, keep one register, plan paragraphs with connectors, use your
  range, count and check.
- Reviews: *Se trata de… / trata de…, El reparto…, Me encantó que* + imperfect subjunctive, *Te
  recomiendo que* + present subjunctive, *Aunque…, Si tuviera que poner un pero…*
- Edit for agreement, accents and mood.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: The DELE B1 exam and review
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This last core lesson of Spanish B1 explains what B1 means, describes the Instituto
Cervantes' DELE B1 exam in general terms, gives strategies for its four tests, and reviews the
course's grammar with three charts. The questions at the end cover the whole course. You don't
have to take the exam, but its free model papers are a good way to measure your level.

## What B1 means

B1 is the third of the six levels of the Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR), the
first level of the "independent user". In plain words, at B1 you can:

- understand the main points of clear, standard speech and writing about familiar things:
  work, studies, free time, the news on topics you know;
- deal with most situations that come up when you travel or live where the language is
  spoken, including unexpected ones (a complaint, a misunderstanding, a change of plan);
- write simple connected texts on familiar topics: an e-mail, a post, a short review, an
  account of an experience;
- describe experiences, events, dreams, hopes and ambitions, and give brief reasons and
  explanations for your opinions and plans.

The exam guide names the Instituto Cervantes' *Niveles de referencia para el español* as the
basis of the exam's content. At B1 you still make mistakes and search for words, but you keep
going and get your message across.

## The DELE B1

The DELE (*Diplomas de Español como Lengua Extranjera*) are the official diplomas of the
Instituto Cervantes, and the Cervantes describes them as having indefinite validity: they don't
expire. The figures below come from the official *Guía del examen DELE B1* (© 2014 Instituto
Cervantes), confirmed on the Cervantes' current DELE B1 page, in this course's own words.

| Test | Time | Tasks | Points |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reading (*Comprensión de lectura*) | 70 minutes | 5 tasks, 30 questions | 25 |
| Listening (*Comprensión auditiva*) | 40 minutes | 5 tasks, 30 questions | 25 |
| Writing (*Expresión e interacción escritas*) | 60 minutes | 2 tasks | 25 |
| Speaking (*Expresión e interacción orales*) | 15 minutes, after 15 minutes to prepare | 4 tasks | 25 |

![A diagram of the DELE B1. Four boxes: reading, 70 minutes; writing, 60 minutes; listening, 40 minutes; speaking, 15 minutes after 15 minutes of preparation; each worth 25 points. Reading and writing form group 1, listening and speaking form group 2, each of 50 points, and each needs at least 30. At the bottom: 30 or more in both groups gives Apto.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The 100 points are split into two groups of 50: group 1 is reading + writing, group 2 is
listening + speaking. You need at least 30 points in each group to be *apto* (pass); a
strong group can't make up for a weak one. Reading and listening give one point per correct
answer, and a wrong answer costs nothing. Writing and speaking are marked by trained examiners
on scales from 0 to 3: an overall impression counts 40 % and a detailed mark 60 %. The detailed
mark looks at four things: for writing, whether the text is *adecuado* (appropriate) to the
genre and task, its *coherencia* (how it hangs together), its correctness and its range; for
speaking, *coherencia*, *fluidez* (fluency), correctness and range.

### What each test asks, in general terms

- Reading: short notices, ads and messages to match with descriptions; an informative
  text; short accounts such as anecdotes or news; a longer practical text with sentences
  removed; and a letter-style text with gaps. You choose from three options, match texts and
  statements, or put sentences back into a text.
- Listening: short messages and announcements; a long talk about someone's experiences; a
  radio or TV news program; several short opinions on one topic; and a conversation between
  two people. Every recording is played twice.
- Writing: a reply of 100–120 words to a short text, and a text of 130–150 words chosen
  from two options (lesson 23).
- Speaking: a short talk on a topic you choose and prepare (2–3 minutes); a conversation
  with the examiner about it (3–4 minutes); describing a photo you choose and talking about it,
  without preparation (2–3 minutes); and a role play of an everyday situation (2–3 minutes).
  You may use the notes you made while preparing in the first two tasks. Two examiners are
  present: one talks with you, the other marks. The official B1 page says the speaking test may
  be held on the day before or after the written tests, as the exam center announces.

Which Spanish? The guide says the exam's texts come from many sources and varieties of Spanish.
In your answers, any educated norm of Spanish is accepted as long as you use it consistently,
so write and speak in the Mexican Spanish of this course and recognize the rest (honors 24h1
helps). Formats, dates and fees can change: check the official pages before you register in a
*convocatoria* (exam session) at a *sede* (exam center).

- [DELE B1 exam guide (PDF, Instituto Cervantes)](https://agenda.cervantes.es/sites/default/files/guia_examen_dele_b1_1.pdf)
- [DELE B1: the official Instituto Cervantes page](https://agenda.cervantes.es/es/node/27166877)
- [Preparing for the DELE: free model exams](https://agenda.cervantes.es/es/node/27166889)

## The words of exam instructions

Instructions address you as *usted*:

| Instruction | Meaning |
|---|---|
| *Lea el enunciado con atención.* | Read the instructions carefully. |
| *Redacte un texto de entre 100 y 120 palabras.* | Write a text of 100 to 120 words. |
| *Exprese su opinión y justifíquela.* | Give your opinion and justify it. |
| *Argumente a favor o en contra.* | Argue for or against. |
| *Resuma la idea principal.* | Summarize the main idea. |
| *Puede tomar notas.* | You may take notes. |
| *Lea la situación.* | Read the situation (for a role play). |

*Redactar* is to write or draft a text; *la redacción* is the composition. *La puntuación* is
your score, and also punctuation. *El apartado* is a section of a document. *Apto* is a pass;
*no apto* a fail; *el diploma* is what you receive.

## Strategies for each test

Reading. Read the questions first. Wrong options often repeat the text's words with a
small change (*todos* / *algunos*, *antes* / *después*). In gap texts, look at both sides of the
gap: a connector, a pronoun or a verb's mood often decides it. Answer everything.

Listening. Predict before each recording; get the main idea the first time and details
the second. Watch for changes of mind (*Iba a ir el lunes, pero al final…*): the final version
counts.

Writing. Follow lesson 23's method. Cover every point, keep one register, use *conectores*
(connectors) and show variety: a *variado* (varied) range of tenses and structures scores
better than a safe, flat text. Be *preciso* (precise): *la película me conmovió* says more than
*la película fue buena*.

Speaking. In the 15 minutes, *tome notas*: a plan in key words, not full sentences. In the
talk, open, give three or four ideas, close. In the photo task, go from general to detail, then
guess (*Parece que…, Seguramente…*). In the role play, react and ask. Your *entonación*
matters: a rise at the end of a yes/no question, a fall at the end of a statement. If you don't understand,
say so: *Perdone, ¿podría repetir la pregunta?* Honors lesson 24h2 has full models.

## Grammar review

### Indicative or subjunctive?

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Indicative or subjunctive?
  accDescr: A decision chart for the verb after que or a conjunction. First question: does the main clause express a wish, influence, a feeling or a value judgment? If yes, use the subjunctive, as in Quiero que vengas, Me alegra que estés aquí, Es importante que lo sepas. If no: does it express doubt, denial or possibility? If yes, subjunctive, as in No creo que llueva. If no: is it purpose, para que or sin que? If yes, subjunctive. If no: is it a time clause about the future, with cuando, en cuanto or hasta que? If yes, subjunctive, as in Cuando llegues, llámame; for habits and the past, use the indicative. If no: is it a relative clause about something unknown or nonexistent? If yes, subjunctive, as in Busco un departamento que tenga jardín. Otherwise, for facts, certainty and what you believe, use the indicative, as in Creo que tiene razón.
  A["The verb after que or a conjunction"] --> B{"Wish, influence, feeling, value judgment?"}
  B -- yes --> S1["Subjunctive: Quiero que vengas. Me alegra que estés aquí. (01-03)"]
  B -- no --> C{"Doubt, denial, possibility?"}
  C -- yes --> S2["Subjunctive: No creo que llueva. (04)"]
  C -- no --> D{"Purpose: para que, sin que?"}
  D -- yes --> S3["Subjunctive: para que lo sepas (06)"]
  D -- no --> E{"Time clause about the future?"}
  E -- yes --> S4["Subjunctive: Cuando llegues, llámame. (07)"]
  E -- no --> F{"Something unknown or nonexistent?"}
  F -- yes --> S5["Subjunctive: Busco un departamento que tenga jardín. (08)"]
  F -- no --> I["Indicative: facts, certainty, belief. Creo que tiene razón. (04)"]
```

The chart is a summary, not the whole story. Some words take either mood with a change of
meaning: *aunque* (lesson 17), *siempre que* (18), *decir que* (15). *Quizás* and *tal vez*
take either mood with little change (04), and *a lo mejor* takes the indicative. And if the
main verb is in the past or the conditional, the subjunctive is the imperfect: *Quería que
vinieras* (15).

### Conditions with *si*

| Kind | *si* + | Main clause | Example | Lesson |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Real, possible | present | present, future, command | *Si llueve, nos quedamos en casa.* | A2, 14 |
| Unlikely or unreal now | imperfect subjunctive | conditional | *Si tuviera tiempo, viajaría más.* | 14 |
| Unreal in the past | pluperfect subjunctive | conditional perfect | *Si hubiera sabido, habría venido.* | honors 16h1 |

Never *si* + present subjunctive or *si* + conditional in the condition: ~~*Si tendría
dinero*~~ → *Si tuviera dinero*. Either clause can come first: *Viajaría más si tuviera tiempo.*

### Reporting in the past

| Direct speech | Reported after *dijo que* | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| present: *"Estoy cansada."* | imperfect: *estaba cansada* | 16 |
| preterite or perfect: *"Terminé." / "He terminado."* | pluperfect: *había terminado* | 16 |
| future: *"Vendré."* | conditional: *vendría* | 16 |
| command: *"Llámame."* | imperfect subjunctive: *que la llamara* | 15 |
| *hoy, mañana, aquí* | *ese día, al día siguiente, allí* | 16 |

If what was said is still true, the tense can stay: *Dijo que vive en Puebla* is also correct
(16).

## Dialogue: la semana del examen

Tom is taking the DELE B1 in Mexico City. His friend Ximena is helping him practice.

> Ximena: ¿Ya sabes en qué sede te toca?
>
> Tom: Sí, en una escuela de idiomas en Coyoacán. Me inscribí en la convocatoria de noviembre: el examen escrito es el viernes, y la prueba oral, el sábado.
>
> Ximena: ¿Y cómo vas con la expresión escrita?
>
> Tom: Mejor. Antes no leía bien el enunciado y se me olvidaba algún punto. Ahora lo subrayo todo.
>
> Ximena: ¿Y lo oral? La semana pasada te pusiste muy nervioso.
>
> Tom: Ya lo sé. Mi profesora dice que mi fluidez está bien, pero que tengo que usar conectores más variados, no solo "y" y "pero".
>
> Ximena: Va. Te propongo algo: tienes quince minutos para preparar un tema. Puedes tomar notas. Luego me lo cuentas y yo te hago preguntas, como en el examen.
>
> Tom: Órale. ¿Y si me quedo en blanco?
>
> Ximena: Respiras y sigues. Si no te sale una palabra, la explicas con otras. Lo importante es que te expreses con claridad.
>
> Tom: Ojalá saque apto. Llevo un año echándole ganas.
>
> Ximena: Vas a ver que sí. ¡Ponte las pilas y a darle!

> Ximena: Do you know which exam center you've been given yet?
>
> Tom: Yes, a language school in Coyoacán. I signed up for the November session: the written exam is on Friday, and the speaking test is on Saturday.
>
> Ximena: And how's the writing going?
>
> Tom: Better. Before, I didn't read the instructions properly and I'd forget a point. Now I underline everything.
>
> Ximena: And the speaking? Last week you got really nervous.
>
> Tom: I know. My teacher says my fluency is fine, but that I need to use more varied connectors, not just "y" and "pero".
>
> Ximena: OK. Here's an idea: you have fifteen minutes to prepare a topic. You can take notes. Then you tell me about it and I ask you questions, like in the exam.
>
> Tom: Deal. And what if my mind goes blank?
>
> Ximena: You breathe and keep going. If a word won't come, you explain it with other words. What matters is that you express yourself clearly.
>
> Tom: I hope I pass. I've been working hard for a year.
>
> Ximena: You'll see you will. Get your act together and go for it!

*¿En qué sede te toca?* = which center have you been given?; *quedarse en blanco* = for your mind
to go blank; *si no te sale una palabra* = if a word won't come out; *¡A darle!* (Mexico,
informal) = let's go for it. Notice *Lo importante es que te expreses* (subjunctive after a value
judgment) and *Ojalá saque apto* (a possible wish).

## What comes next

At B2 you'll use the pluperfect subjunctive in full (*Si me lo hubieras dicho…*), more
connectors, nominalization (verbs turned into nouns in formal writing: *la construcción del
puente*, the building of the bridge) and finer control of register. Keep your reviews and
drills going, read the books on the course's reading list, and talk with people.

## Pronunciation

- *Coherencia*: *co-he-REN-cia*, the *h* is silent; *fluidez*: *flui-DES*.
- *Entonación*: *en-to-na-SIÓN*; plural *entonaciones*, no accent.
- *Convocatoria*: *con-vo-ca-TO-ria*, five syllables; *b* and *v* sound the same.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking the total decides the result: each group needs 30 of its 50 points.
- ~~*Escribir una composición de 200 palabras*~~ when the task asks for 130–150: stay in range.
- For "to take an exam" (as the candidate), Mexicans usually say *presentar un examen* (or
  *hacer un examen*). *Tomar un examen* sounds translated from English, and in some countries
  it is what the examiner does.
- Mixing Mexican and Spain's Spanish in one answer: choose one norm and keep it.
- ~~*Pienso de que…*~~ → *Pienso que…* (no *de*: lesson 22).

## Key points

- B1: you can deal with most everyday situations, follow the main points of clear speech, and
  write connected texts about experiences, opinions and plans.
- DELE B1: reading 70 min, listening 40 min, writing 60 min, speaking 15 min after 15 to
  prepare; 25 points each; group 1 (reading + writing) and group 2 (listening + speaking) each
  need 30 of 50 for *apto*; the diplomas don't expire.
- Any educated norm of Spanish is accepted if you use it consistently.
- Grammar: the subjunctive after wishes, feelings, doubt, purpose, future time and the
  unknown; *si* + imperfect subjunctive → conditional; tense shifts after *dijo que*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson. ¡Felicidades! You have finished the core of Spanish B1.

lessons.title: Honors: The same thing in other countries: everyday words across the Spanish-speaking world
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 21 taught the informal Spanish of Mexico: *la chamba, el cuate, ¡Órale!* Travel a few
hours south or watch a series from Buenos Aires, and the grammar is the same but some everyday
words aren't. This lesson is about recognizing informal words from Colombia, the Caribbean,
Argentina and Spain, so that a Colombian friend's *¡Qué bacano!* or an Argentine's *laburo*
doesn't stop you. You don't need to start using them: the DELE accepts any educated variety of
Spanish used consistently (lesson 24), and this course's norm is Mexico's. But a B1 listener
meets all of them.

Two facts keep this in proportion. First, almost all of the words you've learned are understood
everywhere: the differences are concentrated in informal speech, food, clothes and a few
everyday objects. Second, no country's Spanish is "more correct". Dictionaries record where a
word is used: the RAE's *Diccionario de la lengua española* (DLE) labels many senses with a
country or region (abbreviations like *Méx.*, *Col.*, *Arg.*, *Esp.* or *Am.* for the Americas),
and the Association of Academies' *Diccionario de americanismos* covers the words of the
Americas in detail. When you meet a new word, those labels tell you where it lives.

## Colombia

- *Bacano* (informal): great, cool. *¡Qué bacano!* = How cool! Colombians also say *chévere*, which you know from A2
  honors.
- *El parcero*, often shortened to *el parce* (informal; often linked with Medellín): buddy,
  pal, the Colombian *cuate*. *¿Qué más, parce?* = What's up, man?
- *La plata*: money. You met *la plata* as silver (lesson 12); in much of Latin America,
  including Colombia, Argentina and Chile, it is also the everyday word for money: *No tengo
  plata* = I don't have any money. In Mexico, *el dinero* is the neutral word, and *la lana* is
  the informal one.

## The Caribbean

- *La guagua*: the bus, in Cuba, Puerto Rico, the Dominican Republic and the Canary Islands.
  Careful: in the Andes (Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Chile and nearby areas), *la guagua* is a baby,
  from the Quechua word *wawa*. Same spelling, two very different things.
- *Chévere* (A2): great, cool, very common in Venezuela, Colombia and the islands.

## Argentina

Argentine Spanish (and Uruguayan, which shares much of it) often sounds the most different to
learners of Mexican Spanish, because of *vos* (A1 honors) and its *sh* or *zh* sound for *ll*
and *y* (*SHA-ma* for *llama*). Some of its everyday words:

- *Laburar* (informal): to work; *el laburo*: a job, work. They come from Italian
  (*lavorare, lavoro*), brought by the large Italian immigration of the late 19th and early
  20th centuries. *Estoy buscando laburo* = I'm looking for work (Mexico: *chamba*).
- *El pibe, la piba* (informal): a kid, a young person, a guy or girl. *Es un buen pibe* =
  He's a good guy.
- *La pollera*: a skirt (Mexico: *la falda*). It has nothing to do with *el pollo*.
- *El boliche*: a nightclub, a place to go dancing. In Mexico *el boliche* is bowling (*jugar
  boliche*) and a club is *el antro*, so this one causes real misunderstandings.
- *La pileta*: a swimming pool (Mexico: *la alberca*; Spain: *la piscina*). In some places it is
  also a sink.
- *El colectivo* (A2 honors): the city bus.

## Spain

You met Spain's grammar in notes all through this course: *vosotros*, the perfect for today
(*Hoy he comido*). Its informal vocabulary has two words you'll hear in every conversation:

- *¡Vale!*: OK! *—¿Quedamos a las ocho? —¡Vale!* (Mexico: *Va, Sale, Órale*). It is one of the
  surest signs that a speaker is from Spain.
- *Guay* (informal): cool, great. *¡Qué guay!* (Mexico: *¡Qué padre!, ¡Qué chido!*)

## One thing, five names

![A chart comparing informal words in five places. Rows: bus, buddy, job, cool, swimming pool. Mexico: el camión, el cuate, la chamba, padre or chido, la alberca. Colombia: el bus, el parcero, el trabajo, bacano or chévere, la piscina. The Caribbean: la guagua, el pana, el trabajo, chévere, la piscina. Argentina: el colectivo, el amigo, el laburo, bárbaro, la pileta. Spain: el autobús, el colega, el curro, guay, la piscina.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The chart shows the words most associated with each place, simplified: in every country you'll
also hear the neutral word, and usage varies inside countries too. A few words in it aren't
taught here and are only for recognition: *el camión* (Mexico's city bus), *el pana*
(Venezuela, Puerto Rico: buddy), *bárbaro* (Argentina: great), *el colega* and *el curro*
(Spain: mate, job).

## When a word is harmless in one country and rude in another

This is the part that matters most for your behavior, not just your understanding. A handful
of everyday words in one country are vulgar in another. This course names them in English only:

- In Spain, the ordinary verb for "to catch" or "to take" (a bus, a cold, a ball) is a vulgar
  sexual word in Mexico, Argentina and much of Latin America. In the Americas, take the bus
  with *tomar*: *Tomé el camión.*
- In Argentina and Uruguay, a common word for a seashell is vulgar. In Mexico the same word is
  also the name of a popular sweet bread, which can make a Mexican and an Argentine laugh, or
  blush.
- In Chile, the everyday word for a bird's beak is vulgar slang.

The safe strategy is the one this course follows: keep to neutral Spanish with strangers, use
the informal words of the place you're in once you've heard locals use them, and if people
laugh at something innocent you said, ask: *¿Dije algo raro?* (Did I say something strange?).

## Worked examples

### Example 1: a message from Bogotá

Your friend Camila writes from Colombia:

> *¡Hola! ¿Qué más? El concierto de anoche estuvo bacanísimo. Fui con mi parce Andrés, pero
> no me alcanzó la plata para la camiseta del grupo. ¡Qué pesar!*

Step by step: *¿Qué más?* is a Colombian greeting (what's up?). *Bacanísimo* is *bacano* +
*-ísimo*: really great. *Mi parce* = my buddy. *No me alcanzó la plata* = I didn't have enough
money (*alcanzar* = to be enough, lesson 01's verb in another sense). *¡Qué pesar!* = What a
pity (Colombia). In Mexican Spanish: *¿Qué onda? El concierto de anoche estuvo padrísimo. Fui
con mi cuate Andrés, pero no me alcanzó el dinero para la playera del grupo. ¡Qué lástima!*
(*La playera* is Mexico's word for a T-shirt; Colombia says *la camiseta*.)

### Example 2: un malentendido en Buenos Aires

Mariana, from Monterrey, is visiting her Argentine friend Facundo.

> Facundo: Che, Mariana, ¿querés venir al boliche esta noche?
>
> Mariana: ¿Al boliche? No sé jugar muy bien, pero órale.
>
> Facundo: ¿Jugar? No, es para bailar. Hay música toda la noche.
>
> Mariana: ¡Ah, un antro! En México el boliche es el juego de los bolos.
>
> Facundo: ¡Qué gracioso! Bueno, no nos quedamos hasta muy tarde: mañana tengo que laburar.
>
> Mariana: ¿Laburar? ¿Eso es trabajar?
>
> Facundo: Sí. Mi laburo empieza a las ocho. Después, si hace calor, vamos a la pileta del club.
>
> Mariana: ¿A la alberca? ¡Sí! Pero me tengo que comprar un traje de baño. ¿Hay tiendas cerca?
>
> Facundo: Sí, en la avenida. Y si querés, también hay polleras lindas.
>
> Mariana: ¿Polleras? ¿Venden pollos?
>
> Facundo: ¡No, tonta! Faldas. Acá la falda se llama pollera.

> Facundo: Hey, Mariana, do you want to come to the club tonight?
>
> Mariana: To the bowling alley? I'm not very good at it, but OK.
>
> Facundo: Good at it? No, it's for dancing. There's music all night.
>
> Mariana: Oh, a club! In Mexico *boliche* is the game with the pins.
>
> Facundo: That's funny! Anyway, we won't stay out too late: tomorrow I have to work.
>
> Mariana: *Laburar*? Is that *trabajar*?
>
> Facundo: Yes. My job starts at eight. Afterward, if it's hot, we'll go to the club's pool.
>
> Mariana: To the pool? Yes! But I need to buy a swimsuit. Are there any stores nearby?
>
> Facundo: Yes, on the avenue. And if you like, there are nice skirts too.
>
> Mariana: *Polleras*? Do they sell chickens?
>
> Facundo: No, silly! Skirts. Here a skirt is called a *pollera*.

Facundo uses *vos* forms (*querés*, A1 honors) and *Che* (hey), both typical of Argentina.
*Acá* = here (common in Argentina). Notice that the misunderstandings come from nouns and one verb: the grammar never gets
in the way.

### Example 3: from Argentina to Mexico

Rewrite in Mexican Spanish: *El pibe de mi vecina consiguió laburo en un boliche y ya no viene
a la pileta.*

1. *El pibe* → *El hijo* (if it's her son) or *el chavo* (the young guy, Mexico, informal).
2. *laburo* → *chamba* (informal) or *trabajo* (neutral).
3. *un boliche* → *un antro*.
4. *la pileta* → *la alberca*.

Result: *El hijo de mi vecina consiguió chamba en un antro y ya no viene a la alberca.* — My
neighbor's son got a job at a club and doesn't come to the pool anymore.

## Common mistakes

- Mixing regions in one sentence: ~~*Mi parce consiguió laburo, ¡qué guay!*~~ is three
  countries at once. Pick one variety, ideally the one of the people you're talking to.
- Assuming a word means the same everywhere: *boliche*, *guagua* and *pileta* each mean
  different things in different places.
- Thinking a regional word is slang to be corrected: *la pollera* and *la pileta* are the
  normal words in Argentina, used on the news.
- Using a word you've only heard in films with strangers. Informal words can sound rude or
  silly from a foreigner until you know the people.

## Key points

- The grammar of Spanish is shared; informal words, food, clothes and some objects change by
  country. Dictionaries such as the DLE label where a word is used.
- Colombia: *bacano, el parcero / el parce, la plata* (money). The Caribbean: *la guagua*
  (bus; in the Andes, a baby). Argentina: *laburar, el laburo, el pibe, la pollera, el boliche*
  (nightclub), *la pileta*. Spain: *¡Vale!, guay*.
- Mexico's equivalents: *la chamba, el cuate, padre / chido, el camión, la falda, el antro, la
  alberca*.
- A few words are harmless in one country and vulgar in another: keep to neutral Spanish with
  strangers.

the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: DELE B1 writing and speaking in practice
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 23 gave you a method for B1 texts and lesson 24 described the DELE B1. This lesson puts
both into practice: two writing tasks of the kind the exam sets, each with a first draft, the
corrections and a final model; then a plan and a model for each of the four speaking tasks, with
timing. The tasks are original and only follow the exam's general format, as the official guide
describes it; for real practice papers, use the Instituto Cervantes' free model exams (links in
lesson 24).

Throughout, you'll mark your own work. That's *la autoevaluación* (self-assessment) and *la
autocorrección* (self-correction), the two habits that make study without a teacher work.

## How your writing and speaking are judged

The guide says examiners give an overall mark and a detailed one, using a *rúbrica* (scoring
rubric) with four *criterios* (criteria). In this course's words:

| Writing | Speaking | Ask yourself |
|---|---|---|
| fit to the task and genre | coherence | Did I do what was asked, in the right kind of text? Does it hang together? |
| coherence | fluency | Do my ideas connect (*además, sin embargo, por eso*)? Do I keep talking without long stops? |
| correctness | correctness | Are agreement, tenses and mood right? |
| range | range | Do I use varied words and structures, or the same few? |

From these you can make a *lista de control* (checklist) for every text and talk. The task's
*pautas* (guidelines: the points you must cover) come first on it.

## Writing task 1: a reply

### Example 1: a language exchange

*The task (original):* You read this post in a forum: *"Soy Rodrigo, estudiante de ingeniería
en Guadalajara. Busco a alguien para practicar inglés; a cambio, ayudo con el español.
Escríbanme."* Write a reply of 100–120 words: introduce yourself, explain why you're interested,
suggest when and where to meet, and ask him a question.

Kate's first draft had five problems. Here they are, with her corrections:

| First draft | Second draft | Why |
|---|---|---|
| *estoy preparando por el DELE B1* | *estoy preparando el DELE B1* | *preparar* takes a direct object; no preposition |
| *estoy maestra de idiomas* | *soy maestra de idiomas* | a profession takes *ser* |
| *Te propongo que nos vemos los martes* | *Te propongo que nos veamos los martes* | *proponer que* is influence: subjunctive (lesson 02) |
| *Qué te parece el café…?* | *¿Qué te parece el café…?* | Spanish opens a question with ¿ |
| (no question for Rodrigo) | *Una pregunta: ¿prefieres…?* | one of the *pautas* was missing |

The last row is the important one: a missing point costs more than any single grammar slip.
Here is her final text (110 words, *el número de palabras* counted by computer, greeting and
signature included):

> Hola, Rodrigo:
>
> Leí tu anuncio en el foro de intercambio y me interesa mucho. Me llamo Kate, soy de Toronto y
> vivo en Guadalajara desde marzo. Trabajo en una escuela de idiomas y estoy preparando el DELE
> B1, así que necesito practicar la conversación. Yo te puedo ayudar con el inglés: soy maestra
> de idiomas. Te propongo que nos veamos los martes en la tarde, porque es cuando salgo temprano
> de la escuela. ¿Qué te parece el café que está enfrente de la biblioteca de la universidad?
> Podemos hablar media hora en cada idioma. Una pregunta: ¿prefieres practicar conversación o te
> interesa más la gramática? Espero tu respuesta.
>
> Saludos,
> Kate

*El foro* is a forum; *a cambio* = in exchange. Check it against the *pautas*: she introduces
herself (name, city, job), gives a reason (the DELE), proposes a day, a time and a place, and
asks a question. The register is *tú*, as Rodrigo's post invites.

## Writing task 2: a composition

### Example 2: a decision that changed my life

*The task (original):* A magazine asks its readers to write about a decision that changed
their life. Write 130–150 words: what you decided and why, how the people around you reacted,
how your life is now, and what you would advise others.

Lucía's first draft was 118 words, too short, and had these problems:

| First draft | Second draft | Why |
|---|---|---|
| *pensaron que me había puesto loca* | *pensaron que me había vuelto loca* | "to go crazy" is *volverse loco* (lesson 22) |
| *empecé del cero* | *empecé de cero* | a fixed phrase |
| *Si podría volver atrás* | *Si pudiera volver atrás* | never *si* + conditional (lesson 14) |
| *Mi consejo es que escuchan* | *Mi consejo es que escuchen* | advice: subjunctive |
| *me di cuenta que* | *me di cuenta de que* | careful writing keeps *de* (lesson 22) |
| (nothing on how she feels now) | *Gano menos, pero estoy más tranquila…* | a missing point, which also brought the count up |

The final text (135 words):

> El año pasado tomé una decisión que cambió mi vida: dejé mi trabajo en un banco y me mudé a
> Oaxaca. Durante diez años había trabajado en una oficina en Monterrey. Ganaba bien, pero me
> sentía cansada y casi nunca veía la luz del sol. Un día, en una junta, me di cuenta de que no
> quería seguir así. Al principio mi familia se puso nerviosa y mis amigos pensaron que me
> había vuelto loca. Sin embargo, me atreví. En Oaxaca empecé de cero: tomé un curso de cocina y
> ahora trabajo en un pequeño restaurante. Gano menos, pero estoy más tranquila y he aprendido
> muchísimo. Si pudiera volver atrás, tomaría la misma decisión, aunque me habría gustado
> hacerlo antes. Mi consejo es que escuchen esa voz que les dice que es hora de cambiar.

> Last year I made a decision that changed my life: I left my job at a bank and moved to
> Oaxaca. For ten years I had worked in an office in Monterrey. I earned well, but I felt tired
> and almost never saw the sunlight. One day, in a meeting, I realized that I didn't want to go
> on like that. At first my family got nervous and my friends thought I had gone crazy.
> However, I took the plunge. In Oaxaca I started from scratch: I took a cooking course and now
> I work in a small restaurant. I earn less, but I'm calmer and I've learned a huge amount. If I
> could go back, I'd make the same decision, although I wish I had done it sooner. My advice is
> to listen to that voice that tells you it's time to change.

Count the range: preterite, imperfect, pluperfect and perfect; two verbs of change (*se puso,
se había vuelto*); a hypothetical (*Si pudiera…, tomaría*); the conditional perfect (*me habría
gustado*); a subjunctive of advice. That variety is what "range" means.

## Speaking

You have *el tiempo de preparación*, 15 minutes, for tasks 1 and 2, and you may use your notes
in them. Tasks 3 and 4 aren't prepared. Practice with a timer: *cronometrar* (to time) your talk
is the only way to know what two or three minutes feel like.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Using the 15 minutes of preparation
  accDescr: A plan for the preparation time. Minutes 0 to 2: read both options and choose one. Minutes 2 to 10: write a plan in key words, one line per point, with a connector for each. Minutes 10 to 13: note useful words and two or three questions you might be asked. Minutes 13 to 15: say your first and last sentences quietly to yourself.
  A["0-2 min: read both options, choose one"] --> B["2-10 min: key-word plan, one line per point, a connector each"]
  B --> C["10-13 min: useful words; questions you might be asked"]
  C --> D["13-15 min: rehearse your first and last sentence"]
```

### Example 3: the talk (task 1)

*Topic (original):* *Un lugar que es importante para mí.* Kate's notes:

- *Intro*: el mercado de mi barrio, Guadalajara
- *Primero*: llegué → no conocía a nadie → la señora de las frutas, palabras nuevas
- *Además*: corazón del barrio: platicar, noticias, ayudarse
- *Por otro lado*: precios, supermercado → *me preocupa que…*
- *Opinión*: la ciudad debería apoyar → *para que…*
- *En resumen* + recomendación

Her talk (158 words; at a calm learner's pace, about a minute and a half, so in the exam she
would add an example or answer the examiner's follow-up):

> Voy a hablar de un lugar muy importante para mí: el mercado de mi barrio en Guadalajara. Primero,
> les voy a contar por qué es especial. Cuando llegué a México, no conocía a nadie y no hablaba
> bien español. Todos los sábados iba al mercado, y la señora del puesto de frutas me enseñaba
> palabras nuevas: así aprendí qué es un mamey y cómo se pide medio kilo. Además, el mercado es
> el corazón del barrio: ahí la gente platica, se entera de las noticias y se ayuda. Por otro
> lado, también es un lugar con problemas: los precios han subido mucho y algunos jóvenes
> prefieren el supermercado. Me preocupa que los mercados desaparezcan. En mi opinión, la
> ciudad debería apoyarlos para que sigan abiertos. En resumen, para mí el mercado no es solo un
> lugar para comprar: es donde empecé a sentirme en casa. Si alguna vez visitan Guadalajara, les
> recomiendo que vayan a uno. Muchas gracias.

*El mamey* is a tropical fruit with orange flesh. The notes are key words only; she never
reads a sentence aloud.

### Example 4: the conversation (task 2)

The examiner asks about the talk, and about your experiences and opinions. Answer in two or
three sentences, with a reason, and keep the conversation going:

> Examinadora: ¿Usted cree que los mercados van a desaparecer?
>
> Kate: Espero que no. Es verdad que el supermercado es más cómodo, pero en el mercado la fruta es más fresca. Además, creo que muchos jóvenes están volviendo a los mercados.
>
> Examinadora: ¿Y en su país hay mercados así?
>
> Kate: Hay mercados de agricultores, pero solo los fines de semana. Si hubiera más, yo iría todos los días.

Notice the moods: *Espero que no* (a wish), *Es verdad que… es* and *creo que… están*
(certainty: indicative), *Si hubiera…, iría* (a hypothetical). *El mercado de agricultores* is
a farmers' market.

### Example 5: describing a photo (task 3)

You choose one of two photos and describe it without preparation, then answer questions. Use a
fixed route: general view, then the people, then the details, then a guess.

![A park on a sunny day. In the center, a fountain. On the left, an older couple sit on a bench next to a tree. On the right, a girl rides a bicycle and a boy holds a red balloon. In the background, a family has a picnic on a blanket, and there is a swing.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

> En la foto se ve un parque en un día de sol. En el centro hay una fuente. A la izquierda,
> junto a un árbol, una pareja de señores mayores está sentada en una banca; parece que están
> platicando tranquilamente. A la derecha, una niña anda en bicicleta y un niño tiene un globo
> rojo. Al fondo, una familia está haciendo un día de campo y hay un columpio. Creo que es fin
> de semana, porque hay mucha gente y nadie parece tener prisa. Seguramente es un parque de
> barrio, como los que hay en muchas ciudades de México.

Route words: *En la foto se ve…, En el centro, A la izquierda / derecha, Al fondo* (A2), *parece
que…, Creo que…, Seguramente…* for guesses. A picture printed on a card for describing, like
this one, is *una lámina*.

### Example 6: the role play (task 4)

The examiner plays a part in an everyday situation related to the photo. Here: you bought a
jacket last week, and the zipper broke; you go back to the store.

> Kate: Buenas tardes. Compré esta chamarra la semana pasada y se le rompió el cierre.
>
> Empleado: ¿Trae su ticket?
>
> Kate: Sí, aquí está. Me gustaría que me la cambiaran por otra igual.
>
> Empleado: Lo siento, ya no tenemos de su talla.
>
> Kate: Entonces, ¿sería posible que me devolvieran el dinero?
>
> Empleado: Claro, si me deja la chamarra, le hago el reembolso.
>
> Kate: Perfecto. Muchas gracias por su ayuda.

*La chamarra* is a jacket (Mexico); *el cierre* a zipper. She uses *usted*, polite imperfect
subjunctives (*Me gustaría que…, ¿Sería posible que…?*, lessons 15 and 20) and *el reembolso*
(lesson 08). She opens, explains, asks, reacts to a problem and closes: five moves in seven
lines.

## Common mistakes

- Writing a fine text that misses a *pauta*. Check the task's points first on your *lista de
  control*.
- Counting badly: write to the middle of the range (about 110 and 140 words).
- Reading your notes aloud in the talk. Write key words, not sentences.
- Describing a photo with a list of nouns (*un árbol, una fuente, un perro*): add verbs,
  positions and guesses.
- Forgetting *usted* in the role play with a stranger, or switching halfway.
- Practicing without a timer: *cronometra* every talk.

## Key points

- Judge your work with the four *criterios*: for writing, fit to the task and genre, coherence,
  correctness and range; for speaking, coherence, fluency, correctness and range.
- Writing: a first draft, a *lista de control*, a second draft; every *pauta* covered; 100–120
  and 130–150 words.
- Speaking: plan in key words in the 15 minutes; describe photos from general to detail with
  guesses; in role plays, open, explain, ask, react and close in *usted*.
- *Autoevaluación* and *autocorrección* are the core of studying alone.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: Canciones: Latin American popular music
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Music is one of the easiest ways into a language: you hear real Spanish, with real
pronunciation, again and again, and you want to understand it. This lesson tells the story of
seven kinds of Latin American popular music in brief, from the Cuban bolero of the 1880s to
today's reguetón, and gives you the words to describe and review a song. It uses three tools
from this course: the passive for history (*fue compuesta en…, se popularizó en…*, lesson 12),
relative clauses for description (*un género que…, el músico con el que…*, lesson 08), and the
connectors of lessons 10, 17 and 19.

No lyrics are quoted here: song lyrics are protected by copyright, so you'll find titles and
facts only. Look the songs up and listen while you read.

![A timeline of Latin American popular music with places. 1883, Santiago de Cuba: Tristezas, often called the first bolero. 1910 to 1920, Mexico: corridos of the Revolution. 1930s to 1950s, Mexico: rancheras in the golden age of Mexican cinema. Late 1960s and 1970s, Cuba: the nueva trova. 1990s, Panama and Puerto Rico: reguetón. 2011: UNESCO lists mariachi. 2023: UNESCO lists the bolero, for Cuba and Mexico. A side box: son jarocho, southern Veracruz; cumbia, the Caribbean coast of Colombia.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Seven genres in brief

### El bolero

The bolero is a slow, romantic song, usually about love and heartbreak. Its history is usually
traced to Santiago de Cuba, where José "Pepe" Sánchez wrote *Tristezas* in 1883, often called
the first bolero. From Cuba it spread to Mexico, Puerto Rico and the rest of Latin America, and
Mexico became one of its great centers: Agustín Lara (born in 1897 or 1900, by different accounts; died 1970) wrote some of its best-known
songs, and trios with guitars made it popular across the continent. In 2023 UNESCO added the
bolero, nominated by Cuba and Mexico, to its list of the intangible cultural heritage of
humanity.

### La ranchera

*La canción ranchera* is a Mexican song about the countryside, love, pride and loss, sung with
a strong, open voice and usually accompanied by mariachi. It was made famous across Latin
America by the golden age of Mexican cinema (roughly the 1930s to the 1950s), whose stars, such
as Jorge Negrete and Pedro Infante, sang in their films. José Alfredo Jiménez (1926–1973) is
the composer most associated with it. Mariachi, the ensemble that plays rancheras, corridos,
boleros and much more, was added to the UNESCO list in 2011.

### El corrido

The corrido is a Mexican narrative ballad: it tells a story, often of battles, heroes, crimes
or love affairs, verse after verse, with the same melody. Its best-known period is the Mexican
Revolution (1910–1920), when corridos spread the news of events and leaders from town to town;
*La Adelita* is one of the most famous titles. Corridos are still written today, about all kinds
of subjects.

### El son jarocho

*El son jarocho* is the traditional music of southern Veracruz, on the Gulf of Mexico. It is
played with the *jarana* (a small guitar that keeps the rhythm), the *requinto* (a small guitar
that plays the melody) and often the harp, while dancers stamp out a rhythm on a wooden
platform (*la tarima*). It mixes Spanish, African and Indigenous roots. Its best-known song is
*La Bamba*: Ritchie Valens's rock version, released in 1958, made it famous in the United
States.

### La trova

*La trova* is the song of the *trovador*: a singer who accompanies himself or herself on the
guitar, with poetic lyrics. It has deep roots in Cuba, especially in Santiago, and in Mexico in
Yucatán (*la trova yucateca*). In the late 1960s and the 1970s, the Cuban *nueva trova* brought
socially committed lyrics; Silvio Rodríguez and Pablo Milanés are its best-known names. Today a
*cantautor* (singer-songwriter) of any style is often linked to this tradition.

### La cumbia

The cumbia was born on the Caribbean coast of Colombia, from African, Indigenous and European
roots. In the mid-20th century it spread across Latin America, and it took on a life of its own
in many countries: Mexico, Peru and Argentina each have their own styles. In Mexico it is the
music of countless parties, from Monterrey to Mexico City.

### El reguetón

*El reguetón* (also spelled *reggaetón*) grew out of two scenes. In Panama, in the 1980s,
young people of Jamaican and Caribbean descent sang Jamaican reggae and dancehall in Spanish;
in Puerto Rico, in the early 1990s, an underground hip-hop scene took up that sound, and the
name *reguetón* stuck. Its typical rhythm is called *dembow*. Since the 2000s it has become one
of the most popular kinds of music in the Spanish-speaking world.

## Words for describing music

- *El compositor, la compositora* writes the music; *el cantautor, la cantautora* writes and
  sings their own songs. *Componer* is conjugated like *poner*: *compongo, compuso, ha
  compuesto*; *La canción fue compuesta en 1950* (passive).
- *La melodía* is the tune; *el ritmo* (A1) the rhythm; *la letra* the lyrics (A1's *la letra*,
  "letter of the alphabet", in a new sense); *el estribillo* the chorus or refrain, the part
  that repeats (in everyday Mexican speech you'll also hear *el coro*, which is also a choir).
- *Pegajoso* = catchy (literally sticky); *bailable* = good for dancing; *nostálgico* =
  nostalgic.
- Describing with relatives: *Es un género que nació en Cuba. Es un ritmo con el que todo el
  mundo baila. Es la canción de la que te hablé* (the song I told you about).

## Worked examples

### Example 1: a genre in three sentences

Task: describe the son jarocho in three sentences, using a passive, a relative clause and a
connector.

1. History, with the *se* passive: *El son jarocho se toca en el sur de Veracruz desde hace
   siglos.* (Son jarocho has been played in southern Veracruz for centuries.)
2. Description, with a relative: *Es una música en la que la jarana, el requinto y el arpa
   dialogan con los bailarines.* (It's a music in which the jarana, the requinto and the harp
   talk with the dancers.)
3. A fact with a connector: *Además, su canción más conocida, "La Bamba", fue grabada como rock
   en 1958.* (Besides, its best-known song, "La Bamba", was recorded as rock in 1958.)

Check: *se toca* agrees with *el son* (singular); *en la que* refers to *una música*
(feminine); *fue grabada* agrees with *su canción* (feminine).

### Example 2: comparing two genres

Task: compare the bolero and the corrido using *mientras que* and *en cambio*.

*El bolero es una canción lenta y romántica que habla del amor, mientras que el corrido cuenta
una historia, verso tras verso. El bolero nació en Cuba; el corrido, en cambio, es mexicano.*
— The bolero is a slow, romantic song about love, while the corrido tells a story, verse after
verse. The bolero was born in Cuba; the corrido, on the other hand, is Mexican.

Notice where *en cambio* goes: between commas, right after the new subject (*el corrido, en
cambio, es…*), a common position in written comparisons.

### Example 3: a short song review

The song and the group are invented, so the review can be original. Read it and notice the
structure of lesson 23: presentation, description, opinion with a reaction, a reservation, a
recommendation (123 words).

> *"Luna de Tlacotalpan"* es la primera canción del nuevo disco de Las Jaraneras, un grupo de
> cuatro mujeres de Veracruz. Fue compuesta por la cantautora del grupo, que la escribió después
> de un fandango en su pueblo. La canción mezcla el son jarocho tradicional con una base de
> cumbia, y el resultado es sorprendente: la jarana y el arpa llevan la melodía, mientras que el
> bajo invita a bailar. El estribillo es tan pegajoso que lo vas a cantar todo el día. Lo que más
> me gustó fue que no perdieran las raíces del son, aunque lo modernizaran. Si tuviera que poner
> un pero, diría que es un poco corta. Aun así, es muy recomendable para quien quiera descubrir
> la música de Veracruz.

*El disco* = the album; *el fandango* = a son jarocho party where people play, sing and dance
together; *el bajo* = the bass; *las raíces* = the roots. The review uses the *ser* passive
(*fue compuesta por*), a relative (*que la escribió*), a past reaction with the imperfect
subjunctive (*fue que no perdieran*), *aunque* + subjunctive, a hypothetical, and *quien* +
subjunctive.

## Common mistakes

- *La música* is feminine, but genres are nouns with their own gender: *el bolero, el corrido,
  el son, el reguetón*; *la ranchera, la trova, la cumbia*.
- ~~*La canción fue compuesto*~~ → *La canción fue compuesta* (the participle agrees with the
  subject in the passive).
- ~~*Componió*~~ → *compuso* (like *puso*).
- Quoting lyrics in a review you publish: describe them instead (*La letra habla de…*).

## Key points

- Bolero (Cuba, 1880s; UNESCO 2023 with Mexico), ranchera (Mexico, with mariachi; golden age of
  cinema), corrido (Mexican narrative ballad; the Revolution), son jarocho (southern Veracruz),
  trova (Cuba, Yucatán; *nueva trova*), cumbia (Colombia's Caribbean coast), reguetón (Panama
  and Puerto Rico, 1980s–1990s).
- *El compositor, el cantautor, la melodía, el estribillo, componer* (*compuso, compuesto*).
- Describe music with the passive (*fue compuesta*), relatives (*un género que…*) and
  connectors (*mientras que, en cambio, además*).

lessons.title: Poesía: how Spanish verse works
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 10 introduced *el poema* among the genres. This lesson teaches you to read poems the way
Spanish speakers learn to at school: counting syllables, hearing the rhyme, recognizing the classic
forms and noticing images and figures of speech. Spanish verse follows clear, countable rules,
which makes this easier than in English. Every poem here is original, written for this course in
simple Spanish; at the end you'll meet five great poets through their lives and books, and find
out where to read them free.

## Words for talking about poems

A poem is made of lines, *los versos*, grouped in stanzas, *las estrofas*. Careful: *un verso* is
one line, not a whole poem or a stanza. Lines that sound alike at the end *riman* (rhyme):
*"corazón" rima con "canción"*. A book of poems is *un poemario*. To say a poem from memory is
*recitar*; to perform it dramatically before an audience is *declamar*, as in the school
*concursos de declamación* (recitation contests) held in many Mexican schools. A poet's inspiration is traditionally *la musa*, after the
nine Muses of Greek myth.

## Counting syllables

Spanish verse is measured by syllables, and the count follows three rules. A syllable counted
this way is a **[[metrical syllable]]** (*sílaba métrica*), and the system of measuring lines is
called **[[meter]]** (*la métrica*).

1. Count the syllables as you say them, not as you write them. Silent *h* doesn't count.
2. **[[Sinalefa]]**. When one word ends in a vowel and the next begins with a vowel (or with silent
   *h*), the two vowels are joined into one syllable: *se apaga* is said *sea-pa-ga*, three
   syllables, not four. The conjunction *y* between vowels joins too.
3. The last word changes the count. The basic count assumes the line ends in a *palabra
   llana* (stress on the second-to-last syllable, like most Spanish words). If the line ends in a
   *palabra aguda* (stress on the last syllable: *luz, Ramón*), add one. If it ends in a *palabra
   esdrújula* (stress on the third-to-last: *pájaro*), subtract one.

There are finer points (poets can also split or squeeze vowels for the meter), but these three
rules cover most lines.

![Two lines of verse divided into syllables. First line, Cuando se apaga la tarde: cuan, do, sea, pa, ga, la, tar, de. An arc joins se and a into one syllable, labeled sinalefa. Total: 8 syllables. Second line, Llega temprano la luz: lle, ga, tem, pra, no, la, luz. Seven syllables plus one because luz is a palabra aguda: 8.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 1: counting a line

*Una niña pide un globo* (a girl asks for a balloon):

1. Split it as you say it: *u-na-ni-ña-pi-de-un-glo-bo*, nine written syllables.
2. *pide un*: *-de* ends in a vowel and *un* begins with one, so they join: *pi-deun*. Now it's
   *u-na-ni-ña-pi-deun-glo-bo* = 8.
3. *globo* is *llana*, so nothing changes. The line has eight syllables: an **[[octosyllable]]**
   (*octosílabo*).

Now an *esdrújula* ending: *canta en la rama un pájaro* (a bird sings on the branch) is *can-taen-
la-ra-maun-pá-ja-ro*: eight after the two sinalefas, minus one for *pájaro*, so seven.

## The octosyllable and the *romance*

The octosyllable is the most popular line in Spanish. It is the line of the medieval
*romances* (ballads), of many Mexican *corridos* and of countless songs; it is often said to match the natural length
of a Spanish phrase. Lines of eight syllables or fewer are
called *de arte menor*; lines of nine or more, *de arte mayor*.

Here is an original poem in octosyllables. Read it aloud, slowly.

> #### Mañana de mercado
>
> Llega temprano la luz
> a los puestos de la plaza,
> y don Ramón acomoda
> su montaña de naranjas.
>
> Una niña pide un globo
> y su abuela la regaña;
> toda la calle se llena
> de voces y de palabras.
>
> Cuando se apaga la tarde,
> Ramón recoge su caja,
> y el mercado se despide
> hasta el sol de la mañana.

Translation: "Market morning. / The light arrives early / at the stalls in the square, / and Don
Ramón arranges / his mountain of oranges. / A little girl asks for a balloon / and her
grandmother scolds her; / the whole street fills / with voices and words. / When the evening
fades, / Ramón packs up his crate, / and the market says goodbye / until the morning sun."

Every line has eight metrical syllables. Check line 7 yourself (*to-da-la-ca-lle-se-lle-na*), and
line 12, which needs a sinalefa (*has-tael-sol-de-la-ma-ña-na*). The first line ends in *luz*,
an *aguda*: seven written syllables plus one.

## Assonant and consonant rhyme

Look at the ends of the even lines of *Mañana de mercado*: *plaza, naranjas, regaña, palabras,
caja, mañana*. They don't rhyme in the English sense, but they share the same vowels from the
stressed one on: *á-a*. This is **[[assonant rhyme]]** (*rima asonante*): only the vowels match.
The odd lines don't rhyme at all. Octosyllables with assonance in the even lines are exactly the
form of the traditional *romance*.

In **[[consonant rhyme]]** (*rima consonante*), everything from the stressed vowel on matches,
vowels and consonants: *libreta / secreta, decir / escribir*. Here is an original stanza of four
octosyllables with consonant rhyme in the pattern ABBA (line 1 with 4, line 2 with 3):

> #### Libreta
>
> Escribo en una libreta
> lo que no te sé decir,
> y la noche, al escribir,
> se vuelve azul y secreta.

Translation: "Notebook. / I write in a notebook / what I can't find the words to tell you, / and
the night, as I write, / turns blue and secret."

Count line 2: *lo-que-no-te-sé-de-cir* is seven, and *decir* is *aguda*, so eight. To find the
rhyme, start at the last stressed vowel: *libreta* and *secreta* share *-eta* (A), *decir* and
*escribir* share *-ir* (B).

| | Assonant rhyme | Consonant rhyme |
|---|---|---|
| What matches | the vowels from the last stressed vowel on | vowels and consonants from the last stressed vowel on |
| Examples | *plaza / naranjas* (á-a), *luna / duda* (ú-a) | *libreta / secreta*, *corazón / canción* |
| Typical forms | the *romance*, popular songs | the sonnet, most "learned" poetry until the twentieth century |

## The sonnet

The **[[sonnet]]** (*el soneto*) came from Italy, took hold in Spanish in the sixteenth century
and became the great form of Spanish poetry. Its rules:

- fourteen lines of eleven syllables each, the **[[hendecasyllable]]** (*endecasílabo*);
- two stanzas of four lines (*cuartetos*) and two of three (*tercetos*);
- consonant rhyme, usually ABBA ABBA in the quatrains and a freer pattern in the tercets, such as
  CDC DCD or CDE CDE.

![A diagram of a sonnet as fourteen bars in four groups. The first two groups have four bars each, labeled cuarteto, with rhyme letters A B B A. The last two groups have three bars each, labeled terceto, with rhyme letters C D C and D C D. A note says: 14 versos endecasílabos, rima consonante.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Here is an original *cuarteto*, the first quarter of a sonnet, in hendecasyllables:

> #### Domingo
>
> El tiempo pasa lento en la ventana
> y el gato duerme al sol, muy descansado;
> el aire sabe a pan recién dorado
> y nadie piensa en lunes ni en mañana.

Translation: "Sunday. / Time passes slowly at the window / and the cat sleeps in the sun, nice
and rested; / the air tastes of freshly browned bread / and nobody thinks about Monday or
tomorrow."

### Example 2: checking a hendecasyllable

Line 2, *y el gato duerme al sol, muy descansado*:

1. Sinalefas: *y el* → *yel*; *duerme al* → *duer-meal*.
2. Count: *yel-ga-to-duer-meal-sol-muy-des-can-sa-do* = 11.
3. *descansado* is *llana*: no change. Eleven syllables.
4. Rhyme: *descansado / dorado* share *-ado* (B, consonant); *ventana / mañana* share *-ana*
   (A).

Hendecasyllables also have a rhythm: the stress usually falls on the sixth syllable, or on the
fourth and eighth, and always on the tenth. In line 1, *El TIEM-po PA-sa LEN-to en la ven-TA-na*,
the stresses fall on 2, 4, 6 and 10.

## Images and figures of speech

Poems speak through **[[imagery]]** (*las imágenes*): words that make you see, hear, smell or taste.
*El aire sabe a pan recién dorado* gives the reader a taste and a smell at once. And they use
**[[figures of speech]]** (*figuras retóricas*), ways of saying one thing through another:

| Figure | What it does | Example (original) |
|---|---|---|
| **[[metaphor]]** (*la metáfora*) | says something *is* something else | *su montaña de naranjas* (a pile of oranges is a mountain); *Tu risa es una ventana abierta.* |
| **[[simile]]** (*el símil, la comparación*) | compares with *como* or *parecer* | *Acomoda las papayas como si fueran joyas* (lesson 91); *blanco como la leche* |
| **[[personification]]** (*la personificación*) | gives human actions to things | *el mercado se despide; la noche se vuelve secreta* |
| **[[hyperbole]]** (*la hipérbole*) | exaggerates on purpose | *Te lo he dicho mil veces. Me muero de hambre.* |

A symbol is an image that stands for an idea: in many poems the night stands for sadness or
mystery, the sun for hope, autumn for old age. *Simbolizar* (*simbolicé*) works like English: *¿Qué
simboliza la luz en el primer verso?*

### Example 3: reading for imagery

In *Libreta*: what do I see? A notebook, the night, the color blue. What is said through
something else? *La noche se vuelve azul y secreta*: the night can't change color or keep secrets
(personification and metaphor): writing changes how the speaker feels the night. What is the
feeling? *Lo que no te sé decir*: love or regret that can only be written. A poem rarely says "I'm
sad"; it shows it.

## Reading poems aloud

Join the sinalefas (*se apaga* sounds like *seapaga*), pause briefly at the end of each line
and longer at the end of a stanza, and let the rhyme be heard without singing it.

```speak lang=es-MX
# Read aloud: Mañana de mercado
Llega temprano la luz a los puestos de la plaza,
= The light arrives early at the stalls in the square,
y don Ramón acomoda su montaña de naranjas.
= and Don Ramón arranges his mountain of oranges.
Cuando se apaga la tarde, Ramón recoge su caja,
= When the evening fades, Ramón packs up his crate,
y el mercado se despide hasta el sol de la mañana.
= and the market says goodbye until the morning sun.
```

## Five poets to read

These five wrote long ago, so their works are in the public domain and free to read online. The
Biblioteca Virtual Miguel de Cervantes (cervantesvirtual.com), a free digital library of Spanish
and Latin American literature, has editions and pages on many of them: search for the author's
name. The Spanish Wikisource (es.wikisource.org) also has many of their books.

- Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz (New Spain, today Mexico; born in San Miguel Nepantla in 1648 or
  1651, the date is disputed; died in Mexico City in 1695). A nun of the Hieronymite order who
  read everything, she wrote sonnets, plays and the long philosophical poem *Primero sueño*
  (1692). In her *Respuesta a sor Filotea de la Cruz* (1691) she defended a woman's right to
  study. Her contemporaries called her *la décima musa*, "the tenth Muse", and she is on Mexico's
  100-peso note (2020). Read: her sonnets, and her verses criticizing men who blame women for the
  faults they themselves cause.
- José Martí (Cuba; born in Havana in 1853, died at Dos Ríos in 1895). Poet, journalist and
  leader of Cuban independence, he lived mostly in New York from 1880 to 1895. He published
  *Ismaelillo* (1882), poems for his son, the children's magazine *La Edad de Oro* (1889) and
  *Versos sencillos* (1891), short poems in octosyllables. Verses from *Versos sencillos* were
  later adapted in the song "Guantanamera". Read: *Versos sencillos*, and count the syllables of
  the first stanza yourself.
- Gustavo Adolfo Bécquer (Spain; born in Seville in 1836, died in Madrid in 1870). His short,
  intense love poems, known as the *Rimas*, were collected by his friends and published after his
  death, in 1871, together with his *Leyendas* (legends in prose). Read: the *Rimas*; most use
  assonant rhyme.
- Rubén Darío (Nicaragua; born in Metapa in 1867, died in León in 1916). The leader of
  *modernismo*, he renewed the rhythm and the images of Spanish poetry on both sides of the
  Atlantic. His books include *Azul…* (1888, published in Chile), *Prosas profanas* (1896) and
  *Cantos de vida y esperanza* (1905). Read: *Cantos de vida y esperanza*, and look for sonnets
  and long lines.
- Amado Nervo (Mexico; born in Tepic in 1870, died in Montevideo in 1919, while serving as
  a Mexican diplomat). Close to *modernismo*, he wrote quiet, spiritual poems and books such as
  *Perlas negras* and *Místicas* (both 1898). *La amada inmóvil*, poems about the death of the
  woman he loved, was published after his death. Read: his poems about peace and acceptance.

## Common mistakes

- Using *el verso* for a whole poem. *Un verso* is one line; the poem is *el poema*, a stanza is
  *la estrofa*.
- Counting syllables as written and forgetting the sinalefa: *se apaga* is three syllables.
- Forgetting the last-word rule: *luz* at the end of a line adds one; *pájaro* takes one away.
- Calling *plaza / naranjas* "not a rhyme". In Spanish it's assonant rhyme (á-a).
- Thinking *la poeta* is wrong for a woman: both *la poeta* and *la poetisa* are used.

## Key points

- Spanish verse is counted in metrical syllables: join vowels between words (sinalefa); add one
  after an *aguda*, subtract one after an *esdrújula*.
- The octosyllable is the popular line (*romances*, *corridos*, songs); the hendecasyllable is
  the line of the sonnet.
- Assonant rhyme matches vowels only (*plaza / naranjas*); consonant rhyme matches everything
  from the stressed vowel (*libreta / secreta*).
- The sonnet: 14 hendecasyllables, two *cuartetos* and two *tercetos*, consonant rhyme (often ABBA
  ABBA CDC DCD).
- Figures of speech: metaphor, simile, personification, hyperbole; images that appeal to the
  senses.
- Sor Juana, Martí, Bécquer, Darío and Nervo are in the public domain: read them free at the
  Biblioteca Virtual Miguel de Cervantes or Wikisource.
