lessons.title: La crónica y la columna de opinión: reading the press
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The press brings together everything this course has taught: the past tenses, the subjunctive
of doubt and value judgments, *si* clauses and the connectors of an argument (lessons 17–19).
This lesson reads two genres central to Latin American journalism: the *crónica*, a true story
told with a writer's eye, and the *columna de opinión*, a signed opinion piece. Both texts are
original and describe the same invented market in Mexico City, so you can compare genres.

You'll practice telling fact from opinion, noticing **[[hedging]]** (words that avoid stating
something as certain) and bias, and reading a long text without getting lost, as the longer
texts of the DELE B1 reading test require.

## Three kinds of newspaper text

| Genre | What it does | What it sounds like |
|---|---|---|
| *la noticia* (news story) | Reports what happened, most important facts first. | Third person, no opinions: *Se inauguró el mercado en 1958.* |
| *la crónica* | Tells a true story with scenes and voices. *El cronista* or *la cronista* may say *yo*. | Dialogue, description: *A las seis, el mercado ya está despierto.* |
| *la columna de opinión* | Defends a position, signed by *el columnista* or *la columnista*. | First person, connectors, value judgments: *Es una lástima que nadie lo vea.* |

A news story tries to be *objetivo* and *imparcial*. A *crónica* tells only true things but
chooses what to show, so it is partly subjective. A column is openly *subjetivo*: nobody expects
*objetividad* from an opinion. The problem is opinion dressed up as fact.

The genre goes back to the sixteenth-century chronicles of the Americas, such as Bernal Díaz del
Castillo's *Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España* (published in Madrid in 1632,
after his death). In twentieth-century Mexico it became an art: Carlos Monsiváis
(1938–2010) wrote about popular culture in books such as *Amor perdido* (1977) and *Los rituales
del caos* (1995), and Elena Poniatowska (born in Paris in 1932; Premio Cervantes 2013) told the
1985 earthquake through the voices of survivors in *Nada, nadie*.

![A newspaper front page. At the top, the paper's name, El Diario de la Colonia, and the date, sábado 14 de noviembre de 2026. Below, a large headline: Quedan 60 puestos en el mercado Santa Clara. Under it, a photo of market stalls with awnings and a line of text below the photo. On the right, a narrow column headed Opinión, with the columnist's name, Julia Esparza, and a small portrait. At the bottom, a strip with section names: Ciudad, Cultura, Deportes.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*La primera plana* (the front page) has *el titular* (headline, A2), photos with *el pie de foto*
(caption) and often a short signed column.

## Text 1: a *crónica*

The market and its people are invented, but the scene is typical of Mexico City's public markets
(the city has more than three hundred). Read it once quickly, then again with the glosses.

> #### Seis de la mañana en el mercado Santa Clara
>
> *Un día entre puestos, voces y tortillas recién hechas*
>
> A las seis de la mañana, cuando la colonia todavía duerme, el mercado Santa Clara ya está
> despierto. Don Ernesto sube la cortina metálica de su puesto de frutas con un ruido que se oye
> hasta la esquina. "Llevo cuarenta y dos años abriendo a esta hora", me dice mientras acomoda
> las papayas como si fueran joyas. "Antes de que llegue el primer cliente, todo tiene que estar
> en su lugar."
>
> En el pasillo de las comidas, doña Lupe ya calienta el comal. Huele a maíz, a café de olla, a
> cebolla frita. Una fila de albañiles espera sus tacos de guisado. Nadie habla mucho; todos
> miran el reloj.
>
> A las ocho llegan las familias. Una niña le pide a su mamá que le compre un globo; la mamá le
> contesta que primero van por las verduras. En el puesto de chiles, un señor discute el precio
> del chile poblano. "Ayer estaba a cuarenta el kilo", protesta. "Ayer era ayer, joven", le
> responde la vendedora, y los dos se ríen.
>
> Don Ernesto me cuenta que el mercado ha cambiado mucho. "Cuando yo empecé, aquí había más de
> cien puestos. Hoy quedan sesenta y tantos." Algunos locatarios se jubilaron y sus hijos no
> quisieron seguir; otros cerraron cuando abrió un supermercado a dos cuadras. Según los
> vendedores con los que hablé, la tendencia es la misma en otros mercados de la zona: menos
> puestos y clientes cada vez mayores.
>
> Pero a mediodía el mercado no parece triste. Tres estudiantes graban un video frente al puesto
> de jugos. Una pareja compra flores para su boda. A doña Lupe ya no le quedan tortillas.
>
> A las seis de la tarde, don Ernesto baja la cortina. "¿Y mañana?", le pregunto. "Mañana, a las
> seis, como siempre", me contesta. "Mientras haya gente que quiera fruta buena, aquí voy a
> estar."

Glosses: *la cortina metálica* (metal shutter), *acomodar* (to arrange), *el comal* (griddle),
*el café de olla* (spiced coffee brewed in a clay pot), *el albañil* (construction worker), *los tacos de guisado*
(tacos filled with stews), *ir por* (to go and get, Mexico), *estar a
cuarenta* (to cost forty: a price that changes), *sesenta y tantos* (sixty-odd), *el locatario*
(stallholder in a market, Mexico), *mayor* (here: older).

In brief: the cronista spends a day at the market. Don Ernesto has opened his fruit stall at six
for forty-two years; Doña Lupe sells stew tacos to construction workers; a customer and a vendor
joke about yesterday's price. The market has gone from over a hundred stalls to sixty-odd, and
customers are getting older, but at noon young people are there too. At closing, Don Ernesto says
he'll be back tomorrow: "As long as there are people who want good fruit, I'll be here."

What makes it a *crónica*: it moves hour by hour; the writer is present (*me dice, le pregunto*);
people speak in their own words; details do the work adjectives would do in a column. Grammar you know: *como si fueran joyas* (13), *antes de que llegue*
(07), *le pide que le compre* (02), *mientras haya gente que quiera* (18, 08).

## Fact or opinion?

A fact can be checked: a date, a number, something someone said, something that happened.
An opinion is a judgment someone could disagree with. Spanish gives you clear signals:

| Usually a fact | Usually an opinion |
|---|---|
| dates and figures: *quedan sesenta y tantos puestos* | opinion verbs: *creo que, me parece que, opino que* |
| quoted speech: *"Llevo cuarenta y dos años…", me dice* | value judgments + subjunctive: *es una lástima / es injusto que…* |
| a named source: *según los vendedores, de acuerdo con el INEGI* (Mexico's statistics office) | evaluative adjectives: *maravilloso, lamentable, absurdo* |
| neutral verbs: *abrió, cerraron, se jubilaron* | *deber* and the conditional: *las autoridades deberían…* |

*Según* and *de acuerdo con* introduce *la fuente*: a fountain in A2, but in journalism the
source of information. *Contrastar la información* means checking it against other sources.

### Example 1: sorting sentences

1. *El supermercado abrió a dos cuadras del mercado.* — Fact: it can be checked.
2. *Ningún supermercado ofrece lo que ofrece un mercado.* — Opinion: an absolute judgment.
3. *Según don Ernesto, antes había más de cien puestos.* — A fact about what he said; the number
   is his memory, which a journalist would contrast with records.
4. *Es una lástima que los jóvenes no vengan.* — Opinion (value judgment + subjunctive).

## Hedging and bias

Writers who aren't sure hedge, mostly with words you know: *al parecer, por lo visto,
supuestamente* (16); *parece que* + indicative, *es posible que / puede que* + subjunctive,
*quizás* (04); *se dice que, se cree que*. News headlines in many countries also use the
conditional for something unconfirmed: *El alcalde renunciaría esta semana* (the mayor will
reportedly resign). Some newspapers' style guides reject this *condicional de rumor* (*El
País* in Spain bans it) because readers can take a rumor for news: recognize it, but write *Según fuentes no oficiales, el
alcalde va a renunciar*.

Hedging is responsible when evidence is weak. **[[Bias]]** (*el sesgo*) is different: a slant in what
a text says and how. It hides in word choice (*los vendedores protestan* vs *exigen sus
derechos*), in which sources speak, and in what is left out.

### Example 2: removing the slant

Biased: *Los ambulantes* (street vendors) *invadieron otra vez la calle, como siempre, ante la
mirada indiferente de las autoridades.*

1. Find the loaded words: *invadieron* (a military verb), *como siempre* (a generalization),
   *indiferente* (a judgment).
2. Replace them with checkable facts: *El sábado, unos veinte vendedores ambulantes instalaron
   sus puestos en la calle Fresno. La alcaldía no ha respondido a nuestras preguntas.* (On
   Saturday, about twenty street vendors set up stalls on Fresno Street. The borough office
   hasn't answered our questions.)

## Text 2: a *columna de opinión*

Now the same market through a columnist's eyes. Look for the connectors of lesson 19 and the
subjunctive of value judgments and doubt.

> #### Los mercados no son nostalgia
>
> *Por Julia Esparza*
>
> Cada vez que cierra un mercado, alguien escribe un texto triste sobre el olor a cilantro y las
> abuelas que regateaban. Yo no voy a hacer eso. Desde mi punto de vista, defender los mercados
> públicos no es una cuestión de nostalgia, sino de ciudad.
>
> En primer lugar, un mercado es mucho más que un lugar para comprar. Es un espacio donde los
> vecinos se conocen, donde un niño aprende a contar el cambio y donde una señora que vive sola
> encuentra con quién platicar. Ningún supermercado ofrece eso, por muy limpio que esté.
>
> Asimismo, los mercados dan trabajo. Detrás de cada puesto hay una familia, y muchas veces tres
> generaciones. Es una lástima que las autoridades solo se acuerden de ellos cuando hay un
> incendio o una elección.
>
> Se dice que los jóvenes ya no van al mercado. Es posible que vayan menos, pero no creo que sea
> por falta de interés. Si los mercados abrieran por la tarde, aceptaran pagos con tarjeta y
> tuvieran baños dignos, muchos jóvenes volverían. No es verdad que el mercado sea algo del
> pasado; lo que es del pasado es la manera de administrarlo.
>
> Por lo tanto, propongo tres medidas sencillas: horarios más amplios, pagos electrónicos en
> todos los puestos y un fondo para reparar techos y drenaje. Nada de esto es una utopía.
>
> Aunque la tendencia sea negativa, todavía estamos a tiempo. El día que perdamos los mercados,
> no perderemos solo un lugar para comprar jitomates: perderemos una manera de vivir juntos.

Glosses: *sino* (but rather, after a negative), *por muy limpio que esté* (however clean it may
be: *por muy* + adjective + *que* + subjunctive), *digno* (decent,
dignified), *administrar* (to run, to manage), *amplio* (wide; here: longer), *estar a tiempo* (to
still have time).

In brief: Julia Esparza argues that markets matter for the city, not out of nostalgia: they are
places where neighbors meet and they give work to families. Young people may go less, she says,
but not for lack of interest; longer hours, card payments and decent restrooms would bring them
back. She proposes three measures and ends: losing markets would mean losing a way of living
together.

How the column works: a hook, the position (*desde mi punto de vista…*), two arguments (*en
primer lugar, asimismo*), a counterargument answered (*Se dice que… Es posible que… pero no creo
que…*), a proposal with *si* + imperfect subjunctive, and *aunque* + subjunctive conceding a
known fact as unimportant (lesson 17). The facts are the crónica's; only the column tells you what
to think.

## Reading a long text

1. Read the questions first: they tell you what to look for.
2. Skim the title and the first sentence of each paragraph. Decide the genre.
3. Scan for each answer, expecting paraphrase: the question says *don Ernesto piensa seguir
   trabajando*, the text says *aquí voy a estar*.
4. Watch the traps: a choice that copies the text's words but changes the meaning, one that is
   true in general but not in the text, and negatives (*no creo que…*).
5. Don't stop at unknown words; come back only if a question needs one.

### Example 3: a paraphrase question

*Según la columnista, ¿por qué van menos jóvenes al mercado?* (a) *porque no les interesa*, (b)
*porque los horarios y los servicios no les convienen*. She writes *no creo que sea por falta de
interés*, which rules out (a), and lists afternoon hours, card payments and restrooms: (b) is the
paraphrase.

## Common mistakes

- Taking a quotation for the writer's opinion. In the *crónica*, *Mientras haya gente que quiera
  fruta buena…* is don Ernesto's voice, not the cronista's.
- Reading *Es posible que vayan menos* as a fact. It's a hedge: the columnist concedes a
  possibility.
- Confusing *objetivo* (objective) with *el objetivo* (goal).
- Writing *el columnista* for a woman: *la columnista*, like *la periodista*.

## Key points

- *La noticia* reports, *la crónica* tells a true story with scenes and voices, *la columna*
  argues a signed opinion.
- Facts can be checked; opinions carry opinion verbs, evaluative adjectives, *deber*, and value
  judgments + subjunctive.
- *La fuente* = source; *contrastar* = check against other sources.
- Hedging: *al parecer, se dice que, es posible que* + subjunctive; recognize the *condicional de
  rumor*. *El sesgo* hides in word choice, sources and omissions.
- Long texts: questions first, skim, scan, expect paraphrase.

lessons.title: Teatro: El mole de la abuela, a one-act comedy
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

A play is all conversation: people interrupt, exaggerate, report what someone said and get it
wrong, switch between *tú* and *usted*, and use idioms without thinking. That makes it a perfect
review of reported speech (16), the subjunctive (01–04, 15), register (20) and idioms (21). This
lesson shows how a play is written, gives you the words of the theater, and presents an original
one-act comedy set in a Mexican family, part of which you'll perform aloud.

## How a play is written

A play (*una obra de teatro*, or just *una obra*) is written by *un dramaturgo* or *una
dramaturga*. Mexico has a strong theater tradition: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz wrote comedies in
the seventeenth century (lesson 90 tells her story), Rodolfo Usigli (1905–1979) wrote *El
gesticulador* in 1938, and Emilio Carballido (1925–2008) wrote dozens of plays, among them
*Rosalba y los llaveros*, first staged in 1950.

A play has *actos* (acts) and *escenas* (scenes); a short one may have a single act. On the page:

- Dialogue: each speech starts with the character's name, usually in capitals with a period and
  a dash: *ROSA.— Veinte, veintiuno…*
- **[[Stage directions]]** (*acotaciones*), in parentheses and italics, describe the set, movements
  and tone, in the present tense and third person, often verb first: *(Entra TOÑO corriendo.)*,
  *(Bajando la voz.)*.

A list of *personajes* comes first; *Se abre el telón* opens the play, *Cae el telón* and *Fin*
close it.

![A theater seen from the audience. A red curtain is pulled to both sides of the stage. On the stage, a table with two clay pots and a small box on it, labeled la utilería, and at the back a rack of hanging costumes, labeled el vestuario. The wooden floor is labeled el escenario and the curtain el telón. In the foreground, three rows of red theater seats, labeled las butacas, with two people sitting in them.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Before opening night *el elenco* (the cast; *el reparto* is also used, especially for films)
*ensaya*: each session is *un ensayo* (rehearsal; also essay). Someone prepares *el vestuario*
(the costumes) and *la utilería* (the props; Spain *el atrezo*): a plastic ring is *de utilería*.
The audience sits in *las butacas*, and at the end comes *el aplauso*.

## The play: *El mole de la abuela*

*Mole poblano* is a sauce from Puebla made with dried chiles, chocolate, sesame seeds and many
spices, often for big celebrations. Read the play once for the story, then with the glosses.

> #### El mole de la abuela
>
> *Comedia en un acto*
>
> PERSONAJES: DOÑA CARMEN, la abuela, que cumple ochenta años mañana. ROSA, su hija. TOÑO, hijo
> de Rosa, diecisiete años. VALERIA, sobrina de Rosa, veintiún años. DON FERMÍN, el vecino.
>
> *(La cocina de una casa en Puebla, un sábado por la mañana. Una mesa grande, una estufa, ollas
> de barro en la pared. ROSA cuenta sillas. VALERIA lee un libro. Se abre el telón.)*
>
> ROSA.— Veinte, veintiuno, veintidós… Valeria, ¿cuántos vienen mañana?
>
> VALERIA.— *(Sin levantar la vista.)* Treinta y cinco, tía. Treinta y seis si viene el novio de
> Lupita.
>
> ROSA.— ¿No te parece raro que tu abuela no haya empezado el mole? Siempre lo empieza dos días
> antes.
>
> VALERIA.— Estará cansada. Tiene ochenta años, tía, no dieciocho.
>
> *(Entra TOÑO corriendo, con el celular en la mano.)*
>
> TOÑO.— ¡Mamá! ¡Prima! Tengo que contarles algo, pero júrenme que no se van a enojar.
>
> ROSA.— Ay, Toño, ¿ahora qué hiciste?
>
> TOÑO.— Yo, nada. Es la abuela. La oí hablando por teléfono en el patio. *(Bajando la voz.)* Dijo
> que ya no iba a hacer el mole. Que estaba harta. Que este año lo hicieran otros.
>
> ROSA.— *(Se sienta.)* ¿Mi mamá dijo eso? No creo que mi mamá diga algo así ni en broma.
>
> TOÑO.— Y eso no es todo. Dijo que mañana temprano se iba con Fermín. Textualmente: "Mañana
> temprano me voy con Fermín."
>
> VALERIA.— ¿Con don Fermín? ¿El vecino?
>
> ROSA.— ¡Híjole! ¡A los ochenta años! ¿Y por qué no me dijo nada a mí? Si yo fuera ella, se lo
> diría primero a mi hija.
>
> VALERIA.— A lo mejor quiere anunciarlo mañana, en la fiesta, delante de todos.
>
> ROSA.— ¡Ni lo mande Dios! Imagínate: treinta y seis invitados, el pastel, las velas, y de
> repente: "Hijos, me voy con Fermín."
>
> TOÑO.— Sería la fiesta más famosa de la colonia.
>
> ROSA.— Tú cállate, que no estás ayudando.
>
> VALERIA.— Tía, no se ponga así. A lo mejor Toño entendió mal. Ya sabe que siempre está en las
> nubes. Como la vez que nos dijo que el maestro había cancelado el examen… y no lo había
> cancelado.
>
> TOÑO.— ¡Eso fue diferente!
>
> ROSA.— Bueno, si mi mamá ya no quiere cocinar, está en su derecho. Pero ¿quién va a hacer el mole
> para treinta y seis personas? Ella nunca ha escrito la receta.
>
> VALERIA.— Pues lo hacemos nosotros. No puede ser tan difícil.
>
> ROSA.— *(Se ríe.)* Lleva veintitantos ingredientes, mija. No es pan comido.
>
> *(Suena el timbre. Todos se miran.)*
>
> TOÑO.— ¡Aguas! Debe de ser él.
>
> *(Entra DON FERMÍN con dos bolsas enormes.)*
>
> DON FERMÍN.— Buenos días, Rosita. Buenos días, jóvenes. ¿Está su mamá?
>
> ROSA.— *(Muy seria.)* Está en el patio, don Fermín. Pero antes de que la vea, quisiera hablar con
> usted. Mire, yo respeto mucho a mi mamá. Si ella quiere irse con usted, nadie se lo va a impedir.
> Pero me gustaría que me lo dijera ella misma.
>
> DON FERMÍN.— *(Confundido.)* ¿Irse conmigo? ¿Adónde?
>
> TOÑO.— No se haga, don Fermín. Mañana temprano. Lo oí todo.
>
> DON FERMÍN.— ¡Ah, eso! *(Se ríe.)* Mañana temprano su abuela y yo vamos al mercado, muchacho. Me
> pidió que la llevara en la camioneta, porque le faltan el ajonjolí y el chocolate. Y estos chiles
> me los encargó ayer. *(Pone las bolsas sobre la mesa.)* Mulato, ancho y pasilla, como siempre.
>
> VALERIA.— *(A TOÑO.)* Ya decía yo.
>
> *(Entra DOÑA CARMEN con un delantal y un cuaderno viejo.)*
>
> DOÑA CARMEN.— ¿Qué tanto platican?
>
> ROSA.— Mamá, Toño nos dijo que usted ya no quería hacer el mole.
>
> DOÑA CARMEN.— Y es verdad. Este año no lo voy a hacer yo. *(Pausa. Todos miran a TOÑO, que
> sonríe.)* Lo van a hacer ustedes. Yo voy a estar sentada en esa silla, dando órdenes. Tengo
> ochenta años: ya es hora de que alguien más aprenda.
>
> VALERIA.— ¿Y por qué dijo que estaba harta?
>
> DOÑA CARMEN.— Porque estoy harta de ser la única que sabe hacerlo. *(Abre el cuaderno.)* Por eso
> anoche escribí la receta. Por primera vez en sesenta años.
>
> TOÑO.— *(Lee por encima del hombro de su abuela.)* "Paso uno: que Toño lave las ollas sin
> quejarse."
>
> DOÑA CARMEN.— Eso también es parte de la receta.
>
> TOÑO.— ¡Me está tomando el pelo, abuela!
>
> DOÑA CARMEN.— Un poquito. Pero las ollas sí las vas a lavar.
>
> DON FERMÍN.— Bueno, yo me retiro, que aquí van a trabajar.
>
> DOÑA CARMEN.— Usted no se va a ningún lado, Fermín. Usted muele los chiles. Toño, el chocolate.
> Valeria, el ajonjolí. Y tú, Rosa, cuidas que nadie meta la pata.
>
> ROSA.— ¿Y usted, mamá?
>
> DOÑA CARMEN.— Yo, como les dije, doy órdenes. *(Se sienta.)* ¡A ver, échenle ganas, que el mole
> no se hace solo!
>
> *(Todos se ponen a trabajar al mismo tiempo y chocan unos con otros. DOÑA CARMEN sonríe y abre
> una revista. Las luces bajan poco a poco. Cae el telón.)*
>
> FIN

Glosses: *la olla de barro* (clay pot), *sin levantar la vista* (without looking up), *Estará
cansada* (she must be tired: the future of probability, A2), *júrenme* (swear to me), *ni en
broma* (not even as a joke), *no se ponga así* (don't get so worked up), *estar en su derecho* (to
be within one's rights), *la receta* (here: recipe), *veintitantos* (twenty-odd), *el timbre* (here: doorbell), *mija* (*mi hija*, my dear: affectionate,
Mexico), *Debe de ser él* (it must be him), *impedir* (to stop, to prevent), *¡Ni lo mande Dios!* (God forbid!), *No se haga* (don't
play dumb: Mexico, informal), *la camioneta* (pickup truck, van), *el ajonjolí* (sesame seeds,
Mexico), *Ya decía yo* (I knew it), *el delantal* (apron), *¿Qué tanto platican?* (what are you all
talking about so much?), *por encima del hombro* (over the shoulder), *me
retiro* (I'll be going), *moler* (to grind; *muele*), *chocar* (to bump into).

Seven idioms from lesson 21 are here: *estar en las nubes, ser pan comido, ¡Aguas!, ¡Híjole!,
tomar el pelo, meter la pata, echarle ganas*. Find each one and say what it means in context.

## What the play does with grammar

### Reported speech and the misunderstanding

Doña Carmen said on the phone, more or less: *"Ya no voy a hacer el mole. Estoy harta. Que este
año lo hagan otros. Mañana temprano me voy con Fermín."* Toño reports it with every shift right
(lesson 16):

| What she said | What Toño reports |
|---|---|
| *Ya no voy a hacer el mole.* | *Dijo que ya no iba a hacer el mole.* |
| *Estoy harta.* | *(Dijo) que estaba harta.* |
| *Que este año lo hagan otros.* | *(Dijo) que este año lo hicieran otros.* |
| *Mañana temprano me voy con Fermín.* | *Dijo que mañana temprano se iba con Fermín.* |

The grammar is perfect; the interpretation is wrong. *Irse con alguien* can mean going somewhere
with someone or leaving home for someone. *Mañana* stays *mañana* because the day is still in
the future when Toño speaks.

### The subjunctive in natural speech

*¿No te parece raro que no haya empezado…?* (03), *No creo que mi mamá diga…* (04), *antes de que
la vea* (07), *Si yo fuera ella, se lo diría* (14), *me gustaría que me lo dijera* and *Me pidió
que la llevara* (15), *ya es hora de que alguien aprenda* (*es hora de que* + subjunctive), and the
recipe's *que Toño lave las ollas* (an instruction with *que* alone).

### Register

Rosa and Valeria say *usted* to their elders (*¿Y usted, mamá?*, *Tía, no se ponga así*), but the
grandmother says *tú* to her daughter and grandson (*Y tú, Rosa, cuidas…*). In many Mexican
families, especially traditional ones, *usted* upward and *tú* downward is a sign of respect and
affection, not distance; in others everyone says *tú*.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: writing stage directions

A narrator writes: *Toño entró corriendo. Rosa se sentó porque estaba sorprendida.*

1. Use the present tense, verb first, name in capitals: *(Entra TOÑO corriendo.)*
2. Show, don't explain: an actor can't play *porque estaba sorprendida*, so give an action or a
   tone: *(Se deja caer en una silla, sorprendida.)* (She drops into a chair, surprised.)

### Example 2: reporting a scene

After the play, Valeria tells a friend what happened. Report these lines in the past:

- DON FERMÍN: *"Mañana su abuela y yo vamos al mercado."* → *Don Fermín nos explicó que al día
  siguiente la abuela y él iban al mercado.* (Here *mañana* does shift: Valeria is telling it
  days later.)
- DOÑA CARMEN: *"Lo van a hacer ustedes."* → *La abuela dijo que lo íbamos a hacer nosotros.*
  (*ustedes* becomes *nosotros* because Valeria was one of them.)
- The recipe's step one as a command, *"Toño, lava las ollas."* → *Le dijo a Toño que lavara las
  ollas.* (a command → imperfect subjunctive)

## Perform it

Play each line, repeat it, then read the exchange at speed. Stage directions tell you the tone:
Rosa is *muy seria* (flat and slow); Don Fermín is confused, then laughs. Yes/no questions
(*¿Irse conmigo?*) usually rise at the end; questions with a question word (*¿Adónde?*) usually
fall.

```dialogue lang=es-MX
# El mole de la abuela: la llegada de don Fermín
Rosa: Si ella quiere irse con usted, nadie se lo va a impedir. Pero me gustaría que me lo dijera ella misma.
= If she wants to leave with you, nobody's going to stop her. But I'd like her to tell me herself.
Don Fermín: ¿Irse conmigo? ¿Adónde?
= Leave with me? Where to?
Toño: No se haga, don Fermín. Mañana temprano. Lo oí todo.
= Don't play dumb, Don Fermín. Tomorrow morning. I heard everything.
Don Fermín: ¡Ah, eso! Mañana temprano su abuela y yo vamos al mercado, muchacho.
= Oh, that! Tomorrow morning your grandmother and I are going to the market, my boy.
```

The play in brief: Toño overhears his grandmother saying she won't make the mole, that others
should make it, and that she's going off with Fermín early tomorrow. Rosa is shocked; Valeria
suspects a misunderstanding. Don Fermín arrives with chiles: he's only driving her to the market.
Doña Carmen explains that this year the family will cook while she gives orders, and that she has
written the recipe down for the first time. Step one: Toño washes the pots.

## Common mistakes

- Stage directions in the past: ~~*(Entró Toño.)*~~ → *(Entra TOÑO.)*
- *El telón* is the stage curtain (a window curtain is *la cortina*); *la butaca* is a theater
  seat (any seat: *el asiento*).
- *El ensayo* in a theater is a rehearsal, not an essay.
- Shifting *mañana* mechanically in reported speech when the day is still to come.
- Assuming *usted* always means distance: in a family it can mean respect and affection.

## Key points

- A play has *actos* and *escenas*; speeches start *ROSA.—*; *acotaciones* are in the present, in
  parentheses: *(Entra TOÑO corriendo.)* *Se abre el telón… Cae el telón. Fin.*
- Theater words: *la obra de teatro, el dramaturgo, el elenco, el ensayo, ensayar, el vestuario,
  la utilería, la butaca, el telón, el aplauso, la acotación.*
- Dialogue uses the whole course: reported speech, the subjunctive, *tú* and *usted*, idioms.
- Read plays aloud: intonation carries half the meaning.

lessons.title: Ciencia para todos: a popular-science article and podcast
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

*La divulgación científica* is science explained for everyone: magazine articles, museum
panels, videos and podcasts. It is a great genre for a B1 learner because so many science words
are cognates (*el virus, la célula, la evolución*), and because it uses exactly the grammar you
have learned: the **[[passive voice]]** and the **[[passive se]]** for processes (lesson 12: *la vacuna
fue aprobada; se compara a los dos grupos*), the subjunctive and the conditional for caution
(*es posible que, podría*), numbers and dates.

This lesson has two original texts: an article on how a vaccine is tested and a podcast
interview on how the brain learns a language. You'll learn to read the "certainty level" of a
scientific claim, and a method for listening to a long recording like the radio programs and
monologues of the DELE B1 listening test.

## Text 1: an article

Read it once for the general idea, then again with the glosses.

> #### ¿Cómo se prueba una vacuna?
>
> *Antes de llegar a tu brazo, una vacuna pasa años en pruebas. Te explicamos cómo funcionan.*
>
> La historia empieza en Inglaterra. El 14 de mayo de 1796, el médico Edward Jenner le puso a un niño
> de ocho años material de una lechera que tenía la viruela de las vacas, una enfermedad leve.
> Después comprobó que el niño ya no se enfermaba de viruela, una enfermedad mucho más grave. Del
> latín *vacca* (vaca) viene la palabra *vacuna*.
>
> Hoy sabemos por qué funcionó. Una vacuna enseña al sistema inmunitario a reconocer un virus o una
> bacteria sin que tengamos que enfermarnos. Algunas vacunas usan el microbio muerto o debilitado;
> otras, solo una parte de él; y otras llevan las instrucciones genéticas para que nuestras propias
> células fabriquen esa parte.
>
> Probar una vacuna es aplicar el método científico: hacer una pregunta, proponer una hipótesis,
> diseñar un experimento y analizar los datos. Primero, la vacuna se estudia en el laboratorio y
> en animales. Si los resultados son buenos, empiezan los ensayos clínicos con personas, en tres
> fases. En la fase 1 participan unas decenas de voluntarios sanos, y se comprueba sobre todo si
> la vacuna es segura. En la fase 2 participan cientos, y se mide si el cuerpo responde. En la
> fase 3 participan miles, a menudo en varios países: en uno de los ensayos de las vacunas contra
> la COVID-19 hubo más de 40 000 voluntarios.
>
> En la fase 3, los voluntarios se dividen al azar en dos grupos. Un grupo recibe la vacuna y el
> otro, un placebo. Ni los voluntarios ni los médicos saben quién recibió qué. Al final, se compara
> cuántas personas se enfermaron en cada grupo. Solo así se puede concluir que la vacuna protege.
>
> Después, los resultados son revisados por la agencia sanitaria de cada país (en México, la
> COFEPRIS) y suelen publicarse en una revista científica. Y la vigilancia no termina: cuando
> millones de personas reciben la vacuna, pueden aparecer efectos muy raros que ningún ensayo
> habría detectado.
>
> ¿Por qué hay que vacunarse contra la gripe cada año? Por la evolución: el virus de la gripe
> cambia constantemente, y la vacuna se actualiza para que corresponda a los virus que circulan.

Glosses: *poner (una vacuna, material)* (to give, to inject), *la lechera* (milkmaid), *la
viruela* (smallpox; *la viruela de las vacas*, cowpox), *leve* (mild), *el sistema inmunitario*
(immune system), *debilitado* (weakened), *proponer* (to put forward), *la hipótesis* (hypothesis,
same in the plural), *el ensayo clínico* (clinical trial: lesson 92's *ensayo* in another sense),
*la decena* (about ten; *unas decenas* = a few dozen), *al azar* (at random), *el placebo* (a dummy
treatment with no active ingredient), *la agencia sanitaria* (health regulator), *la vigilancia*
(monitoring), *la gripe* (flu), *actualizar* (to update), *corresponder a* (to match).

In brief: Jenner's 1796 experiment gave vaccines their name. A vaccine teaches the immune system to
recognize a virus or bacterium without making us sick. It is tested in the laboratory and in
animals, then in three phases with more and more volunteers; in phase 3 a random half gets a
placebo, and nobody knows who got what. Regulators review the results, which are usually
published in a scientific journal, and monitoring continues. Flu vaccines change every year
because the virus evolves.

### The grammar of a process

Science texts describe processes without caring who does each step, so they are full of the
passive. Find these in the article:

- *se*-passive (lesson 12, the usual choice): *la vacuna se estudia, se comprueba si…, se mide,
  se compara, la vacuna se actualiza*. Also impersonal *se*: *se puede concluir*.
- *ser* + participle (formal, often with *por* + agent): *los resultados son revisados por la
  agencia sanitaria*.
- reflexive with things: *los voluntarios se dividen en dos grupos*.

Other things to notice: *sin que tengamos* and *para que… fabriquen* (06), *se comprueba si la
vacuna es segura* (an indirect yes/no question with *si*, lesson 16), and *habría
detectado* (the conditional perfect, lesson 11: would have detected).

The phase 3 design has two names in English: a **[[placebo]]**-controlled trial, because one group
gets a dummy treatment, and a **[[double-blind]]** trial, because neither volunteers nor doctors know
who got what. Both protect the results from wishful thinking.

## How sure is the author?

Popular science must translate research without promising more than it shows. Every claim carries
a level of certainty, and Spanish marks it clearly. This is **[[hedging]]** again (lesson 91), now in
its scientific form:

![A horizontal scale from very sure on the left to not sure on the right, with five boxes. Demuestra que, confirma que: plus indicative. Indica que, sugiere que: plus indicative. Es probable que: plus subjunctive. Es posible que, podría: plus subjunctive or infinitive. No está claro si, no se sabe si: plus indicative. Below, an example for each.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Certainty | Spanish | Example |
|---|---|---|
| very high | *demuestra / confirma que* + indicative | *El ensayo demuestra que la vacuna protege.* |
| good evidence | *indica / sugiere que* + indicative | *Los datos sugieren que dormir ayuda a recordar.* |
| likely | *es probable que* + subjunctive | *Es probable que haga falta una segunda dosis.* |
| possible | *es posible que* + subjunctive; *podría* + infinitive | *El virus podría cambiar.* |
| unknown | *no está claro si* + indicative; *todavía no se sabe* | *No está claro si funciona en niños.* |

Notice *sugerir*: with the indicative it means "to suggest (that something is true)": *Los datos
sugieren que el cerebro cambia*. With the subjunctive it means "to recommend" (lesson 02): *Los
médicos sugieren que nos vacunemos*. *Concluir que* takes the indicative: *El estudio concluyó
que la vacuna funciona*.

### Example 1: spotting an overstatement

Headline: *¡Científicos demuestran que el chocolate te hace más inteligente!* The study behind it
measured 60 students once and found a small difference.

1. Find the certainty verb: *demuestran*, the top of the scale.
2. Check the evidence: one small sample (*una muestra pequeña*), one measurement, no control
   group.
3. Rewrite it honestly: *Un estudio pequeño sugiere que el chocolate podría mejorar la memoria a
   corto plazo, pero hacen falta más datos.* (A small study suggests chocolate might improve
   short-term memory, but more data are needed.)

## Text 2: a podcast

Before you listen, predict: the title is about the brain and languages, so expect *el cerebro,
las neuronas, aprender, la memoria*. Listen once without reading (use Hide the words), then again
with the text.

```dialogue lang=es-MX
# Ciencia de bolsillo, episodio 48: ¿Cómo aprende idiomas el cerebro?
Daniela: Bienvenidos a Ciencia de bolsillo, el pódcast de divulgación para gente curiosa. Hoy está con nosotros Itzel Mora, neurocientífica. Itzel, ¿qué pasa en el cerebro cuando aprendemos una palabra nueva?
= Welcome to Ciencia de bolsillo, the popular-science podcast for curious people. With us today is Itzel Mora, a neuroscientist. Itzel, what happens in the brain when we learn a new word?
Itzel: Bueno, el cerebro humano tiene unos ochenta y seis mil millones de neuronas, según un estudio de 2009. Cada neurona se conecta con miles de otras. Cuando aprendes algo, ciertas conexiones se vuelven más fuertes. Por eso repetir funciona.
= Well, the human brain has about eighty-six billion neurons, according to a 2009 study. Each neuron connects with thousands of others. When you learn something, certain connections get stronger. That's why repetition works.
Daniela: ¿Y hay una parte del cerebro para el lenguaje?
= And is there a part of the brain for language?
Itzel: Hay zonas muy importantes. En 1861, el médico francés Paul Broca estudió el cerebro de un paciente que había perdido el habla y encontró una lesión en el lóbulo frontal izquierdo. Esa zona hoy se llama área de Broca. Pero el lenguaje usa redes de muchas zonas, no un solo lugar.
= There are very important areas. In 1861 the French doctor Paul Broca studied the brain of a patient who had lost the ability to speak and found damage in the left frontal lobe. That area is called Broca's area today. But language uses networks of many areas, not a single place.
Daniela: Mucha gente cree que después de los veinte años ya no se puede aprender un idioma. ¿Es verdad?
= Many people believe that after the age of twenty you can't learn a language anymore. Is that true?
Itzel: No, no es verdad que sea imposible. El cerebro cambia toda la vida. Muchos estudios sugieren que quienes empiezan de niños suelen tener un acento más parecido al nativo, pero los adultos aprenden vocabulario y gramática muy rápido, sobre todo al principio.
= No, it isn't true that it's impossible. The brain changes all through life. Many studies suggest that people who start as children usually end up with a more native-like accent, but adults learn vocabulary and grammar very fast, especially at the beginning.
Daniela: ¿Y existe un gen de los idiomas? Yo siempre digo que no lo tengo.
= And is there a language gene? I always say I don't have it.
Itzel: Hasta ahora no se ha encontrado un solo gen que explique el talento para los idiomas. Hay genes relacionados con el habla, pero la práctica pesa muchísimo.
= So far no single gene has been found that explains a talent for languages. There are genes linked to speech, but practice counts for a great deal.
Daniela: Entonces, para terminar, ¿qué nos recomiendas?
= So, to finish, what do you recommend?
Itzel: Tres cosas. Repasar poco y seguido, no todo un día antes. Dormir bien, porque hay datos que indican que el sueño ayuda a fijar la memoria. Y usar el idioma con gente real, aunque te equivoques.
= Three things. Review a little, often, not everything the day before. Sleep well, because there's evidence that sleep helps memory consolidate. And use the language with real people, even if you make mistakes.
Daniela: Itzel Mora, muchas gracias. Y a ustedes, nos escuchamos la próxima semana.
= Itzel Mora, thank you very much. And to all of you, see you next week.
```

Glosses: *de bolsillo* (pocket-sized), *el pódcast* (podcast; plural *los pódcast*), *el habla*
(speech; feminine, *el habla*), *la lesión* (injury, damage), *el lóbulo* (lobe), *la red* (network),
*parecido a* (similar to), *pesar* (here: to count, to weigh), *poco y seguido* (a little and
often), *fijar* (to fix, to consolidate), *equivocarse* (to make a mistake), *nos escuchamos* (we'll
hear from each other: a podcast goodbye). The guest and the podcast are invented; the facts she
gives are real (see the key points).

English 86 billion is Spanish *86 000 millones*: *un billón* is a million million.

## Listening to a long recording

The DELE B1 listening test includes longer recordings, such as a monologue or a radio program,
each played twice. Before listening, read the questions and predict the words. The first time,
listen for the general idea and the speaker's attitude. The second time, listen for numbers,
names and certainty words (*según, sugieren, no es verdad que, hasta ahora no se ha encontrado*),
and for signposts (*por eso, pero, para terminar, tres cosas*). Expect the choices to paraphrase.

### Example 2: a listening question

Question: *Según la neurocientífica, los adultos…* (a) *no pueden aprender un idioma nuevo*, (b)
*aprenden vocabulario y gramática rápidamente al principio*, (c) *tienen mejor acento que los
niños*.

She says *no es verdad que sea imposible* (rules out a) and that people who start as children
*suelen tener un acento más parecido al nativo* (rules out c). The answer is (b), a paraphrase of
*los adultos aprenden vocabulario y gramática muy rápido, sobre todo al principio*.

## Common mistakes

- Reading *sugiere que* as proof: it reports evidence.
- The subjunctive after *demostrar, concluir, indicar*: ~~*demuestra que la vacuna proteja*~~ →
  *demuestra que la vacuna protege* (after *no*, the subjunctive becomes possible).
- *los virus* (not ~~*viruses*~~), *los genes*, *la célula* (stress on *cé-*).
- 86 billion = *86 000 millones*, not ~~*86 billones*~~.

## Key points

- Popular science uses the passive (*se estudia, son revisados por*), numbers and careful hedging.
- Vaccine trials: laboratory; phase 1 (dozens, safety), 2 (hundreds, response), 3 (thousands,
  vaccine vs placebo, double-blind); the regulator (COFEPRIS in Mexico); then monitoring.
- Jenner, 14 May 1796; Broca, 1861; about 86 billion neurons (Azevedo and colleagues, 2009).
- Certainty: *demuestra que* + ind. → *sugiere que* + ind. → *es probable / posible que* + subj.,
  *podría* → *no está claro si*.
- Long recordings: predict, gist first, then details and certainty words.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

sections.name: Deseos, consejos y sentimientos (wishes, advice and feelings)
Instrucciones, propósitos y planes (instructions, purposes and plans)
Contar con detalle (telling it in detail)
Hablar con naturalidad y el DELE B1 (speaking naturally and the B1 exam)
Honors: Prensa, literatura y ciencia (press, literature and science)

questions.stem: Which genre tells a true story with scenes, voices and details, often with the writer present ("me dice", "le pregunto")?
questions.explanation: A crónica is narrative journalism: everything in it is true, but it is told like a story, with scenes, quoted voices and the cronista present. A noticia reports the facts with the most important first, a column argues an opinion, and a titular is a headline.

questions.stem: At the end of the crónica, don Ernesto says: "Mientras haya gente que quiera fruta buena, aquí voy a estar." What does he mean?
choices: He will close the stall when the supermarket gets better fruit.
He is waiting for customers who want good fruit to arrive.
He will keep working as long as there are people who want good fruit.
He doesn't know whether he will open tomorrow.
questions.explanation: Mientras + subjunctive (haya) means "as long as" (lesson 18), and "gente que quiera" is a relative clause in the subjunctive because those people may or may not exist (lesson 08). "Aquí voy a estar" = I'll be here. He has just said he'll open tomorrow at six, as always.

questions.stem: Which of these sentences are opinions rather than facts? Select all that apply.
choices: Es una lástima que las autoridades solo se acuerden de los mercados en las elecciones.
El supermercado abrió a dos cuadras del mercado en 2019.
Ningún supermercado ofrece lo que ofrece un mercado.
Algunos locatarios se jubilaron el año pasado.
Las autoridades deberían reparar los techos del mercado.
questions.explanation: Opinions: a value judgment + subjunctive (es una lástima que… se acuerden), an absolute judgment someone could dispute (ningún supermercado ofrece…), and a recommendation with deber in the conditional (deberían). The other two report events with dates or numbers that can be checked.

questions.stem: A reader writes to the newspaper: "¿Cuál es la fuente de esta información?" What is the reader asking?
choices: Where the fountain in the photo is.
questions.explanation: In journalism la fuente is the source of information (según una fuente oficial = according to an official source). Its everyday sense, fountain, makes no sense in this question.

questions.stem: Complete with contrastar in the preterite: "Antes de publicar la noticia, la periodista ___ la información con otras dos fuentes."
questions.explanation: Contrastar is a regular -ar verb: ella contrastó (she checked it against two other sources). Contrastar la información is exactly what a careful journalist, and reader, does.

questions.stem: A headline says: "El alcalde renunciaría esta semana." What does the conditional tell the reader?
choices: The information isn't confirmed; the mayor will reportedly resign.
The mayor would resign if people asked him to.
The mayor has refused to resign.
questions.explanation: This is the condicional de rumor of the press: it presents news as unconfirmed ("reportedly"). Recognize it, but in your own writing say it honestly with según: "Según fuentes no oficiales, el alcalde va a renunciar."

questions.stem: Match each word to what it is.
choices: Reports what happened; the most important facts go first
Tells a true story with scenes and voices
A signed text that defends a position
The front page of a newspaper
questions.explanation: A noticia reports, a crónica narrates true events like a story, a columna argues an opinion and is signed by its columnista, and la primera plana is the front page. A book of poems is un poemario (lesson 90).

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this newspaper front page.

image.alt: A newspaper front page with five numbered parts: the large headline, the date line under the paper's name, the line of text under the photo, the narrow opinion column on the right, and the strip of section names at the bottom.

questions.explanation: 1 is el titular (the headline), 2 la fecha (the date), 3 el pie de foto (the caption under the photo), 4 la columna (the signed opinion column, with its columnist's name and photo) and 5 las secciones (Ciudad, Cultura, Deportes). A capítulo is a chapter of a book; there is no ad on this page.

questions.stem: Which word gives this sentence its strongest slant? "Los vendedores ambulantes invadieron la calle Fresno el sábado."
questions.explanation: Invadir is a military verb: it turns setting up stalls into an attack. A neutral report would say "instalaron sus puestos en la calle Fresno". The other words are neutral facts.

questions.stem: Which sentence from the column concedes a possibility without stating it as a fact?
choices: Es posible que los jóvenes vayan menos.
Yo no voy a hacer eso.
questions.explanation: Es posible que + subjunctive (vayan) is a hedge: the columnist accepts that it may be true without asserting it. The other three are a claim, a proposal and a statement of intention, all said with certainty.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: It's a shame that the authorities don't listen to the vendors.
questions.explanation: A value judgment (es una lástima que) takes the subjunctive: no escuchen. The whole que clause can also come first: Que las autoridades no escuchen a los vendedores es una lástima. The indicative no escuchan is wrong after a value judgment.

questions.stem: A reading question says "Los clientes del mercado son cada vez de más edad." Which line of the crónica does it paraphrase?
choices: Una pareja compra flores para su boda.
Tres estudiantes graban un video frente al puesto de jugos.
Llevo cuarenta y dos años abriendo a esta hora.
menos puestos y clientes cada vez mayores
questions.explanation: "Cada vez mayores" = older and older; "de más edad" says the same with other words. Reading questions usually paraphrase. The students and the couple show the opposite (young customers), and forty-two years is don Ernesto's own time at the market.

questions.stem: What does el sesgo mean in "Este artículo tiene un sesgo evidente"?
questions.explanation: El sesgo is a bias or slant. Source is la fuente, trend is la tendencia and headline is el titular.

questions.stem: Which writer told the story of the 1985 Mexico City earthquake through the voices of survivors in Nada, nadie?
choices: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz
questions.explanation: Elena Poniatowska (born in Paris in 1932; Premio Cervantes 2013) wrote Nada, nadie about the 1985 earthquake. Monsiváis (1938–2010) wrote crónicas about popular culture, Bernal Díaz wrote a sixteenth-century chronicle of the conquest, and Sor Juana was a seventeenth-century poet.

questions.stem: In Spanish plays, which tense are stage directions (acotaciones) usually written in?
questions.explanation: Stage directions describe what happens on stage now: (Entra TOÑO corriendo.), (Se sienta.). They use the present tense and the third person, often with the verb first.

questions.stem: Toño reports: "Dijo que ya no iba a hacer el mole." What words did his grandmother actually say?
choices: Ya no voy a hacer el mole.
Ya no fui a hacer el mole.
questions.explanation: After a past reporting verb, ir a in the present (voy a hacer) shifts to the imperfect (iba a hacer), lesson 16. So the original was "Ya no voy a hacer el mole."

questions.stem: Why do Rosa and Toño think the grandmother is leaving home?
choices: Don Fermín told them she was moving to his house.
Toño heard "Mañana temprano me voy con Fermín" and took it to mean she was leaving home with him.
The grandmother wrote it in her old notebook.
Valeria saw her packing her things.
questions.explanation: Toño reported her words correctly, but irse con alguien can mean going somewhere with someone or leaving home for someone. She meant the trip to the market in Don Fermín's pickup.

questions.stem: Report the command. Doña Carmen: "Toño, lava las ollas." → "Le dijo a Toño que ___ las ollas."
questions.explanation: A reported command after a past verb takes the imperfect subjunctive (lesson 15): que lavara (or lavase) las ollas.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of the theater.

image.alt: A theater seen from the audience with five numbered parts: the red curtain at the side, the pots on the table on stage, the rack of costumes at the back, the wooden stage floor, and the rows of red seats.

questions.explanation: 1 el telón (the stage curtain), 2 la utilería (the props: pots and a box), 3 el vestuario (the costumes), 4 el escenario (the stage), 5 las butacas (the theater seats). Applause can't be seen, and a titular is a newspaper headline.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
questions.explanation: El ensayo is a rehearsal (also an essay), el elenco the cast, la acotación a stage direction and el dramaturgo the playwright. The audience is el público.

questions.stem: How do Rosa and her mother address each other in the play?
choices: Rosa says tú to her mother; the grandmother says usted to Rosa.
Rosa says usted to her mother; the grandmother says tú to Rosa.
questions.explanation: Rosa says "¿Y usted, mamá?", and the grandmother says "Y tú, Rosa, cuidas…". In many Mexican families, especially traditional ones, usted toward a parent and tú toward a child show respect and affection, not distance.

questions.stem: Toño tells Don Fermín: "No se haga, don Fermín." What does he mean?
questions.explanation: In Mexico, informal no te hagas / no se haga means "don't pretend you don't know, don't play dumb". Toño thinks Don Fermín is hiding the plan.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: She asked me to take her in the pickup.
questions.explanation: Pedir que after a past verb takes the imperfect subjunctive: me pidió que la llevara. The object pronoun la goes before the conjugated verb. Llevaba, an imperfect indicative, would report a fact, not a request.

questions.stem: Doña Carmen says: "Ya es hora de que alguien más aprenda." Why is aprenda in the subjunctive?
choices: Because alguien is an unknown person.
Because she is reporting what someone said.
Because es hora de que is always followed by the subjunctive.
Because the sentence is in the past.
questions.explanation: Es hora de que (it's time that) expresses what should happen, and it always takes the subjunctive: ya es hora de que alguien aprenda. The sentence is in the present, and alguien is the subject of the subjunctive, not an unknown antecedent of a relative clause.

questions.stem: Which are correctly written stage directions? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Stage directions are in the present, often verb first, and show actions or tone: (Entra TOÑO corriendo.), (Se sienta.), (Bajando la voz.). The other two are in the past, like a narrator, and the last one explains a feeling the actor can't play.

questions.stem: What does "Cae el telón" mark in a play?
choices: The end of the act or the play
The entrance of a new character
questions.explanation: The curtain comes down at the end: Cae el telón (or just Telón), then Fin. At the start, Se abre el telón.

questions.stem: Rosa says: "Lleva veintitantos ingredientes, mija. No es pan comido." What does she mean?
choices: The mole has no bread in it.
questions.explanation: Ser pan comido (lesson 21) means to be very easy, "a piece of cake". No es pan comido = it isn't easy. Lleva veintitantos ingredientes = it has twenty-odd ingredients.

questions.stem: Days later, Valeria reports Don Fermín's words "Mañana su abuela y yo vamos al mercado." Which report is correct?
choices: Don Fermín nos explicó que mañana su abuela y yo vamos al mercado.
Don Fermín nos explicó que al día siguiente la abuela y él fueran al mercado.
Don Fermín nos explicó que al día siguiente la abuela y él iban al mercado.
Don Fermín nos explicó que ayer la abuela y él iban al mercado.
questions.explanation: Reported days later, mañana becomes al día siguiente, yo becomes él, and the present vamos becomes the imperfect iban. Fueran is wrong: this reports information, not a request. The first choice changes nothing, and ayer is the wrong day.

questions.stem: In phase 3 of a vaccine trial, why does one group get a placebo?
choices: So that fewer volunteers need the real vaccine.
So the researchers can compare how many people get sick with and without the vaccine.
Because the placebo makes the vaccine work better.
Because the regulator gives the vaccine only to the other group.
questions.explanation: The volunteers are divided at random; one group gets the vaccine, the other a placebo (a dummy treatment). Comparing how many get sick in each group is what shows whether the vaccine protects: "Al final, se compara cuántas personas se enfermaron en cada grupo."

questions.stem: What did Edward Jenner do on 14 May 1796, according to the article?
choices: He gave a boy material from cowpox and later showed that the boy didn't catch smallpox.
He discovered the flu virus under a microscope.
He described the part of the brain that controls speech.
He organized the first trial with 40,000 volunteers.
questions.explanation: Jenner gave an eight-year-old boy material from a milkmaid with cowpox, a mild disease, and then showed he no longer caught smallpox. The word vacuna comes from Latin vacca, cow. The brain discovery is Broca's (1861); the 40,000-volunteer trial was for a COVID-19 vaccine.

questions.stem: Which sentences describe a step without saying who does it, with se or with ser + participle? Select all that apply.
choices: La vacuna se estudia en el laboratorio.
Los resultados son revisados por la agencia sanitaria.
Se compara cuántas personas se enfermaron.
Edward Jenner comprobó que la vacuna funcionaba.
questions.explanation: Se estudia and se compara use the se passive or impersonal se (lesson 12), and son revisados is ser + participle (the agent, la agencia, is optional). The other two are ordinary active sentences with a subject who does the action.

questions.stem: Put the steps of testing a vaccine in order.
choices: Fase 3: miles de voluntarios, vacuna o placebo
questions.explanation: Laboratory and animal studies come first; then three phases with more and more volunteers (dozens for safety, hundreds for the body's response, thousands to see whether it protects); then the regulator (COFEPRIS in Mexico) reviews the results; monitoring continues after approval.

questions.stem: Which headline claims the highest certainty?
choices: Un estudio sugiere que dormir ayuda a recordar.
Es posible que dormir ayude a recordar.
No está claro si dormir ayuda a recordar.
Un estudio demuestra que dormir ayuda a recordar.
questions.explanation: Demostrar que (to show, to prove) is at the top of the certainty scale. Sugerir que reports evidence, es posible que a possibility, and no está claro si says nobody knows yet.

questions.stem: Complete with the right form of proteger: "Es probable que la vacuna ___ también a los niños."
questions.explanation: Es probable que is a judgment of likelihood and takes the subjunctive: proteja (proteger → protejo → proteja, with g → j before a).

questions.stem: What does sugerir mean in "Los médicos sugieren que nos vacunemos"?
questions.explanation: With the subjunctive (vacunemos), sugerir is a verb of influence: to recommend (lesson 02). With the indicative it reports evidence: "Los datos sugieren que el cerebro cambia" (the data suggest that the brain changes).

questions.stem: Listen. How many neurons does the speaker say the human brain has?

audio.text: El cerebro humano tiene unos ochenta y seis mil millones de neuronas, según un estudio de 2009.

questions.explanation: Ochenta y seis mil millones = 86,000 million = 86 billion in English. Spanish un billón is a million million (an English trillion), so listen for mil millones in very large numbers.

questions.stem: Listen to the neuroscientist. What does she say about learning a language after the age of twenty?

audio.text: No, no es verdad que sea imposible. El cerebro cambia toda la vida.

choices: It is possible, because the brain keeps changing all through life.
It is impossible, because the brain stops changing.
It is true that it is very difficult.
Only people who started as children can do it.
questions.explanation: "No es verdad que sea imposible" (it isn't true that it's impossible) denies the belief; "el cerebro cambia toda la vida" gives the reason. Listen for the negation: no es verdad que + subjunctive.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
questions.explanation: La célula (stressed on cé-) is a cell, la neurona a nerve cell, el gen (plural los genes) a gene and la muestra a sample. A vaccine is la vacuna.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: The study concluded that the vaccine works.
questions.explanation: Concluir que states a result and takes the indicative: funciona. The subject can follow the verb (Concluyó el estudio que…, funciona la vacuna). Funcione, a subjunctive, would need a doubt or a negation (No concluyó que funcione).

questions.stem: What does Itzel mean by "Hasta ahora no se ha encontrado un solo gen que explique el talento para los idiomas"?
choices: Scientists have found the language gene.
Only one gene explains talent for languages.
So far, no single gene that explains a talent for languages has been found.
Genes have nothing to do with speech.
questions.explanation: No se ha encontrado = has not been found (se passive in the perfect); un solo gen que explique = a single gene that would explain (subjunctive: no such gene is known). She adds that some genes are linked to speech, so the last choice goes too far.

questions.stem: How do you write 86 billion (86,000,000,000) in Spanish?
questions.explanation: English billion = Spanish mil millones: 86 000 millones. Spanish un billón is a million million, so 86 billones would be a thousand times too big.

questions.stem: When a long recording is played twice, what should you focus on the first time?
choices: Writing down every number you hear
The general idea and the speaker's attitude
The unknown words, so you can look them up
questions.explanation: First listening: who is talking, about what, and how sure or how positive they are. Second listening: details such as numbers, names and certainty words (según, sugieren, no es verdad que). Translating or chasing unknown words makes you lose the thread.

questions.stem: What is un verso in Spanish poetry?
questions.explanation: Un verso is one line. A stanza is una estrofa, a poem is un poema and a book of poems is un poemario. English "verse" can mean a stanza, which makes this a classic mistake.

questions.stem: How many metrical syllables does this line have? "Cuando se apaga la tarde" (Give the number.)
questions.explanation: Cuan-do-se-a-pa-ga-la-tar-de is nine written syllables, but se + a join by sinalefa: cuan-do-sea-pa-ga-la-tar-de = 8. Tarde is a palabra llana, so nothing is added or taken away: an octosyllable.

questions.stem: How many metrical syllables does "canta en la rama un pájaro" have?
questions.explanation: With the sinalefas (taen, maun) it's can-taen-la-ra-maun-pá-ja-ro = 8, and a line ending in a palabra esdrújula (pájaro) counts one less: 7.

questions.stem: Which pair has assonant rhyme but not consonant rhyme?
questions.explanation: From the last stressed vowel, plaza gives -aza and naranjas -anjas: only the vowels á-a match, so it's assonant rhyme. In the other pairs everything from the stressed vowel matches (-eta, -ón, -ir): consonant rhyme.

questions.stem: Which pairs have consonant rhyme? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Consonant rhyme matches vowels and consonants from the last stressed vowel on: -eta, -ir, -ana. Plaza / caja (á-a) and luna / duda (ú-a) share only the vowels: assonant rhyme.

questions.stem: Match each example to its figure of speech.
left: Tu risa es una ventana abierta.
Te lo he dicho mil veces.
questions.explanation: A metaphor says one thing is another (your laugh is an open window); a simile compares with como; personification gives human actions to things (a market can't say goodbye); hyperbole exaggerates on purpose. Rhyme is about sound, not a figure of meaning.

questions.stem: Put the lines of the stanza Libreta in order. Its rhyme is ABBA.
choices: lo que no te sé decir,
questions.explanation: The sentence reads: I write in a notebook what I can't tell you, and the night, as I write, turns blue and secret. The rhyme confirms it: libreta (A), decir (B), escribir (B), secreta (A).

questions.stem: Which description fits the classic Spanish sonnet?
choices: Eight-syllable lines with assonant rhyme in the even lines
Three lines of five, seven and five syllables
Any number of lines with no fixed rhyme
Fourteen eleven-syllable lines in two cuartetos and two tercetos, with consonant rhyme
questions.explanation: El soneto has 14 hendecasyllables: two quatrains (cuartetos, usually ABBA ABBA) and two tercets (tercetos, for example CDC DCD), all in consonant rhyme. Octosyllables with assonance in the even lines are the romance.

questions.stem: Which poet was a seventeenth-century nun in New Spain, was called la décima musa, and appears on Mexico's 100-peso note?
choices: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz
questions.explanation: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz (born in 1648 or 1651, died in 1695) wrote sonnets, plays and Primero sueño, defended women's right to study, and is on the 100-peso note issued in 2020. Nervo was a Mexican poet of the early twentieth century, Darío a Nicaraguan and Bécquer a Spaniard.

questions.stem: Which book by José Martí, published in 1891, is made of short poems in octosyllables?
questions.explanation: Versos sencillos (1891); verses from it were later adapted in the song "Guantanamera". Azul… (1888) is Rubén Darío's, the Rimas are Bécquer's and Primero sueño is Sor Juana's.

questions.stem: Rubén Darío (1867–1916) was the leader of which literary movement?
questions.explanation: Darío led modernismo, which renewed the rhythm and imagery of Spanish poetry at the end of the nineteenth century, with books such as Azul… (1888) and Cantos de vida y esperanza (1905). Magical realism belongs to twentieth-century fiction.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: That poem always moves me.
questions.explanation: The poem is the subject (conmueve, third person, o → ue) and me is the direct object (a ella la conmueve). The adverb and the subject can move: Siempre me conmueve ese poema, Ese poema me conmueve siempre. Conmuevo would mean "I move".

questions.stem: What is un poemario?
questions.explanation: Un poemario is a book or collection of poems: Versos sencillos es un poemario de José Martí. A person who writes poems is un poeta / una poeta.

questions.stem: Which statement about Bécquer's Rimas is correct?
choices: Bécquer published them as a book in Mexico City.
They were collected by his friends and published after his death, in 1871.
They are long poems in hendecasyllables about the conquest.
They were written in the twentieth century.
questions.explanation: Bécquer (Seville 1836 – Madrid 1870) died before they appeared as a book; his friends published them in 1871 with his prose Leyendas. They are short love poems, most of them with assonant rhyme.

questions.stem: Complete: "Quiero que tú ___ a mi fiesta." (venir)
questions.explanation: Querer que + a new subject (tú) takes the present subjunctive: vengas, from the yo form vengo. Vienes and vendrás are indicative; venir would need the same subject (Quiero venir = I want to come).

questions.stem: How do you say "I want to go to the party"?
choices: Quiero que voy a la fiesta.
Quiero que vaya a la fiesta.
questions.explanation: The person who wants and the person who goes are the same (yo), so Spanish uses the infinitive: Quiero ir. Quiero que vaya means "I want him / her to go" (a different subject). Que voy is indicative, and a subjunctive never follows without que.

questions.stem: Complete: "Mi mamá espera que yo ___ la tarea antes de cenar." (hacer)
questions.explanation: Esperar que + a new subject takes the subjunctive. Start from the yo present hago, drop the -o and add -a: haga. Hago and hace are present indicative; hice is the preterite.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ojalá que mis primos ___ temprano." (llegar)
questions.explanation: Llegar keeps its hard g sound before e by adding u: lleguen (like the preterite llegué). Llegen would sound like "lle-HEN"; llegan is indicative; lleguan doesn't exist (-ar verbs take e, not a).

questions.stem: Complete: "La abuela quiere que nosotros ___ un deseo con cada uva." (pedir)
questions.explanation: -ir stem changers change in nosotros too: pedir → pidamos (as in the gerund pidiendo). Pedamos keeps the plain stem (that happens only with -ar and -er verbs: pensemos, podamos); pidemos has an -ar ending; piedamos has the wrong change.

questions.stem: Your friend asks: "¿Vienes a mi boda en junio?" You answer: "¡Ojalá!" What do you mean?
questions.explanation: Ojalá alone means "I hope so!": you would like to, but you aren't sure you can. "Of course" would be ¡Claro!; "definitely not" is ¡Claro que no!; "I don't know yet" is Todavía no sé.

questions.stem: Look at the card. What do Daniel and Mariana hope?

image.alt: A New Year's card with stars and a clock at midnight. It reads: ¡Feliz Año Nuevo 2027! Querida tía Rosa: Te deseamos un año lleno de paz, salud y felicidad. Que se cumplan todos tus deseos y que alcances tus metas. Ojalá que nos veamos pronto en Oaxaca. Con cariño y de corazón, Daniel y Mariana.

choices: That tía Rosa visits them in Puebla.
That tía Rosa finds a new job.
That she sends them a card soon.
That they see each other soon in Oaxaca.
questions.explanation: "Ojalá que nos veamos pronto en Oaxaca" = I hope we see each other soon in Oaxaca. The card also wishes her peace, health and happiness, and that her wishes come true and she reaches her goals. It says nothing about a job or about Puebla.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: Espero que te guste el regalo.
Prefiero que nos quedemos en casa.
Ojalá que no llueva el sábado.
questions.explanation: Espero que te guste, prefiero que nos quedemos and ojalá que no llueva all have a wish + subjunctive. Quiero que me ayudas needs the subjunctive (ayudes). Quiero que yo vaya has the same subject twice: say Quiero ir contigo.

questions.stem: Write the present subjunctive of tener: "Te deseo que ___ un año lleno de salud." (tú)
questions.explanation: tener → yo tengo → teng- + -as: tengas. Desear que + a new subject takes the subjunctive.

questions.stem: Complete with the present subjunctive of ser and saber: "Ojalá que el examen no ___ difícil y que yo ___ todas las respuestas."
questions.explanation: Ser and saber are two of the six verbs whose subjunctive doesn't come from the yo present (soy, sé): sea and sepa.

questions.stem: Match each verb to its present subjunctive (yo form).
questions.explanation: The six verbs to learn by heart: ser sea, ir vaya, estar esté, dar dé, saber sepa, haber haya. Va and sabe are present indicative forms.

questions.stem: Put the steps for making the present subjunctive of tener in order.
choices: Add the endings with the other vowel: tenga, tengas…
questions.explanation: The subjunctive is built on the yo present, so its irregular g carries through: tener → tengo → teng- → tenga.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: I hope you like the gift.
questions.explanation: Esperar que + subjunctive: guste, not the indicative gusta. The thing liked (el regalo) can come after the verb or before te: Espero que te guste el regalo / Espero que el regalo te guste.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: My grandmother wants us to make a wish.
questions.explanation: A wish for someone else: quiere que + subjunctive. Pedir changes e → i in nosotros in the subjunctive: pidamos. Pedimos is the present indicative.

questions.stem: Complete: "Te pido que me ___ mañana." (llamar)
questions.explanation: Pedir que + a new subject takes the subjunctive: llames. Te (the person asked) and -s in llames (the person who calls) are the same person, tú.

questions.stem: Complete: "Mis papás no me dejan ___ entre semana." (salir)
questions.explanation: Dejar often takes a plain infinitive: No me dejan salir. No me dejan que salga is also correct, but it needs que; salga alone and the indicative que salgo are wrong.

questions.stem: Your mom tells you: "¡Llega temprano!" Later you tell a friend: "Mi mamá dice que ___ temprano."
questions.explanation: Decir que + subjunctive reports a command: Mi mamá dice que llegue temprano (My mom says I should come home early). Dice que llego temprano would report a fact (that I do come home early).

questions.stem: General advice for everyone: "It's important to sleep eight hours." Which sentence fits?
choices: Es importante que dormir ocho horas.
Es importante que duermes ocho horas.
Es importante a dormir ocho horas.
questions.explanation: For a general statement, an impersonal expression takes the infinitive with nothing in between: Es importante dormir. For one person you would say Es importante que duermas (subjunctive), never que + infinitive or the indicative duermes.

questions.stem: Complete: "Mi hermano insiste en que no ___ su culpa." (He insists it wasn't his fault.)
questions.explanation: Insistir en que pushes someone to act when it takes the subjunctive; when it insists that something is true, it takes the indicative. "It wasn't his fault" is a past fact: fue. Es would mean "it isn't".

questions.stem: Complete: "Los papás de Ana le ___ que salga sola de noche." (They forbid her to go out alone at night.)
questions.explanation: Prohibir puts a written accent on the stressed í: prohíbo, prohíbes, prohíbe, prohíben. Prohíban is the subjunctive (the main verb here is a plain statement, so indicative); prohibimos is "we".

questions.stem: Look at the poster. When do the children get their allowance?

image.alt: A poster titled Reglas de la casa, familia Treviño, with six rules beside pictures: Lavar los platos después de cenar. Sacar la basura los martes y viernes. Nada de celulares en la mesa. Llegar antes de las 10 p. m. (fines de semana: 11). Pedir permiso para invitar amigos. Mesada: los domingos, si cumples con tus quehaceres.

choices: On Sundays, if they do their chores.
At the end of the month.
questions.explanation: "Mesada: los domingos, si cumples con tus quehaceres" = allowance on Sundays, if you do your chores. Tuesdays and Fridays are for taking out the trash.

questions.stem: In Mexico, what is "la mesada"?
choices: Money parents give a child regularly.
questions.explanation: La mesada is an allowance (pocket money); in Mexico it is also called el domingo. Spain says la paga. A school's rules are las normas or el reglamento.

questions.stem: Which sentences correctly say "My parents don't let me go out"? Select all that apply.
choices: Mis papás no me dejan salir.
Mis papás no me dejan que salga.
Mis papás no me dejan que salgo.
Mis papás no dejan que salir.
Mis papás no me permiten salir.
questions.explanation: Dejar and permitir take either an infinitive (no me dejan salir, no me permiten salir) or que + subjunctive (no me dejan que salga). Que salgo is indicative, and que is never followed by an infinitive here.

questions.stem: Write the present subjunctive: "Te sugiero que ___ más y que ___ ayuda." (dormir, pedir; tú)
questions.explanation: Sugerir que + subjunctive. dormir → duermo → duermas; pedir → pido → pidas. The stem changes as in the yo present.

questions.stem: Match each verb to its meaning.
questions.explanation: aconsejar = to advise, exigir = to demand, rogar = to beg, prohibir = to forbid, criar = to raise (a child). To obey is obedecer and to scold is regañar.

questions.stem: Match each picture on the house-rules poster to its rule.

image.alt: The house-rules poster with pictures but no words, and six numbered markers: on the stack of plates, the trash bag, the crossed-out phone over a table, the clock showing ten, the door with two people, and the pile of coins.

choices: nada de celulares en la mesa
questions.explanation: 1 lavar los platos (the plates), 2 sacar la basura (the trash bag), 3 nada de celulares en la mesa (the crossed-out phone), 4 llegar antes de las diez (the clock), 5 pedir permiso para invitar amigos (the door and two friends), 6 la mesada (the coins). No picture shows a dog or a broom.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: I advise you to talk to your teacher. (tú; the teacher is a woman)
questions.explanation: Aconsejar que + subjunctive: hables. Te before aconsejo is the person advised; hables says the same person will talk.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: It's important that you all respect the rules.
questions.explanation: An impersonal expression about specific people takes que + subjunctive: respeten (ustedes). The que clause can also come first: Que respeten las reglas es importante. Respetan is indicative.

questions.stem: Complete: "Me molesta que mis vecinos ___ tanto ruido." (hacer)
questions.explanation: A feeling about what someone else does takes que + subjunctive, even when it is true: hagan (from hago). Hacen and harán are indicative; the infinitive would need the same person.

questions.stem: Complete: "___ que mis hijos lleguen tarde." (It bothers me that my children come home late.)
questions.explanation: With gustar-type verbs, the que clause is the subject, and a clause counts as one thing: me molesta (singular), even though lleguen is plural. Me molesto means "I get annoyed"; molesto means "I bother".

questions.stem: How do you say "I'm glad to see you"?
questions.explanation: The person who is glad and the person who sees are the same (yo), so use the infinitive: Me alegra verte (or Me alegro de verte). Que + a verb is for someone else's action; me alegro que verte mixes both and drops the de.

questions.stem: Your friend has just arrived after a long trip. You say: "I'm glad you've come."
questions.explanation: For something that has happened, a feeling takes the perfect subjunctive: haya, hayas… + participle: Me alegra que hayas venido. Has venido and habías venido are indicative; vienes is the present indicative.

questions.stem: Complete: "Me alegro ___ que estés mejor."
questions.explanation: Alegrarse takes de: me alegro de que + subjunctive. The RAE's Diccionario panhispánico de dudas lists Me alegro de que… as the correct form. (Me alegra que… with alegrar needs no de.)

questions.stem: Your friend says: "Estoy decepcionada." How does she feel?
questions.explanation: Decepcionado is a false friend: it means disappointed. Deceived is engañado; excited is emocionado; embarrassed is avergonzado (in Mexico also me da pena).

questions.stem: In the dialogue "Buenas y malas noticias", why is Andrés also a little sad?
choices: He and Carmen will live far apart.
He didn't get the job in Monterrey.
His mother is angry with him.
His old boss wants him to stay.
questions.explanation: Andrés says: "Me da tristeza que vivamos tan lejos" (It makes me sad that we'll live so far apart). He did get the job, his mother is worried but happy, and his old boss doesn't come into it.

questions.stem: Complete: "¡Qué ___ que no puedas venir a la boda!" (What a shame…)
questions.explanation: ¡Qué lástima! = What a pity, what a shame. Orgullo is pride, alegría is joy and envidia is envy (¡Qué envidia! = Lucky you!).

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: Me preocupa que no duermas bien.
Estoy harta de que me interrumpen.
Mis papás están orgullosos de que yo estudie medicina.
questions.explanation: Correct: me preocupa que + duermas, me encanta que + hayas escrito, están orgullosos de que + estudie. Estoy harta de que needs the subjunctive (interrumpan). Me sorprenden should be singular: me sorprende que no llamen.

questions.stem: Complete with the perfect subjunctive of llegar: "Me preocupa que mis papás todavía no ___." (They haven't arrived yet.)
questions.explanation: Perfect subjunctive = haya, hayas, haya, hayamos, hayan + participle. Mis papás = ellos: hayan llegado.

questions.stem: These words look like English words but mean something else. Match each to its meaning.
questions.explanation: decepcionado = disappointed (deceived is engañado); sensible = sensitive (reasonable, "sensible", is sensato); la ilusión = excitement, hope; emocionado = excited or moved; la decepción = disappointment.

questions.stem: How does each person feel?

image.alt: Five cartoon faces without captions, each with a numbered marker on the forehead: 1 a smiling face with a medal; 2 a sad face above a gift box broken in two; 3 a frowning face with angry eyebrows, crossed arms and a stack of papers; 4 a face with closed eyes and a small smile wiping a drop of sweat from its forehead; 5 a grinning face with stars for eyes above a ticket.

questions.explanation: 1 orgulloso (proud, with a medal), 2 decepcionado (disappointed by a broken gift), 3 harto (fed up with a pile of work), 4 aliviado (relieved, wiping the sweat away), 5 emocionado (excited about a ticket). Nobody looks in love or ill.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: It bothers me that they arrive late.
questions.explanation: A feeling about someone else's action takes que + subjunctive: lleguen. The que clause can also come first: Que lleguen tarde me molesta. Llegan is indicative.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: I'm glad you've come. (tú)
questions.explanation: Something that has happened, after a feeling: the perfect subjunctive hayas venido, not the indicative has venido. The que clause can also come first, though Me alegra que hayas venido is the usual order.

questions.stem: Complete: "No creo que esa luz ___ un ovni." (ser)
questions.explanation: A negated opinion (no creo que) takes the subjunctive: sea. Creo que es un ovni (positive) would take the indicative.

questions.stem: Complete: "Creo que ___ razón." (tener, tú)
questions.explanation: Creo que presents something as true, so it takes the indicative: tienes. The subjunctive comes after no creo que (No creo que tengas razón).

questions.stem: Complete: "A lo mejor ___ mañana." (llover)
questions.explanation: A lo mejor takes only the indicative: A lo mejor llueve. With quizás or tal vez, either mood is correct (Quizás llueve / Quizás llueva).
